In the 1990s, directors took inspiration from the success of [[David Lynch]]'s ''[[Blue Velvet (film)|Blue Velvet]]'' (1986) and [[Peter Greenaway]]'s ''[[The Cook, the Thief, His Wife & Her Lover]]'' (1989) and created films with bizarre alternative worlds and elements of surrealism. Japanese director Akira Kurosawa's ''[[Dreams (1990 film)|Dreams]]'' (1990) depicted his imaginative reveries in a series of vignettes that range from idyllic pastoral country landscapes to horrific visions of tormented demons and a blighted post-nuclear war landscape. The [[Coen Brothers]]' ''[[Barton Fink]]'' (1991), which won the [[Palme d'Or]] at the [[Cannes Film Festival]], features various literary allusions in an enigmatic story about a writer who encounters a range of bizarre characters, including an alcoholic, abusive novelist and a serial killer. ''[[Lost Highway (film)|Lost Highway]]'' (1997), from the same director as ''Blue Velvet'', is a psychological [[Thriller film|thriller]] that explores fantasy worlds, bizarre time-space transformations, and mental breakdowns using surreal imagery.

Other directors in the 1990s explored philosophical issues and themes such as identity, chance, death, and existentialism. [[Gus Van Sant]]'s ''[[My Own Private Idaho]]'' (1991) and [[Wong Kar-wai]]'s ''[[Chungking Express]]'' (1994) explored the theme of identity. The former is an independent road movie/buddy film about two young street hustlers, which explores the theme of the search for home and identity. It was called a "high-water mark in '90s independent film",<ref>Filmcritic.com critic Jake Euler.{{full citation needed|date=August 2023}}</ref> a "stark, poetic rumination",<ref>Reviewer Nick Schager.{{full citation needed|date=August 2023}}</ref> and an "exercise in film experimentation"<ref>Critic Matt Brunson.{{full citation needed|date=August 2023}}</ref> of "high artistic quality".<ref name="Allmovie.com" /> ''Chungking Express''<ref>Prior to Chungking Express, he directed ''[[Days of Being Wild]]''. Later in the 1990s, Kar-wai directed ''[[Happy Together (1997 film)|Happy Together (film)]]'' (1997).</ref> explores themes of identity, disconnection, loneliness, and isolation in the "metaphoric concrete jungle" of modern Hong Kong. [[Todd Haynes]] explored the life of a suburban housewife and her eventual death from toxic materials in the 1995 critical success, ''[[Safe (1995 film)|Safe]]''.<ref>{{cite web|url = http://www.tasteofcinema.com/2017/pulling-focus-safe-1995/ |title = Pulling Focus: Safe (1995) |work = Taste of Cinema|date = January 17, 2017|first= Shane|last = Scott-Travis}}</ref>

In 1991, another important film of [[Edward Yang]], a Taiwanese New Wave director, ''[[A Brighter Summer Day]]'' is portrayal of one normal teenager life that evacuated from China to Taiwan which affacted by political situation, school situation, and family situation that make a main protagonist murders a girl in the end. In 1992, ''[[Rebels of the Neon God]]'', first feature film of [[Tsai Ming-liang]], second generation of Taiwanese New Wave, it has his unique style of filmmaking like alienation, slow movement of actor (his recurring cast, [[Lee Kang-sheng]]), slow-paced, and a few dialogues.

Daryush Shokof's film ''[[Seven Servants]]'' (1996) is an original high art cinema piece about a man who strives to "unite" the world's races until his last breath. One year after ''[[Seven Servants]]'', [[Abbas Kiarostami]]'s film ''[[Taste of Cherry]]'' (1997),<ref name="ReferenceB">In 1990, Kiarostami directed ''[[Close-Up (1990 film)|Close-up]]''.</ref> which won the Palme d'Or at the Cannes Film Festival, tells a similar tale with a different twist; both films are about a man trying to hire a person to bury him after he commits suicide. ''[[Seven Servants]]'' was shot in a minimalist style, with long takes, a leisurely pace, and long periods of silence. The film is also notable for its use of long shots and overhead shots to create a sense of distance between the audience and the characters. [[Zhang Yimou]]'s early 1990s works such as ''[[Ju Dou]]'' (1990), ''[[Raise the Red Lantern]]'' (1991), ''[[The Story of Qiu Ju]]'' (1992) and ''[[To Live (1994 film)|To Live]]'' (1994) explore human emotions through poignant narratives. ''[[To Live (1994 film)|To Live]]'' won the Grand Jury Prize.

Several 1990s films explored existentialist-oriented themes related to life, chance, and death. [[Robert Altman]]'s ''[[Short Cuts]]'' (1993) explores themes of chance, death, and infidelity by tracing 10 parallel and interwoven stories. The film, which won the [[Golden Lion]] and the Volpi Cup at the [[Venice Film Festival]], was called a "many-sided, many mooded, dazzlingly structured eclectic jazz mural" by ''Chicago Tribune'' critic Michael Wilmington. [[Krzysztof Kieślowski]]'s ''[[The Double Life of Véronique]]'' (1991) is a drama about the theme of identity and a political allegory about the East/West split in Europe; the film features stylised cinematography, an ethereal atmosphere, and unexplained supernatural elements.

<!-- Commented out: [[File:Cremaster1.png|thumb|left|250px|'Goodyear' (played by Marti Domination) from ''[[The Cremaster Cycle|Cremaster 1]]'' (1995).]] -->
[[Darren Aronofsky]]'s film ''[[π (film)|Pi]]'' (1998) is an "incredibly complex and ambiguous film filled with both incredible style and substance" about a paranoid mathematician's "search for peace".<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.filmcritic.com/misc/emporium.nsf/ddb5490109a79f598625623d0015f1e4/a29bee8a645baf0b882567c0005e8d55?OpenDocument|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20051230151045/http://www.filmcritic.com/misc/emporium.nsf/ddb5490109a79f598625623d0015f1e4/a29bee8a645baf0b882567c0005e8d55?OpenDocument |archive-date=30 December 2005 |title=Pi Movie Review, DVD Release – |publisher=Filmcritic.com |access-date=6 October 2010}}</ref> The film creates a [[David Lynch]]-inspired "eerie ''[[Eraserhead]]''-like world"<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.filmthreat.com/index.php?section=reviews&Id=997|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080623211405/http://www.filmthreat.com/index.php?section=reviews&Id=997|archive-date=23 June 2008 |title=Current Movie Reviews, Independent Movies – Film Threat |publisher=Filmthreat.com |date=15 June 1998 |access-date=6 October 2010}}</ref> shot in "black-and-white, which lends a dream-like atmosphere to all of the proceedings" and explores issues such as "metaphysics and spirituality".<ref>Critic James Berardinelli.{{full citation needed|date=August 2023}}</ref> [[Matthew Barney]]'s ''[[The Cremaster Cycle]]'' (1994–2002) is a cycle of five symbolic, allegorical films that creates a self-enclosed aesthetic system, aimed to explore the process of creation. The films are filled with allusions to reproductive organs and sexual development, and use narrative models drawn from biography, mythology, and geology.

In 1997, [[Terrence Malick]] returned from a 20-year absence with ''[[The Thin Red Line (1998 film)|The Thin Red Line]]'', a war film that uses poetry and nature to stand apart from typical war movies. It was nominated for seven [[71st Academy Awards|Academy Awards]], including Best Picture and Best Director.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.oscars.org/oscars/ceremonies/1999|title=The 71st Academy Awards &#124; 1999|date=18 November 2016|website=www.oscars.org}}</ref>

Some 1990s films mix an ethereal or surreal visual atmosphere with the exploration of philosophical issues. ''[[Satantango|Sátántangó]]'' (1994), by the [[Hungarian cinema|Hungarian director]] [[Béla Tarr]], is a {{frac|7|1|2}}-hour-long film, shot in black and white, that deals with Tarr's favorite theme, inadequacy, as [[confidence trick|con man]] Irimias comes back to a village at an unspecified location in Hungary, presenting himself as a leader and [[false Messiah|Messiah figure]] to the gullible villagers. Kieslowski's ''[[Three Colors]]'' trilogy (1993–94), particularly ''[[Three Colors: Blue|Blue]]'' (1993) and ''[[Three Colors: Red|Red]]'' (1994), deal with human relationships and how people cope with them in their day-to-day lives. The trilogy of films was called "explorations of spirituality and existentialism"<ref>Emanuel Levy, [http://www.emanuellevy.com/review/three-colors-blue/ review of ''Three Colors: Blue'']. Retrieved 9 January 2012.</ref> that created a "truly transcendent experience".<ref>Matt Brunson.</ref> ''The Guardian'' listed ''[[Breaking the Waves]]'' (1996) as one of its top 25 arthouse films. The reviewer stated that "[a]ll the ingredients that have come to define [[Lars von Trier]]'s career (and in turn, much of modern European cinema) are present here: high-wire acting, innovative visual techniques, a suffering heroine, issue-grappling drama, and a galvanising shot of controversy to make the whole thing unmissable".<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.theguardian.com/film/2010/oct/20/breaking-waves-trier-arthouse|title=Breaking the Waves: No 24 best arthouse film of all time|author=Steve Rose|work=The Guardian|date=20 October 2010 |access-date=21 April 2015}}</ref>

===2000s===
Lewis Beale of ''[[Film Journal International]]'' stated that Australian director [[Andrew Dominik]]'s western film ''[[The Assassination of Jesse James by the Coward Robert Ford]]'' (2007) is "a fascinating, literary-based work that succeeds as both art and genre film".<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.filmjournal.com/filmjournal/reviews/article_display.jsp?vnu_content_id=1003639817 |title=The assassination of Jesse James by the coward Robert Ford |access-date=27 September 2007 |author=Lewis Beale |publisher=[[Film Journal International]] |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071011214428/http://www.filmjournal.com/filmjournal/reviews/article_display.jsp?vnu_content_id=1003639817 |archive-date=11 October 2007 |url-status=dead}}</ref> Unlike the action-oriented [[Jesse James]] films of the past, Dominik's unconventional epic perhaps more accurately details the outlaw's relinquishing psyche during the final months of his life as he succumbs to the paranoia of being captured and develops a precarious friendship with his eventual assassin, [[Robert Ford (outlaw)|Robert Ford]].

In 2009, director [[Paul Thomas Anderson]] claimed that his 2002 film ''[[Punch-Drunk Love]]'' about a shy, repressed rage-aholic was "an art house [[Adam Sandler]] film", a reference to the unlikely inclusion of "frat boy" comic Sandler in the film; critic Roger Ebert claims that ''Punch Drunk Love'' "may be the key to all of the Adam Sandler films, and may liberate Sandler for a new direction in his work. He can't go on making those moronic comedies forever, can he? Who would have guessed he had such uncharted depths?"<ref>{{cite news| url=https://www.rogerebert.com/reviews/punch-drunk-love-2002 | work=RogerEbert.com | title=Punch-Drunk Love|date = 18 October 2002}}</ref>

===2010s===
[[Apichatpong Weerasethakul]]'s ''[[Uncle Boonmee Who Can Recall His Past Lives]]'', which won the 2010 Cannes Palme d'Or, "ties together what might just be a series of beautifully shot scenes with moving and funny musings on the nature of death and reincarnation, love, loss, and karma".<ref>Satraroj, Nick. Movie review: [http://www.cnngo.com/bangkok/play/uncle-boonmee-who-can-recall-his-past-lives-art-film-everyone-487790 "Uncle Boonmee", an art film for everyone] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100823040713/http://www.cnngo.com/bangkok/play/uncle-boonmee-who-can-recall-his-past-lives-art-film-everyone-487790 |date=23 August 2010 }}. CNN. Retrieved 2 October 2010.</ref> Weerasethakul is an independent film director, screenwriter, and film producer, who works outside the strict confines of the Thai film studio system. His films deal with dreams, nature, sexuality, including his own homosexuality,<ref>"Creating His Own Language: An Interview With Apichatpong Weerasethakul", Romers, H. ''Cineaste'', page 34, vol. 30, no. 4, Fall 2005, New York.</ref> and Western perceptions of [[Thailand]] and Asia. Weerasethakul's films display a preference for unconventional narrative structures (such as placing titles/credits at the middle of a film) and for working with non-actors.

[[Terrence Malick]]'s ''[[The Tree of Life (film)|The Tree of Life]]'' (2011) was released after decades of development and won the Palme d'Or at the [[2011 Cannes Film Festival]]; it was highly praised by critics. At the Avon Theater in [[Stamford, Connecticut]], a message was posted about the theater's no-refund policy due to "some customer feedback and a polarized audience response" to the film. The theater stated that it "stands behind this ambitious work of art and other challenging films".<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.indiewire.com/article/avon_theatre_director_talks_about_his_tree_of_life_disclaimer/|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110626031334/http://www.indiewire.com/article/avon_theatre_director_talks_about_his_tree_of_life_disclaimer/|archive-date=26 June 2011|title=INTERVIEW: Here's the Story Behind That Theater's No Refund Policy for "Tree of Life"|publisher=indieWIRE|date=24 June 2011|author=Austin Dale|access-date=16 July 2011}}</ref> ''[[Drive (2011 film)|Drive]]'' (2011), directed by [[Nicolas Winding Refn]],<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.dazeddigital.com/film-tv/article/36668/1/the-best-and-worst-arthouse-film-remakes|title= The best and worst arthouse film remakes|work=Dazed|first = Nick|last = Chen|date = 7 July 2017}}</ref> is commonly called an [[arthouse action film]].<ref name= "RottenTomatoes">{{cite web |url=https://www.rottentomatoes.com/m/drive_2011 |title=Drive (2011) |work=[[Rotten Tomatoes]] |publisher=[[Flixster]] |access-date=17 September 2011}}</ref> Also in 2011, director [[Lars von Trier]] released ''[[Melancholia (2011 film)|Melancholia]]'', a movie dealing with [[Depressive episode|depression]] and other mental disorders while also showing a family's reaction to an approaching planet that could collide with the Earth. The movie was well received, some claiming it to be Von Trier's masterpiece with others highlighting [[Kirsten Dunst]]'s performance, the visuals, and realism depicted in the movie.

[[Jonathan Glazer]]'s [[Under the Skin (2013 film)|''Under the Skin'']] (an example of "[[arthouse science fiction film|arthouse sci-fi]]"<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://screenrant.com/best-genre-blending-sci-fi-horror-movies/|title=20 Best Sci-Fi Horror Movies (That Blend The Genres Perfectly)|first=Ben|last=Sherlock|date=23 May 2020|website=ScreenRant}}</ref>) was screened at the [[2013 Venice Film Festival]] and received a theatrical release through indie studio [[A24]] the following year. The film, starring [[Scarlett Johansson]], follows an [[Extraterrestrial life|alien]] in human form as she travels around [[Glasgow]], picking up unwary men for sex, harvesting their flesh and stripping them of their humanity. Dealing with themes such as sexuality, humanity, and objectification, the film received positive reviews<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.rottentomatoes.com/m/under_the_skin_2013/|title=Under the Skin|date=4 April 2014|publisher=Rotten Tomatoes|access-date=21 April 2015}}</ref> and was hailed by some as a masterpiece;<ref>{{cite news|first=Robbie|last=Collin|url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/film/under-the-skin/review/ |archive-url=https://ghostarchive.org/archive/20220112/https://www.telegraph.co.uk/film/under-the-skin/review/ |archive-date=12 January 2022 |url-access=subscription |url-status=live|title=Under the Skin: 'simply a masterpiece'|newspaper=[[The Daily Telegraph]]|date=13 March 2014|access-date=22 February 2018}}{{cbignore}}</ref> critic [[Richard Roeper]] described the film as "what we talk about when we talk about film as art".<ref>{{cite web|first=Richard|last=Roeper|url=http://blog.richardroeper.com/?p=6233|title='Under the Skin': Brilliant mood piece about a fascinating femme fatale|work=[[Chicago Sun-Times]]|date=13 April 2014|access-date=21 April 2015|via=Richard Roeper Blog}}</ref>

This decade also saw a re-emergence of "[[art horror]]"<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://screenrant.com/sci-fi-movies-every-decade-change-define-how/|title=How Sci-Fi Movies Have Changed In Each Decade (& Why)|first=Chrishaun|last=Baker|date=9 August 2020|website=ScreenRant}}</ref> with the success of films like ''[[Beyond the Black Rainbow]]'' (2010), ''[[Black Swan (film)|Black Swan]]'' (2010), ''[[Stoker (film)|Stoker]]'' (2013), ''[[Enemy (2013 film)|Enemy]]'' (2013), ''[[The Babadook]]'' (2014), ''[[Only Lovers Left Alive]]'' (2014), ''[[A Girl Walks Home Alone at Night]]'' (2014), ''[[Goodnight Mommy]]'' (2014), ''[[Nightcrawler (film)|Nightcrawler]]'' (2014), ''[[It Follows]]'' (2015), ''[[The Witch (2015 film)|The Witch]]'' (2015), ''[[The Wailing (2016 film)|The Wailing]]'' (2016), ''[[Split (2016 American film)|Split]]'' (2016), the [[social thriller]] ''[[Get Out]]'' (2017), ''[[Mother!]]'' (2017), ''[[Annihilation (film)|Annihilation]]'' (2018), ''[[A Quiet Place (film)|A Quiet Place]]'' (2018), ''[[Hereditary (film)|Hereditary]]'' (2018), ''[[Suspiria (2018 film)|Suspiria]]'' (2018; [[Suspiria|a remake of the 1977 film of the same name]]), ''[[Mandy (2018 film)|Mandy]]'' (2018), ''[[The Nightingale (2018 film)|The Nightingale]]'' (2018), ''[[The House That Jack Built (2018 film)|The House That Jack Built]]'' (2018), ''[[Us (2019 film)|Us]]'' (2019), ''[[Midsommar (film)|Midsommar]]'' (2019), ''[[The Lighthouse (2019 film)|The Lighthouse]]'' (2019), ''[[Color Out of Space (film)|Color Out of Space]]'' (2019) and the [[Academy Award for Best Picture]] winner ''[[Parasite (2019 film)|Parasite]]'' (2019).<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.joblo.com/trippy-horrorfantasy-beyond-the-black-rainbow-gets-new-synopsis-dvdblu-ray-release-date/|title=Trippy horror/fantasy Beyond the Black Rainbow gets DVD/Blu-ray release date|first=Jake|last=Dee|date=31 August 2012}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|first=Donald|last=Clarke|url=https://www.irishtimes.com/culture/film/black-swan-1.1278785|title=Black Swan|newspaper=[[The Irish Times]]|date=21 January 2011|access-date=14 March 2016}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|first=Bilge|last=Ebiri|url=https://www.vulture.com/2014/04/under-the-skin-and-a-history-of-art-horror-film.html|title=Under the Skin and a History of Art-Horror Film|work=[[Vulture (blog)|Vulture]]|date=17 April 2014|access-date=14 March 2016}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|first=Anthony|last=D'Alessandro|url=https://deadline.com/2015/10/goodnight-mommy-oscars-austria-foreign-film-entry-radius-1201597760/|title=Radius Horror Film 'Goodnight Mommy' Set To Wake Up Oscar Voters As Austria's Entry|work=Deadline Hollywood|date=29 October 2015|access-date=14 March 2016}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|first=Benjamin|last=Lee|url=https://www.theguardian.com/film/filmblog/2016/feb/23/did-arthouse-horror-hit-the-witch-trick-us-multiplex-audiences|title=Did arthouse horror hit The Witch trick mainstream US audiences?
|newspaper=[[The Guardian]]|date=22 February 2016|access-date=26 February 2017}}</ref>

[[Roma (2018 film)|''Roma'']] (2018), is a film by [[Alfonso Cuarón]] inspired by his childhood living in 1970s Mexico. Shot in black-and-white, it deals with themes shared with Cuarón's past films, such as mortality and class. The film was distributed through [[Netflix]], earning the streaming giant their first [[Academy Awards|Academy Award]] nomination for [[Academy Award for Best Picture|Best Picture]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://variety.com/2019/film/news/roma-netflix-first-best-picture-oscar-nomination-1203113407/|title='Roma' Becomes Netflix's First Best Picture Oscar Nominee|first1=Kristopher|last1=Tapley|date=22 January 2019}}</ref>

[[Arthouse animation]] (with Oscar-nominated titles like ''[[Song of the Sea (2014 film)|Song of the Sea]]'' and ''[[Loving Vincent]]'') was also gaining momentum during this era as an alternative to mainstream animated features alongside the works of acclaimed animators [[Makoto Shinkai]], [[Satoshi Kon]], [[Don Hertzfeldt]] and [[Ari Folman]] from the previous decade.<ref name="amctheatres.com">{{Cite web|url=https://www.amctheatres.com/amc-scene/5-unique-animated-movies-to-look-out-for-from-now-until-christmas|title=Animated Movies To Look Forward To|website=amctheatres.com}}</ref><ref name="hollywoodreporter.com">{{Cite web|url=https://www.hollywoodreporter.com/news/euro-animated-films-offer-darker-arthouse-alternative-hollywood-exec-says-1066701|title=Euro Animated Films Offer "Darker" Art House Alternative to Hollywood, Exec Says|website=The Hollywood Reporter|date=15 December 2017 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://thefilmstage.com/the-criterion-channels-july-2021-lineup-includes-wong-kar-wai-neo-noir-art-house-animation-more/|title=The Criterion Channel's July 2021 Lineup Includes Wong Kar Wai, Neo-Noir, Art-House Animation & More|first=Leonard|last=Pearce|date=24 June 2021}}</ref>

[[Tom Shone]] said of the work of [[Christopher Nolan]]: "He has completed eleven features, [...] all ticking the boxes of studio entertainment, yet indelibly marked with the kind of personal themes and obsessions that are more traditionally the preserve of the art house: the passage of time, the failures of memory, our quirks of denial and deflection, the intimate clockwork of our interior lives, set against landscapes in which the fault lines of late [[Industrialisation|industrialism]] meet the fissure points and paradoxes of the [[information age]]."<ref>{{Cite book |last=Shone |first=Tom |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=-ITjDwAAQBAJ&pg=PT433 |title=The Nolan Variations: The Movies, Mysteries, and Marvels of Christopher Nolan |date=2020-11-03 |publisher=Faber & Faber |isbn=978-0-571-34800-8 |language=en}}</ref>

=== 2020s ===
During the 2020s, [[art film|art-house cinema]] expanded globally through online platforms. The [[COVID-19 pandemic]] accelerated this shift: major [[film festival|festivals]] went virtual, enabling global audiences (critics and cinephiles alike) to see independent and experimental films without travel.<ref>{{cite web |title=Film Festivals Go Virtual |url=https://variety.com/2020/film/global/film-festivals-virtual-1234646021/ |website=Variety |date=2020-06-15}}</ref> Many art-house cinemas also launched virtual programs and [[streaming media|streaming services]] to reach broader audiences.

New storytelling forms emerged. "[[Screenlife|Desktop cinema]]" films―narratives unfolding entirely on computer or mobile screens―treat the screen as both camera and canvas, reflecting contemporary online culture.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Grønstad |first=Asbjørn |title=The Poetics of the Desktop: Essay Film in the Age of Screenlife |journal=NECSUS: European Journal of Media Studies |year=2022 |url=https://necsus-ejms.org/desktop-documentary-from-artefact-to-artistic-emotions/}}</ref>

==Criticism==
Criticisms of art films includes being too pretentious, oppressive, insufferable, overly vague, abstract and self-indulgent for mainstream audiences.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/culture/film/film-blog/10283912/The-Top-10-Most-Pretentious-Films.html |archive-url=https://ghostarchive.org/archive/20220112/https://www.telegraph.co.uk/culture/film/film-blog/10283912/The-Top-10-Most-Pretentious-Films.html |archive-date=12 January 2022 |url-access=subscription |url-status=live|title=The Top 10 Most Pretentious Films|first=Anne|last=Billson|date=5 September 2013|work=The Daily Telegraph}}{{cbignore}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.tasteofcinema.com/2019/10-famous-arthouse-movies-that-are-too-self-indulgent/|title= 10 Famous Arthouse Movies That Are Too Self-Indulgent|first=Mert|last=Dekin|date=1 October 2019|publisher=Taste of Cinema}}</ref><ref>{{cite magazine|url=https://www.wired.com/2019/08/geeks-guide-pretentious-sci-fi/ |title=Are Sci-Fi Movies Getting Too Pretentious?|magazine=WIRED|date = 10 August 2019}}</ref><ref>[https://www.theyoungfolks.com/film/161962/why-critics-hate-the-movies-you-love/ Why Critics Hate the Movies You Love|The Young Ones]</ref><ref name="worstarthouse">[https://collider.com/arthouse-movies-worst-ranked/ 10 Worst Arthouse Movies, Ranked|Collider]</ref>

''[[LA Weekly]]'' film critic Michael Nordine cited the films ''[[Gummo]]'' (1997) as being an "art-house [[exploitation film|exploitation flick]]" and ''[[Amores Perros]]'' (2000) exemplifying "the art-house stereotype of featuring more dead dogs than ''[[Where the Red Fern Grows]]'' and every other book you had to read in middle school".<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.laweekly.com/20-worst-hipster-movies-of-all-time/ |title=20 Worst Hipster Movies of All Time |work= LA Weekly|first = Michael|last = Nordine|date = 17 July 2014}}</ref>

Jeremy Urquhart of ''[[Collider (website)|Collider]]'' cited "exceptionally difficult" yet "sometimes clunky" arthouse fare that "might well irritate more than they enlighten" such as [[Michael Snow]]'s 1967 [[structural film]] ''[[Wavelength (1967 film)|Wavelength]]'', [[David Cronenberg]]'s [[Naked Lunch (film)|1991 adaptation of ''Naked Lunch'']]  and [[Francis Ford Coppola]]'s 1982 musical ''[[One from the Heart]]''.<ref name="worstarthouse"/>

==Related concepts==
===Arthouse television===
{{see also|Quality television}}
[[Quality artistic television]],<ref>{{cite book|first=John|last=Thornton Caldwell|title=''Televisuality: Style, Crisis, and Authority in American Television''|url=https://archive.org/details/televisualitysty00cald|url-access=registration|publisher=Rutgers University Press|year=1995|page=[https://archive.org/details/televisualitysty00cald/page/67 67]|isbn=9780585241135 }}</ref> a [[television genre]] or style which shares some of the same traits as art films, has been identified. Television shows, such as David Lynch and Mark Frost's ''[[Twin Peaks]]'' and Dennis Potter's ''[[The Singing Detective]]'', also have "a loosening of causality, a greater emphasis on psychological or anecdotal realism, violations of classical clarity of space and time, explicit authorial comment, and ambiguity".<ref>{{cite book|first=Kristin|last=Thompson|title=''Storytelling in Film and Television''|publisher=Harvard University Press|location=Cambridge, Massachusetts|year=2003}}</ref>

As with much of Lynch's other work (notably the film ''[[Blue Velvet (film)|Blue Velvet]]''), ''Twin Peaks'' explores the gulf between the veneer of small-town respectability and the seedier layers of life lurking beneath its surface. The show is difficult to place in a defined television genre; stylistically, it borrows the unsettling tone and supernatural premises of horror films and simultaneously offers a bizarrely comical parody of American soap operas with a [[Camp (style)|campy]], melodramatic presentation of the morally dubious activities of its quirky characters. The show represents an earnest moral inquiry distinguished by both [[Surreal humor|weird humor]] and a deep vein of [[surrealism]], incorporating highly stylised vignettes, surrealist and often inaccessible artistic images alongside the otherwise comprehensible narrative of events.

[[HBO]]'s ''[[The Wire]]'' might also qualify as "artistic television", as it has garnered a greater amount of critical attention from academics than most television shows receive. For example, the [[film theory]] journal ''[[Film Quarterly]]'' has featured the show on its cover.<ref>{{cite web|first=D.|last=Driscoll|url=http://machines.pomona.edu/152-2009/2009/11/02/the-wire-being-taught-at-harvard/|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110720033154/http://machines.pomona.edu/152-2009/2009/11/02/the-wire-being-taught-at-harvard/|archive-date=20 July 2011 |title=''The Wire'' Being Taught at Harvard |publisher=Machines.pomona.edu |date=2 November 2009|access-date=6 October 2010}}</ref>

==In popular media==
Art films have been part of popular culture from animated sitcoms like ''[[The Simpsons]]''<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.imdb.com/title/tt1225549/|title=Any Given Sundance|publisher= IMDb}}</ref> and ''[[Clone High]]'' spoofing and satirizing them<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.imdb.com/title/tt0542907/|title=Film Fest: Tears of a Clone|publisher= IMDb}}</ref> to even the comedic film review webseries ''Brows Held High'' (hosted by Kyle Kallgren).<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.geek.com/movies/real-good-you-guys-kyle-kallgren-and-brows-held-high-1721593/ |title=Real Good You Guys: Kyle Kallgren and Brows Held High|date=7 November 2017|access-date=12 September 2019 |archive-date=15 August 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180815041155/https://www.geek.com/movies/real-good-you-guys-kyle-kallgren-and-brows-held-high-1721593/ |url-status=dead}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://the-avocado.org/2018/06/03/brows-held-high-night-thread/ |title=Brows Held High Night Thread |work= The Avocado|first = Sam|last = Aronow|date = 3 June 2018}}</ref><ref name="top15essayistsonyoutube">{{Cite web|url=https://raindance.org/top-15-video-essayists-youtube/|title=Top 15 Video Essayists on Youtube|first=Bruno Savill De|last=Jong|date=27 June 2017}}</ref><ref name="essaysof2017">{{Cite web |last1=Lee |first1=Kevin B. |last2=Verdeure |first2=David |date=2010-01-10 |title=The best video essays of 2017 |url=https://www2.bfi.org.uk/news-opinion/sight-sound-magazine/polls-surveys/annual-round-ups/best-video-essays-2017 |access-date=2020-12-24 |website=[[British Film Institute]] |language=en}}</ref>

'''''Barbie'''''{{efn|group=lower-alpha|Also known in promotional material as '''''Barbie the Movie'''''<ref>{{cite web |date=31 July 2023 |title=Barbie The Movie |url=https://creations.mattel.com/pages/barbie-the-movie |access-date=31 July 2023 |publisher=[[Mattel]] |archive-date=July 28, 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230728042726/https://creations.mattel.com/pages/barbie-the-movie |url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite magazine |last=Chan |first=Tim |date=27 July 2023 |title=Flashback: See Margot Robbie and 'Barbie' Cast React to Their Official Barbie Dolls for the First Time |url=https://www.hollywoodreporter.com/lifestyle/shopping/margot-robbie-barbie-movie-doll-buy-online-1235507777/ |access-date=31 July 2023 |magazine=[[The Hollywood Reporter]] |archive-date=July 28, 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230728121634/https://www.hollywoodreporter.com/lifestyle/shopping/margot-robbie-barbie-movie-doll-buy-online-1235507777/ |url-status=live}}</ref>}} is a 2023 satirical [[fantasy comedy film]] directed by [[Greta Gerwig]] from a screenplay she wrote with her husband, [[Noah Baumbach]]. Based on the [[Barbie|fashion dolls]] by [[Mattel]], it is the first live-action Barbie film after numerous [[List of Barbie animated films|animated films and specials]]. Starring [[Margot Robbie]] as the title character and [[Ryan Gosling]] as [[Ken (doll)|Ken]], the film follows them on a journey of self-discovery through Barbieland and the real world following an [[existential crisis]]. The supporting cast includes [[America Ferrera]], [[Michael Cera]], [[Kate McKinnon]], [[Issa Rae]], [[Rhea Perlman]], and [[Will Ferrell]].

A live-action Barbie film was announced in September 2009 by [[Universal Pictures]] with [[Laurence Mark]] producing. Development began in April 2014, when [[Sony Pictures]] acquired the [[film rights]]. Following multiple writer and director changes and the casting of [[Amy Schumer]] and later [[Anne Hathaway]] as Barbie, the rights were transferred to [[Warner Bros. Pictures]] in October 2018. Robbie was cast in 2019, and Gerwig was announced as director and co-writer with Baumbach in 2020. The rest of the cast was announced in early 2022. [[Principal photography]] occurred primarily at [[Warner Bros. Studios Leavesden]], England, and at the [[Venice Beach Skatepark]] in Los Angeles from March to July 2022.

''Barbie'' premiered at the [[Shrine Auditorium]] in Los Angeles on July 9, 2023, and was released in the United States on July 21. Its concurrent release with [[Universal Pictures]]' ''[[Oppenheimer (film)|Oppenheimer]]'' was the catalyst of the "[[Barbenheimer]]" phenomenon, encouraging audiences to see both films as a [[double feature]]. The film grossed $1.448{{nbsp}}billion and achieved several milestones, becoming Warner Bros.' highest-grossing film, the [[2023 in film#Highest-grossing films|highest-grossing film of 2023]] and the [[List of highest-grossing films|<!--This is the PEAK POSITION the film achieved NOT the CURRENT. Please do NOT adjust!-->14th<!--This is the PEAK POSITION the film achieved NOT the CURRENT. Please do NOT adjust!--> highest-grossing film of all time]] at the time of its release.

Named one of the top ten films of 2023 by the [[National Board of Review]] and the [[American Film Institute]], ''Barbie'' received widespread critical acclaim and [[List of accolades received by Barbie (film)|other accolades]], including eight [[Academy Award]] nominations (among them [[Academy Award for Best Picture|Best Picture]]), winning [[Academy Award for Best Original Song|Best Original Song]] for "[[What Was I Made For?]]"; the song also won the [[Golden Globe Award for Best Original Song]] while the film received the inaugural [[Golden Globe Award for Cinematic and Box Office Achievement]].{{TOC limit|3}}

==Plot==
<!--Please thoughtfully consider any additions to the plot and its structure, e.g., consider avoiding using clauses that just repeat the meaning of the main clauses with synonyms. Plots are generally 400-700 words; current count: 535-->
A "[[stereotypical]]" [[Barbie]] resides with many different versions of herself in Barbieland, a [[matriarchal]] society created by the collective human imagination, along with [[Ken (doll)|Ken]]s and a group of discontinued models treated like outcasts due to their unconventional traits. While the Kens spend their days playing at the beach, considering it their profession, the Barbies hold prestigious jobs in law, science, politics, media, and so on. Ken ("Beach Ken") is only happy when he is with Barbie, and he seeks a closer relationship with her, but she rebuffs him in favor of other activities and female friendships.

One evening at a dance party, Barbie is suddenly stricken with [[Mortality salience|worries about mortality]]. Overnight, she develops bad breath, [[cellulite]], and [[flat feet]], disrupting her routines and impairing the aura of classic perfection experienced by the Barbies. Weird Barbie, a disfigured doll, tells Barbie to find the child playing with her in the real world to cure her afflictions. Barbie travels to the real world, with Beach Ken joining her by stowing away in her convertible.

After arriving in [[Venice, Los Angeles|Venice Beach]], Barbie punches a man for groping her, and is briefly arrested. She and Ken are then both arrested after not paying for new clothes. Alarmed by the dolls' presence in the real world and remembering the "[[Skipper (Barbie)|Skipper]] incident", the CEO of [[Mattel]] orders their recapture. Barbie tracks down her owner, a teenage girl named Sasha, who criticizes Barbie for encouraging unrealistic beauty standards. Distraught, Barbie discovers that Gloria, a Mattel employee and Sasha's mother, inadvertently caused Barbie's [[existential crisis]] after starting to play with Sasha's old Barbie dolls and drawing Barbies with dark emotions and thoughts. Mattel finds Barbie and attempts to put her in a toy box for remanufacturing, but a mysterious elderly woman named Ruth helps her escape. Gloria and Sasha arrive just in time to rescue Barbie from Mattel's executives, and the three travel to Barbieland with the executives in pursuit.

Meanwhile, Ken learns about [[patriarchy]] and feels respected for the first time. He returns to Barbieland to persuade the other Kens to take it over. The Kens begin to [[indoctrinate]] the Barbies into submissive roles, such as agreeable girlfriends, housewives, and maids. Barbie arrives and attempts to convince the Barbies to be independent again, but becomes depressed when she fails. Gloria expresses her frustration with the [[Sexism|conflicting standards that real-world women are expected to follow]], and her speech restores Barbie's confidence.

Aided by Sasha, Weird Barbie, [[Alan (Barbie character)|Allan]], Writer Barbie and the discontinued dolls, Gloria uses her knowledge from the real world to [[deprogram]] the Barbies from their indoctrination. The Barbies then [[Manipulation (psychology)|manipulate]] the Kens into fighting among themselves, which distracts them from enshrining male superiority into Barbieland's constitution, allowing the Barbies to regain power. Having now experienced systemic [[oppression]] for themselves, the Barbies resolve to rectify the faults of their previous society, emphasizing better treatment of the Kens and all [[Outcast (person)|outcast]]s. Barbie and Ken make amends, acknowledging their past mistakes. When Ken bemoans his lack of purpose without Barbie, she encourages him to find an autonomous identity. Barbie, who remains unsure of her own identity, meets with the ghost of [[Ruth Handler]], Mattel co-founder and creator of the Barbie doll,<!--There is debate among editors about whether to call Handler "inventor" of Barbie (or similar) due the fact that the doll was based at least in part by the Bild Lilli doll. Since pretty much all RS and the movie refer to Handler as Barbie's creator, that's how we present her in the article. See talk page topic "Did Ruth Handler invent Barbie?"--> who explains that Barbie's story has no set ending and her ever-evolving history surpasses her roots.

After bidding goodbye to the other dolls and Mattel executives, Barbie decides to become human again and return to the real world. Sometime later, Gloria, her husband, and Sasha take Barbie, now going by the name "Barbara Handler", to her first [[gynecologist]] appointment.

==Production==
===Development===
The concept of a live-action ''Barbie'' film was in development at [[Cannon Films]] in the mid-1980s.<ref>{{cite news |last=Broeske |first=Pat H. |date=May 25, 1986 |title=More Blasts from Cannon |url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1986-05-25-ca-6926-story.html |access-date=September 12, 2023 |newspaper=Los Angeles Times |archive-date=September 15, 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230915043006/https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1986-05-25-ca-6926-story.html |url-status=live}}</ref> Renewed development on a film based on the ''Barbie'' toy line began in September 2009, when it was announced that [[Mattel]] had signed a partnership with [[Universal Pictures]] and producer [[Laurence Mark]], but nothing came to fruition.<ref>{{cite magazine |last1=Fleming |first1=Michael |last2=Graser |first2=Marc |date=September 23, 2009 |title=Barbie's a Living Doll at Universal Pictures with Big Screen Plans |url=https://variety.com/2009/film/markets-festivals/barbie-s-a-living-doll-at-universal-1118009027/ |url-status=live |magazine=[[Variety (magazine)|Variety]] |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220719133530/https://variety.com/2009/film/markets-festivals/barbie-s-a-living-doll-at-universal-1118009027/ |archive-date=July 19, 2022 |access-date=May 23, 2022}}</ref> In April 2014, Mattel teamed with [[Sony Pictures]] to produce the film, which would have [[Jenny Bicks]] writing the screenplay and [[Laurie MacDonald]] and [[Walter F. Parkes]] producing through their [[Parkes+MacDonald Image Nation]] banner. Filming was anticipated to begin by the end of the year.<ref>{{cite web |last=Fleming |first=Mike Jr |date=April 23, 2014 |title=Sony Pictures Teams With Mattel To Fashion Film Franchise Based On Barbie Toyline |url=https://deadline.com/2014/04/sony-pictures-teams-with-mattel-to-fashion-film-franchise-based-on-barbie-toyline-718667/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211022213045/https://deadline.com/2014/04/sony-pictures-teams-with-mattel-to-fashion-film-franchise-based-on-barbie-toyline-718667/ |archive-date=October 22, 2021 |access-date=October 22, 2021 |website=[[Deadline Hollywood]]}}</ref> In March 2015, [[Diablo Cody]] was brought onto the project to rewrite the screenplay, and [[Amy Pascal]] joined the producing team.<ref>{{cite web |last=Fleming |first=Mike Jr. |date=March 4, 2015 |title=Diablo Cody Set To Rewrite 'Barbie' |url=https://deadline.com/2015/03/diablo-cody-barbie-sony-pictures-1201386146/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211022213539/https://deadline.com/2015/03/diablo-cody-barbie-sony-pictures-1201386146/ |archive-date=October 22, 2021 |access-date=October 22, 2021 |website=[[Deadline Hollywood]]}}</ref> Sony ordered further rewrites by [[Lindsey Anderson Beer|Lindsey Beer]], [[Bert V. Royal]] and Hillary Winston, who submitted separate drafts.<ref>{{cite web |last=Fleming |first=Mike Jr. |date=December 15, 2015 |title='Barbie' Movie: Sony Trying Three Poses With Three Scripts |url=https://deadline.com/2015/12/barbie-movie-writers-three-scripts-lindsey-beer-bert-royal-hilary-winston-1201667609/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200224060242/https://deadline.com/2015/12/barbie-movie-writers-three-scripts-lindsey-beer-bert-royal-hilary-winston-1201667609/ |archive-date=February 24, 2020 |access-date=October 22, 2021 |website=[[Deadline Hollywood]]}}</ref>

In December 2016, [[Amy Schumer]] entered negotiations for the title role with Winston's screenplay. She helped rewrite the script with her sister, Kim Caramele.<ref>{{cite news |last=Fleming |first=Mike Jr. |date=December 2, 2016 |title=Amy Schumer Playing ''Barbie'' |url=https://deadline.com/2016/12/amy-schumer-barbie-movie-sony-pictures-mattel-1201863294/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211022213951/https://deadline.com/2016/12/amy-schumer-barbie-movie-sony-pictures-mattel-1201863294/ |archive-date=October 22, 2021 |access-date=October 22, 2021 |website=[[Deadline Hollywood]]}}</ref> In March 2017, she exited negotiations, initially saying it was due to scheduling conflicts with the planned June 2017 filming; she revealed in 2023 that she left due to creative differences with the film's producers.<ref>{{cite news |last=Hipes |first=Patrick |date=March 23, 2017 |title=Amy Schumer Says Bye-Bye To ''Barbie'' |url=https://deadline.com/2017/03/amy-schumer-exits-barbie-movie-1202050379/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211022214450/https://deadline.com/2017/03/amy-schumer-exits-barbie-movie-1202050379/ |archive-date=October 22, 2021 |access-date=October 22, 2021 |website=[[Deadline Hollywood]]}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last=Sharf |first=Zack |date=June 9, 2023 |title=Amy Schumer Dropped Out of ''Barbie'' Because Original Script Wasn't "Feminist and Cool" Enough: "There's a New Team Behind It" Now |url=https://variety.com/2023/film/news/amy-schumer-barbie-not-feminist-dropped-out-1235638574/ |access-date=June 10, 2023 |magazine=[[Variety (magazine)|Variety]] |archive-date=June 10, 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230610164949/https://variety.com/2023/film/news/amy-schumer-barbie-not-feminist-dropped-out-1235638574/ |url-status=live}}</ref> That July, [[Anne Hathaway]] was considered for the title role; Sony hired Olivia Milch to rewrite the screenplay and approached [[Alethea Jones]] to direct as a means of interesting Hathaway in signing.<ref>{{cite web |last=Busch |first=Anita |title=Anne Hathaway Circling ''Barbie'' At Sony |url=https://deadline.com/2017/07/anne-hathaway-barbie-movie-sony-1202135188/ |website=Deadline Hollywood |access-date=October 22, 2021 |date=July 24, 2017 |archive-date=October 22, 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211022214450/https://deadline.com/2017/07/anne-hathaway-barbie-movie-sony-1202135188/ |url-status=live}}</ref> Jones was attached to direct by March 2018.<ref>{{cite web |last=N'Duka |first=Amanda |date=March 23, 2018 |title=Female Directors Scorecard: Sony's ''Barbie'', ''Charlie's Angels'' And More |url=https://deadline.com/2018/03/sony-female-directors-scorecard-2018-1202351662/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211022214734/https://deadline.com/2018/03/sony-female-directors-scorecard-2018-1202351662/ |archive-date=October 22, 2021 |access-date=October 22, 2021 |website=[[Deadline Hollywood]]}}</ref>

In August 2018, Mattel CEO [[Ynon Kreiz]] hired film executive [[Robbie Brenner]], who was later appointed head of [[Mattel Films]].<ref name="Jacobs-2023">{{cite web |last=Jacobs |first=Matthew |date=July 20, 2023 |title=The Woman Who Rescued ''Barbie'' from Development Hell |url=https://www.vulture.com/2023/07/the-mattel-exec-who-rescued-barbie-from-development-hell.html |url-access=limited |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230721230027/https://www.vulture.com/2023/07/the-mattel-exec-who-rescued-barbie-from-development-hell.html |archive-date=July 21, 2023 |access-date=July 21, 2023 |website=[[Vulture (website)|Vulture]]}}</ref><ref name="Wagmeister-2023">{{cite magazine |last=Wagmeister |first=Elizabeth |title='This Is Not About Selling Toys': Mattel Bosses on 'Barbie's' Long Development, Needing a Female Director and More |url=https://variety.com/2023/film/news/barbie-movie-mattell-execs-toy-adaptations-1235674597/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230721232631/https://variety.com/2023/film/news/barbie-movie-mattell-execs-toy-adaptations-1235674597/ |archive-date=July 21, 2023 |access-date=July 21, 2023 |magazine=[[Variety (magazine)|Variety]]|date=July 20, 2023}}</ref> Sony's option on the project expired in October 2018, and film rights were transferred to [[Warner Bros. Pictures]], causing Hathaway, Jones, Macdonald, Parkes and Pascal to leave the project. [[Margot Robbie]] entered early talks for the role, and [[Patty Jenkins]] was briefly considered as director.<ref>{{cite web |last=D'Alessandro |first=Anthony |date=October 5, 2018 |title=''Barbie'' Zooming From Sony To Warner Bros; Margot Robbie In Early Talks |url=https://deadline.com/2018/10/anne-hathaway-barbie-movie-to-open-2020-1202267729/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180826073131/https://deadline.com/2018/01/anne-hathaway-barbie-movie-to-open-2020-1202267729/ |archive-date=August 26, 2018 |access-date=October 22, 2021 |website=[[Deadline Hollywood]]}}</ref> Kreiz was determined to cast Robbie after meeting with her; both he and Brenner felt that Robbie's appearance resembled that of a conventional Barbie doll and were impressed by her ideas. Initial meetings occurred at the [[Polo Lounge]] located in [[The Beverly Hills Hotel]].<ref>{{cite magazine |last=Dockterman |first=Eliana |date=June 27, 2023 |title=How ''Barbie'' Came to Life |url=https://time.com/6289864/barbie-time-cover-story/ |url-access=limited |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230627110127/https://time.com/6289864/barbie-time-cover-story/ |archive-date=June 27, 2023 |access-date=July 24, 2023 |magazine=[[Time (magazine)|Time]]}}</ref><ref name="Wagmeister-2023"/> Brenner eventually partnered with Robbie's production company, [[LuckyChap Entertainment]], and Robbie's husband [[Tom Ackerley]] and Josey McNamara were enlisted as producers.<ref name="Jacobs-2023"/><ref name="Wagmeister-2023"/> Robbie's casting was confirmed in July 2019.<ref name="RobbieCast">{{cite web |last=N'Duka |first=Amanda |title=Greta Gerwig, Noah Baumbach To Script Warner Bros' Live-Action ''Barbie'' Film |url=https://deadline.com/2019/07/greta-gerwig-noah-baumbach-warner-bros-barbie-script-1202646509/ |website=[[Deadline Hollywood]] |access-date=October 22, 2021 |date=July 15, 2019 |archive-date=October 22, 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211022215849/https://deadline.com/2019/07/greta-gerwig-noah-baumbach-warner-bros-barbie-script-1202646509/ |url-status=live}}</ref>

In her capacity as a producer, Robbie pitched ''Barbie'' to Warner Bros. herself. During the green-light meeting, she compared the film to [[Steven Spielberg]]'s ''[[Jurassic Park]]'' (1993) and also suggested at the time in jest that it would gross over $1&nbsp;billion.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Nemiroff |first1=Perri |last2=Jones |first2=Tamera |date=July 19, 2023 |title=Margot Robbie Sold 'Barbie' By Comparing It to Steven Spielberg's 'Jurassic Park' |url=https://collider.com/barbie-margot-robbie-interview-ryan-gosling/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230720223600/https://collider.com/barbie-margot-robbie-interview-ryan-gosling/ |archive-date=July 20, 2023 |access-date=July 21, 2023 |website=[[Collider (website)|Collider]]}}</ref> Later on, she approached [[Greta Gerwig]]—whose previous films, particularly ''[[Little Women (2019 film)|Little Women]]'' (2019), Robbie enjoyed—to screenwrite. Gerwig was in [[post-production]] for another film, and took the assignment on the condition that her husband, [[Noah Baumbach]], also write the script.<ref name="Barasch-2023">{{cite magazine |last=Barasch |first=Alex |date=July 2, 2023 |title=After 'Barbie', Mattel is Raiding Its Entire Toy Box |url=https://www.newyorker.com/magazine/2023/07/10/after-barbie-mattel-is-raiding-its-entire-toybox |url-access=limited |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230710191533/https://www.newyorker.com/magazine/2023/07/10/after-barbie-mattel-is-raiding-its-entire-toybox |archive-date=July 10, 2023 |access-date=July 21, 2023 |magazine=[[The New Yorker]]}}</ref><ref name="Marriott-2023">{{cite magazine |last=Marriott |first=Hannah |date=July 19, 2023 |title=It's Greta's World&nbsp;... The Director Talks Boiler Suits, New Babies, And Barbie-Mania |url=https://www.elle.com/uk/life-and-culture/a44525742/greta-gerwig-barbie-digital-cover/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230721225044/https://www.elle.com/uk/life-and-culture/a44525742/greta-gerwig-barbie-digital-cover/ |archive-date=July 21, 2023 |access-date=July 21, 2023 |magazine=[[Elle (magazine)|Elle]]}}</ref> Gerwig would sign on to also direct the film in July 2021.<ref>{{cite magazine |last=Jackson |first=Angelique |date=July 9, 2021 |title=Greta Gerwig to Direct ''Barbie'' With Margot Robbie, Filming to Start in 2022 |url=https://variety.com/2021/film/news/greta-gerwig-barbie-movie-director-margot-robbie-noah-baumbach-1235015427/ |url-status=live |magazine=[[Variety (magazine)|Variety]] |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210709161914/https://variety.com/2021/film/news/greta-gerwig-barbie-movie-director-margot-robbie-noah-baumbach-1235015427/ |archive-date=July 9, 2021 |access-date=October 22, 2021}}</ref> Robbie said the film aimed at subverting expectations and giving audiences "the thing you didn't know you wanted".<ref>{{cite magazine |last=Rose |first=Lacey |date=December 18, 2020 |title=Margot Robbie and LuckyChap Partners Talk Their Producing Strategy: "If It's Not a 'F***, Yes,' It's a 'No'" |url=https://www.hollywoodreporter.com/movies/movie-news/margot-robbie-and-luckychap-partners-talk-their-producing-strategy-if-its-not-a-f-yes-its-a-no-4105712/ |url-status=live |magazine=[[The Hollywood Reporter]] |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220414144857/https://www.hollywoodreporter.com/movies/movie-news/margot-robbie-and-luckychap-partners-talk-their-producing-strategy-if-its-not-a-f-yes-its-a-no-4105712/ producer.<ref>{{cite magazine |last1=Donnelly |first1=Matt |last2=Lang |first2=Brent |date=August 14, 2023 |title='Barbie's' Big Payday: Margot Robbie Will Earn $50 Million in Salary and Box Office ===Writing===
{{Multiple image
| perrow            = 2
| total_width       = 270
| image1            = Greta Gerwig Berlinale 2018.jpg
| alt1              = Greta Gerwig at the 2018 Berlin International Film Festival in Berlin, Germany.
| image2            = Noah Baumbach Cannes 2017.jpg
| alt2              = 
| footer            = Director [[Greta Gerwig]] co-wrote the screenplay with her husband, [[Noah Baumbach]].
}}

As writers, Gerwig and Baumbach were given full creative freedom. They worked on the screenplay during the 2020–2021 [[COVID-19 pandemic lockdowns]] at their house in Long Island. Baumbach felt he understood the film's purpose once Gerwig had shown him the first scene, identifying the "element" as "embracing mortality and sadness and sickness and everything that it means to be human". Gerwig was also inspired by the real-life story of Barbie creator [[Ruth Handler]].<ref>{{cite web |last=Thompson |first=Anne |date=December 5, 2023 |title=Greta Gerwig Explains the Exhilarating Freedom of Imagining Her Hit 'Barbie' |url=https://www.indiewire.com/features/interviews/greta-gerwig-freedom-indiewire-honors-interview-1234931987/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231205213202/https://www.indiewire.com/features/interviews/greta-gerwig-freedom-indiewire-honors-interview-1234931987/ |archive-date=December 5, 2023 |access-date=January 18, 2024 |publisher=[[IndieWire]]}}</ref> Gerwig's [[film treatment]] consisted of an [[abstract poem]] on Barbie influenced by the [[Apostles' Creed]]. For the narrative arc, she was partially inspired by the non-fiction book ''[[Reviving Ophelia]]'' (1994) by [[Mary Pipher]], which accounts the effects of societal pressures on American teenage girls. She also found inspiration in classic [[Technicolor]] musicals such as ''[[The Red Shoes (1948 film)|The Red Shoes]]'' (1948) and ''[[The Umbrellas of Cherbourg]]'' (1964), and said: "They have such a high level of what we came to call authentic artificiality. You have a painted sky in a soundstage. Which is an illusion, but it's also really there. The painted backdrop is really there. The tangibility of the artifice is something that we kept going back to."<ref name="vogue.com">{{cite magazine |last=Aguire |first=Abby |date=May 24, 2023 |title=Barbiemania! Margot Robbie Opens Up About the Movie Everyone's Waiting For |url=https://www.vogue.com/article/margot-robbie-barbie-summer-cover-2023-interview |url-status=live |magazine=[[Vogue (magazine)|Vogue]] |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230524133039/https://www.vogue.com/article/margot-robbie-barbie-summer-cover-2023-interview |archive-date=May 24, 2023 |access-date=May 24, 2023}}</ref> The script also contains candid criticism of [[Mattel]], which created skepticism among Mattel officials when they received the first version. However, Kreiz decided to trust Gerwig. Brenner noted that "being safe in this world doesn't work" as she interpreted Barbie to be a "bold" and "trailblazer" figure. As a result, [[Will Ferrell]]'s portrayal as the Mattel CEO was meant to be an [[allegory]] for corporate America. Kreiz praised Ferrell and said that while Mattel officials took their brands seriously, they did not take themselves seriously.<ref name="Wagmeister-2023"/> Gerwig and Robbie had felt the film was "most certainly a feminist film", but Mattel officials rejected the description because of the inherent sexism and misandry. Gerwig and Robbie informed the studio that they would explore the controversies and problematic parts of Barbie, but also convinced the studio that they would respect the product.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Ferguson |first1=Sarah |last2=Freri |first2=Marina |date=July 11, 2023 |title=Greta Gerwig and Margot Robbie discuss Barbie's surprising feminism |url=https://www.abc.net.au/news/2023-07-11/margot-robbie-greta-gerwig-barbie-and-feminism-730/102565304 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230711111605/https://www.abc.net.au/news/2023-07-11/margot-robbie-greta-gerwig-barbie-and-feminism-730/102565304 |archive-date=July 11, 2023 |access-date=July 24, 2023 |publisher=[[Australian Broadcasting Corporation]]}}</ref>

Gerwig was also influenced by her childhood experiences with Barbie. Her mother discouraged her from purchasing such dolls, but eventually allowed her to.<ref name="Moshakis-2023">{{cite news |last=Moshakis |first=Alex |date=July 9, 2023 |title='It had to be totally bananas': Greta Gerwig on bringing Barbie to life |url=https://www.theguardian.com/film/2023/jul/09/it-had-to-be-totally-bananas-greta-gerwig-on-bringing-barbie-back-to-life |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230709072541/https://www.theguardian.com/film/2023/jul/09/it-had-to-be-totally-bananas-greta-gerwig-on-bringing-barbie-back-to-life |archive-date=July 9, 2023 |access-date=July 12, 2023 |newspaper=[[The Guardian]]}}</ref> Opting to acknowledge the controversial nature of the Barbie doll, Gerwig chose to create a film where she would be both "doing the thing and subverting the thing", in the sense that she would be celebrating the feminism behind Barbie while also noting the controversial beauty standards associated with it. She was also fascinated by the idea that humans created dolls, which in turn imitate humans, feeling that "we're in constant conversation with inanimate objects" while also conveying an affirmative message to the audience to "just be yourself and know that that's enough". The film deliberately juxtaposed contradictory messaging, such as critiquing [[consumerism]] yet glamorizing plastic products; and in the film's ending, where Barbie desires to be more than just a plastic doll. Gerwig made the film as an "earnest attempt to make amends" between affirming women's worth and conveying the impossibility of perfection, which some perceived to be standards associated with Barbie.<ref name="Paskin"/><ref>{{cite web |last1=Tong |first1=Scott |last2=Perkins Mastromarino |first2=James |last3=Hagan |first3=Allison |date=July 21, 2023 |title=Barbie' director Greta Gerwig explains how the movie deconstructs a toy icon |url=https://www.wbur.org/hereandnow/2023/07/21/greta-gerwig-barbie |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230721223806/https://www.wbur.org/hereandnow/2023/07/21/greta-gerwig-barbie |archive-date=July 21, 2023 |access-date=July 21, 2023 |publisher=[[WBUR-FM]]}}</ref>

Reflecting upon the [[maximalism]] of Barbie, Gerwig said the "[[ontology]] of Barbie" was similar to what she perceived as [[William Shakespeare]]'s maximalism, which she enjoyed in his works. She grounded the film in what she described as a "heightened theatricality that allows you to deal with big ideas in the midst of anarchic play".<ref>{{cite magazine |last=Laffly |first=Tomris |date=July 21, 2023 |title=How Greta Gerwig Brought Indie Spirit to ''Barbie'' |url=https://www.wmagazine.com/culture/greta-gerwig-barbie-interview |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230721223036/https://www.wmagazine.com/culture/greta-gerwig-barbie-interview |archive-date=July 21, 2023 |access-date=July 21, 2023 |magazine=[[W (magazine)|W]]}}</ref> She also described the film as being anarchic, unhinged, and humanist.<ref name="Moshakis-2023"/><ref name="Hiatt-2023"/> She felt the film originated from the "deep isolation of the [[COVID-19 pandemic|pandemic]]", opining that the line in which Barbie says "Do you guys ever think about dying?" exemplifies the film's anarchic nature. She also found the idea of Barbie being "constrained in multitudes" as "all of these women are Barbie and Barbie is all of these women" to be "trippy" and felt as a result, Barbie did not need to have her own personal life, as she was attuned to her environment. She also described the story as mirroring a girl's journey from childhood to adolescence, though she did not deem it to be a [[coming of age]] film and felt that the film ultimately "ends up, really, about being human".<ref name="Moshakis-2023"/>

Primarily, she began her writing by interpreting Barbie as living in a [[utopia]] and eventually experiencing reality, where she would have to "confront all the things that were shielded from them in this place [Barbieland]". She also drew parallels to the story of [[Adam and Eve]] and taking inspiration from [[John Milton]]'s ''[[Paradise Lost]]'', particularly being inspired by the concept that there is "no poetry without pain".<ref name="Marriott-2023"/> To underscore the tragic elements of Barbie and Ken facing the real world, she focused on elements of dissonance.<ref name="Barasch-2023"/> As such, she chose to keep a scene featuring Robbie's Barbie telling an older woman that she is beautiful after being requested to remove it, as she felt that the scene epitomized "the heart of the movie". She also desired to provide a "counterargument" to Barbie by featuring a scene in which Barbie learns that some women do not like her, and felt it gave the film "real intellectual and emotional power".<ref name="Hiatt-2023"/> As such, a scene is featured in which Barbie is being stared at inappropriately on the Venice Beach, which Gerwig chose to feature as she felt it was a universal experience, being especially relevant for actors. She was inspired by an audition she did in which she wore overalls and felt that she did not perform well in.<ref name="Bahr-2023">{{cite news |last=Bahr |first=Lindsey |date=July 20, 2023 |title='Barbie' filmmaker Greta Gerwig wants to embrace the mess |url=https://apnews.com/article/greta-gerwig-interview-barbie-ed61b918097f2fc43e024f4872a7225e |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230721225753/https://apnews.com/article/greta-gerwig-interview-barbie-ed61b918097f2fc43e024f4872a7225e |archive-date=July 21, 2023 |access-date=July 20, 2023 |publisher=[[Associated Press]]}}</ref>

The ending of the film features Barbie saying the line "I'm here to see my gynecologist", with Gerwig describing it as a "mic drop kind of joke". She had chosen to include the line as she had wanted to instill confidence in younger girls, as she had been embarrassed about her body when she was younger.<ref>{{cite news |last=Ryan |first=Patrick |date=July 22, 2023 |title='Barbie' ending: Greta Gerwig talks 'emotional' final line, creator Ruth Handler (Spoilers!) |url=https://www.usatoday.com/story/entertainment/movies/2023/07/22/barbie-moving-ending-spoilers/70429263007/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230722155319/https://www.usatoday.com/story/entertainment/movies/2023/07/22/barbie-moving-ending-spoilers/70429263007/ |archive-date=July 22, 2023 |access-date=July 24, 2023 |newspaper=[[USA Today]]}}</ref> ''Barbie'' also explores the negative consequences of hierarchical power structures, with Gerwig saying that she extrapolated that "Barbies rule and Kens are an underclass" and felt it was similar to the ''[[Planet of the Apes]]''.<ref name="Hiatt-2023"/> Ken has low self-esteem and seeks approval from Barbie, which Gerwig identified as a good source for a story. Gosling compared Gerwig's vision to [[Milton Glaser]]'s [[I Love New York]] logo, as he felt Gerwig created the film's characters as a way of understanding the contemporary world.<ref>{{cite news |last=Olsen |first=Mark |date=July 11, 2023 |title=Ryan Gosling and Greta Gerwig on how Ken became the subversive center of 'Barbie' |url=https://www.latimes.com/entertainment-arts/movies/story/2023-07-11/greta-gerwig-ryan-gosling-ken-barbie |url-access=limited |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230721235731/https://www.latimes.com/entertainment-arts/movies/story/2023-07-11/greta-gerwig-ryan-gosling-ken-barbie |archive-date=July 21, 2023 |access-date=July 21, 2023 |newspaper=[[Los Angeles Times]]}}</ref> Ken has the only [[Sentimental ballad|power ballad]] in the film, and Gerwig had identified it as the moment in which she felt the film transcended what a Barbie film traditionally should have been.<ref name="Paskin"/><ref>{{cite magazine|url=https://variety.com/2023/film/news/barbie-noah-baumbach-greta-gerwig-terrible-idea-1235772481/|title=Barbie' Co-Writer Noah Baumbach Initially Thought Film Was a 'Terrible Idea,' but Greta Gerwig 'Signed Me Up': 'You've Gotta Get Us Out of This'|date=October 30, 2023|magazine=Variety|access-date=October 30, 2023|archive-date=October 30, 2023|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231030142554/https://variety.com/2023/film/news/barbie-noah-baumbach-greta-gerwig-terrible-idea-1235772481/|url-status=live}}</ref>

===Set design===
[[Sarah Greenwood]] and [[Katie Spencer]] were the set designer and decorator, respectively, for ''Barbie''. For the [[Barbie Dreamhouse]], they drew inspiration from [[mid-century modern]]ist architecture found in [[Palm Springs]], including the 1946 [[Kaufmann Desert House]] by [[Richard Neutra]], and the photography of [[Slim Aarons]]. Gerwig wanted to capture "what was so ridiculously fun about the Dreamhouses", alluding to its previous models, and referenced ''[[Pee-wee's Big Adventure]]'' (1985), the paintings of [[Wayne Thiebaud]], and the apartment of [[Gene Kelly]]'s character in the Technicolor musical ''[[An American in Paris (film)|An American in Paris]]'' (1951). "Everything needed to be tactile, because toys are, above all, things you touch", Gerwig said of the use of [[practical effect]]s instead of [[computer-generated imagery]] (CGI) to capture the sky and the [[San Jacinto Mountains]]. The set design is also noted for its extensive use of a specific shade of pink, Pantone 219. [[Rosco Laboratories]], the film's paint supplier, faced international [[shortage]]s due to [[COVID-19]]-related supply-chain issues, as well as freezing temperatures that damaged stock; the film's sets required the company's entire remaining stock of pink.<ref>{{cite web |last=Malle |first=Chloe |author-link=Chloe Malle |date=May 30, 2023 |title=Inside the Barbie Dreamhouse, a Fuchsia Fantasy Inspired by Palm Springs |url=https://www.architecturaldigest.com/story/inside-the-barbie-dreamhouse-a-fuchsia-fantasy-inspired-by-palm-springs |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230616190629/https://www.architecturaldigest.com/story/inside-the-barbie-dreamhouse-a-fuchsia-fantasy-inspired-by-palm-springs |archive-date=June 16, 2023 |access-date=May 30, 2023 |website=Architectural Digest}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.latimes.com/entertainment-arts/movies/story/2023-06-03/barbie-production-design-shortage-pink-paint-greta-gerwig |title='Barbie' production emptied a company's worldwide supply of pink paint |website=[[Los Angeles Times]]|first=Jonah|last=Valdez |date=June 3, 2023 |access-date=July 27, 2023 |archive-date=July 26, 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230726232648/https://www.latimes.com/entertainment-arts/movies/story/2023-06-03/barbie-production-design-shortage-pink-paint-greta-gerwig |url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.npr.org/2023/06/05/1180133265/barbie-movie-pink-paint-shortage |title=Did the 'Barbie' movie really cause a run on pink paint? Let's get the full picture |publisher=[[NPR]] |first=Rachel|last=Treisman|date=June 5, 2023 |access-date=August 3, 2023 |archive-date=July 25, 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230725030441/https://www.npr.org/2023/06/05/1180133265/barbie-movie-pink-paint-shortage |url-status=live}}</ref> Because Gerwig also wanted to use practical builds,<ref name="Nemiroff-2023"/> and had to film sequences in miniature models, then composite the footage onto the actual image. She began discussing the production design with cinematographer Rodrigo Prieto, Greenwood, and costume designer [[Jacqueline Durran]] a year in advance of filming.<ref name="Nemiroff-2023">{{cite web |last1=Nemiroff |first1=Perri |last2=Amin |first2=Arezou |date=July 20, 2023 |title=Greta Gerwig Revived 1950s Techniques to Create the World of 'Barbie' |url=https://collider.com/barbie-greta-gerwig-interview/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230721235458/https://collider.com/barbie-greta-gerwig-interview/ |archive-date=July 21, 2023 |access-date=July 21, 2023 |website=[[Collider (website)|Collider]]}}</ref> She also called director [[Peter Weir]] for inspiration on Barbieland, with the idea of creating it as an "interior soundstage world".<ref name="Bahr-2023"/>

===Costumes, hair, and makeup===
[[File:Barbie and Ken costumes from Barbie movie at Warner Bros. Studio Tour Hollywood.jpg|thumb|upright|right|''Barbie'' costumes on display at the [[Warner Bros. Studio Tour Hollywood]]]]
Costume designer [[Jacqueline Durran]], who previously collaborated with Gerwig on ''[[Little Women (2019 film)|Little Women]]'' (2019), employed a practical approach to create Barbie's wardrobe: "The defining characteristic of what she wears is where she's going and what she's doing, [i]t's about being completely dressed for your job or task." To match the film's Barbieland setting, Durran and her team created costumes made of roughly fifteen color combinations "that riffed off the idea of a [[French Riviera]] beach in the early 1960s" and drew inspiration from actress [[Brigitte Bardot]]. For Ken's outfits, Durran zeroed in a look composed of colorful sportswear from the [[1980s in fashion|1980s]], while actor Ryan Gosling suggested a Ken-branded underwear for the character. Durran closely adapted outfits from past iterations of Barbie dolls, such as the 1993 "Western Stampin{{'"}} dolls and the 1994 "Hot Skatin{{'"}} dolls. She noted the Barbie dolls as "a very useful way to look at different ideas of [[femininity]]: what that means, who owns it, and who it's aimed at" and reflected this idea in how she dressed the characters. While the majority of the clothing featured in the film were sourced by Durran and her team, they also pulled pieces from the fashion archives of [[Chanel]].<ref>{{cite web |last=Mukhtar |first=Amel |date=June 12, 2023 |title=Exclusive: ''Barbie'' Costume Designer Jacqueline Durran On Vintage Chanel, Ken's Pants And Styling The Film Of The Summer |url=https://www.vogue.co.uk/article/barbie-costumes-jacqueline-durran |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230616183259/https://www.vogue.co.uk/article/barbie-costumes-jacqueline-durran |archive-date=June 16, 2023 |access-date=June 12, 2023 |magazine=[[British Vogue]]}}</ref> [[Ivana Primorac]] was the lead hair and makeup artist for the film.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.nylon.com/beauty/barbie-movie-make-up-artist-ivana-primorac-interview|title=Dreamy Hair and Makeup Brought The Dolls To Life In 'Barbie'|date=July 26, 2023|first=Sam |last=Neibart|access-date=July 26, 2023|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230726212331/https://www.nylon.com/beauty/barbie-movie-make-up-artist-ivana-primorac-interview|archive-date=July 26, 2023|magazine=[[Nylon (magazine)|Nylon]]|url-status=live}}</ref> In 2024, Primorac and Marie Larkin and Clare Corsick jointly won the [[Make-Up Artists and Hair Stylists Guild Award for Best Period and/or Character Hair Styling in a Feature-Length Motion Picture]] for ''Barbie''.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.msn.com/en-us/lifestyle/beauty/maestro-saltburn-barbie-win-film-prizes-at-make-up-artists-hair-stylists-guild-awards-full-list/ar-BB1iuJSu?OCID=ansmsnnews11 | title=MSN | website=[[MSN]] | access-date=February 19, 2024 | archive-date=March 13, 2024 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240313191142/https://www.msn.com/en-us/lifestyle/beauty/maestro-saltburn-barbie-win-film-prizes-at-make-up-artists-hair-stylists-guild-awards-full-list/ar-BB1iuJSu?OCID=ansmsnnews11 | url-status=live}}</ref>

===Filming===
[[Principal photography]] began on March 22, 2022, at [[Warner Bros. Studios Leavesden]] in England and wrapped on July 21.<ref>{{cite news |last=Hayes |first=Dade |date=July 21, 2022 |title=Mattel Speeds Past Wall Street's Q2 Estimates On Same Day ''Barbie'' Wraps Shooting |url=https://deadline.com/2022/07/mattel-speeds-past-wall-street-second-quarter-forecasts-barbie-1235074207/ |access-date=July 21, 2022 |website=Deadline Hollywood |archive-date=August 1, 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220801092821/https://deadline.com/2022/07/mattel-speeds-past-wall-street-second-quarter-forecasts-barbie-1235074207/ |url-status=live}}</ref> Among the notable [[Location shooting|locations]] was the [[Venice Beach Skatepark]] in Los Angeles, California.<ref>{{cite news |last=Keane |first=Daniel |date=June 28, 2022 |title=Margot Robbie and Ryan Gosling rollerskate down Venice Beach while filming 'Barbie' in Los Angeles |url=https://www.standard.co.uk/showbiz/margot-robbie-ryan-gosling-rollerskate-venice-beach-barbie-b1008757.html |access-date=May 29, 2023 |newspaper=[[Evening Standard]] |archive-date=May 29, 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230529141205/https://www.standard.co.uk/showbiz/margot-robbie-ryan-gosling-rollerskate-venice-beach-barbie-b1008757.html |url-status=live}}</ref> [[Rodrigo Prieto]] served as cinematographer.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.theknowledgeonline.com/the-knowledge-bulletin/post/2022/03/22/uk-shoot-begins-on-margot-robbies-barbie-|title=UK shoot begins on Margot Robbie's ''Barbie''|date=March 22, 2022|website=The Knowledge|access-date=March 26, 2022|archive-date=March 25, 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220325163524/https://www.theknowledgeonline.com/the-knowledge-bulletin/post/2022/03/22/uk-shoot-begins-on-margot-robbies-barbie-|url-status=live}}</ref> Prior to filming, Gerwig organized a [[sleepover]] with the female cast members for them to establish positive relationships, also feeling that it "would be the most fun way to kick everything off".<ref name="Moshakis-2023"/> She opted to use filming techniques from the 1950s (as Barbie had been a popular toy since 1959) to create a period-accurate look.<ref name="Nemiroff-2023"/> She also watched [[Powell and Pressburger]]'s ''[[A Matter of Life and Death (1946 film)|A Matter of Life and Death]]'' (1946) to understand how pre-digital visual effects were used to create theatricality. To highlight the tragic nature of Barbie and Ken facing the difficulties of the real world, she directed Robbie and Gosling to act as if they were in a drama.<ref name="Barasch-2023"/>

===Post-production===
Editor Nick Huoy returned to collaborate with Greta Gerwig, having also cut ''[[Lady Bird (film)|Lady Bird]]'' and ''[[Little Women (2019 film)|Little Women]]''.<ref>{{cite web |last=Strauss |first=Bob |date=2023-12-11 |title='Barbie' editor Nick Houy on cutting America Ferrera's now-famous speech and that tricky '2001' opening |url=https://www.latimes.com/entertainment-arts/awards/story/2023-12-11/barbie-editor-nick-houy-greta-gerwig-margot-robbie |access-date=2024-04-29 |website=Los Angeles Times |archive-date=February 23, 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240223120004/https://www.latimes.com/entertainment-arts/awards/story/2023-12-11/barbie-editor-nick-houy-greta-gerwig-margot-robbie |url-status=live}}</ref> Finding the tone of the film was a playful experiment working collaboratively with Gerwig and VFX supervisor Glen Pratt and VFX producer Nick King.<ref>{{cite web |last=Blair |first=Iain |date=12 October 2023 |title=Barbie Editor Nick Houy Talks Workflow and VFX |url=https://postperspective.com/barbie-editor-nick-houy-talks-workflow-and-vfx/ |access-date=April 29, 2024 |archive-date=May 18, 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240518173744/https://postperspective.com/barbie-editor-nick-houy-talks-workflow-and-vfx/ |url-status=live}}</ref> Pratt focused on blending the practical with the digital.<ref>{{cite web |date=2023-12-18 |title=Glen Pratt On Incorporating the Concept of Play into the Visual Effects Language of 'Barbie' |url=https://www.awardsdaily.com/2023/12/18/glen-pratt-on-incorporating-the-concept-of-play-into-the-visual-effects-language-of-barbie/ |access-date=2024-04-29 |website=Awardsdaily |archive-date=April 29, 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240429101710/https://www.awardsdaily.com/2023/12/18/glen-pratt-on-incorporating-the-concept-of-play-into-the-visual-effects-language-of-barbie/ |url-status=live}}</ref> Practical miniatures were built, scanned and captured with photogrammetry inspiring the creation of hundreds of digital miniatures to populate Barbieland vistas, set extensions, backdrops and full CGI shots.<ref>{{cite web |title=No Visual Effects in 'Barbie'? Glen Pratt Reveals the Truth |url=https://www.awn.com/vfxworld/no-visual-effects-barbie-glen-pratt-reveals-truth |access-date=2024-04-29 |website=[[Animation World Network]] |archive-date=February 6, 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240206145849/https://www.awn.com/vfxworld/no-visual-effects-barbie-glen-pratt-reveals-truth |url-status=live}}</ref> Pratt worked with visual effects studios [[Framestore]] on Barbieland scenes and UPP on the invisible effects deployed in the real world and a car pursuit sequence.

The palette chosen for the scenes in Barbieland was inspired by the classic three-strip Technicolor look, and was named TechnoBarbie. This required the creation of a software called PPL, a color correcting program which separates the image into the three basic components of blue, green, and red, which can then be manipulated individually.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.gq.com/story/barbie-greta-gerwig-barbie-land-technobarbie-new-color-pink |title=How Greta Gerwig Recaptured Old Hollywood Technicolor Magic for Barbie |date=August 11, 2023 |access-date=June 3, 2024 |archive-date=June 3, 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240603022533/https://www.gq.com/story/barbie-greta-gerwig-barbie-land-technobarbie-new-color-pink |url-status=live}}</ref>

Despite fan expectations for the 1997 song "[[Barbie Girl]]" by the pop band [[Aqua (band)|Aqua]] to feature in the film, Ulrich Møller-Jørgensen, manager for Aqua lead singer [[Lene Nystrøm]], said that it was not used; ''[[Variety (magazine)|Variety]]'' speculated that it was due to bad relations between Mattel and [[MCA Records]], the song's American publisher, who engaged in [[Mattel, Inc. v. MCA Records, Inc.|a series of lawsuits]] over it from 1997 to 2002.<ref>{{cite magazine |url=https://variety.com/2022/film/news/barbie-girl-movie-aqua-1235254222/ |title=Aqua's 'Barbie Girl' Song Won't Appear in the Margot Robbie ''Barbie'' Movie |magazine=[[Variety (magazine)|Variety]] |date=April 29, 2022 |last=Yossman |first=K. A first-look image of the film was revealed during a Warner Bros. presentation at [[CinemaCon]] in April 2022.
