==Production==

===Background===
{{further|Brandon Teena}}
Brandon Teena was a trans man who was gang raped and murdered by a group of male acquaintances in December 1993, when he was 21.{{refn|Brandon Teena was never his legal name; other names may include his legal name, as well as "Billy Brinson", "Teena Ray", or "Charles Brayman".<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.chicagotribune.com/1994/01/17/deadly-deception/ |title=Deadly Deception |work=[[Chicago Tribune]] |last=Worthington |first=Rogers |date=January 17, 1994 |access-date=April 25, 2015 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150508000231/http://articles.chicagotribune.com/1994-01-17/features/9401170002_1_john-lotter-falls-city-lincoln |archive-date=May 8, 2015}}</ref>|group=nb}}<ref name=8thcircuit /><ref name=Howey /> Kimberly Peirce, at the time a [[Columbia University]] film student, became interested in the case after reading a 1994 ''[[The Village Voice|Village Voice]]'' article by [[Donna Minkowitz]].<ref>{{cite news|last=Minkowitz|first=Donna|date=April 19, 1994|title=Love hurts: Brandon Teena was a woman who lived and loved as a man. She was killed for carrying it off|work=[[The Village Voice]]|page=24}}</ref><ref name=DVDcommentary /><ref name=SanJoseMercury /> Peirce became engrossed in Brandon's life and death; she said, "the minute I read about Brandon, I fell in love. With the intensity of his desire to turn himself into a boy, the fact that he did it with no role models. The leap of imagination that this person took was completely overwhelming to me."<ref name=Meyer /> The sensationalist news coverage of the case prolonged her interest.<ref name=DVDcommentary /> Peirce said she looked beyond the brutality of the case and instead viewed the positive aspects of Brandon's life as part of what eventually caused his death.<ref name="Sragow" /> She admired Brandon's audacity, ability to solve complicated problems, and what she perceived as the sense of fantasy invoked by his personality.<ref name=Sragow />

Peirce wanted to tell the story from Brandon's perspective. She was familiar with Brandon's desire to wear men's clothing: "I started looking at all the other coverage and a great deal of it was sensational. People were focusing on the spectacle of a girl who had passed as a boy because that is so unfamiliar to so many people. Where to me, I knew girls who had passed as boys, so Brandon was not some weird person to me. Brandon was a very familiar person."<ref name=allen /> Peirce was influenced by the public perception of the case, believing the American public was generally misinformed: she said, "People were also focusing on the crime without giving it much emotional understanding and I think that's really dangerous, especially with this culture of violence that we live in".<ref name=allen /> Peirce began working on a concept for the film and gave it the working title ''Take It Like a Man''.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.polfilms.com/boysdontcry.html |title=Boys Don't Cry |work=Political Film Society |access-date=April 25, 2015 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304000326/http://www.polfilms.com/boysdontcry.html |archive-date=March 4, 2016}}</ref>

The project drew interest from various production companies. [[Diane Keaton]]'s production company, Blue Relief, showed interest in the screenplay in the mid-1990s. Initially, the film was to be largely based on [[Aphrodite Jones]]' 1996 [[true crime]] book ''All She Wanted'', which told the story of Brandon's final few weeks.<ref name="The Hollywood Reporter" /> Earlier drafts of the script incorporated scenes featuring Brandon's family background, including his sister Tammy and mother Joann, as well as some of Teena's ex-girlfriends. However, Peirce modified the script to fit her vision to focus on the relationship between Brandon and his 19-year-old girlfriend Lana Tisdel, which Peirce termed a "great love story",<ref name=DVDcommentary /><ref name=Seiler /> in contrast to ''All She Wanted'', which did not place an emphasis on the relationship.<ref name="The Hollywood Reporter" />

To fund the writing and development of the project, Peirce worked as a [[paralegal]] on a midnight shift and as a [[35mm movie film|35mm film]] projectionist; she also received a grant from the [[New York Foundation for the Arts]].<ref name=Hart /> The project attracted the attention of producer [[Christine Vachon]], who had seen a short film Peirce had made for her thesis in 1995 about the case.<ref name=Meyer /> [[IFC Films]], Hart Sharp Entertainment, and [[Killer Films]], Vachon and [[Eva Kolodner]]'s production company, provided financing for the project. IFC contributed roughly $1 million, but the film's eventual budget remained under $2 million.<ref name="MovieMaker">{{cite web|url=http://www.moviemaker.com/archives/moviemaking/directing/articles-directing/kimberly-peirce-3334/ |title=Kimberly Peirce |work=[[MovieMaker]] |last=Basoli |first=A.G. |date=November 16, 1999 |access-date=June 15, 2015 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150528224539/http://www.moviemaker.com/archives/moviemaking/directing/articles-directing/kimberly-peirce-3334/ |archive-date=May 28, 2015}}</ref> Peirce co-wrote the screenplay with Andy Bienen. They worked together for 18 months on the final drafts and were careful not to "mythologize" Brandon; the aim was to keep him as human as possible.<ref name="Sragow" /> In the editing stage of the script, Peirce sent the draft to [[Fox Searchlight Pictures]], which agreed to produce and distribute the film while giving Peirce [[artistic license]].<ref name="MovieMaker" />

Prior to filming, Peirce researched the facts by interviewing the people surrounding the case.<ref name="Filmmaker" /> She immersed herself in the information available about the murder, including trial transcripts. She met Lana Tisdel at a convenience store and interviewed her at Tisdel's home.<ref name="DVDcommentary" /> Tisdel, who began dating Brandon just two weeks before he was murdered, was 19 years old at the time of the murders and lived in Falls City with her mother.<ref>{{cite magazine|url=https://www.newyorker.com/magazine/1997/01/13/the-humboldt-murders |title=The Humboldt Murders |magazine=The New Yorker |last=Dunne |first=John Gregory |date=January 13, 1997 |access-date=January 31, 2016 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160102190519/http://www.newyorker.com/magazine/1997/01/13/the-humboldt-murders |archive-date=January 2, 2016}}</ref> Peirce also interviewed Tisdel's mother and Brandon's acquaintances. However, she was unable to interview Brandon's mother or any of his biological family.<ref name=DVDcommentary /><ref name=allen /> Much factual information, including Nissen being a convicted arsonist, was incorporated into ''Boys Don't Cry''.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.friedmanlaw.com/Articles/Teena-Brandon-An-American-Tragedy.shtml |title=Teena Brandon, An American Tragedy |work=Friedman Law Offices |access-date=April 25, 2015 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150611174600/http://www.friedmanlaw.com/Articles/Teena-Brandon-An-American-Tragedy.shtml |archive-date=June 11, 2015}}</ref>

===Casting===
[[File:Hilary Swank at 28th Tokyo International Film Festival.jpg|thumb|left|upright|alt=Hilary Swank, the lead actress of the film, in 2010|[[Hilary Swank]]]]
The filmmakers retained the names of most of the case's real-life protagonists, but the names of several supporting characters were altered. For example, the character of Candace was named Lisa Lambert in real life.<ref name="Berardinelli" /> The casting process for ''Boys Don't Cry'' lasted almost four years.<ref name=Vaughan /> [[Drew Barrymore]] was an early candidate to star in the film.<ref name="The Hollywood Reporter" /> Peirce scouted the [[LGBTQ people|LGBTQ]] community, looking mainly for masculine, lesbian women for the role of Brandon Teena. Peirce said the LGBT community was very interested in the project because of the publicity surrounding the murder.<ref name=DVDcommentary /> High-profile actors avoided Peirce's auditions at the request of their agents because of the stigma associated with the role.

At one point, the project was nearly abandoned because Peirce was not satisfied with most of the people who auditioned.<ref name=Loos /> In 1996, after a hundred female actors had been considered and rejected, the relatively unknown actor Hilary Swank sent a videotape to Peirce and was signed on to the project.<ref name=DVDcommentary /><ref name="Jane Summer" /> Swank successfully [[Passing (gender)|passed]] as a boy to the doorman at her audition.<ref name="Swank Times">{{cite web|url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1999-oct-22-ca-24840-story.html |title=Actress Got Lost in the Story of Brandon Teena |work=[[Los Angeles Times]] |last=Rauzi |first=Robin |date=October 22, 1999 |access-date=June 16, 2015 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151026030333/http://articles.latimes.com/1999/oct/22/entertainment/ca-24840 |archive-date=October 26, 2015}}</ref> During her audition, Swank, who was 22, lied to Peirce about her age. Swank said that, like Brandon, she was 21 years of age. When Peirce later confronted her about her lie, Swank responded, "But that's what Brandon would do."<ref name=TorontoStar /> Swank's anonymity as an actor persuaded Peirce to cast her; Peirce said she did not want a "known actor" to portray Teena.<ref name=PhilippineDaily /> In addition, Peirce felt that Swank's audition was "the first time I saw someone who not only blurred the gender lines, but who was this beautiful, androgynous person with this cowboy hat and a sock in her pants, who smiled and loved being Brandon."<ref name="MovieMaker" />

Peirce required that Swank "make a full transformation" into a male.<ref name="MovieMaker" /> Immediately after being cast, Peirce took Swank to a hairdresser, where her lower-back length hair was cut and dyed chestnut brown.<ref name="Swank Times" /> When she saw her then-husband, [[Chad Lowe]], again, he barely recognized her.<ref name="Swank Times" /> Swank prepared for the role by dressing and living as a man for at least a month, including [[breast binding|wrapping her chest in tension bandages]] and putting socks down the front of her trousers as Brandon Teena had done. Her masquerade was convincing; Swank's neighbors believed the "young man" coming and going from her home was Swank's visiting brother. She reduced her body fat to seven percent to accentuate her facial structure and refused to let the cast and crew see her out of costume.<ref name=PhilippineDaily /><ref name=PRInside /> Swank earned $75 per day for her work on ''Boys Don't Cry'', totaling $3,000.<ref name=Guardian01 /><ref>{{cite news|title=Cashing In|work=The Chicago Tribune|date=February 2003}}</ref> Her earnings were so low that she did not qualify for health insurance.<ref name=Leung />

[[File:Chloe Sevigny Horror premiere 2015.jpg|thumb|upright|alt=Chloë Sevigny, who plays Lana Tisdel in the film, depicted in 2010|[[Chloë Sevigny]]]]
For the role of Brandon's girlfriend, Lana Tisdel, Peirce had envisioned a teenage [[Jodie Foster]].<ref name=DVDcommentary /> The role was also offered to [[Reese Witherspoon]] and [[Sarah Polley]].<ref>{{cite magazine |url=http://new.oystermag.com/from-the-archives-oyster-53-cover-star-chloe-sevigny |title=The Archives: Oyster #53 Cover Star Chloë Sevigny |magazine=[[Oyster (magazine)|Oyster]] |date=May 11, 2015 |access-date=October 6, 2015 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151008140648/http://new.oystermag.com/from-the-archives-oyster-53-cover-star-chloe-sevigny |archive-date=October 8, 2015}}</ref> Peirce ultimately decided to cast Chloë Sevigny based on her performance in ''[[The Last Days of Disco]]'' (1998).<ref>{{cite video|people =Sevigny, Chloë|title = The Last Days of Disco|medium = DVD| publisher = [[The Criterion Collection]]|date =2009}}</ref><ref name="Guardian08" /> Sevigny had auditioned for the role of Brandon,<ref name=FrancescaMiller /><ref name="Kennedy" /> but Peirce decided Sevigny would be more suited to playing Lana because she could not picture Sevigny as a man.<ref name=Guardian08 /><ref name=Kennedy />
{{blockquote|There's a moment in ''The Last Days of Disco'' when Chloë does this little dance move and flirts with the camera [...] She has this mix of attractiveness, flirtation and sophistication that she gives you, but then takes away very quickly so that you want more: you want to reach into the screen and grab her. When I saw that, and her confidence and wit, I thought: if she could flirt with Brandon and the audience in that way, that's exactly what we need for Lana. I said to her, "Will you please audition to play Lana?" She said, "No." And I said, "OK, you can have the role."<ref name="Guardian08" />}}

Sevigny dyed her hair red for the role to match Lana's strawberry blonde hair. Peirce later said, "Chloë just surrendered to the part. She watched videos of Lana. She just became her very naturally."<ref name="Kennedy" />

Peter Sarsgaard played John Lotter, Lana's former boyfriend, who raped and murdered Teena. Sarsgaard was one of the first choices for the role. He later said he wanted his character to be "likable, sympathetic even", because he wanted the audience "to understand why they would hang out with me. If my character wasn't necessarily likable, I wanted him to be charismatic enough that you weren't going to have a dull time if you were with him."<ref name=Olsen /> In another interview, Sarsgaard said he felt "empowered" by playing Lotter.<ref name=GlasgowHerald /> In an interview with ''[[The Independent]]'', Sarsgaard said, "I felt very sexy, weirdly, playing John Lotter. I felt like I was just like the sheriff, y'know, and that everyone loved me."<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.independent.co.uk/news/people/profiles/ive-never-been-more-repulsive-peter-sarsgaard-on-playing-linda-lovelaces-abusive-husband-8761948.html |title='I've Never Been More Repulsive': Peter Sarsgaard on Playing Lina Lovelace's Abusive Husband |work=[[The Independent]] |last=Mottram |first=James |date=August 18, 2013 |access-date=May 2, 2015 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150612035217/http://www.independent.co.uk/news/people/profiles/ive-never-been-more-repulsive-peter-sarsgaard-on-playing-linda-lovelaces-abusive-husband-8761948.html |archive-date=June 12, 2015}}</ref> Sarsgaard recalled watching footage of and reading about Lotter to prepare for the role.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.tcm.com/tcmdb/person/170209%7C201499/Peter-Sarsgaard/ |title=Overview for Peter Sarsgaard |work=[[Turner Classic Movies]] |access-date=May 2, 2015 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150612055816/http://www.tcm.com/tcmdb/person/170209%7C201499/Peter-Sarsgaard/ |archive-date=June 12, 2015}}</ref> Peirce cast [[Lecy Goranson|Alicia Goranson]], known for playing Becky on the sitcom ''[[Roseanne]]'', as Candace because of her likeness to Lisa Lambert.<ref name=DVDcommentary /> Like Sevigny, Goranson had also initially auditioned for the lead role.<ref name=FrancescaMiller />

===Principal photography===
[[File:Greenville August 2015 28 (Lee Street).jpg|left|upright=1.2|thumb|alt=A street corner with no people|''Boys Don't Cry'' was primarily shot in [[Greenville, Texas]].]]
Initially, ''Boys Don't Cry'' was scheduled to film for thirty days.<ref name="MovieMaker" /> However, principal photography for the film lasted from October 19 to November 24, 1998. The small budget dictated some of the filming decisions, including the omission of some incidents to speed up the overall pacing. Timing constraints and Peirce's visions relating to the plot limited what could be achieved with the narrative.<ref name=DVDcommentary /> For example, the film portrays a double murder when in actuality a third person, Phillip DeVine—a black disabled man—was also killed at the scene. At the time, he had been dating Lana Tisdel's sister, Leslie, who was omitted from the story.<ref name=Ramsland2 /><ref name=Ramsland5 /> ''Boys Don't Cry'' was primarily filmed in [[Greenville, Texas]], a small town about {{Convert|45|miles|km|abbr=on}} northeast of [[Dallas]]. Most of the incidents in the case took place in [[Falls City, Nebraska]],<ref name="NYTimes" /> but budget constraints led the filmmakers to choose locations in Texas.<ref name=DVDcommentary />

Peirce initially wanted to shoot in Falls City, but Vachon told her that filming there would not be possible.<ref name="MovieMaker" /> Afterwards, the film was going to be shot in [[Omaha, Nebraska]], but Peirce felt that "none of [the places] looked right."<ref name="MovieMaker" /> In addition, Peirce also scouted filming locations in Kansas and Florida before deciding on Texas.<ref name="MovieMaker" /> One of Peirce's main goals was for the audience to sympathize with Brandon. On the film's DVD commentary track, Peirce said, "The work was informing me about how I wanted to represent it. I wanted the audience to enter deeply into this place, this character, so they could entertain these contradictions in Brandon's own mind and would not think he was crazy, would not think he was lying, but would see him as more deeply human."<ref name=DVDcommentary /><ref name=allen />

Some scenes in ''Boys Don't Cry'' required emotional and physical intensity; these were allocated extended periods of filming. The scene in which Brandon, at the wishes of his friends, bumper-skis on the back of a pickup truck, was delayed when a police officer, just arriving at a shift change, required a large lighting crane to be moved from one side of the road to the other. The scenes took six hours to shoot and were filmed at sunrise, resulting in a blue sky being seen in the background.<ref name=DVDcommentary /> There were some technical complications: some of the filming equipment got stuck in the mud, and radio wires in some of the scenes conflicted with the sound production. Swank required a stunt double for a scene in which she falls off the back of a truck. Teena's rape scene was given an extended filming time; Sexton, who portrayed one of the attackers, walked away in tears afterward.<ref name=DVDcommentary /> Swank found portraying her character daunting and felt the need to "keep a distance" from the reality of the actual event. When scenes became difficult, Swank requested the company of her husband on set.<ref name=Loos /> At times, Peirce worked for seventeen hours a day to complete more work, but the other crew members told her that this was taking up potential nighttime filming hours.<ref name="MovieMaker" />

===Cinematography===
[[File:Boys Don't Cry passage to manhood.jpg|thumb|upright=1.2|alt=A screenshot of one of the opening scenes of the film, in which Brandon passes through a dimly lit set into a roller rink.|Brandon's "passage to manhood". Peirce had intended the [[roller skate]] scene to be a metaphor for Brandon's formal entrance into masculinity. This image illustrates the dim lighting used throughout the film, giving a particular emphasis on artificial light stemming from the film's focus on confined interiors.]]
Peirce, who had originally sought a career in photography before moving into filmmaking, applied techniques she had learned to the film.<ref name="Index Magazine" /> She described the film's mood as an "artificial night".<ref name="DVDcommentary" /> Director of Photography [[Jim Denault]] showed her the work of photographer [[Jan Staller]], whose long-exposure night photography under artificial lighting inspired Denault to avoid using "moonlight" effects for most of the film. As a way to further incorporate the sense of artificial night, John Pirozzi, who had been experimenting with [[time-lapse photography]] using a non-motion-controlled moving camera, was invited to create the transition shots seen throughout the film.<ref name="DVDcommentary" />

The film's visual style depicts the [[Midwestern United States]] in a "withdrawn",<ref name=Tatara /> dark and understated light to give a "surreal" effect.<ref name="Herald Journal" /> Denault shot ''Boys Don't Cry'' in flat, spherical format on [[35mm movie film|35mm film]] using [[List of motion picture film stocks|Kodak Vision]] film stock. The film was shot with a [[Moviecam Compact]] camera fitted with [[Carl Zeiss AG|Carl Zeiss]] super speed lenses. For the scene in which Brandon is stripped, a hand-held camera was used to give a sense of subjectivity and intimacy.

The use of low natural light and heavy artificial light is illustrated early in the film in the opening roller rink scene in which Brandon pursues his first relationship with a young woman. For this scene, Peirce used a three-shot method similar to that used in a scene in ''[[The Wizard of Oz (1939 film)|The Wizard of Oz]]'' (1939) in which Dorothy leaves her house and enters Oz.<ref name=DVDcommentary /> The scene consists of a three-shot sequence meant to symbolize Brandon's metaphorical "entrance to manhood", or Brandon's social transition from a woman to a man. Some scenes were given a prolonged shooting sequence to induce a feeling of hallucination. An example is the sequence in which Brandon and Lana first have sex, followed by a shot of her, Brandon, Candace, and Kate driving in a car against a city skyline backdrop.<ref name="DVDcommentary" /> The scene in which John and Tom strip Brandon was filmed with three cameras due to time constraints, even though Peirce wanted six cameras to film it. The scene took an hour and a half to film in total.<ref name="MovieMaker" />

Peirce drew inspiration from the filming style of [[John Cassavetes]] and the early work of [[Martin Scorsese]], and she incorporated [[Neorealism (art)|neo-realist]] techniques into the film.<ref name="AV Club"/> She was also influenced by a second style of work—the "magical" films of [[Michael Powell]] and [[Kenji Mizoguchi]].<ref name="AV Club" /> The former style is used when Brandon joins the social circle of John, Tom, Lana and her mother, while the latter is used when Brandon and Lana begin to depart from that life.<ref name="Sragow" /> The film was also influenced by ''[[Bonnie and Clyde (film)|Bonnie and Clyde]]'' (1967).<ref name="AV Club" /> Peirce incorporated influences from ''[[Raging Bull]]'' (1980) by opening the film with a shot of Brandon traveling along a highway, as seen from the character's imaginative or dream perspective, similar to the beginning of ''Raging Bull''.<ref name=DVDcommentary /> When a character expresses a dream or hopeful assertion, Peirce cuts to an "eerily lit" dream landscape.<ref name=Zacharek /> ''[[The Pawnbroker (film)|The Pawnbroker]]'' (1964) inspired the cinematography and editing of Brandon's rape scene, particularly in its use of [[fast cutting]].<ref name="AV Club">{{cite web|url=https://www.avclub.com/article/kimberly-peirce-13626 |title=Kimberly Peirce: Interview |work=[[The A.V. Club]] |last=Tobias |first=Scott |date=October 27, 1999 |access-date=April 25, 2015 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150614032033/http://www.avclub.com/article/kimberly-peirce-13626 |archive-date=June 14, 2015}}</ref>

===Music===
Because the film is set in the rural Midwestern United States, the ''Boys Don't Cry'' soundtrack album features a compilation of country, blues and rock music. [[Nathan Larson (musician)|Nathan Larson]] and [[Nina Persson]] of [[The Cardigans]] composed an instrumental version of [[Restless Heart]]'s 1988 country-pop song "[[The Bluest Eyes in Texas]]", a variation of which was used as the film's love theme and score.<ref name=DVDcommentary /> The song itself is heard during a [[karaoke]] scene, sung by Sevigny's character, and at the end of the film. The title of the film is taken from [[Boys Don't Cry (The Cure song)|the song of the same name]] by British rock band [[The Cure]].<ref name="NME.com">{{cite web|url=https://www.afi.com/news/afi-movie-club-boys-dont-cry/|title=AFI Movie Club: Boys Don't Cry|work=AFI|access-date=18 October 2020|archive-date=October 19, 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201019234151/https://www.afi.com/news/afi-movie-club-boys-dont-cry/|url-status=live}}</ref> An American cover of the song, sung by Nathan Larson, plays in the background in the scene in which Lana bails Brandon out of jail and during one of their sex scenes. However, the song is not included in the released soundtrack. Songs by [[Lynyrd Skynyrd]] ("[[Tuesday's Gone]]"), [[Paisley Underground]] band [[Opal (band)|Opal]] ("She's a Diamond") and [[The Charlatans (American band)|The Charlatans]] ("Codine Blues") also appear in the film, as do cover versions of other songs. The soundtrack was released on November 23, 1999, by [[Koch Records]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.soundtrack.net/album/boys-dont-cry/ |title=Boys Don't Cry Soundtrack |work=Soundtrack.net |access-date=April 26, 2015 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150614004054/http://www.soundtrack.net/album/boys-dont-cry/ |archive-date=June 14, 2015}}</ref> "The Bluest Eyes in Texas" was played when Hilary Swank went onstage to receive her [[Academy Award for Best Actress]] in 2000.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://article.wn.com/view/2014/09/24/Hilary_Swank_to_be_honoured_for_Boys_Don_t_Cry_role/ |title=Hilary Swank to be Honoured for 'Boys Don't Cry' role |work=[[World News Network]] |date=September 24, 2014 |access-date=April 26, 2015 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150616070020/http://article.wn.com/view/2014/09/24/Hilary_Swank_to_be_honoured_for_Boys_Don_t_Cry_role/ |archive-date=June 16, 2015}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2zD5L-ja8O0 |title=Hilary Swank Wins Best Actress: 2000 Oscars |via=[[YouTube]] |date=October 26, 2010 |access-date=July 14, 2015 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150702122401/https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2zD5L-ja8O0 |archive-date=July 2, 2015}}</ref> The song also plays over the film's end credits.<ref name="Dando" />

==Themes and analysis==
{{quote box|width=25%|quote=Unlike most films about mind-numbing tragedy, this one manages to be full of hope.|source=[[Janet Maslin]] of ''The New York Times''<ref name="Maslin" />}}
''Boys Don't Cry'' has been widely discussed and analyzed by scholars and others. [[Roger Ebert]] described the film as a "romantic tragedy" embedded in a working class American setting, calling it "''Romeo and Juliet'' set in a Nebraska trailer park".<ref name=Ebert /> Philosopher Rebecca Hanrahan argued that the question of identity—particularly Brandon's—is alluded to frequently in ''Boys Don't Cry'' and that Peirce poses the nature of [[Personal identity|identification]] and [[self]] as the film's main question.<ref>[[#Hanrahan|Hanrahan (2005)]], pp. 78–80</ref> Journalist [[Janet Maslin]] said the film is about accepting identity, which in turn means accepting the fate predisposed for that identity.<ref name=Maslin /> Paula Nechak called the film a "bold cautionary tale";<ref name="Rotten Tomatoes" /> she regarded the film as a negative, dismal depiction of Midwestern America, writing that "[Peirce's film has] captured the mystique and eerie loneliness" and "isolation of the Midwest, with its dusty desolation and nowhere-to-go frustration that propels people to violence and despair".<ref name="Rotten Tomatoes" />

Christine Vachon, the film's executive producer, said, "It's not just about two stupid thugs who killed somebody. It's about these guys whose world is so tenuous and so fragile that they can't stand to have any of their beliefs shattered", referring to John and Tom's views of their lives, Brandon's aspirations and his biological sex.<ref name="Maslin" /><ref>{{cite magazine|url=https://content.time.com/time/specials/packages/article/0,28804,2095385_2095462_2095494,00.html |title=Boys Don't Cry (1999) – Bullying: What Kids, Teens, and Adults Need to Know |magazine=[[Time (magazine)|Time]] |last=Melnick |first=Meredith |date=September 28, 2011 |access-date=April 26, 2015 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150614060257/http://content.time.com/time/specials/packages/article/0%2C28804%2C2095385_2095462_2095494%2C00.html |archive-date=June 14, 2015}}</ref> Along with other turn-of-the-millennium films such as ''[[In the Company of Men]]'' (1997), ''[[American Beauty (1999 film)|American Beauty]]'' (1999), ''[[Fight Club (film)|Fight Club]]'' (1999), and ''[[American Psycho (film)|American Psycho]]'' (2000), Vincent Hausmann said ''Boys Don't Cry'' "raises the broader, widely explored issue of masculinity in crisis".<ref name="Hausmann 117">{{harvnb|Hausmann|2004|p=117}}</ref> Jason Wood said the film, together with [[Patty Jenkins]]'s ''[[Monster (2003 film)|Monster]]'' (2003), is an exploration of "social problems".<ref name="Wood">[[#Wood|Wood (2004)]], pp. 19–20</ref>

===Romantic and platonic relationships===
[[File:Roger Ebert cropped.jpg|thumb|upright=1|alt=Roger Ebert, one of the film's positive reviewers and commentators, in 2006.|Roger Ebert praised the film and called it "''Romeo and Juliet'' set in a Nebraska trailer park."]]
Several scholars commented on the relationship between Brandon and Lana as well as Brandon's relationship with John and Tom. Carol Siegel regarded the film as a thematically rich love story between two ill-fated lovers, similar to ''[[Romeo and Juliet]]''.<ref name=Genders /> [[Jack Halberstam]] attributed ''Boys Don't Cry''{{'}}s success to its ostensible argument for tolerance of [[sexual diversity]] by depicting a relationship between two unlikely people.

This tragic aspect of the love story led Halberstam to compare Brandon and Lana's relationship and subsequent drama to classic and modern romances including ''Romeo and Juliet'', often using the term [[star-crossed lovers]].<ref name="Halberstam">[[#Halberstam|Halberstam (2005)]], p. 82</ref> In the ''Journal for Creativity in Mental Health'', Jinnelle Veronique Aguilar discussed Brandon's ability to create [[interpersonal relationships]] in the film. She opined that Brandon wanted to create close relationships, but he could not due to his transgender status until he became close with Lana. "Although Brandon can make a brief but authentic connection with Lana, he continues to experience a sense of aloneness in the world. He consistently faces a sense of fear related to the power-over dynamics that he and others who are transsexual face…Brandon experiences the central relational paradox, in which he yearns for connection; however, due to the real threat he faces, he is unable to make that connection."<ref>{{cite journal|last=Aguilar|first=Jinnelle Veronique|title=''Boys Don't Cry'', a Movie Review: Implications for Counseling Persons Who are Transgendered|journal=Journal of Creativity in Mental Health|volume=5|issue=4|pages=440–446|year=2010|doi=10.1080/15401383.2010.527819|s2cid=145329257}}</ref>

Myra Hird, in the ''[[International Feminist Journal of Politics]]'', argued that John and Brandon exemplify two different and contrasting types of masculinity, and that Brandon's version is preferred by the film's female characters, comparing them to [[Arnold Schwarzenegger]] and [[Jimmy Stewart]], respectively. "Throughout the film, John offers the viewer a typified narrative of heteronormative masculinity. […] Against this [[hegemonic masculinity]], Brandon offers a masculinity reminiscent of a by-gone era of chivalry." Furthermore, she contended that John was threatened by Brandon's version of masculinity. "Gender boundaries are taken extremely seriously in Western society, and ''Boys Don't Cry'' depicts how intensely threatened John and Tom are by Brandon's superior portrayal of a masculinity 'schedule'. John cannot abide Brandon's desire, and clear ability, to access [[male privilege]], and his reaction is to force Brandon to ''be'' female through the act of rape."<ref>{{cite journal|last=Hird|first=Myra|title=Appropriating Identity: Viewing 'Boys Don't Cry'|journal=[[International Feminist Journal of Politics]]|volume=3|issue=3|pages=435–442|year=2001|doi= 10.1080/14616740110078211|s2cid=144866276}}</ref>

===Causes of violence against LGBT people===
[[File:Jack Halberstam 03.jpg|thumb|left|upright=1.1|alt=Jack Halberstam, one of the film's main commentators.|Jack Halberstam believed that Brandon's murder as depicted in the film partly arose from [[homophobia]], not just [[transphobia]].]]
Other commentators discussed the more complex psychological causes of Brandon's murder. Halberstam commented on the complicated causes of the murder, and whether it was due to [[transphobia]] or [[homophobia]]: "Ultimately in ''Boys'' [''Don't Cry''], the double vision of the transgender subject gives way to the universal vision of humanism, the transgender man and his lover become lesbians and the murder seems instead to be the outcome of vicious homophobic rage."<ref>{{cite journal|last=Halberstam|first=Jack|author-link= Jack Halberstam|title=The Transgender Gaze in ''Boys Don't Cry''|journal=[[Screen (journal)|Screen]]|volume=42|issue=3|pages=294–298|doi=10.1093/screen/42.3.294|year=2001}}</ref> Ebert called the film a "sad song about a free spirit who tried to fly a little too close to the flame".<ref name=Ebert />

In the same journal, Julianne Pidduck commented on the film's rape and murder scenes, "Effectively, the viewer is asked to experience the rape from the victim's point of view. The film invites political, emotional and corporeal allegiances linked to known and imagined risk, especially for female and/or queer viewers. An allegiance with Brandon's outsider status aligns the viewer with Brandon's initial exhilaration at his transgressive success as a boy, drawing us through to the film's disturbing finale."<ref>{{cite journal|last=Pidduck|first=Julianne|title=The ''Boys Don't Cry'' Debate: Risk and Queer Spectatorship|journal=[[Screen (journal)|Screen]]|volume=42|issue=1|pages=97–102|year=2001|doi= 10.1093/screen/42.1.97}}</ref>

===Self and transgender identity===
Many scholars addressed the various performances of gender by the characters in the film; Moss and Lynne Zeavin offered a [[psychoanalytic]] analysis,{{refn|The essay uses female pronouns to refer to Brandon, which will be reserved for the purposes of quotes.|group=nb}} calling the film a "case report" that "presents [Brandon's] transsexual inclinations as a series of euphoric conquests" and "focuses on a range of anxious reactions to her {{sic}} transsexuality. […] or a case not for what they might reveal about female hysteria, but for what they might reveal about misogyny".<ref>[[#Moss, Zeavin|Moss and Zeavin (2001)]], p. 221</ref> Elaborating on the themes of the film, they wrote:

<blockquote>In her film, Pierce [''sic''] inserts the unconventional problems of transsexuality into a conventional narrative structure. Throughout the film Brandon is presented as a doomed, though beguiling and beautiful rascal, recognizably located in the lineage of well-known cinematic bad-boys like James Dean, Steve McQueen, and Paul Newman. Like these predecessors, Brandon's heroic stature derives from her [''sic''] unwillingness to compromise her [''sic''] identity … Pierce [''sic''] presents Brandon's struggles against [[biological determinism]] as the struggles of a dignified renegade.<ref>[[#Moss, Zeavin|Moss and Zeavin (2001)]], p. 222</ref></blockquote>
Brenda Cooper, in ''Critical Studies in Media Communication'', argued that the film "can be read as a liberatory narrative that queers the centers of heteronormativity and hegemonic masculinity by privileging female masculinity and celebrating its differences from heterosexual norms."<ref name="Cooper44">[[#Cooper|Cooper (2004)]], p. 44</ref> She argued that the film challenged heteronormativity by criticizing the concept of the [[Heartland (United States)|American Heartland]], by presenting problems with [[Heterosexuality|heterosexual]] masculinity and its internalised aggression, by "centering female masculinity", and blurring gender boundaries.<ref name="Cooper44" />

Later on in the same essay, she commented that Brandon both embodied and rejected traditional masculinity, providing a new outlook on what it means to be a man which excited and thrilled the women in the film: "Brandon’s performance of masculinity, however, can be interpreted as operating on two levels in the narratives: When Brandon tries to establish his male identity with his new buddies, he imitates the kind of overly aggressive macho machismo that John and Tom represent. But Lana falls for Brandon because of his version of masculinity, which contradicts and challenges traditional assumptions about what it takes to be a man and to please a woman. Brandon’s articulation of manhood effectively mocks sexist masculine ideals and appropriates the codes of normative masculinity."<ref>[[#Cooper|Cooper (2004)]], p. 54</ref> Michele Aaron, in ''[[Screen (journal)|Screen]]'', claimed that the film was primarily centered on "the spectacle of [[transvestism]]" and that the film as a whole was "a tale of passing".<ref>{{cite journal|last=Aaron|first=Michele| title=The ''Boys Don't Cry'' Debate: Pass/Fail|journal=[[Screen (journal)|Screen]]|volume=42|issue=1|pages=92–96|year=2001|doi=10.1093/screen/42.1.92}}</ref>

Jennifer Esposito wrote that "We watch onscreen as Brandon binds his breasts, packs a [[dildo]], fixes his hair in a mirror. His masculinity is carefully scripted. John and Tom…are never shown preparing for masculinity. They are already masculine."<ref>{{cite journal|last=Esposito|first=Jennifer|title=The Performance of White Masculinity in 'Boys Don't Cry': Identity, Desire, (Mis)Recognition|journal=[[Cultural Studies ↔ Critical Methodologies]]|volume=3|issue=2|pages=229–241|year=2003|doi=10.1177/1532708603003002007|s2cid=145332933}}</ref> Melissa Rigney argued that the film defied traditional portrayals of transgender characters by not confining Brandon to certain [[stereotypes]]. "On the surface, ''Boys Don't Cry'' appears to hold the potential of rendering gender in excess: the figure of Brandon Teena can be read variously as butch, male, lesbian, transgender, transsexual, and heterosexual. […] Although female masculinity comes to the forefront in this film, I argue that the film attempts to subsume the transgressive potential of the gender outlaw within a lesbian framework and narrative, one that reduces and, ultimately, nullifies Brandon's gender and sexual excess."<ref>{{cite journal|last=Rigney|first=Melissa|title=Brandon Goes to Hollywood: 'Boys Don't Cry' and the Portrayal of the Transgender Body in Film|journal=Film Criticism|volume=28|issue=2|year=2003|pages=4–23}}</ref>

In contrast, Annabelle Wilcox opined that the film primarily reinforced the gender binary by showing that "Brandon's body is branded by such rhetoric and representation, and is assumed to be a site of 'truth' that closes the question that being transgender poses for subjectivity, gender, and sexuality." She also went on to note that many film critics either disregarded Brandon's male identity or used female pronouns when referring to him.<ref>{{cite journal|last=Wilcox|first=Annabelle|title=Branding Teena: (Mis)Representations in the Media|journal=[[Sexualities (journal)|Sexualities]]|volume=6|issue=3|year=2003|pages=407–425|doi=10.1177/136346070363009|s2cid=146731065}}</ref> Rachel Swan, writing for ''[[Film Quarterly]]'', wrote that Brandon's masculinity was often contrasted with Lana's femininity as a means of illustrating the two sides of the gender binary. In addition, she regarded John and Tom's rape of Brandon as an attempt to psychologically [[Castration|castrate]] him.<ref>{{cite journal|last=Swan|first=Rachel|title=Reviews: Boys Don't Cry|journal=[[Film Quarterly]]|volume=54|issue=3|year=2001|pages=47–52|doi=10.1525/fq.2001.54.3.47}}</ref>

In another piece, Halberstam compared the media portrayal of Brandon to that of [[Billy Tipton]], a jazz musician who no one knew was transgender until the post-mortem discovery that he was assigned female at birth. He wrote, "On some level Brandon's story, while cleaving to its own specificity, needs to remain an open narrative—not a stable narrative of FTM transsexual identity nor a singular tale of queer bashing, not a cautionary fable about the violence of rural America nor an advertisement for urban organizations of queer community; like the narrative of Billy Tipton, Brandon's story permits a dream of transformation."<ref name="Halberstam3">{{cite journal|last=Halberstam|first=Jack|title=Telling Tales: Brandon Teena, Billy Tipton, and Transgender Biography|journal=Auto/Biography|volume=15|issue=1|pages=62–81|doi=10.1080/08989575.2000.10815235|year=2000|s2cid=161915460}}</ref> Christine Dando argued that "masculinity is associated with outside and femininity with interior spaces."<ref name="Dando" />

===Social class and race===
Lisa Henderson commented on the intersection between [[social class]] and gender in the film, particularly Brandon's [[working-class]] status: "My reading of ''Boys'' [''Don't Cry''] through the lens of class representation is not born of a univocal search for so-called positive images, but I do recoil at what appears to me to be a new instalment in a long history of popular images of working-class pathology. […] But that is not the whole story. Within this universe of feeling and reaction structured by lack and tinted blue by country lyrics and a protective and threatening night-time light, characters imbricate gender and class through their longings for love, acceptance and a better life."<ref>{{cite journal|last=Henderson|first=Lisa|title=The Class Character of ''Boys Don't Cry''|journal=[[Screen (journal)|Screen]]|volume=42|issue=3|pages=299–303|year=2001|doi=10.1093/screen/42.3.299}}</ref>

Jennifer Devere Brody commented on the film's exclusion of Philip DeVine, a [[disability|disabled]] [[African-American]] man who was another victim of the shooting. "Perhaps one can only speculate about the motivations behind this decision. But the effects are familiar ones in the history of racist representations. The erasure of DeVine from the narrative places the white female bodies as the only true victims of crime; and the film's inability to show DeVine as violated rather than violator perpetuates the myth of the black man as always already a perpetrator of crime."<ref>{{cite journal|last=Brody|first=Jennifer Devere|title=Boyz Do Cry: Screening History's White Lies|journal=[[Screen (journal)|Screen]]|volume=43|issue=1|pages=91–96|year=2002|doi=10.1093/screen/43.1.91}}</ref> Regarding DeVine, Halberstam wrote, "Peirce perhaps thought that her film, already running close to two hours, could not handle another subplot, but the story of Philip DeVine is important and it is a crucial part of the drama of gender, race, sexuality, and class that was enacted in the heartland. Race is not incidental to this narrative of mostly white, Midwestern small towns and by omitting DeVine's story from ''Boys Don't Cry'', Peirce contributes to the detachment of transgender narratives from narratives about race, consigning the memory of DeVine to oblivion."<ref name="Halberstam3" />

===Culture of the Midwestern United States===
[[File:Aerial View of Falls City, Nebraska 9-2-2013.JPG|thumb|upright=1.2|alt=An aerial view of Falls City, Nebraska, in 2013; this was the city in which the real-life events surrounding Teena's murder took place.|The film's portrayal of [[Falls City, Nebraska]], as well as the [[Great Plains]] generally, provoked discussion among commentators.]]
Several authors commented on the possible impact that the film's setting of Falls City, Nebraska, located in the Midwestern United States, could have had on the film's plot. Maslin called ''Boys Don't Cry'' a tale of a trapped, small town character's search for life beyond the rural existence and the high price he pays for his view of the [[American Dream]].<ref name=Maslin /> Regarding the film's portrayal of Nebraska, Halberstam wrote, "The landscape of Nebraska then serves as a contested site upon which multiple narratives unfold, narratives indeed which refuse to collapse into simply one story. Some of these narratives are narratives of hate, some of desire; others tell of ignorance and brutality; still others of isolation and fear; some allow violence and ignorant prejudices to become the essence of white poor rural identity; still others provoke questions about the deployment of whiteness and the regulation of violence."<ref name="Halberstam3" />

Christina Dando wrote that the typical portrayal of the Midwest as a "frontier" area did not come through in the film until the setting switched from Lincoln to Falls City: "The flat landscape, the spacious sky, the home, evoke two different Plains time periods familiar to many Americans through historic photographs: the early settlement process…and 1930s [[Farm Security Administration]] photographs. It is virtually timeless. There is also a sense of both place and placelessness. While the landscape is distinctively Plains, it could be described as nowhere."<ref name="Dando">{{cite journal|last=Dando|first=Christina|title=Range Wars: The Plains Frontier of 'Boys Don't Cry'|journal=Journal of Cultural Geography|volume=23|issue=1|pages=91–113|year=2005|doi=10.1080/08873630509478233|s2cid=144016376}}</ref>

She went on to argue that the setting is not only conveyed visually, but also through the characters' homes. "While there is no trailer park in Falls City, Brandon's community there occupies the margin: Candace and Lana's homes appear to be on the outskirts of town, or even outside of town. There are no complete families, only the family that that has been created. The men appear to have no homes, relationally or physically: none are shown to have a family.<ref name="Dando" /> Speaking about the film's cinematography and the relation to its themes:
{{blockquote|The Plains frontier landscape as it is constructed in ''Boys Don't Cry'' is dark, literally and figuratively. Most of the scenes are set at night, utilizing night Plains skies with time-lapse clouds, heightening the isolation. Film frames of placeless and timeless. The community also is dark. It is marginal, just managing to get along, and in the end deadly. While the classic Western dichotomy of men associated with exteriors and women with interiors is apparent, so too is Brandon's border-crossing. He appears to be able to easily handle both landscapes, yet belongs to neither.<ref name="Dando" />
}}

Dando compared the film to other tragic books and films that have been set on the Great Plains, including ''[[My Ántonia]]'', ''[[Giants in the Earth (novel)|Giants in the Earth]]'', ''[[The Grapes of Wrath]]'', ''[[In Cold Blood]]'', and ''[[Badlands (film)|Badlands]]'', writing that unlike the other works, "Brandon is [a] character who truly crosses frontiers."<ref name="Dando" />

Writing for ''[[The Brooklyn Rail]]'' in 2025, Charles Switzer wrote, "Nebraska’s Falls City becomes a character as the myopic brains of John (Peter Sarsgaard) and Tom (Brendan Sexton III), the two ex-convicts who befriend and later brutalize Brandon, and even Lana’s mother, Linda (Jeannetta Arnette), are allowed to fester in its near-nomadic desolation. It is a land filled with shift work, unerotic procreation, substance abuse, and Jesus chic,"<ref>{{Cite web |last=Switzer |first=Charles |date=2 September 2025 |title=90s Queer Cinema – Memory, grief, and the 1990s screen haunt another queer cinema. |url=https://brooklynrail.org/2025/09/film/90s-queer-cinema/ |access-date=26 October 2025 |website=The Brooklyn Rail}}</ref>

==Release and reception==

===Premiere and commercial performance===
''Boys Don't Cry'' aired in Canada at the [[Toronto International Film Festival]] (TIFF) in September 1999.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://business.highbeam.com/2012/article-1G1-55716682/boys-dont-cry |title='Boys Don't Cry' |work=[[The Hollywood Reporter]] |last=McGavin |first=Patrick Z. |url-access=subscription  |date=September 3, 1999 |access-date=August 17, 2015 |url-status=usurped |via=[[HighBeam Research]] |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151117131610/https://business.highbeam.com/2012/article-1G1-55716682/boys-dont-cry |archive-date=November 17, 2015  }}</ref> It premiered in the U.S. at the [[New York Film Festival]] on October 8, 1999, to critical acclaim.<ref name="Maslin" /> It was shown at the Reel Affirmations International Gay and Lesbian Film Festival in early October, where it won further praise and appeared at the [[Venice International Film Festival]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.moviemaker.com/blog/item/boys_dont_cry/|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071014024815/http://www.moviemaker.com/blog/item/boys_dont_cry/|date=October 1, 2007|archive-date=October 14, 2007|title=Boys Don't Cry|work=[[MovieMaker]]|last=Fritz|first=Daniel|access-date=June 15, 2015}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.brown.edu/campus-life/events/tedx/brad-simpson |title=Brad Simpson |work=[[Brown University]] |access-date=October 18, 2015 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151117020500/http://www.brown.edu/campus-life/events/tedx/brad-simpson |archive-date=November 17, 2015}}</ref> ''Boys Don't Cry'' was given a special screening in snippets at the [[Sundance Film Festival]]. At that time, the film was still called ''Take It Like a Man''.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.theguardian.com/film/1999/jan/31/sundancefilmfestival1999.festivals |title=Courting the New Sun Kings |work=[[The Guardian]] |last=Forrest |first=Emma |date=January 31, 1999 |access-date=April 26, 2015 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150613150723/http://www.theguardian.com/film/1999/jan/31/sundancefilmfestival1999.festivals |archive-date=June 13, 2015}}</ref> The film received a limited release theatrically on October 22, 1999, in the U.S.,<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.dove.org/review/2420-boys-dont-cry/ |title=Boys Don't Cry |work=[[The Dove Foundation]] |access-date=April 26, 2015 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150613141013/http://www.dove.org/review/2420-boys-dont-cry/ |archive-date=June 13, 2015}}</ref> where it was distributed by Fox Searchlight Pictures, a subsidiary of [[Twentieth Century Fox]] that specializes in independent films.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.foxsearchlight.com/post/2710/itunes-movie-of-the-week-boys-dont-cry-starring-hilary-swank-1999/ |title=iTunes Movie Of the Week: Boys Don't Cry, Starring Hilary Swank (1999) |work=Fox Searchlight Pictures |last=Cook |first=Cameron |date=July 21, 2010 |access-date=April 26, 2015 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150614160312/http://www.foxsearchlight.com/post/2710/itunes-movie-of-the-week-boys-dont-cry-starring-hilary-swank-1999/ |archive-date=June 14, 2015}}</ref> Initially, many viewers complained via email to Peirce that the film was not being shown near them, as the film was only being shown on 25 screens across the country. However, this number increased to nearly 200 by March 2000.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-2000-mar-08-ca-6468-story.html |title='Boys' Is Proving to Be a Hard Sell |work=[[Los Angeles Times]] |last=Munoz |first=Lorenza |date=March 8, 2000 |access-date=June 16, 2015 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150623113718/http://articles.latimes.com/2000/mar/08/entertainment/ca-6468 |archive-date=June 23, 2015}}</ref> The film grossed $73,720 in its opening week. By December 5, the film had grossed in excess of $2 million. By May 2000, it had a U.S. total gross of $11,540,607—more than three times its production budget.<ref name="mojo">{{cite web|url=https://www.boxofficemojo.com/movies/?id=boysdontcry.htm |title=Boys Don't Cry (1999) |work=[[Box Office Mojo]] |access-date=April 26, 2015 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150326091256/http://boxofficemojo.com/movies/?id=boysdontcry.htm |archive-date=March 26, 2015}}</ref> Internationally, the film was released on March 2, 2000, in Australia<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.urbancinefile.com.au/home/view.asp?Article_ID=3284&p=y |title=Boys Don't Cry |work=Urban Cinefile |access-date=April 26, 2015 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150613171439/http://www.urbancinefile.com.au/home/view.asp?Article_ID=3284&p=y |archive-date=June 13, 2015}}</ref> and on April 9, 2000, in the United Kingdom.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.theguardian.com/film/News_Story/Critic_Review/Observer_review/0,4267,157822,00.html |title=Review: Boys Don't Cry |work=[[The Guardian]] |last=French |first=Philip |date=April 9, 2000 |access-date=July 27, 2015 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151117022554/http://www.theguardian.com/film/News_Story/Critic_Review/Observer_review/0%2C4267%2C157822%2C00.html |archive-date=November 17, 2015}}</ref>

===Critical response===
Critics lauded ''Boys Don't Cry'' upon its release, with many calling it one of the best films of 1999.<ref name=Tatara /><ref name=NationalBoardofReview /><ref name=Wilmington /><ref name=AtlantaJournal /><ref name=filmsite /> Review aggregator [[Rotten Tomatoes]] reports 91% of 85 professional critics gave the film a positive review, with an average rating of 7.90/10; the site's consensus states, "Harrowing yet stirring, ''Boys Don't Cry'' powerfully commemorates the life -- and brutally unjust death -- of transgender teen Brandon Teena".<ref name="Rotten Tomatoes" /> Another review aggregator, [[Metacritic]], gave the film an 86 out of 100 based on 33 reviews, indicating "universal acclaim".<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.metacritic.com/movie/boys-dont-cry |title=Boys Don't Cry Review |work=[[Metacritic]] |access-date=June 15, 2021 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150402014008/http://www.metacritic.com/movie/boys-dont-cry |archive-date=April 2, 2015}}</ref> One reviewer said the film was a "critical knockout".<ref name=Sragow />

Critics often praised the performances by Swank and Sevigny; [[Peter Travers]] said the pair "give performances that burn in the memory",<ref>{{cite magazine|title=Boys Don't Cry |magazine=Rolling Stone |date=October 23, 1999 |url=https://www.rollingstone.com/movies/reviews/boys-dont-cry-19991022 |access-date=September 24, 2014 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141009182039/http://www.rollingstone.com/movies/reviews/boys-dont-cry-19991022 |archive-date=October 9, 2014}}</ref> and The Film Stage termed Swank's performance "one of the greatest" Best Actress Oscar-winning performances.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://thefilmstage.com/features/is-annette-bening-really-overdue-for-an-oscar/ |title=Is Annette Bening Really Overdue for an Oscar? |work=The Film Stage |date=January 4, 2011 |access-date=April 26, 2015 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150616095549/http://thefilmstage.com/features/is-annette-bening-really-overdue-for-an-oscar/ |archive-date=June 16, 2015}}</ref> Peter Stack of the ''[[San Francisco Chronicle]]'' lauded the lead acting performances of Swank, Sevigny, Saarsgard, and Sexton III, writing, "It may be the best-acted film of the year".<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.sfgate.com/movies/article/Heartland-Tragedy-in-Boys-Swank-mesmerizing-2763200.php |title=Heartland Tragedy in 'Boys' / Swank Mesmerizing as Troubled Teen |work=[[San Francisco Chronicle]] |last=Stack |first=Peter |date=April 21, 2000 |access-date=April 27, 2015 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160305040214/http://www.sfgate.com/movies/article/Heartland-Tragedy-in-Boys-Swank-mesmerizing-2763200.php |archive-date=March 5, 2016}}</ref> Online film reviewer [[James Berardinelli]] gave the film three and a half stars out of four; he highlighted the performances of Swank and Sevigny as the film's greatest success and likened the film's intensity to that of a train wreck. Berardinelli wrote that Swank "gives the performance of her career" and that "Sevigny's performance is more conventional than Swank's, but no less effective. She provides the counterbalance to the tide of hatred that drowns the last act of the film."<ref name="Berardinelli" /> [[Emanuel Levy]] of ''[[Variety (magazine)|Variety]]'' called the acting "flawless" and concluded that the "stunningly accomplished" and "candid" film could be "seen as a ''Rebel Without a Cause'' for these culturally diverse and complex times, with the two misfits enacting a version of the James Dean—Natalie Wood romance with utmost conviction, searching, like their '50s counterparts, for love, self-worth and a place to call home".<ref name="Levy" /> [[Stephen Hunter]] of ''[[The Washington Post]]'' said the performances are of such "luminous humanity that they break your heart".<ref name=WashingtonPost>{{cite news|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/wp-srv/style/movies/reviews/boysdontcryhunter.htm |title='Boys Don't Cry' |newspaper=[[The Washington Post]] |last=Hunter |first=Stephen |date=October 22, 1999 |access-date=April 27, 2015 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150613102854/http://www.washingtonpost.com/wp-srv/style/movies/reviews/boysdontcryhunter.htm |archive-date=June 13, 2015}}</ref> ''Premiere'' listed Swank's performance as one of the "100 Greatest Performances of All Time".<ref name=Premiere2 /> Owen Gleiberman of ''[[Entertainment Weekly]]'' called Swank a "revelation" and wrote, "by the end, her Brandon/Teena is beyond male or female. It's as if we were simply glimpsing the character's soul, in all its yearning and conflicted beauty."<ref name=Gleiberman />

Other reviewers were positive towards the way ''Boys Don't Cry'' portrayed its subject matter. [[Roger Ebert]] of the ''[[Chicago Sun-Times]]'' listed ''Boys Don't Cry'' as one of the five best films of 1999, saying, "This could have been a clinical movie of the week, but instead it's a sad song about a free spirit who tried to fly a little too close to the flame".<ref name=Ebert /> Janet Maslin of ''[[The New York Times]]'' said the film was "stunning" and gave it four stars out of four stars. Maslin said, "unlike most films about mind-numbing tragedy, this one manages to be full of hope".<ref name=Maslin /> [[Kenneth Turan]] of the ''[[Los Angeles Times]]'' praised the lack of romanticization and dramatization of the characters, and wrote, "Peirce and Bienen and the expert cast engage us in the actuality of these rootless, hopeless, stoned-out lives without sentimentalizing or romanticizing them" and that "''Boys Don't Cry'' is an exceptional—and exceptionally disturbing film".<ref name=Turan /> Mike Clarke of ''[[USA Today]]'' commended Peirce's depth of knowledge of the case and the subject matter, writing, "Peirce seems to have researched her subject with grad-school-thesis intensity".<ref name="Rotten Tomatoes"/>

Jay Carr of ''[[The Boston Globe]]'' wrote, "''Boys Don't Cry'' not only revisits the crime, but convinces us we're being taken inside it".<ref name="Rotten Tomatoes" /> [[Stephanie Zacharek]] of ''[[Salon (website)|Salon]]'' gave a positive review, singling out the directing and acting. She wrote, "Peirce ... covers an extraordinary amount of territory, not just in terms of dealing with Brandon’s sexual-identity and self-fulfillment issues, but also in trying to understand the lives of those around him". Zacharek described Swank's performance as "a continual revelation" and Sevigny's performance as "transformative". She said, "When Brandon dies, ''Boys Don’t Cry'' reaches an emotional intensity that’s almost operatic. The saddest thing, though, is seeing Sevigny’s Lana crumpled over his corpse—the way she plays it, you know that when Brandon went, he took a part of her with him, too".<ref name="Zacharek" /> [[David Edelstein]] of ''[[Slate (magazine)|Slate]]'' was also very positive towards the film, calling it "a meditation on the irrelevance of gender." He went on to praise Swank, Sevigny, and Sarsgaard in their roles, especially Sevigny, writing that she "keeps the movie tantalizing".<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.slate.com/articles/arts/movies/1999/10/boys_do_bleed.html |title=Boys Do Bleed |work=[[Slate (magazine)|Slate]] |last=Edelstein |first=David |date=October 16, 1999 |access-date=June 13, 2015 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150615033224/http://www.slate.com/articles/arts/movies/1999/10/boys_do_bleed.html |archive-date=June 15, 2015}}</ref>

The film was not without detractors, who focused on the film's portrayal of Brandon and his actions. [[Richard Corliss]] of ''[[Time (magazine)|Time]]'' magazine was one of the film's negative reviewers; he wrote, "the film lets down the material. It's too cool: all attitude, no sizzle".<ref name="Rotten Tomatoes" /> Peter Rainer of ''[[New York Magazine]]'' compared the film unfavorably with ''Rebel Without a Cause'' (1954), calling it a "transgendered {{sic}}" version, elaborating that the film "could have used a tougher and more exploratory spirit; for Peirce, there was no cruelty, no derangement in Brandon's impostures toward the unsuspecting," the review repeatedly misgendering Brandon and negatively focusing on him being transgender and the claim that he misled people despite his girlfriend in the film accepting him for who he was.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://nymag.com/nymetro/movies/reviews/2126/ |title=In Brief: "Boys Don't Cry" |last=Rainer |first=Peter |date=January 1, 2000 |access-date=June 13, 2015 |work=[[New York (magazine)|New York]] |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150615194018/http://nymag.com/nymetro/movies/reviews/2126/ |archive-date=June 15, 2015}}</ref> In 2007, ''[[Premiere (magazine)|Premiere]]'' ranked the film on its list of "The 25 Most Dangerous Movies".<ref name=Kenny />

The film was generally well-received by the [[LGBT community]]. ''Boys Don't Cry''{{'}}s release came a year after the murder of a homosexual teenager, [[Matthew Shepard]],<ref name=DallasMN99 /> which occurred October 12, 1998. The murder sparked additional public interest in [[hate crime]] legislation in America and in Brandon Teena, and increased public interest in ''Boys Don't Cry''.<ref name="life">{{cite web |url=http://www.matthewshepard.org/home/transgender-day-of-remembrance |title=Transgender Day of Remembrance |access-date=October 9, 2010|publisher=Matthew Shepard Foundation|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140409103521/http://www.matthewshepard.org/home/transgender-day-of-remembrance|archive-date=April 9, 2014 }}</ref> Cooper wrote that ''Boys Don't Cry'' "is perhaps the only film addressing the issue of female masculinity by a self-described queer filmmaker to reach mainstream audiences and to receive critical acclaim and prestigious awards."<ref>[[#Cooper|Cooper (2004)]], p. 49</ref> However, [[Noelle Howey]], writing for ''[[Mother Jones (magazine)|Mother Jones]]'', wrote that despite the critical acclaim, relatively few critics understood what she perceived as the main point of the film—Brandon being a victim of [[trans bashing]]. Howey said, "Even a cursory glance at reviews of ''Boys Don't Cry'' reveals that while most critics admired the film, few absorbed its main point: that Brandon Teena was a biological girl who felt innately that she was a man. Most of the media instead cast Teena as a [[Yentl (film)|Yentl]] for the new millennium, rather than a victim of anti-transgender bigotry."<ref name="Howey" />

More recently, some have criticized the film's casting of a [[cisgender]] woman (Swank) for the role of a trans man (Brandon Teena), such as during a 2016 protest at a [[Reed College]] screening of the film.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2016-12-14 |title=Reed College Students Protest Visiting "Boys Don't Cry" Filmmaker Over Alleged Transphobia |url=https://www.wweek.com/arts/movies/2016/12/13/reed-college-students-protest-visiting-boys-dont-cry-filmmaker-over-alleged-transphobia/ |access-date=2026-04-25 |website=Willamette Week |language=en}}</ref> In 2019, Swank stated in an interview for [[IndieWire]]: "I’m happy that times are evolving and changing and that people are getting the opportunity to tell their own stories.”<ref>{{Cite web |last=Dry |first=Jude |date=2019-05-16 |title=Hilary Swank Opens Up About ‘Boys Don’t Cry’ Backlash, and Examines Its Legacy |url=https://www.indiewire.com/features/general/hilary-swank-boys-dont-cry-backlash-lgbt-film-transgender-1202142066/ |access-date=2026-04-25 |website=IndieWire |language=en-US}}</ref>

====Factual accuracy====
The accuracy of ''Boys Don't Cry'' was disputed by real-life people involved in the murder. The real Lana Tisdel declared her dislike for the film; she said Brandon never proposed to her and that when she discovered Brandon was transgender, she ended the relationship. Tisdel disliked the way she was portrayed in the film, and called the film the "second murder of Brandon Teena".<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.eonline.com/news/38886/crying-foul-over-boys-don-t-cry |title=Crying Foul Over 'Boys Don't Cry' |publisher=[[E!]] |last=Farache |first=Emily |date=October 21, 1999 |access-date=April 27, 2015 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150615004952/http://www.eonline.com/news/38886/crying-foul-over-boys-don-t-cry |archive-date=June 15, 2015}}</ref> Before the film's theatrical release, Lana Tisdel sued the film's producers, claiming that the film depicted her as "lazy, white trash and a skanky snake"<ref name="Hawker" /> and that her family and friends had come to see her as "a lesbian who did nothing to stop a murder".<ref name="Peirce Times">{{cite web|url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-2000-feb-07-ca-61809-story.html |title=A Filmmaker Fictionalizes to Get at Difficult Truths |work=[[Los Angeles Times]] |last=Harrison |first=Eric |date=February 7, 2000 |access-date=June 16, 2015 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150713181744/http://articles.latimes.com/2000/feb/07/entertainment/ca-61809 |archive-date=July 13, 2015}}</ref> Tisdel settled her lawsuit against Fox Searchlight for an undisclosed sum.<ref name=Hawker /><ref name=ChicagoST /> Sarah Nissen, cousin of murderer Marvin Nissen, was also critical of the film, saying, "There's none of it that's right. It was just weird."<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.historyvshollywood.com/reelfaces/boysdontcry.php |title=Teena Brandon / Brandon Teena |publisher=[[History vs. Hollywood]] |access-date=May 1, 2015 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150219064107/http://www.historyvshollywood.com/reelfaces/boysdontcry.php |archive-date=February 19, 2015}}</ref> Leslie Tisdel, Lana's sister, called the film "a lie of a movie".<ref name="Peirce Times" />

Lana Tisdel's potential involvement in the rape and murder of Brandon Teena was also highlighted. Various people involved in the case, particularly Brandon's family, have alleged that Tisdel was somehow involved with the murders, or had at least set them up in an act of vengeance. Perhaps the most notable admission about Tisdel's motives came from Tom Nissen, who infamously confessed that Tisdel was present at the time of the murders in the car and had even tried knocking on the door of the farmhouse where Brandon, Lambert, and DeVine were staying.<ref>{{cite book|last1=Jones|first1=Aphrodite|title=All She Wanted|url=https://archive.org/details/allshewanted00jone|url-access=registration|date=1996 |publisher=Pocket Books |isbn=978-0671023881 |page=[https://archive.org/details/allshewanted00jone/page/254 254] |edition=Reprint }}</ref>

===Awards and nominations===
{{main|List of accolades received by Boys Don't Cry (film)}}

The film won a variety of awards, most of which went to Swank for her performance. Swank won a [[Academy Award for Best Actress|Best Actress Oscar]] while Sevigny received a nomination in the category of [[Academy Award for Best Supporting Actress|Best Supporting Actress]].<ref name=oscars /> From the [[Hollywood Foreign Press]], the film received two [[Golden Globe]] nominations in the same two categories (Best Actress, Best Supporting Actress) for Swank and Sevigny, winning Best Actress. Swank and Sevigny both received Best Actress Awards from the [[New York Film Critics Circle]], the [[Chicago Film Critics Association Awards]] and an [[Independent Spirit Award]]. The film won three awards at the [[Boston Society of Film Critics Awards]]: Best Actress (Swank), Best Supporting Actress (Sevigny) and Best Director (Peirce). Swank and Sevigny won [[Satellite Award]]s for their performances, and the film was nominated in two categories; Best Picture (Drama) and Best Director. It was named one of the best films of the year by the [[National Board of Review of Motion Pictures]].<ref name=NationalBoardofReview />

The family of Brandon Teena criticized Swank for her repeated use of the male gender pronoun "he" in her Oscar acceptance speech. Teena's mother JoAnn Brandon said her child's transgender identity was a defense mechanism that was developed in response to childhood sexual abuse, rather than being an expression of Teena's gendered sense of self. JoAnn said, "She pretended she was a man so no other man could touch her".<ref name=EntertainmentWeekly1 /><ref name="TheGuardian">{{cite news |title=Nebraska and India slam Oscar injustices |url=https://www.theguardian.com/film/2000/mar/29/oscars2000.oscars |access-date=10 November 2023 |work=The Guardian |date=March 29, 2000 |archive-date=March 8, 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210308172500/https://www.theguardian.com/film/2000/mar/29/oscars2000.oscars |url-status=live }}</ref> Despite the criticism, Kevin O'Keeffe, writing for ''[[Out (magazine)|Out]]'', defended Swank's acceptance speech; he said, "Swank deserves a place in the great acceptance speech canon for being bold, not only as an actress, but as an award winner".<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.out.com/entertainment/popnography/2014/02/27/lgbt-focused-oscar-acceptance-speeches |title=4 LGBT-Focused Oscar Acceptance Speeches |work=[[Out (magazine)|Out]] |last=O'Keeffe |first=Kevin |date=February 27, 2014 |access-date=May 1, 2015 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150614010641/http://www.out.com/entertainment/popnography/2014/02/27/lgbt-focused-oscar-acceptance-speeches |archive-date=June 14, 2015}}</ref>

===Rating and home media===
''Boys Don't Cry'' garnered significant attention for its graphic rape scene.<ref name=Advocate /> The film was initially assigned an [[NC-17]] rating from the [[Motion Picture Association of America]] (MPAA); the content was [[Film censorship in the United States|toned down]] for the U.S. release, where it was [[MPAA rating system#Ratings|rated R]]. Peirce was interviewed for a 2005 documentary titled ''[[This Film Is Not Yet Rated]]'', which discussed the film's problems with the MPAA, particularly the [[Censorship|censoring]] of the sex scenes.<ref name=DickFilm /> The portrayal of a double rape caused significant problems with the MPAA and had to be trimmed to avoid the NC-17 rating.<ref name=MPAA /> Both the Australian and European version are more explicit, particularly the first rape. Peirce was angry because the MPAA wanted the sex scene between Brandon and Lana removed but was satisfied with the level of brutality in the murder scene.<ref name=DickFilm /> She also claimed that one objection from the MPAA was that one scene featured an orgasm that was "too long", and rhetorically asked if anyone had ever been hurt by an orgasm that was too long. The film is rated [[18 (British Board of Film Classification)|18]] by the British Board of Film Classification.<ref name=BBFC/>

''Boys Don't Cry'' was first released on [[home video]] by [[Fox Entertainment Group|Fox Searchlight Pictures]] in September 2000 as part of a "Premiere Series", preceded by a DVD release in April 2000 in the United States and Canada.<ref name="DVD Talk">{{cite web|url=https://www.dvdtalk.com/reviews/560/boys-dont-cry/ |title=Boys Don't Cry: DVD Talk Review of the DVD Video |work=[[DVD Talk]] |last=Belerle |first=Aaron |date=April 18, 2000 |access-date=May 1, 2015 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150616014810/http://www.dvdtalk.com/reviews/560/boys-dont-cry/ |archive-date=June 16, 2015}}</ref> The DVD's special features included a commentary by Kimberly Peirce and a behind-the-scenes featurette containing interviews with Peirce, Swank and Sevigny; there was also a theatrical trailer and three television trailers.<ref name="DVD Talk" /><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.ign.com/articles/2000/04/18/boys-dont-cry |title=Boys Don't Cry |work=[[IGN]] |date=April 18, 2000 |access-date=May 1, 2015 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150614072758/http://www.ign.com/articles/2000/04/18/boys-dont-cry |archive-date=June 14, 2015}}</ref> This same edition was re-released in 2009 with different cover art.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.dvdsreleasedates.com/movies/3484/Boys-Don't-Cry-(1999).html |title=Boys Don't Cry DVD Release Date |work=DVD Release Dates |access-date=May 1, 2015 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150615093200/http://www.dvdsreleasedates.com/movies/3484/Boys-Don%27t-Cry-%281999%29.html |archive-date=June 15, 2015}}</ref> The film was released on [[Blu-ray]] on February 16, 2011, by 20th Century Fox Entertainment in conjunction with Fox Pathé Europa.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.blu-ray.com/movies/Boys-Dont-Cry-Blu-ray/17912/ |title=Boys Don't Cry Blu-ray Release Date February 16, 2011 (Selection Blu-VIP) (France) |access-date=December 2, 2010 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120324185420/http://www.blu-ray.com/movies/Boys-Dont-Cry-Blu-ray/17912/ |archive-date=March 24, 2012}}</ref>
