==Production==
Before the publication of the novel, several Hollywood executives and studios declined to create a film based on it, including [[Louis B. Mayer]] and [[Irving Thalberg]] at [[Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer]] (MGM), [[Pandro S. Berman]] at [[RKO Radio Pictures]], and [[David O. Selznick]] of [[Selznick International Pictures]]. [[Jack L. Warner]] of [[Warner Bros.]] considered purchasing the rights after reading the synopsis, but his biggest star [[Bette Davis]] was not interested at the time, and [[Darryl F. Zanuck]] of [[20th Century-Fox]] had not offered enough money. However, Selznick changed his mind after his story editor [[Kay B. Barrett|Kay Brown]] and business partner [[John Hay Whitney]] urged him to purchase the film rights. In July 1936—a month after it was published—Selznick bought the rights from [[Margaret Mitchell]] for $50,000.<ref name="Friedrich">{{cite book |last=Friedrich |first=Otto |title=City of Nets: A Portrait of Hollywood in the 1940s |year=1986 |publisher=[[University of California Press]] |location=Berkeley / Los Angeles |isbn=978-0-520-20949-7 |pages=[https://archive.org/details/cityofnetsportra00frie/page/17 17]–21 |url=https://archive.org/details/cityofnetsportra00frie/page/17 |author-link=Otto Friedrich}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=The Book Purchase |work=Gone with the Wind Online Exhibit |location=[[University of Texas at Austin]] |publisher=[[Harry Ransom Center]] |url=http://www.hrc.utexas.edu/exhibitions/web/gwtw/book |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140602124241/http://www.hrc.utexas.edu/exhibitions/web/gwtw/book |archive-date=June 2, 2014}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=The Search for Scarlett: Chronology |work=Gone with the Wind Online Exhibit |location=[[University of Texas at Austin]] |publisher=[[Harry Ransom Center]] |url=http://www.hrc.utexas.edu/exhibitions/web/gwtw/scarlett/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140602124241/http://www.hrc.utexas.edu/exhibitions/web/gwtw/scarlett |archive-date=June 2, 2014}}</ref>

===Casting===
[[File:Clark Gable and Vivien Leigh - Wind.jpg|thumb|upright=1|Publicity photo of Clark Gable and Vivien Leigh as Rhett and Scarlett]]
The casting of the two lead roles became a complex, two-year endeavor. For the role of Rhett Butler, Selznick from the start wanted Clark Gable, but Gable was under contract to MGM, which never loaned him to other studios.<ref name="Friedrich" /> [[Gary Cooper]] was considered, but [[Samuel Goldwyn]]—to whom Cooper was under contract—refused to loan him out.<ref name="Lambert">{{cite news |last=Lambert |first=Gavin |author-link=Gavin Lambert |title=The Making of Gone with the Wind, Part I |url=https://www.theatlantic.com/magazine/archive/1973/02/the-making-of-gone-with-the-wind-part-i/306455/?single_page=true |url-status=live |work=[[The Atlantic Monthly]] |date=February 1973 |access-date=March 7, 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130521071143/http://www.theatlantic.com/magazine/archive/1973/02/the-making-of-gone-with-the-wind-part-i/306455/?single_page=true |archive-date=May 21, 2013}}</ref> Warner offered a package of Bette Davis, [[Errol Flynn]], and [[Olivia de Havilland]] for lead roles in return for the distribution rights,<ref name="tcm notes">{{cite web |title=Gone with the Wind (1939) – Notes |work=TCM database |publisher=[[Turner Classic Movies]] |url=https://www.tcm.com/tcmdb/title/414427/gone-with-the-wind#notes |access-date=January 16, 2013 |archive-date=March 10, 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160310052138/http://www.tcm.com/tcmdb/title/414427/Gone-With-the-Wind/notes.html |url-status=dead}}</ref> but Davis refused to star opposite Flynn as Rhett Butler.<ref name="Atlantic" /> By this time, Selznick was determined to get Gable, and in August 1938 he eventually struck a deal with his father-in-law, MGM chief Louis B. Mayer, in which MGM agreed to provide Gable and $1.25{{nbsp}}million for half of the production budget, and would distribute the film. In return, Selznick would have to pay Gable's weekly salary and half the profits would go to MGM.<ref name="Friedrich" /><ref name="Lambert" />

The arrangement to release through MGM meant delaying the start of production until the end of 1938, when Selznick's current distribution deal with [[United Artists]] concluded.<ref name="Lambert" /> Selznick used the delay to revise the script and, more importantly, build publicity through their endeavors to cast [[Scarlett O'Hara#In the 1939 film|the role of Scarlett]]. Selznick began a nationwide [[casting call]] interviewing 1,400 unknowns. The effort cost $100,000 and proved useless for the main objective of casting the role, but created "priceless" publicity.<ref name="Friedrich" /> Early frontrunners included [[Miriam Hopkins]] and [[Tallulah Bankhead]], who were regarded as possibilities by Selznick prior to the purchase of the film rights; [[Joan Crawford]], who was signed to MGM, was also considered as a potential pairing with Gable. After the deal was struck with MGM, Selznick held discussions with [[Norma Shearer]]—who was one of MGM's top female stars at the time—but she withdrew herself from consideration after negative feedback from movie fans. [[Katharine Hepburn]] lobbied hard for the role with the support of her friend, George Cukor, who had been hired to direct, but she was vetoed by Selznick, who felt she was not right for the part.<ref name="Lambert" /><ref name="tcm notes" /><ref name="tcm articles">{{cite web |last1=Miller |first1=Frank |last2=Stafford |first2=Jeff |title=Gone with the Wind (1939) – Articles |work=TCM database |publisher=[[Turner Classic Movies]] |url=https://www.tcm.com/tcmdb/title/414427/gone-with-the-wind#articles-reviews |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130926003430/http://www.tcm.com/tcmdb/title/414427/Gone-With-the-Wind/articles.html|archive-date=September 26, 2013}}</ref>

Many actresses, both known and unknown, were considered, but only thirty, in addition to the eventual choice, Vivien Leigh, were actually tested for the role, including Ardis Ankerson ([[Brenda Marshall]]), [[Jean Arthur]], Tallulah Bankhead, [[Diana Barrymore]], [[Joan Bennett]], [[Nancy Coleman]], [[Frances Dee]], Terry Ray ([[Ellen Drew]]), [[Paulette Goddard]], Edythe Marrenner ([[Susan Hayward]]), [[Anita Louise]], [[Haila Stoddard]], [[Margaret Tallichet]], [[Lana Turner]], and [[Linda Watkins]].<ref>{{cite web |title=The Search for Scarlett: Girls Tested for the Role of Scarlett |work=Gone with the Wind Online Exhibit |location=[[University of Texas at Austin]] |publisher=[[Harry Ransom Center]] |url=http://www.hrc.utexas.edu/exhibitions/web/gwtw/scarlett/girltest.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140105182706/http://www.hrc.utexas.edu/exhibitions/web/gwtw/scarlett/girltest.html |archive-date=January 5, 2014}}</ref> Although Margaret Mitchell refused to publicly name her choice, the actress who came closest to winning her approval was Miriam Hopkins, whom Mitchell felt was just the right type of actress to play Scarlett as written in the book. However, Hopkins was in her mid-thirties at the time and was considered too old for the part.<ref name="Lambert" /><ref name="tcm notes" /><ref name="tcm articles" /> Four actresses, including Jean Arthur and Joan Bennett, were still under consideration by December 1938; however, only two finalists, Paulette Goddard, and Vivien Leigh, were tested in [[Technicolor]], both on December 20.<ref>{{cite book |first=Ronald |last=Haver |author-link=Ronald Haver |title=David O. Selznick's Hollywood |location=New York |publisher=[[Alfred A. Knopf]] |year=1980 |isbn=978-0-394-42595-5}}</ref> Goddard almost won the role, but controversy over her marriage to [[Charlie Chaplin]] caused Selznick to change his mind.<ref name="Friedrich" />

Selznick had been quietly considering Vivien Leigh, a young English actress who was still little known in America, for the role of Scarlett since February 1938 when Selznick saw her in ''[[Fire Over England]]'' and ''[[A Yank at Oxford]]''. Leigh's American agent was the London representative of the [[Myron Selznick]] talent agency (headed by David Selznick's brother, one of the owners of Selznick International), and she had requested in February that her name be submitted for consideration as Scarlett. By the summer of 1938, the Selznicks were negotiating with [[Alexander Korda]], to whom Leigh was under contract, for her services later that year.<ref>{{cite book |first=William |last=Pratt |title=Scarlett Fever |location=New York |publisher=[[Macmillan Publishers (United States)|Macmillan Publishers]] |year=1977 |pages=73–74, 81–83 |isbn=978-0-02-598560-5}}</ref> Selznick's brother arranged for them to meet for the first time on the night of December 10, 1938, when the burning of Atlanta was filmed. In a letter to his wife two days later, Selznick admitted that Leigh was "the Scarlett dark horse", and after a series of screen tests, her casting was announced on January 13, 1939.<ref>{{cite book |first=Marianne |last=Walker |title=Margaret Mitchell and John Marsh: The Love Story Behind Gone With the Wind |year=2011 |publisher=Peachtree Publishers |isbn=978-1-56145-617-8 |pages=[https://books.google.com/books?id=quf-7VPsZWEC&pg=PA405 405–406]}}</ref> Just before the shooting, Selznick informed newspaper columnist [[Ed Sullivan]]: "Scarlett O'Hara's parents were French and Irish. Identically, Miss Leigh's parents are French and Irish."<ref>{{cite web |last=Selznick |first=David O. |title=The Search for Scarlett: Vivien Leigh – Letter from David O. Selznick to Ed Sullivan |date=January 7, 1939 |work=Gone with the Wind Online Exhibit |location=[[University of Texas at Austin]] |publisher=[[Harry Ransom Center]] |url=http://www.hrc.utexas.edu/exhibitions/web/gwtw/scarlett/sullivan.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131028095558/http://www.hrc.utexas.edu/exhibitions/web/gwtw/scarlett/sullivan.html |archive-date=October 28, 2013}}</ref>

A pressing issue for Selznick throughout casting was Hollywood's persistent failure to accurately portray [[Southern American English|Southern accents]]. The studio believed that if the accent was not accurately depicted, it could prove detrimental to the success. Selznick hired [[Susan Myrick]] (an expert on Southern speech, manners, and customs recommended to him by Mitchell) and Will A. Price to coach the actors on speaking with a [[Southern drawl]]. Mitchell was complimentary about the vocal work of the cast, noting the lack of criticism when the film came out.<ref name="ut-audtin-cella-gwtw">{{cite web |last1=Cella |first1=Claire |title=Fan Mail: Producing Gone With the Wind |url=https://norman.hrc.utexas.edu/gwtw/?cat=Protests&story=6 |publisher=[[Harry Ransom Center]] |access-date=June 22, 2020 |archive-date=August 1, 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200801060709/https://norman.hrc.utexas.edu/gwtw/?cat=Protests&story=6 |url-status=live }}</ref><ref name="mt-crenshaw">{{cite web |last1=Crenshaw |first1=Wayne |title=Without her, the 'Gone With the Wind' film might not have sounded as Southern |url=https://www.macon.com/living/article114217348.html |work=[[The Macon Telegraph]] |access-date=September 28, 2019 |date=November 11, 2016 |archive-date=July 26, 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200726023103/https://www.macon.com/living/article114217348.html |url-status=live }}</ref>

===Screenplay===
Of the original screenplay writer, [[Sidney Howard]], film historian Joanne Yeck writes: "[R]educing the intricacies of ''Gone with the Wind''{{'}}s epic dimensions was a herculean task ... and Howard's first submission was far too long, and would have required at least six hours of film; ... [producer] Selznick wanted Howard to remain on the set to make revisions ... but Howard refused to leave New England [and] as a result, revisions were handled by a host of local writers".<ref name="Yeck">{{cite encyclopedia |last=Yeck |first=Joanne |title=American Screenwriters |encyclopedia=[[Dictionary of Literary Biography]] |year=1984 |publisher=[[Gale (publisher)|Gale]]}}</ref> Selznick dismissed director George Cukor three weeks into filming and sought out Victor Fleming, who was directing ''[[The Wizard of Oz]]'' at the time. Fleming was dissatisfied with the script, so Selznick brought in the screenwriter [[Ben Hecht]] to rewrite the entire screenplay within five days. Hecht returned to Howard's original draft and, by the end of the week, had succeeded in revising the entire first half of the script. Selznick undertook to rewrite the second half himself but fell behind schedule, so Howard returned to work on the script for one week, reworking several key scenes in part two.<ref name="Bartel">{{cite book |first=Pauline |last=Bartel |title=The Complete Gone with the Wind Trivia Book: The Movie and More |year=1989 |publisher=[[Taylor Trade Publishing]] |isbn=978-0-87833-619-7 |pages=[https://books.google.com/books?id=ZJLb5GC35E8C&pg=PA64 64]–[https://books.google.com/books?id=DJUYAcJN3jgC&pg=PA69 69], [https://books.google.com/books?id=ZJLb5GC35E8C&pg=PA127 127] & [https://books.google.com/books?id=ZJLb5GC35E8C&pg=PA161 161]–[https://books.google.com/books?id=DJUYAcJN3jgC&pg=PA172 172] |url=https://archive.org/details/completegonewith00bart/page/64}}</ref>

[[File:DavidOSelznick.jpg|thumb|left|upright|David O. Selznick in 1940]]
"By the time of the film's release in 1939, there was some question as to who should receive screen credit", writes Yeck. "But despite the number of writers and changes, the final script was remarkably close to Howard's version. The fact that Howard's name alone appears on the credits may have been as much a gesture to his memory as his writing, for in 1939, Sidney Howard died at age 48 in a farm-tractor accident, and before the movie's premiere."<ref name="Yeck" /> Selznick, in a memo written in October 1939, discussed the writing credits: "[Y]ou can say frankly that of the comparatively small amount of material in the picture which is not from the book, most is my own personally, and the only original lines of dialog which are not my own are a few from Sidney Howard and a few from Ben Hecht and a couple more from [[John Van Druten]]. Offhand I doubt that there are ten original words of [[Oliver H. P. Garrett|[Oliver] Garrett]]'s in the whole script. As to construction, this is about eighty per cent my own, and the rest divided between [[Jo Swerling]] and Sidney Howard, with Hecht having contributed materially to the construction of one sequence."<ref name="Selznick">{{cite book |first=David O. |last=Selznick |year=1938–1939 |editor-last=Behlmer |editor-first=Rudy |title=Memo from David O. Selznick: The Creation of Gone with the Wind and Other Motion Picture Classics, as Revealed in the Producer's Private Letters, Telegrams, Memorandums, and Autobiographical Remarks |location=New York |publisher=[[Modern Library]] |publication-date=2000 |isbn=978-0-375-75531-6 |pages=179–180 & 224–225}}</ref>

According to Hecht's biographer William MacAdams, {{Blockquote|At dawn on Sunday, February 20, 1939, David Selznick ... and director Victor Fleming shook Hecht awake to inform him he was on loan from MGM and must come with them immediately and go to work on ''Gone with the Wind'', which Selznick had begun shooting five weeks before. It was costing Selznick $50,000 each day the film was on hold, waiting for a final screenplay rewrite, and time was of the essence. Hecht was in the middle of working on the film ''[[At the Circus]]'' for the [[Marx Brothers]]. Recalling the episode in a letter to screenwriter friend [[Gene Fowler]], he said he hadn't read the novel, but Selznick and director Fleming could not wait for him to read it. They acted in scenes based on Sidney Howard's original script, which needed to be rewritten in a hurry. Hecht wrote: "After each scene had been performed and discussed, I sat down at the typewriter and wrote it out. Selznick and Fleming, eager to continue with their acting, kept hurrying me. We worked in this fashion for seven days, putting in eighteen to twenty hours a day. Selznick refused to let us eat lunch, arguing that food would slow us up. He provided bananas and salted peanuts ... thus on the seventh day I had completed, unscathed, the first nine reels of the Civil War epic."<ref name="MacAdams"/>}}

MacAdams writes: "It is impossible to determine exactly how much Hecht scripted ... In the official credits filed with the [[Screen Writers Guild]], Sidney Howard was of course awarded the sole screen credit, but four other writers were appended ... Jo Swerling for contributing to the treatment, Oliver H. P. Garrett and Barbara Keon to screenplay construction, and Hecht, to dialogue ..."<ref name="MacAdams">{{cite book |last=MacAdams |first=William |title=Ben Hecht |year=1990 |publisher=[[Barricade Books]] |location=New York |isbn=978-1-56980-028-7 |pages=199–201}}</ref>

===Filming===
[[Principal photography]] began on January 26, 1939, and ended on July 1, with post-production work continuing until November 11, 1939. Director George Cukor, with whom Selznick had a long working relationship and who had spent almost two years in pre-production on ''Gone with the Wind'', was replaced after less than three weeks of shooting.<ref name="tcm notes" />{{refn|From a private letter from journalist and on-set technical advisor Susan Myrick to Margaret Mitchell in February 1939: {{blockquote|George [Cukor] finally told me all about it ... He hated [leaving the production] very much he said but he could not do otherwise. In effect he said he is an honest craftsman and he cannot do a job unless he knows it is a good job and he feels the present job is not right. For days, he told me, he has looked at the rushes and felt he was failing ... the thing did not click as it should. Gradually he became convinced that the script was the trouble ... David [Selznick], himself, thinks HE is writing the script.... And George has continually taken script from day to day, compared the [Oliver] Garrett-Selznick version with the [Sidney] Howard, groaned and tried to change some parts back to the Howard script. But he seldom could do much with the scene.... So George just told David he would not work any longer if the script was not better and he wanted the Howard script back. David told George he was a director—not an author and he (David) was the producer and the judge of what is a good script.... George said he was a director and a damn good one and he would not let his name go out over a lousy picture.... And bull-headed David said "OK get out!"<ref name=Myrick>{{cite book |first=Susan |last=Myrick |title=White Columns in Hollywood: Reports from the GWTW Sets |location=Macon, Georgia |publisher=[[Mercer University Press]] |year=1982 |pages=[https://books.google.com/books?id=ctFm2Hetkh0C&pg=PA126 126–127] |isbn=978-0-86554-044-6 |author-link=Susan Myrick}}</ref>}} Selznick had already been unhappy with Cukor, "a very expensive luxury", for not being more receptive to directing other Selznick assignments, even though Cukor had remained on salary since early 1937. In a confidential memo written in September 1938, Selznick flirted with the idea of replacing him with Victor Fleming.<ref name=Selznick/> [[Louis B. Mayer]] had been trying to have Cukor replaced with an MGM director since negotiations between the two studios began in May 1938. In December 1938, Selznick wrote to his wife about a phone call he had with Mayer: "During the same conversation, your father made another stab at getting George off of ''Gone With the Wind''."<ref>{{cite book |first=Scott |last=Eyman |title=Lion of Hollywood: The Life and Legend of Louis B. Mayer |year=2005 |publisher=[[Robson Books]] |pages=[https://books.google.com/books?id=q0ldNR7gZ1oC&pg=PA258 258–259] |isbn=978-1-86105-892-8 |author-link=Scott Eyman}}</ref>|group = nb}} Selznick and Cukor had already disagreed over the pace of filming and the script,<ref name="tcm notes" /><ref name="Myrick" /> but other explanations put Cukor's departure down to Gable's discomfort at working with him.<ref>{{cite book |first=Michelangelo |last=Capua |title=Vivien Leigh: A Biography |year=2003 |publisher=[[McFarland & Company]] |isbn=978-0-7864-1497-0 |pages=[https://books.google.com/books?id=uMdRckjUDvAC&pg=PA59 59]–61}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Levy |first=Emanuel |title=George Cukor: Master of Elegance |publisher=[[William Morrow and Company]] |year=1994 |isbn=978-0-688-11246-2 |author-link=Emanuel Levy |pages=117–118 |url=https://archive.org/details/benchtoptools0000popu/page/117/mode/1up }}</ref> Vivien Leigh and Olivia de Havilland learned of Cukor's firing on the day the Atlanta bazaar scene was filmed, and the pair went to Selznick's office in full costume and implored him to change his mind. [[Victor Fleming]], who was directing ''The Wizard of Oz'', was called in from MGM to complete the film. However, Cukor continued privately to coach Leigh and De Havilland.<ref name="Bartel" /> Another MGM director, [[Sam Wood]], worked for two weeks in May when Fleming temporarily left the production due to exhaustion. Although some of Cukor's scenes were later reshot, Selznick estimated that "three solid reels" of his work remained in the final cut. As of the end of principal photography, Cukor had undertaken eighteen days of filming, Fleming ninety-three, and Wood twenty-four.<ref name="tcm notes" />

Cinematographer [[Lee Garmes]] began the production, but on March 11, 1939—after a month of shooting footage that Selznick and his associates regarded as "too dark"—was replaced with [[Ernest Haller]], working with Technicolor cinematographer [[Ray Rennahan]]. Garmes completed the first third of the film—mostly everything prior to Melanie having the baby—but did not receive a credit.<ref>{{cite book |last=Turner |first=Adrian |title=A Celebration of Gone with the Wind |year=1989 |publisher=[[Paper Tiger Books|Dragon's World]] |page=114}}</ref>

Most of the filming was done on "[[RKO Forty Acres|the back forty]]" studio backlot of Selznick International with all the location scenes being photographed in California, mostly in [[Los Angeles County]] or neighboring [[Ventura County]].<ref>{{cite book |first=Cynthia Marylee |last=Molt |title=Gone with the Wind on Film: A Complete Reference |location=Jefferson, NC |publisher=[[McFarland & Company]] |year=1990 |pages=[https://archive.org/details/gonewithwindonfi0000molt/page/272 272–281] |isbn=978-0-89950-439-1 |url=https://archive.org/details/gonewithwindonfi0000molt/page/272 }}</ref> Tara, the fictional Southern plantation house, existed only as a plywood and papier-mâché façade built on the Selznick studio lot.<ref>{{cite book |last=Bridges |first=Herb |year=1998 |title=The Filming of Gone with the Wind |publisher=[[Mercer University Press]] |isbn=978-0-86554-621-9 |at=[https://books.google.com/books?id=ekvkZo0mAXcC&pg=PT4 PT4]}}</ref> For the burning of Atlanta, new façades were built in front of the Selznick backlot's many old abandoned sets, and Selznick himself operated the controls for the explosives that burned them down.<ref name="Friedrich" /> Sources at the time put the estimated production costs at $3.85&nbsp;million, making it the second most expensive film made up to that point, with only ''[[Ben-Hur (1925 film)|Ben-Hur]]'' (1925) having cost more.<ref name="Time (1939)">{{cite magazine |title=Cinema: G With the W |date=December 25, 1939 |magazine=[[Time (magazine)|Time]] |url=http://content.time.com/time/magazine/article/0,9171,762137,00.html |access-date=July 6, 2011 |pages=[http://content.time.com/time/magazine/article/0%2C9171%2C762137-1%2C00.html 1]–[http://content.time.com/time/magazine/article/0%2C9171%2C762137-2%2C00.html 2] & [http://content.time.com/time/magazine/article/0%2C9171%2C762137-7%2C00.html 7] |archive-date=November 12, 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131112085413/http://content.time.com/time/magazine/article/0,9171,762137,00.html |url-status=live}}</ref>{{refn|''Time'' also reports that ''[[Hell's Angels (film)|Hell's Angels]]'' (1930)—directed by [[Howard Hughes]]—cost more, but this was later revealed to be incorrect; the accounts for ''Hell's Angels'' show it cost $2.8&nbsp;million, but Hughes publicized it as costing $4&nbsp;million, selling it to the media as the most expensive film ever made up to that point.<ref name="Eyman (1997)">{{cite book |last=Eyman |first=Scott |title=The Speed of Sound: Hollywood and the Talkie Revolution, 1926–1930 |year=1997 |publisher=[[Simon & Schuster]] |isbn=978-0-684-81162-8 |page=[https://archive.org/details/speedofsoundholl00eyma/page/253 253] |url=https://archive.org/details/speedofsoundholl00eyma/page/253 |author-link=Scott Eyman}}</ref>|group=nb}}

Although legend persists that the [[Hays Office]] fined Selznick $5,000 for using the word "damn" in [[Frankly, my dear, I don't give a damn|Butler's exit line]], in fact, the [[Motion Picture Association]] board passed an amendment to the Production Code on November 1, 1939, that forbade the use of the words "hell" or "damn" except when their use "shall be essential and required for portrayal, in proper historical context, of any scene or dialogue based upon historical fact or folklore ... or a quotation from a literary work, provided that no such use shall be permitted which is intrinsically objectionable or offends good taste". With that amendment, the [[Production Code Administration]] had no further objection to Rhett's closing line.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Leff |first1=Leonard J. |last2=Simmons |first2=Jerold L. |title=The Dame in the Kimono: Hollywood, Censorship, and the Production Code |publisher=[[University Press of Kentucky]] |year=2001 |page=[https://books.google.com/books?id=bkU7CKBubgMC&pg=PA108 108]}}</ref>

===Music===
Selznick chose [[Max Steiner]] to compose the score, with whom he had worked at RKO Pictures in the early 1930s. Warner Bros.{{emdash}}who had contracted Steiner in 1936{{emdash}}agreed to lend him to Selznick. Steiner spent twelve weeks working on the score, the most prolonged period he had ever spent writing one, and at two hours and thirty-six minutes long, it was also the longest he had ever written. Five orchestrators were hired: [[Hugo Friedhofer]], Maurice de Packh, [[Bernhard Kaun]], [[Adolph Deutsch]] and [[Reginald Hazeltine Bassett]].

The score is characterized by two love themes, one for Ashley and Melanie's sweet love and another that evokes Scarlett's passion for Ashley, though notably, there is no Scarlett and Rhett love theme. Steiner drew considerably on folk and patriotic music, which included [[Stephen Foster]] tunes such as "Louisiana Belle", "Dolly Day", "Ringo De Banjo", "[[Beautiful Dreamer]]", "[[Old Folks at Home]]", and "Katie Belle", which formed the basis of Scarlett's theme; other tunes that feature prominently are: "[[Marching through Georgia]]" by [[Henry Clay Work]], "[[Dixie (song)|Dixie]]", "[[Garryowen (air)|Garryowen]]", and "[[The Bonnie Blue Flag]]". The theme that is most associated with the film today is the melody that accompanies Tara, the O'Hara plantation; in the early 1940s, "Tara's Theme" formed the musical basis of the song "[[My Own True Love (song)|My Own True Love]]" by [[Mack David]]. In all, there are ninety-nine separate pieces of music featured in the score.

Due to the pressure of completing on time, Steiner received some assistance in composing from Friedhofer, Deutsch, and [[Heinz Roemheld]], and in addition, two short cues—by [[Franz Waxman]] and [[William Axt]]—were taken from scores in the MGM library.<ref>{{cite book |first=Laurence E. |last=MacDonald |title=The Invisible Art of Film Music: A Comprehensive History |year=1998 |publisher=[[Scarecrow Press]] |isbn=978-1-880157-56-5 |pages=[https://books.google.com/books?id=bQGbUd83MhYC&pg=PT68 52]–[https://books.google.com/books?id=bQGbUd83MhYC&pg=PT69 53]}}</ref>

===Costuming===
Color, texture, and fabric were used to reinforce Scarlett O'Hara's narrative arc and character development. While early gowns feature light pastels and vibrant primary colors, her post-war attire transitions to darker crimson and burgundy tones as her circumstances become more dire. In the latter part of the film, Scarlett's more extravagant and colorful costumes were used to contrast her against the drabness of the other characters.<ref>{{cite web | last = Bartel | first = Pauline | title = Scarlett's Gowns in Gone With the Wind | website = PaulineBartel.com | url = https://paulinebartel.com/scarletts-gowns-in-gone-with-the-wind/ | access-date = January 14, 2026}}</ref>

The costumes combined historical reference with contemporary Hollywood aesthetics. Costume designer [[Walter Plunkett]] drew on nineteenth-century sources such as illustrations in ''[[Godey's Lady's Book]]'' and surviving 1860s–1870s garments while streamlining volume and ornamentation to suit 1930s screen taste and the practical needs of filming. Plunkett's approach produced gowns that evoked period silhouettes whilst omitting excessive ruffles, bows, and lace in favour of cleaner lines and Hollywood trimmings such as ostrich plumes.<ref>{{cite magazine | last = Morena | first = Jill | title = How Gone With the Wind's Costumes Combined the 1860s and the 1930s | magazine = [[Time (magazine)|Time]]| date = December 17, 2015| url = https://time.com/4154085/gone-with-the-wind-costumes/ | access-date = November 16, 2025}}</ref>

==Release==

===Preview, premiere, and initial release===
On September 9, 1939, Selznick, his wife, [[Irene Mayer Selznick|Irene]], investor [[John Hay Whitney|John "Jock" Whitney]], and film editor [[Hal Kern]] drove to [[Riverside, California]], to watch a [[rough cut]] at the [[Riverside Fox Theater|Fox Theatre]], without incomplete titles and special optical effects. It ran for four hours and twenty-five minutes; the final release was cut to under four hours. A [[double bill]] of ''[[Hawaiian Nights]]'' and ''[[Beau Geste (1939 film)|Beau Geste]]'' was playing, but after the first feature it was announced that instead of the second bill, the theater would be screening a preview of an unnamed upcoming film; the audience were informed they could leave but would not be readmitted once the film had begun, nor would phone calls be allowed once the theater had been sealed. When the title appeared on the screen, the audience cheered, and after it had ended, the film received a standing ovation.<ref name="tcm notes" /><ref name="Bell">{{cite news |last=Bell |first=Alison |title=Inland Empire Cities were Once 'In' with Hollywood for Movie Previews |date=June 25, 2010 |work=[[Los Angeles Times]] |url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-2010-jun-25-la-me-then-20100625-story.html |access-date=January 25, 2013 |archive-date=December 29, 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131229110642/http://articles.latimes.com/2010/jun/25/local/la-me-then-20100625 |url-status=live }}</ref> In his biography of Selznick, [[David Thomson (film critic)|David Thomson]] wrote that the audience's response before the film had even started "was the greatest moment of [Selznick's] life, the greatest victory and redemption of all his failings",<ref>{{cite book |first=David |last=Thomson |author-link=David Thomson (film critic) |title=Showman: The Life of David O. Selznick |location=New York |publisher=[[Knopf]] |year=1992 |isbn=978-0-394-56833-1 |page=314 |url=https://archive.org/details/showmanlifeofdav00thom}}</ref> with Selznick describing the preview cards as "probably the most amazing any picture has ever had".<ref name="Atlantic">{{cite news |first=Gavin |last=Lambert |author-link=Gavin Lambert |work=[[The Atlantic Monthly]] |date=March 1973 |title=The Making of Gone with the Wind, Part II |volume=265 |issue=6 |pages=56–72 |url=https://www.theatlantic.com/past/docs/issues/73mar/wind.htm |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111127011143/http://www.theatlantic.com/past/docs/issues/73mar/wind.htm |archive-date=November 27, 2011}}</ref> When Selznick was asked by the press in early September how he felt about the film, he said, "At noon I think it's divine, at midnight I think it's lousy. Sometimes I think it's the greatest picture ever made. But if it's only a great picture, I'll still be satisfied."<ref name="Time (1939)" />
[[File:Gone With the Wind Atlanta premiere 1939.jpg|thumb|left|The premiere of the film at Loew's Grand, Atlanta]]
About 300,000 people came out in Atlanta for the premiere at the [[Loew's Grand Theatre]] on December 15, 1939. It was the climax of three days of festivities hosted by Mayor [[William B. Hartsfield]], which included a parade of limousines featuring stars from the film, receptions, thousands of [[Confederate flag]]s, and a costume ball. [[Eurith D. Rivers]], the governor of Georgia, declared December 15 a state holiday. An estimated 300,000 Atlanta residents and visitors lined the streets for seven miles to view the procession of limousines that brought stars from the airport. Only Leslie Howard and Victor Fleming chose not to attend: Howard had returned to England due to the outbreak of [[World War II]], and Fleming had fallen out with Selznick and declined to attend any of the premieres.<ref name="Time (1939)" /><ref name="Atlantic" /> Hattie McDaniel was also absent, as she and the other black cast members were prevented from attending the premiere due to Georgia's [[Jim Crow laws]], which kept them from sitting with their white colleagues. Upon learning that McDaniel had been barred from the premiere, Clark Gable threatened to boycott the event, but McDaniel persuaded him to attend.<ref>{{cite book |last=Harris |first=Warren G. |title=Clark Gable: A Biography |publisher=[[Harmony Books]] |year=2002 |page=211}}</ref> President [[Jimmy Carter]] later recalled it as "the biggest event to happen in the South in my lifetime".<ref>{{cite book |first=Hamilton |last=Cravens |title=Great Depression: People and Perspectives |series=Perspectives in American Social History |year=2009 |publisher=[[ABC-CLIO]] |isbn=978-1-59884-093-3 |page=[https://books.google.com/books?id=0gblKwLBrrQC&pg=PA221 221]}}</ref> Premieres in New York and Los Angeles followed; the latter attended by some of the actresses who had been considered for the part of Scarlett, among them Paulette Goddard, Norma Shearer, and Joan Crawford.<ref name="Atlantic" />

From December 1939 to July 1940, the film played only advance-ticket [[Roadshow theatrical release|road show]] engagements at a limited number of theaters at prices upwards of $1—more than double the price of a regular first-run feature—with MGM collecting an unprecedented 70 percent of the box office receipts, as opposed to the typical 30–35 percent of the period. After reaching saturation as a roadshow, MGM revised its terms to a 50 percent cut and halved the prices before it finally entered general release in 1941 at "popular" prices.<ref name="Schatz (1999)">{{cite book |last=Schatz |first=Thomas |title=Boom and Bust: American Cinema in the 1940s |volume=6 |series=History of the American Cinema |year=1999 |publisher=[[University of California Press]] |orig-year=1997 |isbn=978-0-520-22130-7 |pages=[https://books.google.com/books?id=dwf5SUcfousC&pg=PA65 65]–[https://books.google.com/books?id=dwf5SUcfousC&pg=PA66 66]}}</ref> Including its distribution and advertising costs, total expenditure was as high as $7&nbsp;million.<ref name="Atlantic" /><ref name="Shearer">{{cite news |last=Shearer |first=Lloyd |title=GWTW: Supercolossal Saga of an Epic |date=October 26, 1947 |work=[[The New York Times]] |url=https://www.nytimes.com/packages/html/movies/bestpictures/wind-ar6.html |access-date=July 14, 2012 |archive-date=May 31, 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130531030901/http://www.nytimes.com/packages/html/movies/bestpictures/wind-ar6.html |url-status=live |author-link=Lloyd Shearer}}</ref>

===Later releases===
[[File:Gone With The Wind 1967 re-release.jpg|thumb|upright|1967 re-release poster |alt=Poster shows Rhett Butler carrying Scarlett O'Hara against a backdrop of the Burning of Atlanta]]

In 1942, Selznick liquidated his company for tax reasons and sold his share in ''Gone with the Wind'' to his business partner, John Whitney, for $500,000. In turn, Whitney sold it to MGM for $2.8&nbsp;million, giving the studio outright ownership of the film.<ref name="Shearer" /> MGM immediately re-released it in early 1942,<ref name="Bartel"/> and again in 1947 and 1954.<ref name="tcm notes" /> The 1954 reissue was the first time the film was shown in [[widescreen]], compromising the original [[Academy ratio]] and cropping the top and bottom to an aspect ratio of 1.75:1. In doing so, several shots were optically re-framed and cut into the three-strip camera negatives, forever altering five shots.<ref>{{cite book |last=Haver |first=Ronald |author-link=Ronald Haver |year=1993 |title=David O. Selznick's Gone with the Wind |location=New York |publisher=[[Random House]] |pages=84–85}}</ref>

A 1961 rerelease commemorated the [[centennial]] anniversary of the start of the Civil War, and it also included a gala "premiere" at the Loew's Grand Theater. It was attended by Selznick and many other stars of the film, including Vivien Leigh and Olivia de Havilland;<ref name="Brown & Wiley">{{cite book |first1=Ellen F. |last1=Brown | first2=John Jr. |last2=Wiley |title=Margaret Mitchell's Gone With the Wind: A Bestseller's Odyssey from Atlanta to Hollywood |year=2011 |publisher=[[Taylor Trade Publications]] |isbn=978-1-58979-527-3 |pages=[https://books.google.com/books?id=Jb6kAdtMHCQC&pg=PA287 287], [https://books.google.com/books?id=Jb6kAdtMHCQC&pg=PA293 293] & [https://books.google.com/books?id=Jb6kAdtMHCQC&pg=PA322 322]}}</ref> Clark Gable had died the previous year.<ref>{{cite book |first=James Stuart |last=Olson |title=Historical Dictionary of the 1950s |year=2000 |publisher=[[Greenwood Publishing Group]] |isbn=978-0-313-30619-8 |page=[https://books.google.com/books?id=eSBDF5_L3BgC&pg=PA108 108] |author-link=James S. Olson}}</ref> For its 1967 re-release, the film was blown up to [[70mm]],<ref name="tcm notes" /> and issued with updated poster artwork featuring Gable—with his white shirt ripped open—holding Leigh against a backdrop of orange flames.<ref name="Brown & Wiley" /> There were further re-releases in 1971, 1974, and 1989; for the fiftieth-anniversary reissue in 1989, it was given a complete audio and video restoration. It was released in American theaters again in 1998, by [[Time Warner]]-owned [[New Line Cinema]].<ref>{{cite book |editor1-last=Block|editor1-first=Alex Ben|editor2-last=Wilson|editor2-first=Lucy Autrey|year=2010|title=George Lucas's Blockbusting: A Decade-By-Decade Survey of Timeless Movies Including Untold Secrets of Their Financial and Cultural Success|publisher=[[HarperCollins]]|isbn=978-0-06-177889-6|pages=[https://archive.org/details/georgelucassbloc00alex/page/220 220]–221 |url=https://archive.org/details/georgelucassbloc00alex|url-access=registration}}</ref><ref name="Kramer">{{cite book |first=Peter |last=Krämer |title=The New Hollywood: From Bonnie And Clyde To Star Wars |volume=30 |series=Short Cuts |year=2005 |publisher=[[Wallflower Press]] |isbn=978-1-904764-58-8 |page=[https://books.google.com/books?id=B5PjuAbEPooC&pg=PA46 46]}}</ref>

In 2013, a [[4K resolution|4K]] [[Digital cinema|digital restoration]] was released in the United Kingdom to coincide with Vivien Leigh's centenary.<ref>{{cite web |last=Andrew |first=Geoff |title=Gone with the Wind |work=British Film Institute |publisher=[[British Film Institute]] |url=http://www.bfi.org.uk/news-opinion/bfi-film-releases/gone-wind |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131201232515/http://www.bfi.org.uk/news-opinion/bfi-film-releases/gone-wind |archive-date=December 1, 2013 |author-link=Geoff Andrew}}</ref> In 2014, special screenings were scheduled over two days at theaters across the United States to coincide with the film's 75th anniversary,<ref name="75th anniversary screenings">{{cite web |last=Fristoe |first=Roger |title=Gone with the Wind: 75th Anniversary – Screenings and Events |publisher=[[Turner Classic Movies]] |url=https://www.tcm.com/this-month/article/1028229 |access-date=September 28, 2014 |archive-date=September 29, 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140929040858/http://www.tcm.com/this-month/article/1028229%7C0/Gone-With-the-Wind-th-Anniversary.html |url-status=live }}</ref> and again over three days in 2024, to celebrate its 85th anniversary.<ref>{{cite web
|title=''Gone with the Wind'' returning to theaters for 85th anniversary: where to see it near you |date=April 4, 2024 |publisher=[[CBS News]] |url=https://www.cbsnews.com/philadelphia/news/gone-with-the-wind-returning-to-theaters/ |access-date=May 2, 2024 }}</ref>

===Television===
''Gone with the Wind'' premiered on American television on the [[HBO]] cable network on June 11, 1976, and played on HBO fourteen times throughout the rest of the month.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://hboguides.com/guides/1976/1976-06.html |title=The HBO Guide – June 1976 |date=May 1976 |website=The HBO Guide Archive |access-date=December 10, 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180602095355/http://hboguides.com/guides/1976/1976-06.html |archive-date=June 2, 2018 |url-status=usurped}}</ref><ref name="Bartel" /><ref>{{cite magazine|magazine=[[Variety (magazine)|Variety]]|date=July 28, 1976|page=39|title=HBO's 'GWTW' Viewers}}</ref> Other cable channels also broadcast it during June.<ref>{{cite magazine|magazine=[[Variety (magazine)|Variety]]|date=May 5, 1976|page=153|title='GWTW' Sold To Pay-Cable Pre-NBC Play}}</ref> It made its [[network television]] debut in November of that year; [[NBC]] paid $5&nbsp;million for a one-off airing, and it was broadcast in two parts on successive evenings.<ref name="Bartel" /> It became at that time the [[List of most watched television broadcasts in the United States#The highest-rated broadcasts of all time|highest-rated television program]] ever presented on a single network, watched by 47.5 percent of the households sampled in America, and 65 percent of television viewers, still the record for the highest-rated film to ever air on television.<ref name="Bartel" /><ref name="Kramer" />

In 1978, [[CBS]] signed a deal worth $35&nbsp;million to broadcast ''Gone with the Wind'' twenty times over twenty years.<ref name="Bartel" /> [[Turner Entertainment]] acquired the MGM film library in 1986, but the deal did not include the television rights to ''Gone with the Wind'', which were still held by CBS. An agreement was struck in which the rights were returned to Turner Entertainment, and CBS's broadcast rights to ''The Wizard of Oz'' were extended.<ref name="Bartel" /> The film was used to launch two cable channels owned by [[Turner Broadcasting System]]: [[Turner Network Television]] (1988) and [[Turner Classic Movies]] (1994).<ref>{{cite news |first=Kenneth R. |last=Clark |title=TNT Rides in on 'Gone With Wind' |date=September 29, 1988 |work=[[Chicago Tribune]] |url=https://www.chicagotribune.com/1988/09/29/tnt-rides-in-on-gone-with-wind/ |access-date=January 29, 2013 |archive-date=May 26, 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130526004738/http://articles.chicagotribune.com/1988-09-29/features/8802030105_1_basic-cable-industry-jeffrey-selznick-tnt |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last=Osborne |first=Robert |author-link=Robert Osborne |title=Robert Osborne on TCM's 15th Anniversary |publisher=[[Turner Classic Movies]] |url=http://www.tcm.com/this-month/article/236547%7C0/Robert-Osborne-April-2009.html |access-date=January 29, 2013 |archive-date=May 27, 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130527204400/http://www.tcm.com/this-month/article/236547%7C0/Robert-Osborne-April-2009.html |url-status=dead }}</ref> 

=== Home media ===
''Gone with the Wind'' debuted on [[VHS]] in March 1985, where it placed second in the sales charts.<ref name="Bartel" /> It has since been released on [[DVD]] and [[Blu-ray]] formats.<ref name="Brown & Wiley" /> It is to be released in 4K digitally and on [[Ultra HD Blu-ray]] on November 4, 2026, with three separate physical editions which include the standard 4K UHD release, a SteelBook, and a collector's edition sold exclusively through [[Walmart]].<ref>{{cite news |last=Tingley |first=Anna |url=https://variety.com/2026/film/news/gone-with-the-wind-4k-blu-ray-buy-online-1236810525/ |title='Gone With the Wind' Sets First 4K Blu-ray Release With New Restoration and Bonus Features (EXCLUSIVE) |work=Variety |date=July 14, 2026 |access-date=July 15, 2026 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260715202125/https://variety.com/2026/film/news/gone-with-the-wind-4k-blu-ray-buy-online-1236810525/ |archive-date=July 15, 2026 |url-status=live}}</ref>

==Reception==
===Critical response===
[[File:Gone With The Wind featuring McDaniel & de Havilland & Leigh.jpg|thumb|right|upright=1|McDaniel, de Havilland, and Leigh were praised for their performances.]]
Consumer magazines and newspapers generally gave ''Gone with the Wind'' excellent reviews.<ref name="tcm notes" /> ''[[Variety (magazine)|Variety]]'' described it as "a great picture poised for grosses which may be second to none in the history of the business".<ref>{{cite web | last = Tatna | first = Meher | title = Forgotten Hollywood: Vivien Leigh and "Gone with the Wind" (1939) | publisher = Golden Globes | date = September 5, 2022| url = https://goldenglobes.com/articles/forgotten-hollywood-vivien-leigh-and-gone-wind-1939/ | access-date = January 13, 2026}}</ref> While its production values, technical achievements, and scale of ambition were universally recognized, some reviewers of the time found it lengthy and dramatically unconvincing. [[Frank S. Nugent]] of ''[[The New York Times]]'' wrote that, although it was the most ambitious production to date, it was probably not the greatest ever made; he nonetheless described it as an "interesting story beautifully told".<ref name="Nugent">{{cite news |last=Nugent |first=Frank S. |author-link=Frank S. Nugent |title=The Screen in Review; David Selznick's 'Gone With the Wind' Has Its Long-Awaited Premiere at Astor and Capitol, Recalling Civil War and Plantation Days of South—Seen as Treating Book With Great Fidelity |date=December 20, 1939 |work=[[The New York Times]] |url=https://www.nytimes.com/movie/review?res=9807E2DA153EE432A25753C2A9649D946894D6CF |access-date=February 1, 2013 |archive-date=March 8, 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160308195051/http://www.nytimes.com/movie/review?res=9807E2DA153EE432A25753C2A9649D946894D6CF |url-status=live }}</ref> Franz Hoellering of ''[[The Nation]]'' was of the same opinion: "The result is a film which is a major event in the history of the industry but only a minor achievement in motion-picture art. There are moments when the two categories meet on good terms, but the long stretches between are filled with mere spectacular efficiency."<ref name="Hoellering">{{cite news |last=Hoellering |first=Franz |title=Gone With the Wind |year=1939 |work=[[The Nation]] |publication-date=December 16, 2008 |url=http://www.thenation.com/article/gone-wind |access-date=February 1, 2013 |archive-date=May 21, 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140521030825/http://www.thenation.com/article/gone-wind |url-status=live }}</ref>

Although ''Gone with the Wind'' was praised for its fidelity to the novel,<ref name="Nugent" /> this was also singled out as the main factor contributing to the lengthy running time.<ref name="Flinn">{{cite news |last=Flinn | first=John C. Sr. |title=Gone With the Wind |date=December 20, 1939 |work=[[Variety (magazine)|Variety]] |url=https://variety.com/1939/film/reviews/gone-with-the-wind-2-1200412649/ |access-date=June 14, 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130614055311/http://variety.com/1939/film/reviews/gone-with-the-wind-2-1200412649/ |archive-date=June 14, 2013 |url-status=live }} [http://www.varietyultimate.com/archive/issue/WV-12-20-1939-14 Alt URL] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181106235704/https://varietyultimate.com/archive/issue/WV-12-20-1939-14 |date=November 6, 2018 }}</ref> John C. Flinn wrote for ''Variety'' that Selznick had "left too much in", and that as entertainment, it would have benefited if repetitious scenes and dialog from the latter part of the story had been trimmed.<ref name="Flinn" /> ''[[The Manchester Guardian]]'' felt the one serious drawback was that the story lacked the epic quality to justify the outlay of time and found the second half, which focuses on Scarlett's "irrelevant marriages" and "domestic squabbles", mostly superfluous, and the sole reason for their inclusion had been "simply because Margaret Mitchell wrote it that way". ''The Guardian'' believed that if "the story had been cut short and tidied up at the point marked by the interval, and if the personal drama had been made subservient to a cinematic treatment of the central theme—the collapse and devastation of the [[Antebellum South|Old South]]—then ''Gone With the Wind'' might have been a really great film".<ref name="Guardian">{{cite news |title=From the Archive, 28 May 1940: Gone with the Wind at the Gaiety |date=May 28, 1940 |work=[[The Manchester Guardian]] |publication-date=May 28, 2010 |url=https://www.theguardian.com/theguardian/2010/may/28/archive-gone-with-the-wind-1940 |access-date=February 1, 2013 |archive-date=October 20, 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131020121148/http://www.theguardian.com/theguardian/2010/may/28/archive-gone-with-the-wind-1940 |url-status=live }}</ref> Likewise, Hoellering also found the second half of the film weaker. Identifying the Civil War to be the driving force of the first part while the characters dominate in the second part, he concluded this is where the main fault of the film lay, commenting that "the characters alone do not suffice". Despite many excellent scenes, he considered the drama to be unconvincing and that the "psychological development" had been neglected.<ref name="Hoellering" />

Much of the praise was reserved for the casting, with Vivien Leigh, in particular, being singled out for her performance as Scarlett. Nugent described her as the "pivot of the picture" and believed her to be "so perfectly designed for the part by art and nature that any other actress in the role would be inconceivable".<ref name="Nugent" /> Similarly, Hoellering found her "perfect" in "appearance and movements"; he felt her acting best when she was allowed to "accentuate the split personality she portrays" and thought she was particularly effective in such moments of characterization like the morning after the marital rape scene.<ref name="Hoellering" /> Flinn also found Leigh suited to the role physically and felt she was best in the scenes where she displays courage and determination, such as the escape from Atlanta and when Scarlett kills a Yankee deserter.<ref name="Flinn" /> Leigh won in the Best Actress category for her performance at the [[1939 New York Film Critics Circle Awards]].<ref>{{cite web |title=New York Film Critics Circle Awards – 1939 Awards |publisher=[[New York Film Critics Circle]] |url=http://www.nyfcc.com/awards/?awardyear=1939 |access-date=July 21, 2015 |archive-date=July 2, 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150702012120/http://www.nyfcc.com/awards/?awardyear=1939 |url-status=live }}</ref> Of Clark Gable's performance as Rhett Butler, Flinn felt the characterization was "as close to Miss Mitchell's conception—and the audience's—as might be imagined",<ref name="Flinn" /> a view which Nugent concurred with,<ref name="Nugent" /> although Hoellering felt that Gable did not quite convince in the closing scenes, as Rhett walks out on Scarlett in disgust.<ref name="Hoellering" /> Of the other principal cast members, both Hoellering and Flinn found Leslie Howard to be "convincing" as the weak-willed Ashley, with Flinn identifying Olivia de Havilland as a "standout" as Melanie;<ref name="Hoellering" /><ref name="Flinn" /> Nugent was also especially taken with de Havilland's performance, describing it as a "gracious, dignified, tender gem of characterization".<ref name="Nugent" /> Hattie McDaniel's performance as Mammy was singled out for praise by many critics: Nugent believed she gave the best performance after Vivien Leigh,<ref name="Nugent" /> with Flinn placing it third after Leigh's and Gable's performances.<ref name="Flinn" />

===Academy Awards===
At the [[12th Academy Awards]], ''Gone with the Wind'' set a record for [[Academy Award]] wins and nominations, winning in eight of the competitive categories it was nominated in, from a total of thirteen nominations. It won for Best Picture, Best Actress, Best Supporting Actress, Best Director, Best Screenplay, Best Cinematography, Best Art Direction, and Best Editing, and received two further honorary awards for its use of equipment and color (it also became the first color film to win Best Picture).<ref name="Oscars1940">{{cite web |title=Results Page – 1939 (12th) |work=Academy Awards database |publisher=[[Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences]] |url=http://awardsdatabase.oscars.org/ampas_awards/BasicSearch?action=searchLink&displayType=1&BSFromYear=12 |access-date=February 3, 2013 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://archive.today/20130415140512/http://awardsdatabase.oscars.org/ampas_awards/BasicSearch?action=searchLink&displayType=1&BSFromYear=12 |archive-date=April 15, 2013  }}</ref><ref name="Randall">{{cite news |last1=Randall |first1=David |last2=Clark |first2=Heather |title=Oscars – Cinema's Golden Night: The Ultimate Bluffer's Guide to Hollywood's Big Night |date=February 24, 2013 |work=[[The Independent]] |url=https://www.independent.co.uk/arts-entertainment/films/features/oscars--cinemas-golden-night-the-ultimate-bluffers-guide-to-hollywoods-big-night-8508244.html |access-date=March 7, 2013 |archive-date=February 26, 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130226221247/http://www.independent.co.uk/arts-entertainment/films/features/oscars--cinemas-golden-night-the-ultimate-bluffers-guide-to-hollywoods-big-night-8508244.html |url-status=live |author-link=David Randall}}</ref>

The record of eight competitive wins stood until ''[[Gigi (1958 film)|Gigi]]'' (1958) won nine, and its overall record of ten was broken by ''[[Ben-Hur (1959 film)|Ben-Hur]]'' (1959) which won eleven.<ref name="Cutler">{{cite news |last=Cutler |first=David |editor1-last=Goldsmith |editor1-first=Belinda |editor2-last=Zargham |editor2-first=Mohammad |title=Factbox : Key Historical Facts about the Academy Awards |date=February 22, 2013 |work=[[Reuters]] |url=https://www.reuters.com/article/us-oscars-factbox-idUSBRE91L0KM20130222 |access-date=March 7, 2013 |archive-date=February 26, 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130226081535/http://www.reuters.com/article/2013/02/22/us-oscars-factbox-idUSBRE91L0KM20130222 |url-status=live }}</ref> ''Gone with the Wind'' also held the record for most nominations until ''[[All About Eve]]'' (1950) secured fourteen.<ref name="tcm articles" /> It was the longest American sound film made up to that point, and may still hold the record of the longest Best Picture winner depending on how it is interpreted.<ref name="Oscar quotes">{{cite web|title=Beyond the Page: Famous Quotes |publisher=[[Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences]] |url=http://www.oscars.org/events-exhibitions/features/read-the-book/part1_beyond.html |access-date=March 8, 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120905125647/http://www.oscars.org/events-exhibitions/features/read-the-book/part1_beyond.html |archive-date=September 5, 2012}}</ref> The running time for ''Gone with the Wind'' is just under 221&nbsp;minutes, while ''[[Lawrence of Arabia (film)|Lawrence of Arabia]]'' (1962) runs for just over 222&nbsp;minutes; however, including the [[overture]], [[intermission]], [[entr'acte]], and exit music, ''Gone with the Wind'' lasts for 234&nbsp;minutes (although some sources put its full length at 238&nbsp;minutes) while ''Lawrence of Arabia'' comes in slightly shorter at 232&nbsp;minutes with its additional components.<ref name="filmsite">{{cite web |last=Dirks |first=Tim |title=Academy Awards: Best Picture – Facts & Trivia |work=[[Filmsite.org]] |publisher=[[AMC Networks]] |page=2 |url=http://www.filmsite.org/bestpics1.html |access-date=March 7, 2013 |archive-date=January 9, 2010 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100109122738/http://www.filmsite.org/bestpics1.html |url-status=live }}</ref><ref name="Kim">{{cite magazine |last=Kim |first=Wook |title=17 Unusual Oscar Records – Longest Film (Running Time) to Win an Award: 431&nbsp;Minutes |date=February 22, 2013 |magazine=[[Time (magazine)|Time]] |url=https://entertainment.time.com/2013/02/22/17-unusual-oscar-records/slide/war-and-peace/ |access-date=March 7, 2013 |archive-date=February 27, 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130227022821/http://entertainment.time.com/2013/02/22/17-unusual-oscar-records/slide/war-and-peace/ |url-status=live }}</ref>

Hattie McDaniel became the first African-American to win an Academy Award—beating out her co-star Olivia de Havilland, who was also nominated in the same category—but was [[Racial segregation in the United States|racially segregated]] from her co-stars at the awards ceremony at the [[Ambassador Hotel (Los Angeles)|Coconut Grove]]; she and her escort were made to sit at a separate table at the back of the room.<ref name="Haskell">{{cite book |last=Haskell |first=Molly |title=Frankly, My Dear: Gone With the Wind Revisited |series=Icons of America |year=2010 |publisher=[[Yale University Press]] |isbn=978-0-300-16437-4 |pages=[https://books.google.com/books?id=V-g1USyUYIwC&pg=PA213 213]–[https://books.google.com/books?id=V-g1USyUYIwC&pg=PA214 214] |author-link=Molly Haskell}}</ref> Meanwhile, screenwriter Sidney Howard became the first [[List of posthumous Academy Award winners and nominees|posthumous]] Oscar winner and Selznick personally received the [[Irving G. Thalberg Memorial Award]] for his career achievements.<ref name="tcm articles" /><ref name="Oscars1940" />
