===Reactions from African-Americans===
[[File:Studio publicity Hattie McDaniel.jpg|thumb|upright|Hattie McDaniel, the first African-American Oscar winner]]
African-American commentators have criticized ''Gone with the Wind'' since its release for the film's depiction of black people and "whitewashing" of slavery; contemporary white newspapers did not report on such criticism.<ref name="Schuessler">{{cite news |last=Schuessler |first=Jennifer |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2020/06/14/movies/gone-with-the-wind-battle.html |title=The Long Battle Over 'Gone With the Wind' |newspaper=[[The New York Times]] |date=June 14, 2020 |access-date=June 20, 2020 |archive-date=June 20, 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200620000443/https://www.nytimes.com/2020/06/14/movies/gone-with-the-wind-battle.html |url-status=live }}</ref> [[Carlton Moss]], a black dramatist, wrote in an open letter that whereas ''[[The Birth of a Nation]]'' was a "frontal attack on American history and the Negro people", ''Gone with the Wind'' was a "rear attack on the same". He went on to characterize the latter film as a "nostalgic plea for sympathy for a still-living cause of Southern reaction". Moss further called out the stereotypical black characterizations, such as the "shiftless and dull-witted Pork", the "indolent and thoroughly irresponsible Prissy", Big Sam's "radiant acceptance of slavery", and Mammy with her "constant haranguing and doting on every wish of Scarlett".<ref name="Lupack">{{cite book |first=Barbara Tepa |last=Lupack |title=Literary Adaptations in Black American Cinema: From Oscar Micheaux to Toni Morrison |year=2002 |publisher=University of Rochester Press |isbn=978-1-58046-103-0 |pages=[https://books.google.com/books?id=hjO7_Ju7lWUC&pg=PA209 209]–211 |author-link=Barbara Tepa Lupack}}</ref> Similarly, the black poet and educator [[Melvin B. Tolson]] wrote that while, "''Birth of a Nation'' was such a barefaced lie that a moron could see through it. ''Gone with the Wind'' is such a subtle lie that it will be swallowed as truth by millions of whites and blacks alike."<ref name="TimeGajanan2020">{{cite magazine |first=Mahita |last=Gajanan |title=Gone With the Wind Should Not Be Erased, Argue Film Historians. But It Should Not Be Watched in a Vacuum |date=June 12, 2020 |magazine=[[Time (magazine)|Time]] |url=https://time.com/5852362/gone-with-the-wind-film-history/ |access-date=June 17, 2020 |archive-date=June 17, 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200617021842/https://time.com/5852362/gone-with-the-wind-film-history/ |url-status=live}}</ref>

Following Hattie McDaniel's Oscar win, [[Walter Francis White]], the leader of the [[National Association for the Advancement of Colored People]], accused her of being an [[Uncle Tom]]. McDaniel responded that she would "rather make seven hundred dollars a week playing a maid than seven dollars being one"; she further questioned White's qualification to speak on behalf of black people since he was light-skinned and only one-eighth black.<ref name="Haskell" /> Opinion on the film in the wider African-American community was divided. ''Gone with the Wind'' was called by some a "weapon of terror against black America" and an insult to black audiences, and demonstrations were held in various cities.<ref name="Haskell" /> [[Malcolm X]] recalled that "when [[Butterfly McQueen]] went into her act, I felt like crawling under the rug".<ref name="Reynolds">{{cite book |last=Reynolds |first=David |title=America, Empire of Liberty: A New History |year=2009 |publisher=[[Penguin UK]] |isbn=978-0-14-190856-4 |pages=[https://books.google.com/books?id=ohbINLMYW4IC&q=white+women+are+elegant 241]–242 |author-link=David Reynolds (historian)}}</ref> For her part, McQueen was initially unhappy with playing a slave, having expected Selznick to update the novel's story. "But he was very authentic with the script," she recalled in 1989. "I'm glad now that he was, because you can look at the film and see history as it was. You can see where we've come."<ref>{{cite news |last1=Edge|first1=Lynn|date=October 8, 1989|title='GWTW' start toted the load during filming|url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?nid=1454&dat=19891008&id=YVdIAAAAIBAJ&pg=5617,3009053&hl=en|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210418082135/https://news.google.com/newspapers?nid=1454&dat=19891008&id=YVdIAAAAIBAJ&pg=5617,3009053&hl=en|archive-date=April 18, 2021|access-date=May 9, 2016|publisher=Star-News|issue=60}}</ref> Some sections of the black community recognized McDaniel's achievements to be representative of progress; some African-Americans crossed picket lines and praised McDaniel's warm and witty characterization, and others hoped that the industry's recognition of her work would lead to increased visibility on screen for other black actors. In its editorial congratulation to McDaniel on winning her Academy Award, ''[[Opportunity: A Journal of Negro Life]]'' used ''Gone with the Wind'' as a reminder of the "limit" put on black aspiration by old prejudices.<ref name="Haskell" /><ref name="Lupack" />

===Audience response===
''Gone with the Wind'' broke attendance records everywhere. At the [[Capitol Theatre (New York City)|Capitol Theatre]] in New York alone, it averaged eleven thousand admissions per day in late December,<ref name="Schatz (1999)" /> and within four years of its release had sold an estimated sixty million tickets across the United States—sales equivalent to just under [[1940 United States Census|half the population at the time]].<ref name="Young">{{cite magazine |last=Young |first=John |title='Avatar' vs. 'Gone With the Wind' |date=February 5, 2010 |magazine=[[Entertainment Weekly]] |url=http://www.ew.com/article/2010/02/05/avatar-vs-gone-wind |access-date=February 5, 2013 |archive-date=March 8, 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150308205945/http://www.ew.com/article/2010/02/05/avatar-vs-gone-wind |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=About the 1940 Census |work=Official 1940 Census Website |publisher=[[National Archives and Records Administration]] |url=https://1940census.archives.gov/about |access-date=February 5, 2013 |archive-date=February 5, 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130205174839/http://1940census.archives.gov/about/ |url-status=live }}</ref> It repeated its success overseas, and was a sensational hit during [[the Blitz]] in London, opening in April 1940 and playing for four years at the Little Ritz in [[Leicester Square]].<ref>{{cite news |title=London Movie Doings |newspaper=[[The New York Times]]|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1944/06/25/archives/london-movie-doings-wind-ends-historic-run-korda-returns-to.html|date=June 25, 1944 |page=X3|last=Lejeune|first=C. A.|author-link=C. A. Lejeune|access-date=June 15, 2024}}</ref> By the time MGM withdrew it from circulation at the end of 1943, its worldwide distribution had returned a [[gross rental]] (the studio's share of the box office gross) of $32&nbsp;million, making it the [[Timeline of highest-grossing films|most profitable film ever made up to that point]].<ref name="tcm articles" /><ref name="Bartel"/> It eventually opened in Japan in September 1952 and became the highest-grossing foreign film there.<ref>{{cite magazine|magazine=[[Variety (magazine)|Variety]]|title='Wind,' 'Winchester' Top Film Grossers In Japan|date=October 8, 1952|page=14|url=https://archive.org/stream/variety188-1952-10#page/n141/mode/1up|access-date=January 18, 2021|via=[[Archive.org]]}}</ref><ref>{{cite magazine|magazine=[[Variety (magazine)|Variety]]|date=March 7, 1984|title=All-Time Foreign Grossers In Japan|page=89}}</ref>

[[File:Crowds line up to see "Gone with the Wind" in Pensacola, Florida (1947).jpg|thumb|left|Line up to see ''Gone with the Wind'' in Pensacola, Florida (1947)]]

The international response to ''Gone with the Wind'' was volatile, and its immense scale and emotional resonance provoked political intervention. It was banned in Nazi-occupied Europe, although it was reportedly being favored by government officials. Despite the prohibition, copies were smuggled into occupied territories for private screenings, to the dismay of propaganda authorities.<ref name="Singer">{{cite web |last=Singer |first=Saul |date=June 15, 2022|title=Gone With the Wind in Nazi Germany and Eretz Yisrael |url=https://jewishpress.com/sections/features/features-on-jewish-world/gone-with-the-wind-in-nazi-germany-and-eretz-yisrael/2022/06/15/ |website=The Jewish Press |access-date=January 18, 2026}}</ref> In early 1942 Tokyo, a select group of Japanese military officers and filmmakers viewed a double feature of ''Gone with the Wind'' and [[Disney]]'s ''[[Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs (1937 film)|Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs]]'', both obtained after the British surrender in Singapore. Despite Japan's early wartime successes, the advanced technology and production quality of these films caused despair among the viewers, who questioned how Japan could possibly defeat a nation capable of such cinematic achievements.<ref>{{cite news |last=Schaller |first=Michael |date=November 3, 2019 |title='Gone With the Wind' viewed in 1939 Brooklyn, Berlin & Tokyo |url=https://tucson.com/opinion/local/ua-prof-michael-schaller-gone-with-the-wind-viewed-in-1939-brooklyn-berlin-tokyo/article_f6dd3a0d-8bc6-54c7-bbe6-3fd53014e4aa.html |work=[[Arizona Daily Star]] |access-date=January 15, 2026}}</ref> At a gala premiere attended by approximately 2,500 people in the Soviet Union, ''Gone with the Wind'' resonated deeply with audiences amid the country's own period of upheaval. Viewer Nelli Bersineva noted "Scarlett definitely has a Russian character." [[Leningrad]] mayor Anatoly A. Sobchak highlighted the contemporary relevance, saying "we see how American people lived through their war and changed their lives".<ref>{{cite news |last= |first= |date=October 22, 1990|title=A Popular Soviet Premiere |url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1990-10-22-ca-2313-story.html |work=Los Angeles Times |access-date=January 18, 2026}}</ref>

Even though it earned its investors roughly twice as much as the previous record-holder, ''The Birth of a Nation'',<ref name="Finler">{{cite book |last=Finler |first=Joel Waldo |year=2003 |title=The Hollywood Story |publisher=[[Wallflower Press]] |isbn=978-1-903364-66-6 |pages=[https://books.google.com/books?id=rvVhEJmbfrsC&pg=PA47 47], [https://books.google.com/books?id=rvVhEJmbfrsC&pg=PA356 356]–363}}</ref><ref name="Time (1940)">{{cite magazine|title=Show Business: Record Wind |date=February 19, 1940 |magazine=[[Time (magazine)|Time]] |url=http://www.time.com/time/magazine/article/0,9171,763541,00.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100202110029/http://www.time.com/time/magazine/article/0%2C9171%2C763541%2C00.html |archive-date=February 2, 2010 |url-status=dead |access-date=January 19, 2013}}</ref> the [[box-office]] performances of the two films were likely much closer. The bulk of the earnings from ''Gone with the Wind'' came from its roadshow and first-run engagements, where the distributor received 70 percent and 50 percent of the box-office gross, respectively, rather than its general release, which at the time typically saw the distributor's share set at 30–35 percent of the gross.<ref name="Schatz (1999)" /> In the case of ''The Birth of a Nation'', its distributor, Epoch, sold off many of its distribution territories on a "states rights" basis—which typically amounted to 10 percent of the box-office gross—and Epoch's accounts are only indicative of its own profits from the film, and not the local distributors. [[Carl E. Milliken]], secretary of the [[Motion Picture Producers and Distributors Association]], estimated that ''The Birth of a Nation'' had been seen by fifty million people by 1930.<ref name="Stokes">{{cite book |last=Stokes |first=Melvyn |title=D.W. Griffith's the Birth of a Nation: A History of the Most Controversial Motion Picture of All Time |year=2008 |publisher=[[Oxford University Press]] |isbn=978-0-19-533678-8 |pages=[https://books.google.com/books?id=fGJFpiTjbKwC&pg=PA119 119] & [https://books.google.com/books?id=fGJFpiTjbKwC&pg=PA287 287]}}</ref><ref name="Grieveson">{{cite book |last=Grieveson |first=Lee |title=Policing Cinema: Movies and Censorship in Early-Twentieth-Century America |year=2004 |publisher=[[University of California Press]] |isbn=978-0-520-23966-1 |page=[https://archive.org/details/policingcinemamo00grie_0/page/308 308] |url=https://archive.org/details/policingcinemamo00grie_0/page/308}}</ref>

When re-released in 1947, it earned a $5 million rental in the United States and Canada and was one of the year's top ten releases.<ref name="Shearer" /><ref name="Finler" /> Successful re-releases in 1954 and 1961 enabled it to retain its position as the industry's top earner, despite substantial challenges from more recent films such as ''Ben-Hur'',<ref name="Thomas (1963)">{{cite news |last=Thomas |first=Bob |author-link=Bob Thomas (reporter) |agency=[[Associated Press]] |work=[[The Robesonian]] |title=Movie Finances Are No Longer Hidden From Scrutiny |date=August 1, 1963 |page=[https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=QsBVAAAAIBAJ&sjid=iUANAAAAIBAJ&pg=7022,1836881 10] }}</ref> but it was finally overtaken by ''[[The Sound of Music (film)|The Sound of Music]]'' in 1966.<ref name="Berkowitz">{{cite book |last=Berkowitz |first=Edward D. |title=Mass Appeal: The Formative Age of the Movies, Radio, and TV |series=Cambridge Essential Histories |year=2010 |publisher=[[Cambridge University Press]] |isbn=978-0-521-88908-7 |page=[https://books.google.com/books?id=ofKqd-ElfaoC&pg=PA160 160] |author-link=Edward Berkowitz}}</ref>

The 1967 reissue was unusual because MGM chose to roadshow it, which turned it into the most successful re-release in the industry's history. It generated a box-office gross of $68&nbsp;million, making it MGM's most lucrative film after ''[[Doctor Zhivago (film)|Doctor Zhivago]]'' from the latter half of the decade.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Hall |first1=Sheldon |last2=Neale |first2=Stephen |title=Epics, Spectacles, and Blockbusters: A Hollywood History |year=2010 |publisher=[[Wayne State University Press]] |isbn=978-0-8143-3008-1 |pages=[https://books.google.com/books?id=jhvrSwOOsRgC&pg=PA181 181]–[https://books.google.com/books?id=jhvrSwOOsRgC&pg=PA182 182] |author-link=Sheldon Hall (film historian)}}</ref> MGM earned a rental of $41&nbsp;million from the release,<ref name="Thomas (1971)">{{cite news |last=Thomas |first=Bob |author-link=Bob Thomas (reporter) |title=Reissues Playing Big Role in Movie Marketing Today |date=May 6, 1971 |agency=[[Associated Press]] |work=[[The Register-Guard]] |page=[https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=hLRVAAAAIBAJ&sjid=L-EDAAAAIBAJ&pg=6732,1474472 9E]}}</ref> with the U.S. and Canadian share amounting to over $30&nbsp;million, placing it second only to ''[[The Graduate]]'' for that year.<ref name="Finler" /><ref name="Thomas (1971)" /> Including its $6.7&nbsp;million rental from the 1961 reissue,<ref>{{cite book |last=Kay |first=Eddie Dorman |title=Box Office Champs: The Most Popular Movies of the Last 50 Years |year=1990 |publisher=[[Random House Value Publishing]] |isbn=978-0-517-69212-7 |page=92}}</ref> it was the fourth highest-earner of the decade in the North American market, with only ''The Sound of Music'', ''The Graduate'' and ''Doctor Zhivago'' making more for their distributors.<ref name="Finler" /> A further re-release in 1971 allowed it to briefly recapture the record from ''The Sound of Music'', bringing its total worldwide gross rental to about $116&nbsp;million by the end of 1971—more than trebling its earnings from its initial release—before losing the record again the following year to ''[[The Godfather]]''.<ref name="Kramer" /><ref name="Atlantic Monthly (1973)">{{cite news |first=Anna |last=Akhmatova |title=Gone With the Wind |work=[[The Atlantic Monthly]] |year=1973 |volume=231 |page=[https://books.google.com/books?id=38wmAQAAIAAJ&q=%22As%20of%20the%20end%20of%201971,%20GWTW%20stood%20as%20the%20all-time%20money-drawing%20movie%22 2] |quote=As of the end of 1971, GWTW stood as the all-time money-drawing movie, with a take of $116&nbsp;million, and, with this year's reissues, it should continue to run ahead of the second place contender and all-time ''kaffee-mit-schlag'' spectacle.}}</ref>

Across all releases, it is estimated that ''Gone with the Wind'' has sold over [[List of highest-grossing films in Canada and the United States adjusted for inflation|200&nbsp;million tickets in the United States and Canada]],<ref name="Young" /> generating more theater admissions in that territory than any other film.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.boxofficemojo.com/alltime/adjusted.htm?adjust_yr=1&p=.htm |title=Domestic Grosses – Adjusted for Ticket Price Inflation |work=[[Box Office Mojo]] |access-date=February 8, 2013 |archive-date=April 12, 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140412013351/http://www.boxofficemojo.com/alltime/adjusted.htm?adjust_yr=1&p=.htm |url-status=live }}</ref> The film was phenomenally successful in [[Western Europe]] too, generating approximately [[List of highest-grossing films in the United Kingdom by box-office admissions|35&nbsp;million tickets in the United Kingdom]] and over [[List of highest-grossing films in France|16&nbsp;million in France]], respectively becoming the biggest and sixth-biggest ticket-sellers in those markets.<ref>{{cite news |title=Gone with the Wind tops film list |date=November 28, 2004 |work=[[BBC News]] |url=https://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/entertainment/4049645.stm |access-date=June 9, 2011 |archive-date=June 15, 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120615222149/http://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/entertainment/4049645.stm |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=The Ultimate Film Chart |publisher=[[British Film Institute]] |url=http://old.bfi.org.uk/features/ultimatefilm/chart/index.php |access-date=August 9, 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181107001631/http://old.bfi.org.uk/features/ultimatefilm/chart/index.php |archive-date=November 7, 2018 |url-status=dead }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Top 250 tous les temps en France (Reprises incluses) |publisher=JP's Box-Office |url=http://www.jpbox-office.com/top100.php?view=2 |access-date=December 2, 2017 |archive-date=March 31, 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180331112258/http://www.jpbox-office.com/top100.php?view=2 |url-status=live }}</ref> Its appeal has endured overseas, sustaining a popularity similar to its domestic longevity; in 1975 it played to capacity audiences every night during the first three weeks of its run at London's Plaza 2 Theatre, and in Japan it generated over half a million admissions at twenty theaters during a five-week engagement.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Taylor |first1=Richard |title=Peckinpah's latest: Don't do it again, Sam |url=https://newspaperarchive.com/alton-telegraph-dec-20-1975-p-22/ |access-date=April 15, 2022 |work=[[Alton Telegraph]] |via=[[NewspaperArchive]] |date=December 20, 1975 |page=22 |url-access=subscription |quote=Currently, in its sixth reissue in Japan, playing 20 theatres for a five-week engagement, ''Gone With the Wind'' has grossed $1,547,277 and has played to 501,377 customers.<br> In London, playing at the 826-seat Plaza 2 Theatre for the past three weeks, it has grossed over $75,000 with capacity performances every night of the run to date.}}</ref> In total, ''Gone with the Wind'' grossed over $390&nbsp;million globally at the box office;<ref>{{cite web |title=Gone with the Wind |work=[[The Numbers (website)|The Numbers]] |publisher=Nash Information Services |url=http://www.the-numbers.com/movie/Gone-with-the-Wind#tab=summary |access-date=February 8, 2013 |archive-date=March 26, 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140326031139/http://www.the-numbers.com/movie/Gone-with-the-Wind#tab=summary |url-status=live }}</ref> in 2007 Turner Entertainment estimated the gross to be equivalent to approximately $3.3&nbsp;billion when adjusted for [[inflation]] to current prices;<ref name="tcm articles" /> ''[[Guinness World Records]]'' arrived at a figure of $3.44&nbsp;billion in 2014 making it the [[List of highest-grossing films adjusted for inflation|most successful film in cinema history]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Highest Box Office Film Gross – Inflation Adjusted |year=2014 |publisher=[[Guinness World Records]] |url=http://www.guinnessworldrecords.com/world-records/highest-box-office-film-gross-inflation-adjusted/ |access-date=February 9, 2015 |archive-date=February 9, 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150209121955/http://www.guinnessworldrecords.com/world-records/highest-box-office-film-gross-inflation-adjusted/ |url-status=live }}</ref>

''Gone with the Wind'' remains popular with audiences into the 21st century, having been [[List of films considered the best#Audience polls|voted the most popular film]] in two nationwide polls of Americans undertaken by [[Harris Insights & Analytics|Harris Interactive]] in 2008, and again in 2014. The market research firm surveyed over two thousand U.S. adults, with the results weighted by age, sex, race/ethnicity, education, region, and household income, so their proportions matched the composition of the adult population.<ref>{{cite press release |first=Regina A. |last=Corso |title=Frankly My Dear, The Force is With Them as Gone With the Wind and Star Wars are the Top Two All Time Favorite Movies |date=February 21, 2008 |publisher=[[Harris Insights & Analytics|Harris Interactive]] |url=http://media.theharrispoll.com/documents/Harris-Interactive-Poll-Research-Frankly-My-Dear-The-Force-is-With-Them-as-Gone-Wit-2008-02.pdf |access-date=July 9, 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130614055709/http://www.harrisinteractive.com/vault/Harris-Interactive-Poll-Research-Frankly-My-Dear-The-Force-is-With-Them-as-Gone-Wit-2008-02.pdf |archive-date=June 14, 2013 |url-status=dead  }}</ref><ref>{{cite press release |first=Larry |last=Shannon-Missal |title=Gone but Not Forgotten: Gone with the Wind is Still America's Favorite Movie |date=December 17, 2014 |publisher=[[Harris Insights & Analytics|Harris Interactive]] |url=http://www.theharrispoll.com/health-and-life/Gone_but_Not_Forgotten__Gone_with_the_Wind_is_Still_America_s_Favorite_Movie.html |access-date=July 9, 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141228064846/http://www.harrisinteractive.com/NewsRoom/HarrisPolls/tabid/447/ctl/ReadCustom%20Default/mid/1508/ArticleId/1535/Default.aspx |archive-date=December 28, 2014 |url-status=dead}}</ref>

===Critical re-evaluation===
{{Quote box
| title = [[AFI 100 Years... series]]
| source = American Film Institute<ref name="afi-lists">{{cite web |title=AFI's 100 Years...The Complete Lists |work=[[American Film Institute]] |url=http://www.afi.com/100Years/downloads.aspx |access-date=February 27, 2013 |archive-date=April 26, 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140426215135/http://www.afi.com/100years/downloads.aspx |url-status=live }}</ref>
| quote = 
* [[AFI's 100 Years...100 Movies]] – #4
* [[AFI's 100 Years...100 Passions]] – #2
* [[AFI's 100 Years...100 Movie Quotes]]:
** "[[Frankly, my dear, I don't give a damn]]." – #1
** "After all, tomorrow is another day!" – #31
** "As God is my witness, I'll never be hungry again." – #59
* [[AFI's 100 Years of Film Scores]] – #2
* [[AFI's 100 Years...100 Cheers]] – #43
* [[AFI's 100 Years...100 Movies (10th Anniversary Edition)]] – #6
* [[AFI's 10 Top 10]] – #4 [[Epic film]]
| style = "text-align:right;" | salign = right | width = 25em | bgcolor = #F0EAD6
}}
When revisiting ''Gone with the Wind'' in the 1970s, [[Arthur M. Schlesinger Jr.]] believed that Hollywood films generally age well, revealing an unexpected depth or integrity, but in the case of ''Gone with the Wind'' time has not treated it kindly.<ref name="Schlesinger">{{cite news |first=Arthur |last=Schlesinger |author-link=Arthur M. Schlesinger, Jr. |work=[[The Atlantic Monthly]] |date=March 1973 |title=Time, Alas, Has Treated Gone with the Wind Cruelly |volume=231 |issue=3 |page=64 |url=https://www.theatlantic.com/past/docs/issues/73mar/schles.htm |access-date=February 16, 2013 |archive-date=May 21, 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130521215711/http://www.theatlantic.com/past/docs/issues/73mar/schles.htm |url-status=live }}</ref> [[Richard Schickel]] argued that one measure of a film's quality is to ask what the viewer can remember of it, and the film falls down in this regard: unforgettable imagery and dialogue are not present.<ref name="Schickel">{{cite news |first=Richard |last=Schickel |author-link=Richard Schickel |work=[[The Atlantic Monthly]] |date=March 1973 |title=Glossy, Sentimental, Chuckle-headed |volume=231 |issue=3 |page=71 |url=https://www.theatlantic.com/past/docs/issues/73mar/schick.htm |access-date=February 16, 2013 |archive-date=May 21, 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130521070918/http://www.theatlantic.com/past/docs/issues/73mar/schick.htm |url-status=live }}</ref> [[Stanley Kauffmann]], likewise, also found the film to be a largely forgettable experience, claiming he could only remember two scenes vividly.<ref name="Kauffmann">{{cite news |first=Stanley |last=Kauffman |author-link=Stanley Kauffmann |work=[[The Atlantic Monthly]] |date=March 1973 |title=The Romantic Is Still Popular |volume=231 |issue=3 |page=61 |url=https://www.theatlantic.com/past/docs/issues/73mar/kauff.htm |access-date=February 16, 2013 |archive-date=May 21, 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130521071121/http://www.theatlantic.com/past/docs/issues/73mar/kauff.htm |url-status=live }}</ref> Both Schickel and Schlesinger put this down to it being "badly written", in turn describing the dialogue as "flowery" and possessing a "picture postcard" sensibility.<ref name="Schlesinger" /><ref name="Schickel" /> Schickel also believes the film fails as popular art in that it has limited rewatch value{{emdash}}a sentiment that Kauffmann also concurs with, stating that having watched it twice he hopes "never to see it again: twice is twice as much as any lifetime needs".<ref name="Schickel" /><ref name="Kauffmann" /> Both Schickel and [[Andrew Sarris]] identify the film's main failing is in possessing a producer's sensibility rather than an artistic one: having gone through so many directors and writers the film does not carry a sense of being "created" or "directed", but rather having emerged "steaming from the crowded kitchen", where the main creative force was a producer's obsession in making the film as literally faithful to the novel as possible.<ref name="Schickel" /><ref name="Sarris">{{cite news |first=Andrew |last=Sarris |author-link=Andrew Sarris |work=[[The Atlantic Monthly]] |date=March 1973 |title=This Moviest of All Movies |volume=231 |issue=3 |page=58 |url=https://www.theatlantic.com/past/docs/issues/73mar/sarris.htm |access-date=February 16, 2013 |archive-date=May 21, 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130521071117/http://www.theatlantic.com/past/docs/issues/73mar/sarris.htm |url-status=live }}</ref>

Sarris concedes that despite its artistic failings, the film does hold a mandate around the world as the "single most beloved entertainment ever produced".<ref name="Sarris" /> [[Judith Crist]] observes that, kitsch aside, the film is "undoubtedly still the best and most durable piece of popular entertainment to have come off the Hollywood assembly lines", the product of a showman with "taste and intelligence".<ref name="Crist">{{cite news |first=Judith |last=Crist |author-link=Judith Crist |work=[[The Atlantic Monthly]] |date=March 1973 |title=Glorious Excesses |volume=231 |issue=3 |page=67 |url=https://www.theatlantic.com/past/docs/issues/73mar/crist.htm |access-date=February 16, 2013 |archive-date=May 21, 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130521215717/http://www.theatlantic.com/past/docs/issues/73mar/crist.htm |url-status=live }}</ref> Schlesinger notes that the first half of the film does have a "sweep and vigor" that aspire to its epic theme, but agreed with criticisms of the personal lives taking over in the second half, and how it ends up losing its theme in unconvincing sentimentality.<ref name="Schlesinger" /> Kauffmann also finds interesting parallels with ''The Godfather'', which had just replaced ''Gone with the Wind'' as the highest-grosser at the time: both were produced from "ultra-American" best-selling novels, both live within codes of honor that are romanticized, and both in essence offer cultural fabrication or revisionism.<ref name="Kauffmann" />

The critical perception of the film has shifted in the intervening years, which resulted in it being ranked 235th in ''[[Sight & Sound]]''{{'}}s prestigious [[decennial]] critics poll in 2012,<ref name="sight and sound" /> and in 2015 sixty-two international film critics polled by the [[BBC]] voted it the 97th best American film.<ref>{{cite web |title=The 100 Greatest American Films |date=July 20, 2015 |publisher=[[BBC]] |url=http://www.bbc.com/culture/story/20150720-the-100-greatest-american-films |access-date=July 21, 2015 |archive-date=September 16, 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160916105535/http://www.bbc.com/culture/story/20150720-the-100-greatest-american-films |url-status=live }}</ref> To commemorate the twentieth anniversary of [[Turner Classic Movies]] (TCM) in 2014, the channel chose again to screen ''Gone with the Wind'', the first film ever broadcast on TCM.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Drumm |first=Diana |date=April 8, 2014 |title=How Turner Classic Movies Redefines The Idea of Classic Film |url=https://www.indiewire.com/features/general/how-turner-classic-movies-redefines-the-idea-of-classic-film-28037/ |archive-url=https://archive.today/20240618155456/https://www.indiewire.com/features/general/how-turner-classic-movies-redefines-the-idea-of-classic-film-28037/ |archive-date=June 18, 2024 |access-date=June 18, 2024 |website=[[IndieWire]]}}</ref> Discussing its re-release into theaters that year, film historian and TCM host [[Robert Osborne]] stated, "The amazing thing to me is that ''Gone with the Wind'' has endured and triumphed even in a very changed world 75 years later. It still affects people in the same way as it did then."<ref>{{Cite web |last=Alexander |first=Bryan |title=What endures as 'Gone with the Wind' turns 75 |url=https://www.usatoday.com/story/life/movies/2014/09/21/gone-with-the-wind-75th-anniversary/15446623/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140925095944/https://www.usatoday.com/story/life/movies/2014/09/21/gone-with-the-wind-75th-anniversary/15446623/ |archive-date=September 25, 2014 |access-date=June 18, 2024 |website=[[USA Today]]}}</ref>

===Industry recognition===
The film has featured in several high-profile industry polls. It was selected as the greatest film of the past half-century in a 1950 poll conducted by ''[[Variety (magazine)|Variety]]'' of more than 200 professionals who had worked in the film industry for over 25 years.<ref>{{Cite news |date=February 23, 1950 |title=Variety poll, best actor, actress, and film of the past 50 years |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-birmingham-post-variety-poll-best-a/149104495/ |access-date=June 19, 2024 |work=[[The Birmingham Post]] |page=4}}</ref> In 1977 it was voted the most popular film by the [[American Film Institute]] (AFI), in a poll of the organization's membership;<ref name="tcm notes" /> the AFI also ranked the film fourth on its "[[AFI's 100 Years...100 Movies|100 Greatest Movies]]" list in 1998,<ref name="afi-movie">{{cite web |title=AFI's 100 Years...100 Movies |publisher=[[American Film Institute]] |date=June 1998 |url=http://www.afi.com/100Years/movies.aspx |access-date=February 27, 2013 |archive-date=May 15, 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160515202027/http://www.afi.com/100years/movies.aspx |url-status=live }}</ref> with it slipping down to sixth place in the [[AFI's 100 Years...100 Movies (10th Anniversary Edition)|tenth anniversary edition]] in 2007.<ref name="afi-movie-10th">{{cite web |title=AFI's 100 Years...100 Movies (10th Anniversary Edition) |publisher=[[American Film Institute]] |date=June 20, 2007 |url=http://www.afi.com/100Years/movies10.aspx |access-date=February 27, 2013 |archive-date=August 18, 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150818175815/http://www.afi.com/100Years/movies10.aspx |url-status=live }}</ref> In 2014, it placed fifteenth in an extensive poll undertaken by ''[[The Hollywood Reporter]]'', which balloted every studio, agency, publicity firm and production house in the [[Hollywood, Los Angeles|Hollywood]] region.<ref>{{cite news |title=Hollywood's 100 Favorite Films |date=June 25, 2014 |work=[[The Hollywood Reporter]] |url=http://www.hollywoodreporter.com/lists/best-hollywood-movies-all-time-818512 |access-date=July 13, 2014 |archive-date=September 14, 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150914055722/http://www.hollywoodreporter.com/lists/best-hollywood-movies-all-time-818512 |url-status=live }}</ref> Film directors ranked it 322nd in the 2012 edition of the decennial ''Sight & Sound'' poll,<ref name="sight and sound">{{cite web |title=Votes for Gone with the Wind (1939) |year=2012 |publisher=[[British Film Institute]] |url=http://www.bfi.org.uk/films-tv-people/4ce2b6ab5808b/sightandsoundpoll2012 |access-date=February 16, 2018 |archive-date=February 17, 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180217211407/http://www.bfi.org.uk/films-tv-people/4ce2b6ab5808b/sightandsoundpoll2012 |url-status=dead }}</ref> and in 2016 it was selected as the ninth best "directorial achievement" in a [[Directors Guild of America]] members poll.<ref>{{cite web |title=The 80 Best-Directed Films |date=Spring 2016 |publisher=[[Directors Guild of America]] |url=http://www.dga.org/Craft/DGAQ/All-Articles/1602-Spring-2016/80th-Film-Poll.aspx |access-date=May 4, 2016 |archive-date=May 3, 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160503234209/http://www.dga.org/Craft/DGAQ/All-Articles/1602-Spring-2016/80th-Film-Poll.aspx |url-status=live }}</ref> In 2006, the [[Writers Guild of America]] voted its screenplay twenty-third in its list of 101 greatest screenplays.<ref>{{Cite news |title=101 Greatest Screenplays – The List |publisher=[[Writers Guild of America, East]] |date=2006 |url=https://www.wgaeast.org/101-lists/101-greatest-screenplays/list/  |access-date=January 2, 2026 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190629183833/https://www.wgaeast.org/101-lists/101-greatest-screenplays/list/ |archive-date=June 29, 2019 |language=en |url-status=live}}</ref> 

''Gone with the Wind'' was one of the twenty-five inaugural films selected for preservation in the [[National Film Registry]] by the United States [[Library of Congress]] in 1989 for being "culturally, historically, or aesthetically significant".<ref>{{cite web |title=National Film Preservation Board: Film Registry – Complete National Film Registry Listing |publisher=[[Library of Congress]] |url=https://www.loc.gov/programs/national-film-preservation-board/film-registry/complete-national-film-registry-listing/ |access-date=December 14, 2017 |archive-date=October 31, 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161031213743/https://www.loc.gov/programs/national-film-preservation-board/film-registry/complete-national-film-registry-listing/ |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=National Film Preservation Board: Film Registry – Nominate |publisher=[[Library of Congress]] |url=https://www.loc.gov/programs/national-film-preservation-board/film-registry/nominate/ |access-date=December 14, 2017 |archive-date=December 16, 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171216173647/https://www.loc.gov/programs/national-film-preservation-board/film-registry/nominate/ |url-status=live }}</ref>

==Analysis and controversies==

===Historical portrayal===
Though not always historically precise, ''Gone with the Wind'' largely captured the spirit and ethos of the era it depicts. Producer David Selznick wrote "I am most sensitive to the feelings of minority people", and assured his avoidance of promoting intolerance during fascist times.<ref name="Singer"/> Nevertheless, the film has been criticized as having perpetuated [[American Civil War|Civil War]] myths and [[Stereotypes of African Americans|black stereotypes]].<ref name="Hernan">{{cite book |first1=Hernán |last1=Vera |first2=Andrew Mark |last2=Gordon |year=2003 |title=Screen Saviors: Hollywood Fictions of Whiteness |publisher=[[Rowman & Littlefield]] |isbn=978-0-8476-9947-6 |page=[https://books.google.com/books?id=6ZAPD2YdBXYC&pg=PR8 viii] & [https://books.google.com/books?id=6ZAPD2YdBXYC&pg=PA102 102]}}</ref> [[David Reynolds (historian)|David Reynolds]] wrote that, "The white women are elegant, their menfolk are noble or at least dashing. And, in the background, the black slaves are mostly dutiful and content, clearly incapable of an independent existence." Reynolds likened ''Gone with the Wind'' to ''The Birth of a Nation'' and other re-imaginings of the South made during the era of segregation, in which white Southerners are portrayed as defending traditional values, and the issue of slavery is largely ignored.<ref name="Reynolds" /> The film has been described as a "regression" that promotes both the myth of the black rapist and the honorable and defensive role of the [[Ku Klux Klan]] during [[Reconstruction era|Reconstruction]],<ref name="Silk">{{cite book |first1=Catherine |last1=Silk |first2=John |last2=Silk |year=1990 |title=Racism and Anti-Racism in American Popular Culture: Portrayals of African-Americans in Fiction and Film |publisher=[[Manchester University Press]] |isbn=978-0-7190-3070-3 |page=[https://books.google.com/books?id=JtNRAQAAIAAJ&pg=PA141 141]}}</ref> and as a "social propaganda" film offering a "[[white supremacist]]" view of the past.<ref name="Hernan" />

From 1972 to 1996, the [[Atlanta Historical Society]] held several ''Gone with the Wind'' exhibits, among them a 1994 exhibit which was titled "Disputed Territories: ''Gone with the Wind'' and Southern Myths". One of the questions that was explored by the exhibit was "How True to Life Were the Slaves in ''GWTW''?". This section showed that slave experiences were diverse and, as a result, it concluded that the "happy darky" was a myth, as was the belief that all slaves experienced violence and brutality.<ref>{{cite book |last=Dickey |first=Jennifer W. |year=2014 |title=A Tough Little Patch of History: Gone with the Wind and the Politics of Memory |publisher=[[University of Arkansas Press]] |page=[https://books.google.com/books?id=jdtXAwAAQBAJ&pg=PA66 66] |isbn= 978-1-55728-657-4}}</ref> W. Bryan Rommel Ruiz has argued that despite factual inaccuracies in depicting the Reconstruction period, ''Gone with the Wind'' reflects contemporary interpretations of it that were common in the early 20th century. One such viewpoint is reflected in a brief scene in which Mammy fends off a leering [[freedman]]: a politician can be heard offering [[forty acres and a mule|"forty acres and a mule"]] to the emancipated slaves in exchange for their votes. The inference is taken to mean that freedmen are ignorant about politics and unprepared for freedom, unwittingly becoming the tools of corrupt Reconstruction officials.<ref name="Ruiz" /> The phrase "forty acres and a mule" originated with a wartime order proclaimed by General [[William Tecumseh Sherman]], and has come to symbolize the broken promise that [[Reconstruction Era|Reconstruction policies]] would offer economic justice for African Americans.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.freedmen.umd.edu/sfo15.htm|title=Order by the Commander of the Military Division of the Mississippi, January 16, 1865|website=www.freedmen.umd.edu}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |url=http://www.neh.gov/news/humanities/2004-01/reconstruction.html|journal=Humanities|title=Forty Acres and a Mule: The Ruined Hope of Reconstruction|volume=25|issue=1 Jan./Feb|first=Danielle|last=Alexander|year=2004|publisher=National Endowment for the Humanities|location=Washington, D.C.|access-date=19 August 2011|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080916095443/http://neh.gov/news/humanities/2004-01/reconstruction.html|archive-date=16 September 2008|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref>Mitchell, "From Reconstruction to Deconstruction" (2001), p. 506.</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.motherjones.com/politics/2024/06/40-acres-reconstruction-freedmen-bureau-stolen-land/|title=40 Acres and a Lie|website=[[Mother Jones (magazine)|Mother Jones]]|date=2024|access-date=August 12, 2025|archive-date=|archive-url=|url-status=bot: unknown}}</ref>

According Rommel-Ruiz, while perpetuating some [[Lost Cause]] myths, the film makes concessions with regard to others. After Scarlett is attacked in the shanty town by a white man and his black accomplice (and saved by her former slave), a group of men—including Ashley and Scarlett's husband Frank—raid the town; in the novel, they belong to the Ku Klux Klan, representing the common trope of protecting the white woman's virtue, but Rommel Ruiz argues that the filmmakers consciously neutralize the presence of the Klan in the film by simply referring to it as a "political meeting".<ref name="Ruiz">{{cite book |first=W. Bryan |last=Rommel Ruiz |year=2010 |title=American History Goes to the Movies: Hollywood and the American Experience |publisher=[[Taylor & Francis]] |isbn=978-0-203-83373-5 |page=[https://books.google.com/books?id=MEfE-WxwAJwC&pg=PA61 61]}}</ref> Katherine H. Lee writes, "the Klan's presence in the novel is excised from the film—becoming the vigilante group that avenges the attack on Scarlett by changing the race of the attackers from the novel",{{refn|In this respect, Lee's appraisal is incorrect as the film does not change the race of the attackers. As in the novel, the attack is instigated by a white man, assisted by a black man. However, in the film Scarlett is sexually assaulted by the white man, whereas in the novel it is the black man who gropes her.|group=nb}} but characterizes the film as "undeniably racist".<ref>{{cite book |last=Lee |first=Katherine H. |title=The Encyclopedia of Racism in American Films |chapter=Gone with the Wind |editor-last=Jiménez Murguía |editor-first=Salvador |page=226 |publisher=[[Rowman & Littlefield]] |year=2018 |isbn=978-1-4422-6906-4 |chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=c0NRDwAAQBAJ&pg=PA226}}</ref> Richard Alleva remarks that, in the film, "a black man merely restrains Scarlett's horse while his white companion (in a memorable close-up) lowers his leering face toward the unconscious heroine; soon a faithful former slave appears and fights off both attackers. But in the novel, the would-be rapist is black while the white man holds the horse ... Selznick mollified Mitchell's racism throughout."<ref>{{Cite magazine |last=Alleva |first=Richard |title=Hard to Watch |magazine=[[Commonweal (magazine)|Commonweal]] |date=December 19, 2017 |url=https://www.commonwealmagazine.org/hard-watch}}</ref> Jennifer Schuessler of ''The New York Times'' quotes a memo where Selznick wrote, "A group of men can go out and 'get' the perpetrators of an attempted rape without having long white sheets over them."<ref name="Schuessler"/> According to film historian [[Thomas Cripps (film historian)|Thomas Cripps]], Selznick "excised all references to the Ku Klux Klan, renegade Negroes and Southern legends."<ref name="Cripps">{{Cite book |last=Cripps |first=Thomas |title=Recasting: Gone with the Wind in American culture |year=1983 |editor-last=Pyron |editor-first=D. A. |pages=137–141 |chapter=Winds of Change: Gone with the Wind and Racism as a National Issue |publisher=[[University Press of Florida|University Presses of Florida]] |location=Miami |chapter-url=https://archive.org/details/recastinggonewit0000unse/page/137/mode/1up |isbn=0-8130-0747-X |author-link=Thomas Cripps (film historian)}}</ref> Cripps also quotes a memorandum written by Selznick: "I personally feel quite strongly that we should cut out the Klan entirely ... [otherwise, the film] might come out as an unintentional advertisement for intolerant societies in these fascist-ridden times." A solution was to rewrite the rape scene and make (quoting Selznick again) "the negro little more than a spectator."<ref name="Cripps"/>

Thomas Cripps reasons that in some respects, the film undercuts racial stereotypes;<ref name="Smyth">{{cite book |first=J.E. |last=Smyth |year=2006 |title=Reconstructing American Historical Cinema: From Cimarron to Citizen Kane |publisher=[[University Press of Kentucky]] |isbn=978-0-8131-7147-0 |page=[https://archive.org/details/reconstructingam00smyt_0/page/164 164]}}</ref> in particular, the film created greater engagement between Hollywood and black audiences,<ref name="Smyth" /> with dozens of films making small gestures in recognition of the emerging trend.<ref name="Lupack" /> Only a few weeks after its initial run, a story editor at Warner wrote a memorandum to [[Walter Wanger]] about ''Mississippi Belle'', a script that contained the worst excesses of plantation films, suggesting that ''Gone with the Wind'' had made the film "unproducible". More than any film since ''The Birth of a Nation'', it unleashed a variety of social forces that foreshadowed an alliance of white liberals and black people who encouraged the expectation that black people would one day achieve equality. According to Cripps, the film eventually became a template for measuring social change.<ref name="Lupack" />

===21st-century reappraisal===
In the 21st century, criticism of the film's depictions of race and slavery curtailed its availability. In 2017, ''Gone with the Wind'' was pulled from the schedule at the [[Orpheum Theatre (Memphis)|Orpheum Theatre]] in [[Memphis, Tennessee]] after a 34-year run of annual showings.<ref>{{cite news |first=Sasha |last=Savitsky |title='Gone With the Wind' Screenings Pulled from Memphis Theater for Racially 'Insensitive' Content |date=August 28, 2017 |publisher=[[Fox News]] |url=https://www.foxnews.com/entertainment/gone-with-the-wind-screenings-pulled-from-memphis-theater-for-racially-insensitive-content/ |access-date=August 28, 2017 |archive-date=August 28, 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170828141735/http://www.foxnews.com/entertainment/2017/08/28/gone-with-wind-screenings-pulled-from-memphis-theater-for-racially-insensitive-content.html |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{cite news |title=Theatre in Memphis Pulls 'Racially Insensitive' Gone With the Wind |date=August 29, 2017 |work=[[The Guardian]] |url=https://www.theguardian.com/film/2017/aug/29/theatre-in-memphis-pulls-racially-insensitive-gone-with-the-wind |access-date=August 29, 2017 |archive-date=August 29, 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170829013615/https://www.theguardian.com/film/2017/aug/29/theatre-in-memphis-pulls-racially-insensitive-gone-with-the-wind |url-status=live }}</ref> On June 9, 2020, the film was removed from [[HBO Max]] in response to an [[op-ed]] written by screenwriter [[John Ridley]] that was published in that day's edition of the ''[[Los Angeles Times]]'', which called for the streaming service to temporarily remove the film from its content library. He wrote that "it continues to give cover to those who falsely claim that clinging to the iconography of the plantation era is a matter of 'heritage, not hate{{'"}}.<ref>{{cite web |last=Ridley |first=John |title=John Ridley: Why HBO Max should remove 'Gone With the Wind' for now |url=https://www.latimes.com/opinion/story/2020-06-08/hbo-max-racism-gone-with-the-wind-movie |work=Los Angeles Times |date=June 8, 2020 |access-date=June 10, 2020 |archive-date=June 16, 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200616031830/https://www.latimes.com/opinion/story/2020-06-08/hbo-max-racism-gone-with-the-wind-movie |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{cite news |first=Jordan |last=Moreau |title=HBO Max Temporarily Removes 'Gone With the Wind' From Library |date=June 9, 2020 |work=[[Variety (magazine)|Variety]] |url=https://variety.com/2020/film/news/hbo-max-gone-with-the-wind-removed-1234629892/ |access-date=June 10, 2020 |archive-date=June 12, 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200612030331/https://variety.com/2020/film/news/hbo-max-gone-with-the-wind-removed-1234629892/ |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://screenrant.com/hbo-max-removes-gone-wind-protests-racist/|title=HBO Max Silently Removes Gone With The Wind|first=Rebecca|last=Vanacker|work=[[Screen Rant]]|date=June 9, 2020|access-date=June 9, 2020|archive-date=June 10, 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200610024650/https://screenrant.com/hbo-max-removes-gone-wind-protests-racist/|url-status=live}}</ref> A spokesperson for HBO Max said that the film was "a product of its time" and as a result, it depicted "ethnic and racial prejudices" that "were wrong then and are wrong today". It was also announced that the film would return to the streaming service at a later date, although it would incorporate "a discussion of its historical context and a denouncement of those very depictions, but will be presented as it was originally created because to do otherwise would be the same as claiming these prejudices never existed. If we are to create a more just, equitable, and inclusive future, we must first acknowledge and understand our history."<ref>{{cite web | url = https://deadline.com/2020/06/hbo-max-removes-gone-with-the-wind-1202955106/ | title = HBO Max Removes 'Gone With the Wind' From Streaming Platform, Says Film Will Return With "Discussion Of Its Historical Context" | first = Tom | last = Tapp | date = June 9, 2020 | access-date = June 10, 2020 | work = [[Deadline Hollywood]] | archive-date = June 10, 2020 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20200610035615/https://deadline.com/2020/06/hbo-max-removes-gone-with-the-wind-1202955106/ | url-status = live }}</ref>

The film's removal sparked a debate, with film critics and historians criticizing HBO as engaging in [[censorship]].<ref name="TimeGajanan2020" /> Following its withdrawal, the film reached the top of [[Amazon (company)|Amazon]]'s best-sellers sales chart for TV and films, and fifth place on [[Apple Inc.|Apple]]'s [[iTunes Store]] film chart.<ref>{{cite news |first=Todd |last=Spangler |title='Gone With the Wind' Hits No. 1 on Amazon Best-Sellers Chart After HBO Max Drops Movie |date=June 10, 2020 |work=[[Variety (magazine)|Variety]] |url=https://variety.com/2020/digital/uncategorized/gone-with-the-wind-amazon-best-seller-hbo-max-1234630577/ |access-date=June 12, 2020 |archive-date=June 12, 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200612002300/https://variety.com/2020/digital/uncategorized/gone-with-the-wind-amazon-best-seller-hbo-max-1234630577/ |url-status=live }}</ref> HBO Max returned the film to its service later that month, with a new introduction by [[Jacqueline Stewart]].<ref>{{cite interview |interviewer=[[Rachel Martin]] |first=Jacqueline |subject=Stewart |title='Gone With The Wind' Returns To HBO Max With Intro By Expert In African American Film |date=June 29, 2020 |work=[[Morning Edition]] |publisher=[[NPR]] |url=https://www.npr.org/2020/06/29/884551356/gone-with-the-wind-returns-to-hbo-max-with-intro-by-black-scholar |access-date=September 2, 2020 |archive-date=August 6, 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200806122114/https://www.npr.org/2020/06/29/884551356/gone-with-the-wind-returns-to-hbo-max-with-intro-by-black-scholar |url-status=live }}</ref> Stewart described the film, in an op-ed for [[CNN]], as "a prime text for examining expressions of white supremacy in popular culture", and said that "it is precisely because of the ongoing, painful patterns of racial injustice and disregard for Black lives that ''Gone with the Wind'' should stay in circulation and remain available for viewing, analysis and discussion". She described the controversy as "an opportunity to think about what classic films can teach us".<ref>{{cite web |first=Jacqueline |last=Stewart |author-link=Jacqueline Stewart |title=Why we can't turn away from 'Gone with the Wind' |date=June 25, 2020 |publisher=[[CNN]] |url=https://www.cnn.com/2020/06/12/opinions/gone-with-the-wind-illuminates-white-supremacy-stewart/index.html |access-date=September 2, 2020 |archive-date=September 2, 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200902111154/https://www.cnn.com/2020/06/12/opinions/gone-with-the-wind-illuminates-white-supremacy-stewart/index.html |url-status=live }}</ref>

At a political rally in February 2020, President [[Donald Trump]] criticized the [[92nd Academy Awards]] ceremony, stating that ''Gone with the Wind'' and ''[[Sunset Boulevard (film)|Sunset Boulevard]]'' (1950) were more deserving of the award for [[Academy Award for Best Picture|Best Picture]] than that year's winner, the South Korean film ''[[Parasite (2019 film)|Parasite]]''. His comments elicited commentary from critics, and a writer for ''[[Entropy (magazine)|Entropy]]'' magazine opined that they had sparked a backlash from pundits across the political spectrum on [[social media]].<ref>{{Cite web|last=Cooper|first=Kori|date=April 17, 2020|title=A Black Feminist's Response To Trump's Question: 'Can We Get Gone With The Wind Back, Please?'|magazine=[[Entropy (magazine)|Entropy]]|url=https://entropymag.org/a-black-feminists-response-to-trumps-question-can-we-get-gone-with-the-wind-back-please/|access-date=November 28, 2020|archive-date=November 26, 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201126035601/https://entropymag.org/a-black-feminists-response-to-trumps-question-can-we-get-gone-with-the-wind-back-please/|url-status=live |quote=Trump's criticism that films made during Hollywood's Golden Age, namely ''Gone with the Wind'' (1939) and ''Sunset Boulevard'' (1950), films that were not even in the running for the 2020 Oscars, were more deserving of this year's Best Picture Award than ''Parasite'' sparked immediate outcry from pundits across the political spectrum on Twitter.}}</ref>

===Depiction of marital rape===
One of the most notorious and widely condemned scenes in ''Gone with the Wind'' depicts what is now legally defined as [[marital rape]].<ref name="White">{{cite book |last=Sinyard |first=Neil |chapter=Gone With the Wind (1939) |editor1-first=John |editor1-last=White |editor2-first=Sabine |editor2-last=Haenni |year=2009 |title=Fifty Key American Films |series=Routledge Key Guides|publisher=[[Routledge]] |isbn=978-0-203-89113-1 |page=[https://books.google.com/books?id=u7gZRtn44AAC&pg=PA59 59]}}</ref><ref name="Hickok">{{cite book | first=Eugene W. Jr. |last=Hickok |year=1991 |title=The Bill of Rights: Original Meaning and Current Understanding |publisher=[[University of Virginia Press]] |isbn=978-0-8139-1336-0 |page=[https://books.google.com/books?id=Eik_eoTn6KEC&pg=PA103 103] |author-link=Eugene W. Hickok}}</ref> The scene begins with Scarlett and Rhett at the bottom of the staircase, where he begins to kiss her, refusing to be told "no" by the struggling Scarlett;<ref name="Paludi">{{cite book |first=Michele A. |last=Paludi |year=2012 |title=The Psychology of Love |volume=2 |series=Women's Psychology |publisher=[[ABC-CLIO]] |isbn=978-0-313-39315-0 |page=[https://books.google.com/books?id=BtK9MKx8QBQC&pg=PR26 xxvi]}}</ref><ref name="Allison">{{cite book |first1=Julie A. |last1=Allison |first2=Lawrence S. |last2=Wrightsman |year=1993 |title=Rape: The Misunderstood Crime |edition=2 |publisher=[[SAGE Publications]] |isbn=978-0-8039-3707-9 |page=[https://books.google.com/books?id=GI0BXXNQJ-QC&pg=PA90 90] |author2-link=Lawrence Wrightsman}}</ref> Rhett ignores her resistance, scolds her and carries her up the stairs to the bedroom,<ref name="Paludi" /><ref name="Allison" /> and "viewers know that impetuous, strong-willed Scarlett is going to get what's coming to her".<ref name="Pagelow">{{cite book |first1=Mildred Daley |last1=Pagelow |first2=Lloyd W. |last2=Pagelow |year=1984 |title=Family Violence |series=Praeger special studies |publisher=[[ABC-CLIO]] |isbn=978-0-275-91623-7 |page=[https://archive.org/details/familyviolence00page/page/420/mode/2up 420]}}</ref> The next scene, the following morning, shows Scarlett glowing with barely suppressed sexual satisfaction;<ref name="Paludi" /><ref name="Allison" /><ref name="Pagelow" /> Rhett apologizes for his behavior, blaming it on his drinking.<ref name="Paludi" /> The scene has been accused of combining romance and rape by making them indistinguishable from each other,<ref name="Paludi" /> and of reinforcing a notion about [[forced seduction|forced sex]]: that women secretly enjoy it, and it is an acceptable way for a man to treat his wife.<ref name="Pagelow" />

Film critic [[Molly Haskell]] has argued that, nevertheless, for women who are uncritical of the scene, it is by and large consistent with what they have in mind if they [[Rape fantasy|fantasize about being raped]]. Their fantasies revolve around love and romance rather than forced sex; they will assume that Scarlett was not an unwilling sexual partner and wanted Rhett to take the initiative and insist on having sexual intercourse.<ref name="Frus">{{cite book |first=Phyllis |last=Frus |editor-first=J. David |editor-last=Slocum |chapter=Documenting Domestic Violence in American Films |year=2001 |title=Violence in American Cinema |series=Afi Film Readers |publisher=[[Routledge]] |isbn=978-0-415-92810-6 |page=[https://books.google.com/books?id=3bIYD6uo3jQC&pg=RA1-PA231 231]}}</ref>

==Legacy==

===In popular culture===
''Gone with the Wind'' and its production have been explicitly referenced, satirized, dramatized, and analyzed on numerous occasions across a range of media, from contemporaneous works such as ''[[Second Fiddle (1939 film)|Second Fiddle]]''—a 1939 film spoofing the "search for Scarlett"—to current television shows, such as ''[[The Simpsons]]''.<ref name="Hernan" /><ref>{{cite news |last=Nugent |first=Frank S. |author-link=Frank S. Nugent |title=Second Fiddle (1939) The Screen; 'Second Fiddle,' With Tyrone Power and Sonja Heine, Opens at the Roxy—Reports on New Foreign Films |date=July 1, 1939 |work=[[The New York Times]] |url=https://www.nytimes.com/movie/review?res=9E04EFD81F3FE432A25752C0A9619C946894D6CF |access-date=June 19, 2014 |archive-date=August 8, 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140808185412/http://www.nytimes.com/movie/review?res=9E04EFD81F3FE432A25752C0A9619C946894D6CF |url-status=live }}</ref><ref name="Gomez">{{cite book|first=M. Carmen |last=Gómez-Galisteo|title=The Wind Is Never Gone: Sequels, Parodies and Rewritings of Gone with the Wind|year=2011|publisher=[[McFarland & Company]]|isbn=978-0-7864-5927-8|page=173}}</ref> ''[[The Scarlett O'Hara War]]'' (a 1980 television dramatization of the casting of Scarlett),<ref name="allmovie">{{cite web |title=The Scarlett O'Hara War (1980) |work=[[Allmovie]] |publisher=[[Rovi Corporation]] |url=http://www.allmovie.com/movie/the-scarlett-ohara-war-v128737 |access-date=March 2, 2013 |archive-date=June 22, 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130622161527/http://www.allmovie.com/movie/the-scarlett-ohara-war-v128737 |url-status=live }}</ref> ''Moonlight and Magnolias'' (a 2007 play by [[Ron Hutchinson (screenwriter)|Ron Hutchinson]] that dramatizes Ben Hecht's five-day re-write of the script),<ref name="Spencer">{{cite news |first=Charles |last=Spencer |title=Moonlight and Magnolias: Comedy Captures the Birth of a Movie Classic |date=October 8, 2007 |work=[[The Daily Telegraph]] |url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/culture/theatre/drama/3668405/Moonlight-and-Magnolias-Comedy-captures-the-birth-of-a-movie-classic.html |access-date=January 17, 2013 |archive-date=March 23, 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140323113428/http://www.telegraph.co.uk/culture/theatre/drama/3668405/Moonlight-and-Magnolias-Comedy-captures-the-birth-of-a-movie-classic.html |url-status=live |author-link=Charles Spencer (journalist)}}</ref> and "[[Went with the Wind!]]" (a sketch on ''[[The Carol Burnett Show]]'' that parodied the film in the aftermath of its television debut in 1976) are among the more noteworthy examples of its enduring presence in popular culture.<ref name="Bartel" /> It was also the subject of a 1988 documentary, ''[[The Making of a Legend: Gone with the Wind]]'', detailing the film's difficult production history.<ref name="tcm legend">{{cite web |last=Thames |first=Stephanie |title=The Making of a Legend: Gone With The Wind (1988) – Articles |work=TCM database |publisher=[[Turner Classic Movies]] |url=http://www.tcm.com/tcmdb/title/304578/The-Making-Of-A-Legend-Gone-With-The-Wind/articles.html |access-date=March 2, 2013 |archive-date=May 27, 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130527221407/http://www.tcm.com/tcmdb/title/304578/The-Making-Of-A-Legend-Gone-With-The-Wind/articles.html |url-status=dead }}</ref> In 1990, the [[United States Postal Service]] issued a stamp depicting Clark Gable and Vivien Leigh embracing in a scene from the film.<ref name="McAllister">{{cite news |last=McAllister |first=Bill |title=Postal Service Goes Hollywood, Puts Legendary Stars on Stamp |date=March 5, 1990 |work=[[The Daily Gazette]] |page=[https://news.google.com/newspapers?nid=1957&dat=19900303&id=V3UhAAAAIBAJ&sjid=AokFAAAAIBAJ&pg=5191,1080306 B9] }}</ref> In 2003, Leigh and Gable (as Scarlett and Rhett) were ranked number 95 on [[VH1]]'s list of the "200 Greatest Pop Culture Icons of All Time".<ref>{{cite press release |title=The 200 Greatest Pop Culture Icons Complete Ranked List |url=http://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/the-200-greatest-pop-culture-icons-complete-ranked-list-70807437.html |publisher=[[VH1]] |access-date=May 4, 2020 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120114233812/http://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/the-200-greatest-pop-culture-icons-complete-ranked-list-70807437.html |archive-date=January 14, 2012 }}</ref>

The film's release is considered the catalyst in establishing "[[Scarlett (given name)|Scarlett]]" as a feminine given name, shifting its identity away from the [[Scarlet (color)|bright red hue]]. Although the name first appeared in limited numbers following the publication of Margaret Mitchell's novel, it was the film's extraordinary reach and longevity that brought the name into mainstream public consciousness. U.S. birth records show its usage increased more than seven-fold immediately after the film's release, with continued gradual growth in subsequent decades.<ref>{{cite web | title=Baby Name Scarlette | website=Nancy's Baby Names | publisher=Nancy.cc | date=February 29, 2012| url=https://www.nancy.cc/2012/02/29/baby-name-scarlett/ | access-date=January 13, 2026}}</ref>

''Gone with the Wind'' has gone on to develop a [[cult following]], known as "the Windies", who follow the latest news and events surrounding the book and film. They are avid collectors of memorabilia and periodically gather for events, usually in Atlanta, wearing costumes based on the film or dressed as Margaret Mitchell.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Severson |first=Kim |date=April 12, 2011 |title=Frankly, My Dear, the ‘Windies’ Do Live for This |newspaper=[[The New York Times]] |language=en-US |issn=0362-4331 |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2011/04/13/us/13windies.html |access-date=October 10, 2026 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110415015305/https://www.nytimes.com/2011/04/13/us/13windies.html |archive-date=April 15, 2011 |url-access=subscription}}</ref>

===Sequel===
Following the publication of her novel, Margaret Mitchell was inundated with requests for a sequel, but she claimed not to have a notion of what happened to Scarlett and Rhett, and as a result, she had "left them to their ultimate fate". Until her death in 1949, Mitchell continued to resist pressure from Selznick and MGM to write a sequel. In 1975, her brother, Stephens Mitchell (who assumed control of her estate), authorized a sequel that would be jointly produced by MGM and the [[Zanuck/Brown Company]] (through their deal with [[Universal Pictures|Universal Studios]]) on a budget of $12&nbsp;million. [[Anne Edwards]] was commissioned to write the sequel as a novel, which would then be adapted into a screenplay and published in conjunction with the film's release. Edwards submitted a 775-page manuscript which was titled ''Tara, The Continuation of Gone with the Wind'', set between 1872 and 1882 and focusing on Scarlett's divorce from Rhett.<ref name="Bartel" /> [[James Goldman]] was hired to adapt it for the screen, which led to the story being taken in a new direction; whilst Zanuck-Brown was satisfied with Goldman's script, MGM vetoed it, and the deal collapsed.<ref>{{cite news |first=Dennis |last=Brown |title=‘Gone With the Wind’: II : Whatever happened to the sequel? : The attempts to continue Rhett and Scarlett’s tale are a saga in themselves |date=December 10, 1989 |newspaper=[[Los Angeles Times]] |url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1989-12-10-ca-364-story.html |access-date=May 11, 2026}}</ref>

The idea was revived in the 1990s when a sequel was finally produced in 1994 in the form of a television [[miniseries]]. ''[[Scarlett (miniseries)|Scarlett]]'' was based on [[Scarlett (Ripley novel)|the novel]] by [[Alexandra Ripley]], itself a sequel to Mitchell's book. British actors [[Joanne Whalley]] and [[Timothy Dalton]] were cast as Scarlett and Rhett, and the series follows Scarlett's relocation to Ireland after she again becomes pregnant by Rhett.<ref name="scarlett">{{cite web |title=Scarlett (1994) |work=[[Allmovie]] |publisher=[[Rovi Corporation]] |url=http://www.allmovie.com/movie/scarlett-v135447 |access-date=March 3, 2013 |archive-date=March 4, 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140304075741/http://www.allmovie.com/movie/scarlett-v135447 |url-status=live }}</ref>

'''''John Carter''''' (titled on-screen as '''''John Carter of Mars''''') is a 2012 American [[science fiction film|science fiction]] [[action-adventure film]] directed by [[Andrew Stanton]], written by Stanton, [[Mark Andrews (filmmaker)|Mark Andrews]], and [[Michael Chabon]], and based on ''[[A Princess of Mars]]'', the first book in the ''[[Barsoom]]'' series of novels by [[Edgar Rice Burroughs]]. Produced by [[Jim Morris (film producer)|Jim Morris]], [[Colin Wilson (film producer)|Colin Wilson]] and Lindsey Collins, it stars [[Taylor Kitsch]] in the title role, with [[Lynn Collins]], [[Samantha Morton]], [[Mark Strong]], [[Ciarán Hinds]], [[Dominic West]], [[James Purefoy]] and [[Willem Dafoe]] co-starring in supporting roles. It chronicles the first interplanetary adventure of [[John Carter of Mars|John Carter]] and his attempts to mediate [[civil conflict]] amongst the warring kingdoms of [[Barsoom]].

Several attempts to adapt the ''Barsoom'' series had been made since the 1930s by various major studios and producers. Most of these efforts ultimately stalled in [[development hell]]. In the late-2000s, [[Walt Disney Pictures]] began a concerted effort to adapt Burroughs' works to film, after an abandoned venture in the 1980s. The project was driven by Stanton, who had pressed Disney to renew the [[Film rights|screen rights]] from the Burroughs estate. Stanton became the new film's director in 2009. It was his live-action debut, after his directorial work for Disney on [[Pixar]]'s ''[[Finding Nemo]]'' and ''[[WALL-E]]''.<ref name="Den of Geek">{{cite news|url=https://www.denofgeek.com/tv/avengers-endgame-agent-carter-continuity-timeline/|title=What We Know About John Carter|last=Lambie|first=Ryan|date=June 19, 2011|newspaper=Den of Geek|access-date=June 22, 2011}}</ref><ref name="SlashFilmSciretta">{{cite news|url=https://www.slashfilm.com/john-carter-of-mars-to-be-pixars-first-live-action-film-bryan-cranston-joins-cast/|title=John Carter of Mars to be Pixar's First Live Action Film, Bryan Cranston Joins Cast|last=Sciretta|first=Peter|date=January 13, 2011|newspaper=SlashFilm|access-date=June 22, 2011}}</ref> Stanton and his Pixar colleague Andrews wrote the initial draft of the screenplay, which Chabon was brought on to revise.

Filming began in November 2009, with [[principal photography]] underway in January 2010, [[Wrap (filmmaking)|wrapping]] seven months later in July.<ref name="Latino Review">{{cite news|last=Blaber|first=Genevieve|title=Utah is Beginning to Look Like Mars|url=http://www.latinoreview.com/news/utah-is-beginning-to-look-like-mars-7124|access-date=June 22, 2011|newspaper=Latino Review|date=June 12, 2009}}</ref><ref name="standard.net">{{cite news |title=Disney wraps up Mars movie shooting in Utah |newspaper=[[Standard-Examiner]] |date=August 2, 2010 |url=http://www.standard.net/node/47453 |access-date=November 4, 2010 |archive-date=April 2, 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120402054730/http://www.standard.net/node/47453 |url-status=dead }}</ref> [[Michael Giacchino]], who scored many Pixar films, composed the music.<ref name="Los Angeles Times Hero Complex">{{cite news|url=http://herocomplex.latimes.com/2011/06/16/john-carter-andrew-stanton-on-martian-history-comic-con-and-monty-python/|title='John Carter': Andrew Stanton on Martian history, Comic-Con and ... Monty Python?|last=Boucher|first=Geoff|date=June 16, 2011|newspaper=Los Angeles Times|access-date=June 22, 2011}}</ref> As with Pixar's ''[[Brave (2012 film)|Brave]]'' that same year, the film is dedicated to the memory of [[Steve Jobs]], Pixar's CEO and majority shareholder prior to Disney's acquisition in 2006.<ref>{{Cite news|last=Buchanan|first=Kyle|date=February 28, 2012|title=John Carter Dedicated to Steve Jobs|work=[[New York (magazine)|New York]]|url=https://www.vulture.com/2012/02/john-carter-dedicated-to-steve-jobs.html|access-date=June 30, 2020}}</ref>

''John Carter'' had its world premiere at the Regal Cinemas at [[L.A. Live]] in Los Angeles on February 22, 2012, and was released in the United States by [[Walt Disney Studios Motion Pictures]] on March 9, marking the [[centennial]] of the titular character's first appearance. It was presented in [[Disney Digital 3D]], [[RealD 3D]] and [[IMAX 3D]] formats.<ref name="Deadline" /><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.firstshowing.net/2011/first-teaser-poster-for-disneys-john-carter-is-dark-but-not-thrilling/ |title=First Teaser Poster for Disney's 'John Carter' is Dark But Not Thrilling |publisher=FirstShowing.net |date=June 15, 2011 |access-date=January 31, 2016}}</ref><ref name="The Hollywood Reporter">{{cite news|last=McClintock|first=Pamela|title='John Carter of Mars,' 'Frankenweenie' Release Dates Changed|url=https://www.hollywoodreporter.com/news/john-carter-mars-frankenweenie-release-73444|access-date=June 22, 2011|newspaper=The Hollywood Reporter|date=January 19, 2011}}</ref> 

''John Carter'' received mixed reviews, with praise for its visuals, Giacchino's score, and the action sequences, but criticism of the characterization and plot. It failed at the North American box office, but set an opening-day record in Russia.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.hollywoodreporter.com/news/john-carter-box-office-russia-298092 |title='John Carter' Earns Soft $500,000 in Midnight Runs Domestically But Scores Big in Russia |work=[[The Hollywood Reporter]] |date=March 9, 2012 |access-date=April 22, 2012}}</ref> It grossed $284 million at the worldwide box office, resulting in a $200 million [[writedown]] for Disney, becoming one of the [[List of biggest box-office bombs|biggest box office bombs]] in history and also becoming the film with the largest estimated box-office loss adjusted for inflation ever, losing $149–265 million. With a total cost of $350 million, including an estimated production budget of $263 million, it is one of the [[List of most expensive films|most expensive films ever made]]. 

Due to its box office performance, Disney cancelled plans for ''Gods of Mars'' and ''Warlord of Mars,'' the rest of the trilogy Stanton had planned.<ref name="gods" /><ref name="warlord" /> Much of the film's failure has been attributed to its promotion, which has been called "one of the worst marketing campaigns in movie history".<ref name="El País story">{{cite news|last=Güimil|first=Eva|title=A decade on, Disney's 'John Carter' is still remembered for one of the worst marketing campaigns in movie history|url=https://english.elpais.com/culture/2022-03-12/a-decade-on-disneys-john-carter-is-still-remembered-for-one-of-the-worst-marketing-campaigns-in-movie-history.html|newspaper=[[El País]]|date=March 11, 2022|access-date=April 19, 2022}}</ref><ref name="Vulture trailers story">{{cite news|last=Brodesser–Akner|first=Claude|title=The Inside Story of How John Carter Was Doomed by Its First Trailer|url=https://www.vulture.com/2012/03/john-carter-doomed-by-first-trailer.html|newspaper=[[Vulture.com]]|date=March 12, 2012|access-date=April 10, 2012}}</ref><ref name="Washington Post story">{{cite news|last=Cavna|first=Michael|title=The Rant: 'John Carter's' Massive Fallout: Who's to blame for Disney's '$200-million' bomb?|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/blogs/comic-riffs/post/the-rant-john-carters-massive-fallout-whos-to-blame-for-disneys-200-million-bomb/2012/03/19/gIQAOKf6VS_blog.html|newspaper=[[The Washington Post]]|date=March 19, 2012|access-date=April 20, 2022|quote='John Carter' may go down as one of Hollywood's biggest movie flops ever. But it should rightly go down as one of the town's biggest marketing flops ever.}}</ref>

==Plot==
<!--Per [[WP:FILMPLOT]], movie plots are 400 to 700 words ONLY. Please respect this longstanding guideline. -->

In 1881, [[Edgar Rice Burroughs]] arrives at the estate of his recently deceased uncle, John Carter, a former [[American Civil War]] [[Confederate Army]] [[Captain (armed forces)|captain]]. Per Carter's instructions, the body is put in a tomb that can be unlocked only from the inside. His attorney gives Carter's journal to Burroughs, to whom Carter bequeathed his fortune.

In a flashback to 1868 in the [[Arizona Territory]], [[Union Army|Union]] Colonel Powell arrests Carter with hopes that he will help in fighting local [[Apache]]. Carter escapes his holding cell with cavalry soldiers in close pursuit. After a run-in with a band of Apaches, Carter and a wounded Powell hide in a cave that is filled with gold. A mysterious man, later revealed to be a Thern, appears in the cave and attacks them with a knife; Carter kills him but accidentally activates the Thern's medallion and is transported to a ruined and dying planet, Barsoom, known to Carter as Mars. Because of his different bone density and the planet's lower gravity, Carter can jump high and perform feats of incredible strength. He is captured by the Tharks, a nomadic tribe of Green Martians and their Jeddak, Tars Tarkas.

Elsewhere on Barsoom, the Red Martian cities of Helium and Zodanga have been at war for a thousand years. Sab Than, Jeddak of Zodanga, armed with a weapon obtained from the Thern leader Matai Shang, proposes a cease-fire and an end to the war by marrying the Princess of Helium, Dejah Thoris. The Princess escapes and is rescued by Carter.

Carter, Dejah, and Tarkas's daughter, Sola, reach a spot in a sacred river to find a way for Carter to get back to Earth. They discover that the medallions are powered by a "ninth ray" that is also the source of Sab Than's weapon. They are then attacked by a vicious race called the Warhoon under the direction of Shang. Carter and Dejah are taken back to Zodanga. Dejah grudgingly agrees to marry Sab Than and gives Carter instructions on how to use the medallion to return to Earth. Carter decides to stay but is captured by Shang, who explains how Therns manipulate the civilizations of different worlds to their doom, feeding off the planet's resources in the process, and intend to do the same thing with Barsoom by choosing Sab Than to rule the planet. Carter escapes and returns to the Tharks with Sola to request their help. There they discover that a brute, Tal Hajus, has overthrown Tarkas. Carter and an injured Tarkas battle with two enormous Great White-Apes in an arena before Carter kills Hajus, thereby becoming the leader of the Tharks.

The Thark army storms Zodanga, but it is empty; realizing that their army is waiting outside Helium, Carter and the Tharks commandeer the Zodangan airships and fly to Helium. Carter defeats the Zodangan army, while Sab Than is killed and Shang escapes. Carter becomes prince of Helium by marrying Dejah. On their first night, Carter decides to stay on Mars and throws away his medallion. Seizing the opportunity, Shang reappears and gives Carter another challenge by sending him back to Earth. Carter embarks on a long quest to find one of the Therns' medallions on Earth; after several years, he appears to die suddenly and asks for unusual funeral arrangements — consistent with his having found a medallion, since his return to Mars would leave his Earth body in a coma-like state, and makes Burroughs his protector.

Back in the present, Burroughs runs back to Carter's tomb and uses clues to open it. Just as he does, a Thern appears and raises a weapon before Carter appears and shoots the Thern dead. He reveals that he had never found another medallion; instead, he devised a scheme to lure a Thern from hiding, thus winning Shang's challenge. Carter then uses the dead Thern's medallion to return to Barsoom.

* [[Lynn Collins]] as [[Dejah Thoris]], the Princess of Helium.

* [[Willem Dafoe]] as [[Tars Tarkas]], the Jeddak of the Tharks and Sola's father.
* [[Thomas Haden Church]] as Tal Hajus, a vicious Thark who dislikes John Carter and Tars Tarkas.
* [[Mark Strong]] as Matai Shang, the Hekkador of the Therns. 
* [[Ciarán Hinds]] as Tardos Mors, the Jeddak of Helium and Dejah Thoris' father.
* [[Dominic West]] as Sab Than, the Jeddak of Zodanga.
* [[James Purefoy]] as Kantos Kan, the [[Captain|Odwar]] of the ship Xavarian.
* [[Bryan Cranston]] as Colonel Powell, a Union colonel who wants John to help his U.S. cavalry soldiers against the Apache. He is loosely based on James K. Powell from the book.
* [[Daryl Sabara]] as [[Edgar Rice Burroughs|Ned]], John Carter's nephew.
* [[Polly Walker]] as Sarkoja, a merciless Thark who hates Sola.
* [[David Schwimmer]] as a young Thark Warrior, a Thark who informs Tars Tarkas that 18 of the Thark eggs did not hatch.
* [[Jon Favreau]] as the Thark bookmaker, a Thark who collects the bets on any conflict.
* [[Don Stark]] as Dix, a shopkeeper at an Arizona town where John Carter stops.
* [[Nicholas Woodeson]] as Dalton, John Carter's executor who summons Edgar.
* [[Art Malik]] as a Zodangan General.

==Development==
===Origins===
[[File:Princess of Mars large.jpg|right|upright|thumb|Cover of the first edition of ''[[A Princess of Mars]]'' by [[Edgar Rice Burroughs]]]]

{{See also|Barsoom}}
The film is largely based on ''[[A Princess of Mars]]'' (1912), the first in a series of 11 Burroughs novels to feature the interplanetary hero [[John Carter of Mars|John Carter]] (and in later volumes the adventures of his children with [[Dejah Thoris]]). The story was originally serialized in six monthly installments (from February through to July 1912) in the [[pulp magazine]] ''[[The All-Story]]''; those chapters, originally titled "[[Under the Moons of Mars]]", were then collected as a novel and published in hardcover five years later by [[A. C. McClurg]].{{citation needed|date=April 2022}}

===Bob Clampett involvement===
In 1931, director [[Bob Clampett]] approached Edgar Rice Burroughs with the idea of adapting ''A Princess of Mars'' into a feature-length animated film.
