Burroughs responded enthusiastically, recognizing that a regular live-action feature would face various limitations to adapt accurately, so he advised Clampett to write an original animated adventure for John Carter.<ref>{{cite news|first=Jim |last=Korkis |title=Lost Cartoons: The Animated "John Carter of Mars" |publisher=Jim Hill Media |date=June 2, 2003 |url=http://jimhillmedia.com/blogs/jim_korkis/archive/2003/06/02/1093.aspx |access-date=January 2, 2009}}</ref> Working with Burroughs' son John Coleman Burroughs in 1935, Clampett used [[rotoscope]] and other hand-drawn techniques to capture the action, tracing the motions of an athlete who performed John Carter's powerful movements in the reduced Martian gravity, and designed the green-skinned, 4-armed Tharks to give them a believable appearance. He then produced footage of them riding their eight-legged Thoats at a gallop, which had all of their eight legs moving in coordinated motion; he also produced footage of a fleet of rocketships emerging from a Martian volcano. [[Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer]] was originally set to release the cartoons, and the studio heads were enthusiastic about the series.<ref name="glut105-6">{{cite book|last=Glut |first=Donald F. |title=The Frankenstein archive: Essays on the Monster, the Myth, the Movies, and More |pages=105–6 |publisher=McFarland |date=2002 |isbn=0-7864-1353-0}}</ref>

The test footage, produced by 1936,<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.erbzine.com/mag21/2175.html|title=The John Carter Animation Project: Promotional Portfolio by John Coleman Burroughs |publisher= ERBzine (#2175) |date= 2008 |access-date=December 9, 2009}}</ref> received negative reactions from film exhibitors across the U.S., especially in small towns; many gave their opinion that the concept of an Earthman on Mars was too outlandish an idea for midwestern American audiences to accept. The series was not given the go-ahead, and Clampett was instead encouraged to produce an animated ''[[Tarzan]]'' series, an offer that he later declined. Clampett recognized the irony in MGM's decision, as the ''[[Flash Gordon (serial)|Flash Gordon]]'' [[movie serial]], released in the same year by [[Universal Pictures|Universal Studios]], was highly successful. He speculated that MGM believed that serials were played only to children during Saturday matinees, whereas the John Carter tales were intended to be seen by adults during the evening. The footage that Clampett produced was believed lost for many years, until Burroughs' grandson, Danton Burroughs, in the early 1970s found some of the test films in the Edgar Rice Burroughs Inc. archives.<ref name="glut105-6" /> Had ''A Princess of Mars'' been released, it might have preceded [[Walt Disney]]'s ''[[Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs (1937 film)|Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs]]'' (1937) to become the first American feature-length animated film.<ref name="hughes">{{cite book|last=Hughes |first=David |title=The Greatest Science Fiction Movies Never Made |publisher=[[Titan Books]] |date=2008 |pages=311–22 |isbn=978-1-84576-755-6}}</ref>

===Disney progression===
During the late 1950s, [[stop-motion animation]] effects director [[Ray Harryhausen]] expressed interest in filming the novels, but it was not until the 1980s that producers [[Mario Kassar]] and [[Andrew G. Vajna]] bought the rights for [[Walt Disney Studios (division)|the Walt Disney Studios]] via [[Cinergi Pictures]], with a view to creating a competitor to the [[Star Wars original trilogy|original ''Star Wars'' trilogy]] and ''[[Conan the Barbarian (1982 film)|Conan the Barbarian]]''. [[Ted Elliott (screenwriter)|Ted Elliott]] and [[Terry Rossio]] were hired to write, while [[John McTiernan]] and [[Tom Cruise]] were approached to direct and star. The project collapsed because McTiernan realized that visual effects were not yet advanced enough to recreate Burroughs' vision of Barsoom. The project remained at Disney, and [[Jeffrey Katzenberg]] was a strong proponent of filming the novels, but the rights eventually returned to the Burroughs estate.<ref name="hughes" />

===Paramount effort===
Producer [[James Jacks]], who at that time, a partner of Alphaville Films, with [[Sean Daniel]],<ref>{{Cite web |last=McNary |first=Dave |last2=Fleming |first2=Michael |date=2004-03-02 |title=Par, helmer explore ‘Mars’ |url=https://variety.com/2004/film/markets-festivals/par-helmer-explore-mars-1117901036/ |access-date=2026-09-01 |website=Variety |language=en-US}}</ref> read [[Harry Knowles]]' autobiography, which lavishly praised the ''John Carter of Mars'' series. Having read the Burroughs' novels as a child, Jacks was moved to convince [[Paramount Pictures]] to acquire the film rights; a [[bidding war]] with [[Columbia Pictures]] followed. After Paramount and Jacks won the rights, Jacks contacted Knowles to become an adviser on the project and hired [[Mark Protosevich]] to write the screenplay. [[Robert Rodriguez]] signed on in 2004 to direct the film after his friend Knowles showed him the script. Recognizing that Knowles had been an adviser to many other filmmakers, Rodriguez asked him to be credited as a producer.<ref name="hughes" />

Filming was set to begin in 2005, with Rodriguez planning to use the all-digital stages he was using for his production of ''[[Sin City (film)|Sin City]]'', a film based on the [[graphic novel]] series by [[Frank Miller]].<ref name="hughes" /> Rodriguez planned to hire [[Frank Frazetta]], the popular Burroughs and fantasy illustrator, as a designer on the film.<ref>{{cite news|first=Drew |last=McWeeny |title=Holy Crap!! Rodriguez Just Can't Stop!! First SIN CITY, And Now ... PRINCESS OF MARS!!! |work=[[Ain't It Cool News]] |date=March 2, 2004 |url=https://www.aintitcool.com/node/17099 |access-date=December 26, 2011}}</ref> Rodriguez had previously stirred up film industry controversy owing to his decision to credit ''Sin City''{{'}}s artist/creator Miller as co-director on the film adaptation; as a result, Rodriguez decided to resign from the [[Directors Guild of America]]. In 2004, unable to employ a non-DGA filmmaker, Paramount assigned [[Kerry Conran]] to direct and [[Ehren Kruger]] to rewrite the John Carter script. The Australian [[Outback]] was scouted as a shooting location. Conran left the film for unknown reasons and was replaced in October 2005 by [[Jon Favreau]].<ref name="hughes" />

Favreau and screenwriter [[Mark Fergus]] wanted to make their script faithful to Burroughs' novels, retaining John Carter's links to the [[American Civil War]] and ensuring that the Barsoomian [[Tharks]] were {{cvt|15|ft}} tall (previous scripts had made them human-sized). Favreau argued that a modern-day soldier would not know how to fence or ride a horse like Carter, who had been a Confederate officer. The first film he envisioned would have adapted the first three novels in the Barsoom series: ''A Princess of Mars'', ''[[The Gods of Mars]]'', and ''[[The Warlord of Mars]]''. Unlike Rodriguez and Conran, Favreau preferred using [[practical effects]] for his film and cited ''[[Planet of the Apes (1968 film)|Planet of the Apes]]'' (1968) as his inspiration. He intended to use make-up, as well as [[Computer-generated imagery|CGI]], to create the Tharks. In August 2006, Paramount chose not to renew the film rights, preferring instead to focus on its ''[[Star Trek (2009 film)|Star Trek]]'' [[Media franchise|franchise]]. Favreau and Fergus moved on to [[Marvel Studios]]' ''[[Iron Man (2008 film)|Iron Man]]''.<ref name="hughes" />

===Return to Disney, Stanton involvement===
[[File:Andrew Stanton 2012 crop.jpg|thumb|right|Andrew Stanton in 2012]]
[[Andrew Stanton]], director of the [[Pixar Animation Studios]] hits ''[[Finding Nemo]]'' and ''[[WALL-E]]'', lobbied Walt Disney Studios to reacquire the rights from Burroughs' estate. "Since I'd read the books as a kid, I wanted to see somebody put it on the screen," he explained.<ref name="LA Times March 6 story">{{cite news|author=Dawn C. Chmielewski|author2=Rebecca Keegan|title=The planets may not be aligned for 'John Carter'|url=https://www.latimes.com/entertainment/la-xpm-2012-mar-06-la-fi-ct-john-carter-20120306-story.html|newspaper=[[The Los Angeles Times]]|date=March 6, 2012|access-date=April 2, 2012}}</ref>

Stanton then lobbied Disney heavily for the chance to direct the film, [[Pitch (filmmaking)|pitching]] it as "[[Indiana Jones]] on Mars". The studio was initially skeptical. Stanton had never directed a live-action film before, and wanted to make the film without any major stars whose names could guarantee an audience, at least on opening weekend. The screenplay was seen as confusing and difficult to follow. However, since Stanton had overcome similar preproduction doubts to make ''WALL-E'' and ''Finding Nemo'' into hits, the studio approved him as director.<ref name="NYT March 12 article">{{cite news|last=Barnes|first=Brooks|title='Ishtar' Lands on Mars|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2012/03/12/business/media/ishtar-lands-on-mars.html|newspaper=The New York Times|date=March 12, 2012|access-date=April 2, 2012}}</ref> Stanton noted he was effectively being "loaned" to [[Walt Disney Pictures]] because Pixar is an all-ages brand and ''John Carter'', in his words, was "not going to be an all-ages film".<ref>{{cite news|title=WALL-E helmer Andrew Stanton talks John Carter of Mars |first=Fred |last=Topel |work=[[Sci Fi Wire]] |date=January 9, 2009 |url=http://scifiwire.com/2009/01/wall-e-helmer-andrew-stanton-talks-john-carter-of-mars.php |access-date=January 13, 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090218105151/http://scifiwire.com/2009/01/wall-e-helmer-andrew-stanton-talks-john-carter-of-mars.php |archive-date=February 18, 2009}}</ref>

By 2008, the first draft for Part One of a ''John Carter'' film trilogy was completed; the first film is based only on the first novel.<ref>{{cite news|first=Eric |last=Ditzian |title=''John Carter Of Mars'' To Be ''Perfect Definition'' Of Live-Action, CGI Hybrid |work=MTV Movies Blog |date=January 13, 2009 |url=http://moviesblog.mtv.com/2009/01/13/john-carter-of-mars-to-be-perfect-definition-of-live-action-cgi-hybrid/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090115023846/http://moviesblog.mtv.com/2009/01/13/john-carter-of-mars-to-be-perfect-definition-of-live-action-cgi-hybrid/ |url-status=dead |archive-date=January 15, 2009 |access-date=January 18, 2009}}</ref> Stanton and his Pixar colleague [[Mark Andrews (filmmaker)|Mark Andrews]] wrote this draft. In April 2009 author [[Michael Chabon]] confirmed he had been hired to revise Stanton and Andrews' script.<ref name=SlashFilmConnelly>{{cite news|last=Connelly|first=Brendon|title=Michael Chabon|url=https://www.slashfilm.com/michael-chabon-writing-john-carter-of-mars/|access-date=June 23, 2011|newspaper=SlashFilm|date=April 14, 2009}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|title=Chabon Revising ''John Carter of Mars'' Script |work=The Amazing Website of Kavalier & Clay |date=April 9, 2009 |url=http://www.sugarbombs.com/kavalier/?p=166 |access-date=April 9, 2009 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090418054131/http://www.sugarbombs.com/kavalier/?p=166 |archive-date=April 18, 2009  }}</ref><ref name="AOL Cinematical Blog">{{cite news|last=Rappe|first=Elizabeth|title=Michael Chabon Join's Pixar's John Carter of Mars|url=http://blog.moviefone.com/2009/04/15/michael-chabon-joins-pixars-john-carter-of-mars/|access-date=June 23, 2011|newspaper=AOL Cinematical Blog|date=April 15, 2009}}</ref> "I'm really good at structure and collaborating," Stanton explained, "but Michael is just technically, poetically, and intelligence-wise a better writer".<ref name=Friend20110417>{{cite news|last=Friend|first=Ted|title=Second-Act Twist|url=https://www.newyorker.com/reporting/2011/10/17/111017fa_fact_friend?currentPage=all|access-date=April 22, 2012|newspaper=The New Yorker|date=October 17, 2011}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|last=Connelly|first=Brendon|title=John Carter's Producers Talk Me Through Filmmaking: The Andrew Stanton Way|work=Bleeding Cool News And Rumors |date=March 6, 2012 |url=http://www.bleedingcool.com/2012/03/06/john-carters-producers-talk-me-through-filmmaking-the-andrew-stanton-way/|publisher=Bleeding Cool|access-date=April 22, 2012}}</ref>

Following the completion of ''WALL-E'', Stanton visited the archives of [[Edgar Rice Burroughs, Inc.]], in [[Tarzana, California]], as part of his research.<ref name="hughes" /> Jim Morris, [[general manager]] of [[Pixar]], said the film would have a unique look distinct from Frank Frazetta's illustrations, which they both found dated.<ref>{{cite news|first=Patrick |last=Lee |title=New Look For Carter Of Mars? |work=[[Sci Fi Wire]] |date=September 26, 2008 |url=http://www.scifi.com/scifiwire/index.php?category=0&id=60551 |access-date=September 27, 2008 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080926063947/http://www.scifi.com/scifiwire/index.php?category=0&id=60551 |archive-date=September 26, 2008 }}</ref> He also noted that although he had less time for pre-production than for any of his usual animated projects, the task was nevertheless relatively easy since he had read Burroughs' novels as a child and had already visualized many of their scenes.<ref name=SlashFilmTyler>{{cite news|last=Tyler|first=Josh|title=Pixar Talks John Carter of Mars|url=https://www.cinemablend.com/new/Pixar-Talks-John-Carter-Of-Mars-10343.html|access-date=June 23, 2011|newspaper=SlashFilm|date=September 28, 2008|archive-date=August 9, 2011|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110809080915/http://www.cinemablend.com/new/Pixar-Talks-John-Carter-Of-Mars-10343.html|url-status=dead}}</ref> Stanton prepared for directing by losing {{convert|20|lb|kg}}, running {{convert|15|mi|km}} a week, and vowed not to go to his trailer or sit down except when absolutely necessary to avoid looking like "the privileged animation geek who'd cheated his way to the top".<ref name=Friend20110417 />

==Production==

===Casting===
{{Multiple image|perrow = 1|total_width = 200
| align             = right 
| direction         = vertical 
| image1            = Taylor Kitsch 2011 Shankbone.JPG
| caption1          = Taylor Kitsch in 2011
| image2            = Lynn Collins TIFF 2011.jpg
| width2            = 200
| caption2          = Lynn Collins in 2011
}}
Stanton said later he had no grand design for the cast, other than having the villains be played by British actors. "I knew that the cast was going to grow with creatures and it was going to grow with different types of races if we were to continue. And it was going to get a little more fantastical", he said.<ref name="The Wrap story">{{cite news|last=Taylor|first=Drew|title=The Untold Story of Disney's $307 Million Bomb 'John Carter': It's a Disaster'|url=https://www.thewrap.com/john-carter-movie-history-why-it-failed|newspaper=[[TheWrap]]|date=March 9, 2022|access-date=April 9, 2022}}</ref>

Many actors were considered for the title role. Aware that Carter's backstory as an officer in the Confederate Army might be a problem for modern audiences, Stanton envisioned the character as disillusioned and disgusted with war in general, apart from the side he fought on. "I wanted to not absolve him of that, but also not make him pro the side he was on. The best I could do was neutralize him". [[Taylor Kitsch]] quickly became his choice for the part, due to a scene in the ''[[Friday Night Lights (TV series)|Friday Night Lights]]'' television series—his character, angry, is left behind by the bus—that captured Stanton's vision for the character, as Kitsch's pose echoed that of Carter on one cover of the books in Stanton's collection.<ref name="The Wrap story" />

[[Lynn Collins]], a [[Juilliard]] graduate set in her first major movie role as [[Dejah Thoris]] early on, tested with many actors, including [[Josh Duhamel]], using a scene (filmed but cut) where she slaps Carter in the face. "Taylor and I have always had incredible chemistry. It was inevitable that we would get a chance to really explore it and work as a team," she said of her co-star in ''[[X-Men Origins: Wolverine]]'' (2009). She recalls him coming into the dressing room after their test together and, seeing her smoking, told her she would have to quit if she got the part, which she did. At Disney's insistence, she used a British accent.<ref name="The Wrap story" />

Tom Cruise expressed interest in playing the role once production had begun; Collins did not read with him. "I think him and Andrew had some conversations, but I don't think he was ever actually in the mix so to speak", she recalled in 2022, noting that all the actors she read with were 20 years younger than him. Stanton said that as there was at that time the possibility of making two sequels, he kept that in mind. "[I]t would take a while to make these three movies", he recalled. "I'm like, ''How do I feel about how these people might age in the next five to seven years?''"<ref name="The Wrap story" />

[[Willem Dafoe]] and [[Samantha Morton]] played their roles as [[Tharks]] wearing [[motion capture]] suits while walking on [[stilts]]. Cameras attached to their outfits focused on their faces and captured their expressions, which were then used to create their characters' faces. "It's a game, it's a new way of performing", he recalled, noting how physically demanding it was.<ref name="The Wrap story" /> "Always as an actor you're looking for things to jump off from, to find new ways of thinking, new ways of looking, to be turned on in a different way. The stilts were part of that".<ref name="Comingsoon.net Dafoe article">{{cite news|last=Blumeyer|first=Kevin|title=Interview: Willem Dafoe on Becoming Tars Tarkas for 'John Carter'|url=https://www.comingsoon.net/movies/news/563290-john-carter-interview-willem-dafoe-tars-tarkas|newspaper=[[Comingsoon.net]]|date=March 5, 2012|access-date=April 16, 2012}}</ref>

Dafoe also had to do dialogue in Thark, developed for the film by [[Paul Frommer]], who had developed the [[Naʼvi language]] for ''[[Avatar (2009 film)|Avatar]]''. He had worked before with Stanton on ''Finding Nemo'', where he had come to like him. Dafoe found it pleasantly surprising that, given Stanton's background in animation, he refused to rely on the effects. "He really felt like he had to have the movie, so when we started these scenes, there was no 'oh, the CGI will do that' or 'they'll do that in post," he said, which kept the film character-driven.<ref name="Comingsoon.net Dafoe article" />

===Filming===
{{quote box|On '' 'John Carter','' Stanton was crafting a complicated, inter-planetary story with live action period elements and more than 2,000 visual-effects shots delivered by four companies. The director said he coaxed Disney to adopt some of Pixar's iterative style ...|source=—Columnists Dawn C. Chmielewski and Rebecca Keegan, writing in the ''Los Angeles Times''<ref name="LA Times March 6 story" />|align=right|width=30em}}
[[Principal photography]] began at [[Longcross Studios]], England, in January 2010 and ended in [[Kanab, Utah]], in July.<ref name="standard.net" /><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.latinoreview.com/news/john-carter-of-mars-begins-principal-photography-in-london-8994 |title=News: John Carter of Mars Begins Principal Photography In London |publisher=Latino Review |date=January 15, 2010 |access-date=October 7, 2010}}</ref> Other locations in Utah included [[Lake Powell]] and [[Grand County, Utah|Grand]], [[Wayne County, Utah|Wayne]], and [[Kane County, Utah|Kane]] counties.<ref>{{cite news|first=Vince |last=Horiuchi |title=Utah will be stage for Mars in new Disney Pixar film |work=[[The Salt Lake Tribune]] |date=June 12, 2009 |url=http://www.sltrib.com/news/ci_12571320 |access-date=June 15, 2009}}</ref><ref name="Lake Powell Chronicle">{{cite news|last=Forney|first=Matt|title=Disney Plans to Film New Movie in Area|url=http://www.lakepowellchronicle.com/v2_news_articles.php?heading=0&page=77&story_id=1955|access-date=June 23, 2011|newspaper=Lake Powell Chronicle|date=February 2, 2010}}</ref> Cinematographer [[Dan Mindel]] believed that the entire movie should have been shot in the [[Four Corners]] region of the [[southwestern U.S.]], the only place on Earth he felt could convincingly pass for Mars.{{efn|Many contemporary filmmakers, by contrast, have preferred to film  movies set on Mars in [[Jordan]]'s [[Wadi Rum]] desert.<ref>{{cite news|last=Jacobs|first=Harrison|title=An otherworldly desert in Jordan has doubled as distant planets in movies like 'Star Wars' and 'The Martian' — after seeing it myself, I can tell you it's just as breathtaking in person|url=https://www.businessinsider.com/the-martian-prometheus-rogue-one-wadi-rum-jordan-2018-7|newspaper=[[Business Insider]]|date=July 29, 2018|access-date=April 13, 2022}}</ref>}} "A lot of the studio work that we had done was so compromised because of the choice of studio, the size of the stages, the fact that it was all inside when it should have been outside, all that kind of stuff".<ref name="The Wrap story" />

Mindel had taken the job in order to learn how to make a movie with many effects shots. He worked with more restraint than he had been used to. Normally he kept the camera rolling even after the director said "[[Cut (transition)#Verbal command|Cut]]!", a lesson he learned from [[Jackie Chan]] while making ''[[Shanghai Noon]]''. However, for ''John Carter'', Stanton had planned the shots in such great detail before filming began as to leave little room for improvisation.<ref name="The Wrap story" />

Stanton went for a look for the movie's costuming different from what had been planned by Rodriguez and Frazetta when they were attached to the project several years earlier. Stanton felt that Frazetta's look was "very sexist and it's very male, fanboy dominated". While conceding the sex appeal at the heart of the characters, he believed they still had to seem realistic. "I want anything, whether it's a fish or a robot or a toy or a human being, I want them to be seen as dimensional as possible and be seen as somebody with thoughts and opinions and surprise in how they may react to something, and contradictions".<ref name="The Wrap story" />

Throughout production there had been arguments from some of Stanton's friends in Pixar's Braintrust that it would be better for the movie to begin with Carter finding himself on Mars than through the narrative device of having Burroughs, supposedly his nephew, find his late uncle's written account of his time there following his death and then [[Flashback (narrative)|flashing back]] to it. Stanton in response considered that "lazy". He told them "If I do that, then thirty minutes in I'm going to have to stop the film to explain the war, and Dejah, and who everyone is, and we're going to have even bigger problems". They compromised by beginning the movie with the battle on Mars, and then the Zondangans getting the nanofoam gun from the Therns. That shift necessitated 18 new scenes, for which Disney agreed to a reshoot.<ref name="Friend20110417" />

====Cinematography and visual effects====
The film was shot in the [[Panavision]] [[anamorphic format]] on [[Kodak]] [[35 mm movie film|35 mm film stock]]. "I try very hard to persuade whomever I'm working with to allow me to shoot on film, and to shoot anamorphically," Mindel told ''ICG'', the magazine of the [[International Cinematographers Guild]]. "It's the most pure, high-definition way of capturing a scene, short of Showscan or IMAX".<ref name="ICG">{{cite web|last=Heuring |first=David |title=War Lords |url=http://www.icgmagazine.com/wordpress/2012/03/01/war-lords/ |work=[[International Cinematographers Guild|ICG Magazine]] |date=March 1, 2012 |access-date=April 4, 2012 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120406220538/http://www.icgmagazine.com/wordpress/2012/03/01/war-lords/ |archive-date=April 6, 2012 }}</ref>

But Mindel also liked the flaws in that process. Older Panavision lenses have imperfections and aberrations, and "At a purely organic level, the light does unmanageable things when it hits an aberration", he said. "An unquantifiable magic happens, and I love that!" That unpredictability, and the effect on the film's texture and [[Film grain|grain]], gave Mindel images he hoped would "[feel] inherently realistic in spite of the fantastical creatures and the extensive digital-visual-effects technology behind them". For ''John Carter'' he used Panavision's Primo and C-Series anamorphic lenses and ATZ and AWZ [[zoom lens]]es, with [[List of motion picture film stocks#Vision3 color negative (ECN-2 process 2007–present)|Kodak's Vision3 500T Color Negative 5219 and 200T 5213 stock]].<ref name="ICG" />

Shooting with a 3D release in mind was considered but dropped over a year before [[principal photography]]. The camera crew and effects specialists viewed Disney's ''[[Alice in Wonderland (2010 film)|Alice in Wonderland]]'', where space on the set was planned with the 3D release in mind. They realized that the processes used for that film would be outdated before they could expect that they would start ''John Carter'', so there was no point in planning for 3D; Stanton also believed that would be too much to deal with while shooting in any event. Mindel said that was "a huge relief".<ref name="ICG" />

Work on the visual effects had begun earlier, in 2009, before the release of ''Avatar'', which revolutionized the field. The effects team doing proof-of-process tests realized when that movie came out that ''John Carter'' would require extensive use of all the techniques that ''Avatar'' had pioneered, and would go where that film had not with many more interactions between human actors and CGI characters. Peter Chiang, the film's visual effects supervisor at [[DNEG|Double Negative]] in London, wrote a production bible for the latter that described how each character should be composed and framed. Bruce McCleery, the [[second unit]]'s director of photography, said that bible was especially useful for scenes blending humans and CGI characters. "Working that out was much more complex than it sounds".<ref name="ICG" />

Shooting the airship battle on a London soundstage required extensive preproduction work. Mindel and the lighting crew started work designing the lighting rig for that scene long before shooting started. They shared their work with the effects teams, which used [[Lidar]] to map it, as it did for every set. The sets housed the full {{convert|110|ft|m|adj=on}} airship models, mounted on [[gimbal]]s with [[green screen]] on all sides. Ultimately, to stage an aerial battle with light-based weapons where the ships maneuver to block the sunlight that powers their opponents' craft, the lighting crew used 120 [[Balloon light|Spacelights]], 15 Dino light banks, flashing lights and a crane mounted with soft lights and green screens that could fill in [[Available light|ambient light]] from the film's sky.<ref name="ICG" />

Once production moved to the Utah desert, the weather added its own challenges. Heavy winds brought frequent [[sandstorm]]s, forcing many on location to work while wearing goggles and sometimes [[burnous|burnooses]]. Mindel wanted the film to take advantage of these conditions as much as possible, although he had to tone it down slightly so the effects teams could do their job. "All the uncontrollable natural phenomena did give the film a visceral, unpredictable quality, and contributed to its unique, idiosyncratic texture," McCleery said.<ref name="ICG" />

====Reshoots====

Before the formal reshoot, which took place throughout September in the Los Angeles neighborhood of [[Playa Vista]],<ref name="ICG" /> Stanton told ''[[The New Yorker]]'' he had done some smaller-scale reshooting focusing on additional dialogue for some characters in order to address the issues the preview had raised. In London, he shot scenes where West, as Sab Than, clarified the Therns' goals. Back in Los Angeles, Kitsch and Collins filmed Carter's proposal scene. Then Stanton went back to London to film Strong's side of the conversation with Sab Than.<ref name="Friend20110417" /> Stanton denied assertions that he had gone over budget and stated that he had been allowed a longer reshoot because he had stayed on budget and on time.<ref name=thr120217>{{cite news | url = https://www.hollywoodreporter.com/heat-vision/andrew-stanton-john-carter-lie-over-budget-disney-reshoots-292488 | title = Andrew Stanton Slams 'John Carter' Budget Overage Claims: "A Complete and Utter Lie" | first = Todd | last = Gilchrist | work=[[The Hollywood Reporter]] | date = February 17, 2012 | access-date =March 12, 2012 }}</ref>

Stanton reshot much of the movie twice, far more than was common in live action filmmaking at that time. He attributed that to his animation background.<ref name="NYT March 12 article" /> "The thing I had to explain to Disney was, 'You're asking a guy who's only known how to do it this way to suddenly do it with one reshoot.'" he explained later. "I said, 'I'm not gonna get it right the first time, I'll tell you that right now.'"<ref name="LA Times March 6 story" /> Stanton often sought advice from people he had worked with at Pixar on animated films (known as the Braintrust) instead of those with live-action experience working with him.<ref name=Friend20110417 />

Stanton also was quoted as saying, "Is it just me, or do we actually know how to do this better than live-action crews do?"<ref name="Friend20110417" /> [[Rich Ross]], Disney's chairman, successor to [[Dick Cook]], who had originally approved the film for production,{{efn|By some accounts, Cook had [[Green-light#Film industry|greenlit]] ''John Carter'' before he or anyone in the studio's production division had read the script.<ref name="THR pre-release marketing article" />}} came from a television background and had no experience with feature films. The studio's new top marketing and production executives had little more.<ref name="NYT March 12 article" />

''The New Yorker'' writer [[Tad Friend]] visited the set during the reshoot and wrote an article about it, noting that it was "unusually extensive (and expensive)". Collins and Kitsch both made comments on the record about the reshoot that seemed defensive; Stanton told Friend not only that if it had been up to him he would have insisted on a second reshoot but that reshoots should be "mandatory".<ref name=Friend20110417 /> It has subsequently been suggested that this article began the media narrative that ''John Carter'' was in serious trouble,<ref name="The Wrap story" /> as conventional Hollywood wisdom held that ''any'' reshoot was an indicator of a troubled production.<ref name="LAT Sept 2012 article">{{cite news|last=Keegan|first=Rebecca|title=Director Andrew Stanton looks back on 'John Carter's' rocky path|url=https://www.latimes.com/entertainment/movies/la-xpm-2012-sep-08-la-et-mn-john-carter-director-20120908-story.html|url-access=registration|newspaper=[[Los Angeles Times]]|date=September 8, 2012|access-date=April 14, 2022}}</ref>

Collins believes that the reshoot was detrimental for her character. Originally filmed as a strong, independent warrior, the scenes added, such as those with her father, made her seem more vulnerable; and scenes like those in which she had slapped Carter were cut. She believes the studio wanted a softer take on Thoris and was reduced to asking Stanton every day what would work with that and just doing it.<ref name="The Wrap story" />

After the reshoot, considerable work remained in post-production on Stanton's first cut, reportedly almost three hours long.<ref name="Atlantic story">{{cite magazine|last=Meslow|first=Scott|title=Why Did It Take 100 Years for John Carter to Make It to the Big Screen?|url=https://www.theatlantic.com/entertainment/archive/2012/03/why-did-it-take-100-years-for-john-carter-to-make-it-to-the-big-screen/254220/|magazine=[[The Atlantic]]|date=March 8, 2012|access-date=April 22, 2022}}</ref> There were many effects and CGI shots to finish. Stanton recalls that "[t]here were more animated shots in what was left to do on ''Carter'' than an entire animated feature". Animating the Tharks, especially in large numbers during battle scenes, proved particularly challenging; the software had to be upgraded for it, and as one animator recalls, work scenes sometimes took three hours to open. Many of those working on the CGI were particularly appreciative of Stanton, since due to his background he had considerable expertise in the area and made himself more available than directors of such films usually are.<ref name="The Wrap story" />

==Marketing==

''John Carter''{{'}}s marketing has been called "one of the worst marketing campaigns in movie history". The filmmakers believe that the decisions made in marketing the film were the primary reason for its failure.<ref name="El País story" /><ref name="Vulture trailers story" /><ref name="Washington Post story" /> A new studio executive team with minimal experience in that side of the business was in charge, and not as emotionally invested in its success as the filmmakers had been. Furthermore, unbeknownst to them, Disney CEO [[Robert Iger]] had already begun talks with [[George Lucas]] about buying [[Lucasfilm]] and the ''[[Star Wars]]'' franchise, eliminating any incentive the company had to launch a successful competing film franchise.<ref name="The Wrap story" />

The head of Walt Disney Studios Marketing during the production was [[MT Carney]], an industry outsider who previously ran a boutique marketing firm in New York<ref name=Goldstein20120420 /> with no previous experience marketing movies.<ref name="The Wrap story" /> Stanton often rejected marketing ideas from the studio, according to those who worked on the film.<ref name=Vulture20120312>{{cite web|last=Brodesser-Akner|first=Claude|title=The Inside Story of How John Carter Was Doomed by Its First Trailer|url=https://www.vulture.com/2012/03/john-carter-doomed-by-first-trailer.html|work=Vulture|date=March 12, 2012 |publisher=New York Media LLC|access-date=April 22, 2012}}</ref> His ideas were used instead, and he ignored criticism that using a cover version of [[Led Zeppelin]]'s 1975 song "[[Kashmir (song)|Kashmir]]" in the [[Trailer (promotion)|trailer]] released in conjunction with an ad aired during [[Super Bowl XLVI|that year's Super Bowl]] would make it seem less current to the contemporary younger audiences the film sought.<ref name="NYT March 12 article" />

He also chose [[billboard]] imagery that failed to resonate with prospective audiences, and put together a preview reel that did not get a strong reception from a [[Science fiction convention|convention]] audience.<ref name="NYT March 12 article" /> Stanton said, "My joy when I saw the first trailer for ''[[Star Wars (film)|Star Wars]]'' is I saw a little bit of almost everything in the movie, and I had no idea how it connected, and I had to go see the movie. So the last thing I'm going to do is ruin that little kid's experience".<ref>{{cite news|last=Vary|first=Adam|title='John Carter' trailer deep dive: Director Andrew Stanton on those green men, that frog dog, and why he HATES trailer spoilers|url=http://insidemovies.ew.com/2011/12/01/john-carter-trailer-deep-dive-andrew-stanton-exclusive/2/|access-date=April 27, 2012|newspaper=Entertainment Weekly|date=December 1, 2011}}</ref> Following the death of [[Steve Jobs]], Stanton dedicated the film in his memory.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.vulture.com/2012/02/john-carter-dedicated-to-steve-jobs.html|title=John Carter Dedicated to Steve Jobs |work=Vulture |date=April 8, 2012 |access-date=February 28, 2012}}</ref>{{efn|"We didn't always agree on which direction to take every step of the way, but there was never serious contention," Stanton told the ''LA Times'' several months after the film's release, when asked about the film's marketing missteps. "The truth was everyone tried their very best to crack how to sell what we had, but the answer proved elusive."<ref name="LAT Sept 2012 article" />}}

===Effect of other 2011 films' box office===

Disney reportedly grew more concerned about the film's prospects after the 2011 failure of the [[Lionsgate Films]] remake of ''[[Conan the Barbarian (2011 film)|Conan the Barbarian]]'', which was based on a popular fantasy [[media franchise|franchise]] that had been adapted into successful films in the 1980s starring [[Arnold Schwarzenegger]]. Lionsgate's version had cost $90 million and starred [[Jason Momoa]]. Chabon recalls reading a [[Quora]] post by one of its screenwriters, [[Sean Hood]], about how he dealt with the movie's failure, and for the first time worried about the possibility that ''John Carter'' could suffer the same fate.<ref name="The Wrap story" />

''[[Cowboys & Aliens]]'', released in July, also had an effect on ''John Carter''. It, too, had science fiction and western elements, and did not fare well commercially. That was taken as indicating that contemporary audiences were not interested in [[Western (genre)#Film|westerns]], or any film set in the American past. Consequently, those elements would be downplayed in the trailers and other marketing for ''John Carter''.<ref name="Daily Beast story">{{cite news|last=Lee|first=Chris|title='John Carter': Disney's Quarter-Billion-Dollar Movie Fiasco|url=https://www.thedailybeast.com/john-carter-disneys-quarter-billion-dollar-movie-fiasco|newspaper=[[The Daily Beast]]|date=February 21, 2012|access-date=April 20, 2022}}</ref>

One of Disney's own recent big-budget franchise films also added to executives' anxieties about ''John Carter''. The May 2011 release of ''[[Pirates of the Caribbean: On Stranger Tides]]'' had done well at the box office, becoming the third highest-grossing film domestically that year and making over a billion dollars worldwide. However, the film's budget, exceeding $400 million by some estimates, made it [[List of most expensive films|the most expensive film ever produced]].<ref>{{cite web |first=Christian |last=Sylt |title=Fourth Pirates Of The Caribbean Is Most Expensive Movie Ever With Costs Of $410 Million |date=July 22, 2014 |work=[[Forbes]] |url=https://www.forbes.com/sites/csylt/2014/07/22/fourth-pirates-of-the-caribbean-is-most-expensive-movie-ever-with-costs-of-410-million/ |access-date=April 10, 2022}}</ref> Its profits were thus lower than a film that popular might have been expected to generate, making Disney fear the same could happen with ''John Carter''. By the time of the reshoot four months after ''On Stranger Tides'', it was reported that ''John Carter'' would have to make at least $700 million worldwide, more than twice its escalating production costs, to justify a sequel.<ref name="Friend20110417" />

===July 2011 preview screening===

Initially, expectations for the film's commercial success were high. The studio held a [[test screening]] in mid-2011, before the reshoot, in [[Portland, Oregon]]. Stanton, who had been diagnosed with high-functioning [[attention deficit hyperactivity disorder]] early in the process of writing the script, was so nervous he took [[lorazepam]] not just on the flight there but before the preview. Four Disney executives were in attendance to watch the reactions of 400 filmgoers and read their opinions afterwards. The audience reactions seemed to indicate that audiences were engaged with the film and laughed when they were supposed to, which relaxed Stanton.<ref name="Friend20110417" />

Afterwards, many of them rated the film as "very good" or "excellent", for an average audience approval rating of 75 percent, which pleased the studio. Carney said that that number could probably be rounded up to 80, reflecting work that had yet to be done. According to the preview cards, that work would also include improving the pacing of the film's second act, making the motivations of the Therns clearer, and developing the relationship between Carter and Thoris so that their wedding at the end was not so much of a surprise.<ref name="Friend20110417" />

===Title changes===

The film's title was a major issue; there are several accounts of who decided to change it and why. It is largely based on the first book of the series, ''A Princess of Mars'', but was originally titled ''John Carter of Mars''.{{efn|At the end of 2009, the independent film company [[The Asylum]] released ''[[Princess of Mars]]'', a low-budget film released [[Direct-to-video|direct-to-DVD]] in the United States, the only other filmed adaptation of the Barsoom novels. Its marketing, intended to capitalize on ''Avatar''{{'}}s success that year, acknowledges that the story inspired that movie without mentioning Burroughs. Its story, like the pre-2005 versions of the script, had Carter (played by [[Antonio Sabàto Jr.]], (with [[Traci Lords]] as Dejah) as a modern-day U.S. soldier initially fighting in Afghanistan, and, notwithstanding its title, dispensed with the notion of Barsoom as Mars entirely, making it a planet light-years away. Since the novel is in the [[public domain in the United States|public domain]] and thus any filmmaker could adapt it, Stanton has referred to it as an inevitable "crappy knock-off". It was rereleased in 2012 as ''John Carter of Mars''.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://news.moviefone.com/2012/03/07/andrew-stanton-john-carter_n_1327070.html |title=&#124; Moviefone |publisher=News.moviefone.com |access-date=January 31, 2016 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121025001614/http://news.moviefone.com/2012/03/07/andrew-stanton-john-carter_n_1327070.html |archive-date=October 25, 2012 }}</ref>}} Stanton changed the title to that from the book's title early in 2011, "because not a single boy would go". Later he removed "of Mars" to make it more appealing to a broader audience, calling the film an "origin story ... about a guy ''becoming'' John Carter of Mars".<ref name="Bleeding Cool" /> Disney also reportedly believed that the sex appeal of the popular Kitsch being shirtless throughout the movie would draw women to see the film. Since women are believed by Hollywood to be averse to science fiction, in this account, "Mars" was excised from the title.<ref name="The Wrap story" />

Stanton planned to keep "Mars" in the title for the proposed future films in the series.<ref name="Bleeding Cool">{{cite news|last=Brendon|first=Connelly|title=Andrew Stanton Explains Why John Carter Of Mars Became Just John Carter|url=http://www.bleedingcool.com/2011/12/05/andrew-stanton-explains-why-john-carter-of-mars-became-just-john-carter/|access-date=December 9, 2011|newspaper=Bleeding Cool|date=December 5, 2011}}</ref> Kitsch said the title was changed to reflect the character's journey, as John Carter would become "of Mars" only in the film's last few minutes.<ref name=7films>{{cite news|title=7 John Carter Moments + Q&A With Star Taylor Kitsch |url=http://7films.me.uk/news/7-john-carter-moments-qa-star-taylor-kitsch/ |date=January 20, 2012 |access-date=September 4, 2012 |newspaper=7films |url-status=usurped |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120704205908/http://7films.me.uk/news/7-john-carter-moments-qa-star-taylor-kitsch/ |archive-date=July 4, 2012 }}</ref> Former Disney marketing president Carney has also been blamed for suggesting the title change.<ref name=Goldstein20120420>{{cite news|last=Goldstein|first=Patrick|title=Rich Ross ousted at Disney: What went wrong?|url=http://latimesblogs.latimes.com/movies/2012/04/rich-ross-disney-chariman-out-resigns.html|access-date=April 22, 2012|newspaper=Los Angeles Times|date=April 20, 2012}}</ref>

Another reported explanation for the name change was that Disney had suffered a significant loss in March 2011 with ''[[Mars Needs Moms]]''; Carney reportedly conducted a study which noted recent movies with the word "Mars" in the title had not been commercially successful.<ref name=Fernandez20120224>{{cite news|last=Fernandez|first=Jay|title='John Carter': Disney Scrambles to Save its $250 Million Gamble|url=https://www.hollywoodreporter.com/news/john-carter-from-mars-taylor-kitsch-budget-box-office-294822|access-date=April 22, 2012|newspaper=The Hollywood Reporter|date=February 24, 2012}}</ref> Chabon responds that all those films were poorly regarded by critics.<ref name="The Wrap story" />{{efn|Another person who had seen that research called it "the most ridiculous thing I've ever heard"<ref name="THR pre-release marketing article" />}}

Despite the name change, some hints of the original title remain. Some promotional materials used the stylized "JCM" logo, and at the end of the film is a [[title card]] with "John Carter of Mars". The marketing team had yielded to Stanton on that, and he explained that "it means something by the end of the movie, and if there are more movies I want that to be what you remember".<ref name="The Wrap story" />

After the film's release and subsequent failure, the truncated title was seen as part of the problem. "What the hell is John Carter? What's the film about?" asked Peter Sealey, former marketing president at [[Columbia Pictures]], told the ''[[Los Angeles Times]]''. " I don't know who John Carter is. You've got to make that clear".<ref name="LAT post-release column">{{cite news|last1=Chmielewski|first1=Dawn C.|last2=Keegan|first2=Rebecca|title=Why did Disney's 'John Carter' flop?|url=https://www.latimes.com/entertainment/la-xpm-2012-mar-13-la-et-john-carter-flop-20120313-story.html|newspaper=[[Los Angeles Times]]|date=March 13, 2012|access-date=April 12, 2022}}</ref> Stanton reportedly believed there was enough awareness of the books that this would not be a problem, to which another marketing executive responded, "People don't say, 'I know what I'll be for Halloween! I'll be John Carter!{{' "}}<ref name="El País story" />

===Trailers===
{{external media
| float  = right
| width  = 150
| headerimage=[[File:John Carter.svg|alt=Movie title in black capital letters|x100px|center]]
| title  = Trailers
| video1 = [https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=edwLjEB-rAY Teaser trailer] at YouTube
| video2 = [https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=du45ko64LOs Trailer with "Kashmir", aired during Super Bowl], at YouTube
| video3 = [https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-BxeHQY1NuM Fan trailer by JohnCarterFiles.com contributors], at YouTube
}}
The film's [[teaser trailer]] released in August 2011 was also seen as poor marketing. It relied largely on visual imagery from the film, without saying much about the creators and their previous accomplishments,{{efn|Stanton took any references to his successful Pixar films out of the trailer to avoid the film being perceived as meant for children.<ref name="El País story" />}} or Burroughs's work and how it had influenced later science fiction universes like ''Star Wars''. There were few effects and little action; Stanton has denied a rumor that that was because he did not have enough finished effects shots to use.<ref name="The Wrap story" /> Disney executives have faulted Stanton for this, since his success at Pixar allowed him to demand and get control over ''John Carter''{{'}}s trailers.<ref name="Vulture trailers story" />

They reportedly strongly implored him to listen to their suggestions and he refused. "This is one of the worst marketing campaigns in the history of movies," a former studio marketing chief complained to ''[[Vulture.com|Vulture]]'' shortly before the film opened. "It's almost as if they went out of their way to ''not'' make us care". After the full trailer, and the Super Bowl ad derived from it seemed similarly bland,{{efn|Within the industry, the Super Bowl ad was seen as confirmation that the film was in serious trouble. "You know it's gotta be bad when they start breaking up the scenes and doing something conceptual for a Super Bowl spot", one executive at a competing studio said. "It's like, 'Guys, this is your [[Hail Mary pass|Hail Mary]]?'"<ref name="Daily Beast story" /><p>''[[Collider (website)|Collider]]''{{'}}s Adam Chitwood said he was "pleasantly surprised" by it, "but I'm still not convinced that the general audience has a handle on what the film's about."<ref name="Collider Super Bowl ad piece">{{cite web|last=Chitwood|first=Adam|title=Super Bowl Movie Commercials: ''The Avengers'', ''Battleship'', ''John Carter'', ''The Lorax'', ''G.I. Joe 2'', ''The Dictator'' and More|url=https://collider.com/super-bowl-movie-commercials-avengers-battleship/|work=Collider|access-date=February 7, 2012|date=February 5, 2012|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200105172643/https://collider.com/super-bowl-movie-commercials-avengers-battleship/143185/|archive-date=January 5, 2020}}</ref></p>}} enough for Kitsch to publicly concur with criticisms of the film's marketing campaign,<ref name="Vulture trailers story" /> a fan group online put out a competing trailer meant to address the official one's deficiencies.<ref name="The Wrap story" /> During February 2012, new television ads emphasizing story points were launched, and a similarly cut trailer was attached to ''[[Act of Valor]]''.<ref name="THR pre-release marketing article">{{cite news|last1=Fernandez|first1=Jay A.|last2=Kit|first2=Borys|title='John Carter': Disney Scrambles to Save its $250 Million Gamble|url=https://www.hollywoodreporter.com/news/general-news/john-carter-from-mars-taylor-kitsch-budget-box-office-294822/|newspaper=[[The Hollywood Reporter]]|date=February 24, 2012|access-date=April 20, 2012}}</ref>

===Early 2012===

After several weeks away from her office, Carney left at the beginning of 2012,<ref>{{cite news|url=http://www.hollywoodreporter.com/news/disney-marketing-exit-memo-mt-carney-279784 |title=Disney's MT Carney Bids Farewell In Internal Memo to Studio | work=The Hollywood Reporter |date=January 9, 2012|access-date=April 13, 2022}}</ref> with four years remaining on her contract,<ref name="The Wrap story" /> to be replaced by Ricky Strauss, former president of [[Participant Media]],{{efn|Strauss had never run a major studio's marketing division, which supposedly led to [[Steven Spielberg]], whose [[DreamWorks Pictures|DreamWorks]] films are distributed by Disney, angrily confronting Ross at the [[Critics' Choice Movie Awards]] dinner over why he was not consulted on the hiring.<ref>{{cite news|last=Masters|first=Kim|title=Why an Angry Steven Spielberg Confronted Disney's Rich Ross at Dinner|url=https://www.hollywoodreporter.com/news/general-news/steven-spielberg-disney-rich-ross-282936/|newspaper=[[The Hollywood Reporter]]|date=January 18, 2012|access-date=April 20, 2022}}</ref>}} for the beginning of the period immediately preceding the film's release when promotional efforts become more intensive. He committed to spending over $100 million to that end.<ref name="THR pre-release marketing article" /> Sealey called the change in marketing leadership "[t]he worst thing that can happen to a movie" as it adversely affects the morale of the cast and crew, who often have to promote the film personally in the media.<ref name="LAT post-release column" />

Disney moved the film's release up to early March 2012 from June,<ref name="The Hollywood Reporter" /> giving it two box office weekends before the release of Lionsgate's ''[[The Hunger Games (film)|The Hunger Games]]'', widely expected to do very well and compete for the same audience.<ref name="Deadline tracking story">{{cite news|last=Finke|first=Nikki|authorlink=Nikki Finke|title='John Carter' Tracking Shockingly Soft: 'Could Be Biggest Writeoff Of All Time'|url=https://deadline.com/2012/02/john-carter-early-tracking-shockingly-soft-could-be-biggest-writeoff-of-all-time-229292/|newspaper=[[Deadline Hollywood]]|date=February 16, 2012|access-date=April 20, 2022}}</ref> As that date approached, the usual aspects of Disney's marketing pushes for big-budget [[Tent-pole (entertainment)|tentpole films]] were absent. There were no large merchandise displays in the company's [[Disney Store|online and retail stores]], nor at [[big-box store]]s like [[Target Corporation|Target]].{{efn|Ross had done these things in 2010 before the release of ''[[Tron: Legacy]]'', a similar big-budget franchise film that was expected to succeed, in the hope of being able to claim some credit for the film's success. While it did perform well at the box office, the merchandising did not do as well since Ross did not have the proper marketing expertise at the studio, leaving Disney with unsold videogames and T-shirts.<ref name="Daily Beast story" />}} Nor were there prominently placed ads in the company's theme parks, or coverage on Disney-owned media such as the [[American Broadcasting Company|ABC]] broadcast network or [[Disney Channel]].<ref name="The Wrap story" /> "It needs to feel like an event, and right now it doesn't feel like an event," an unnamed marketing expert told ''[[The Hollywood Reporter]]''.<ref name="THR pre-release marketing article" />

Instead, the company tried some alternative marketing approaches. Stanton gave a [[TED talk]] on storytelling that had a short scene from ''John Carter'' as an example of one of his points.<ref>{{cite AV media |people=[[Andrew Stanton]]|date=February 2012|title=Andrew Stanton: The clues to a great story|url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=KxDwieKpawg|access-date=April 19, 2022|location=[[Long Beach, California]], USA |publisher=[[TED (conference)|TED]]}}</ref> While that was seen as effective, some other promotions were not, such as an "Are You The Real John Carter?" contest; men who could prove that their real name was John Carter were encouraged to enter, and winners would be invited to a special fan screening.<ref name="The Wrap story" />

As the premiere date neared, some of the filmmakers were unaware of the negative press coverage already attached to the movie. Mindel and Stanton later stated that they were somewhat oblivious due to largely being in contact only with those whom they had been working with in post-production. Collins said those who worked for her and followed media coverage kept that information from her.<ref name="The Wrap story" />

Dafoe, on the other hand, was aware that the media were lowering the public and the industry's expectations for the film: "[M]y recollection was that even before it was released, there were grumblings about it ... everything from the name change to regime change to poor publicity. But I remember before the movie was even seen, people were counting it out".<ref name="The Wrap story" />

====Poor tracking====

Tracking data, the results of long-term surveys of likely filmgoers to judge their interest in seeing an upcoming film upon its release, with a prediction of its opening weekend box office, for ''John Carter'' was returned to Disney in mid-February and shared both within and without the company. [[Nikki Finke]] reported in ''[[Deadline Hollywood]]'' that the numbers pointed to a serious failure. Barely half the likely audience was aware of the film, 27 percent said they were interested in seeing it, and 3 percent said it would be their first choice that weekend.<ref name="Deadline tracking story" />

An executive at a rival studio told Finke that demographic data with the "shocking" tracking for such a costly film showed that women in particular "have flat out rejected the film" and expected "the biggest writeoff of all time". Finke reported that she had heard estimates of a loss around $100 million, but allowed that soft numbers had been widely expected as Disney's in-house surveys had been showing them for some time. Disney told her that the Super Bowl ad had given the film an expected "pop of awareness" and the studio remained committed to a full marketing push before the release.<ref name="Deadline tracking story" />

Chabon says that on the eve of the premiere, he was in a hotel down the street and Disney's marketing department was showing the team the latest tracking. "None of it was good", he recalled. Despite doubts and awareness of previous occasions when such dire forecasts had been wide of the mark, {{nowrap|"[w]e}} just all kind of knew at that point it was going to be bad. It was not going to go well".<ref name="The Wrap story" />

Just before the film was released, an [[Evercore]] analyst who followed Disney more than doubled his estimate of the likely loss, to $165 million, because of the tracking. Other analysts had similarly revised their estimates upward, to $100 million or more.<ref name="THR anticipated writedown story">{{cite news|last1=Szalai|first1=George|last2=Bond|first2=Paul|title='John Carter' Debacle: Analysts Predict $150 Mil Write-Down for Disney|url=https://www.hollywoodreporter.com/news/general-news/john-carter-box-office-disney-flop-298610/|newspaper=[[The Hollywood Reporter]]|date=March 12, 2012|access-date=April 21, 2022}}</ref>

===Premiere===

Disney scheduled the late February premiere for [[Regal Cinemas|Regal]]'s LA Live Theatre in [[downtown Los Angeles]], rather than the [[El Capitan Theatre]] in [[Hollywood, California|Hollywood]], which it owned and had renovated extensively. The choice of venue has been described as "odd", since Disney had held most of its premieres, particularly of big-budget franchise films, at the El Capitan. In a [[news release]] announcing the premiere, Disney highlighted that the movie would be shown in [[3D film|3D]] on a {{convert|70|ft|m|adj=on}} screen to an audience of 800 in three theaters, ranging from the cast and crew and company executives to critics, [[D23 (Disney)|D23]] members and winners of contests.<ref name="The Wrap story" />

Collins, still unaware of the negative media perception of the film, recalls walking in and going down the [[red carpet]] behind Kitsch. She saw [[Rich Ross]] call him over and whisper something in his ear, after which he suddenly stepped back. When she caught up to Kitsch, she asked what Ross had told him that had so affected him. "'It's a disaster.' He just told me, 'It's going to be a fucking disaster.'"<ref name="The Wrap story" />

===Post-release criticisms===

In the ''LA Times'' the week after the release, industry insiders suggested two reasons the film might have struggled to succeed with audiences regardless of how well it had been made or marketed. One was that more recent franchises, such as ''Star Wars'', that had derived and borrowed from Burroughs' original concepts in the century since it had been written had exhausted the potential for audiences to be enthralled by any modern adaptation of his work. James Jacks, the producer who had tried to make a film of the work in the early 2000s, recalled having given director [[Robert Zemeckis]] the novels in order to interest him in the project. "I don't think so," Zemeckis told him after reading them. "[[George Lucas|George [Lucas]]] has really plundered these books".<ref name="LAT post-release column" />

Another industry marketing person, speaking anonymously, told the ''Times'' that modern audiences have a "[[cognitive dissonance]]" problem with films set on Mars based on older works. At the time Burroughs wrote, little was known about conditions on Mars, allowing an author to fill in those gaps with invented details. However, modern audiences know from the many actual [[List of missions to Mars|uncrewed missions to Mars]] that that planet is [[Mars in fiction#Human survival|uninhabitable and apparently devoid of life]]. "You're not able to sell [Burroughs's vision]", he said.<ref name="LAT post-release column" />

Two of the film's supporting cast members weighed in later in the year on the role marketing played in its poor box office performance in separate interviews with ''[[The A.V. Club]]''. In July, Bryan Cranston called its cool reception "unwarranted" and blamed it on TV stations around the country focusing on commercial news about how ''John Carter'' had underperformed and not even won its opening weekend rather than offering a review of the film, leading viewers to make their decisions about what movie to see on that basis. "Why is it all of a sudden important for average Americans to know how much money a movie made at the box office?"<ref>{{cite interview |last=Cranston|first=Bryan|subject-link=Bryan Cranston|interviewer=Will Harris|title=Bryan Cranston on ''Breaking Bad''{{'}}s craziest season and what's next|work=[[The A.V. Club]]|date=July 11, 2012|url=https://www.avclub.com/bryan-cranston-on-breaking-bads-craziest-season-and-wha-1798232190|access-date=April 19, 2012}}</ref>

"I don't know why it's done so badly, or that it's perceived as being the [biggest] flop in Hollywood history", Dominic West said four months later. "It's not that bad at all". He defended Stanton and the film, calling the former "a fucking ''genius''" and noting that the reviews actually had not been very bad. West disclosed also that after production, in 2010, he had seen a marketing plan for the film that was never used, which he believed would have been much more effective than what Disney chose to do.<ref>{{cite interview|last=West|first=Dominic|subject-link=Dominic West|interviewer=Will Harris|title=Dominic West on ''The Hour'', ''John Carter'', and yes, ''The Wire''|work=[[The A.V. Club]]|date=November 26, 2012|url=https://www.avclub.com/dominic-west-on-the-hour-john-carter-and-yes-the-wir-1798234909|access-date=April 19, 2022}}</ref>

In 2020, ''[[Screen Rant]]''{{'}}s Kayleigh Donaldson reiterated the earlier arguments that Stanton's Pixar-based filmmaking process had unnecessarily increased costs, and that the film's ensuing bloated production budget made it harder to be profitable, as had been the case with ''Pirates of the Caribbean: On Stranger Tides''. She noted that all but one of the ten [[most expensive films ever made]] had been made in the last decade, and all but one of those nine had been Disney productions. "This is now the status quo for blockbuster cinema, an era of [[too-big-to-fail]] filmmaking that is almost exclusively reliant on international grosses just to break even". Of those eight Disney films, ''John Carter'' was the only one not part of an existing franchise. That large budget was necessary to faithfully and credibly replicate Burroughs's vision onscreen, but at the same time audiences were accustomed enough to expensive CGI and effects spectacles that that alone could not be expected to impress them.<ref name="Screen Rant piece">{{cite news|last=Donaldson|first=Kayleigh|title=John Carter: Everything That Went Wrong With Disney's Movie|url=https://screenrant.com/john-carter-movie-problems-bad-flop-reasons-explained/|work=[[Screen Rant]]|date=June 15, 2020|access-date=April 14, 2022}}</ref>

Donaldson also criticized the titling, noting that the early decision to not use the book title, ''A Princess of Mars'', "raised a lot of questions over who Disney wanted to sell the movie to", implying that the studio feared that men might not be interested in a movie with "Princess" in the title, despite Disney's own experience to the contrary with [[Disney princess|its many princess]] movies. Stripping it down to just ''John Carter'' "robbed the movie of its identity ... as a title [it] conveyed nothing to potential audiences about the movie they were being sold".<ref name="Screen Rant piece" /> Henry Hards, a writer at ''Giant Freakin Robot'', agreed in 2023, calling ''John Carter'' "the most generic title possible ...  Don't tell me that [''A Princess of Mars''] wouldn't have looked a lot better on a movie poster".<ref name="Giant Freakin Robot">{{cite news|last=Hards|first=Henry|title=John Carter's Posters Accidentally Illustrate Why The Movie Failed And How The Reboot Can Fix It|url=https://www.giantfreakinrobot.com/ent/scifi/john-carter-poster-fail.html|newspaper=Giant Freakin Robot|date=December 29, 2023|access-date=January 5, 2024}}</ref>

Stanton's stated reason for the latter move, that the narrative is about how John Carter becomes John Carter of Mars, also, to Donaldson, points to another problem that has beset other films adapted from series with multiple books. "In an effort to play catch-up to a franchise that spent years developing its intricately woven multiple narratives, many studios tried to do the work of three or four movies in one", she wrote. "This resulted in a lot of franchise non-starters because audiences had little interest in films that existed solely to set up a bunch of sequels for a property they didn't care about". Among these she included ''[[Artemis Fowl (film)|Artemis Fowl]]'', ''[[Robin Hood (2010 film)|Robin Hood]]'', and ''[[King Arthur: Legend of the Sword]]''. Likewise with ''John Carter'', the realization of Barsoom onscreen "wasn't enough to sustain a movie and didn't entice enough people to invest in a trilogy that would never see the light of day".<ref name="Screen Rant piece" />

Donaldson argued that in addition to being overtaken by works influenced by it, the Carter franchise was no longer popular enough to sustain an expensive film franchise by 2012, a century after the first book was published, an issue unintentionally highlighted by the use of "Kashmir" in the trailer. There still were fans, she conceded, but "[n]ame recognition alone does not make a movie hit. Just ask [[The Legend of Tarzan (film)|the most recent ''Tarzan'' reboot]] for evidence of that, or [[The Lone Ranger (2013 film)|Disney's own attempt]] to make ''[[Lone Ranger|The Lone Ranger]]'' a 21st century action favorite", which also failed at the box office.<ref name="Screen Rant piece" />

Hards also said his complaints about the title led to another area where the marketing failed the film: its posters. "They work, but they also highlight the biggest problem the movie has. They all scream family-friendly". Burroughs's books, by contrast, depict "a violent barbarian warrior-style ... world in which women don't wear clothes", or at least that was how they had been depicted on older covers of the books, pointing to one on which Dejah is shown in a very scanty bikini. "Martian women are strong, confident, and have no body shame. They don't need clothes. Or at least that's the premise Burroughs presents as the reality of life on Mars". The franchise was "an R-rated, ''Conan''-style story set in space" and should have been filmed that way, although Hards allowed that might alienate early 20th-century, even though it might have seemed liberating when Burroughs wrote the books.<ref name="Giant Freakin Robot" />

==Music and soundtrack==
{{main|John Carter (soundtrack)}}
In February 2010, [[Michael Giacchino]] revealed in an interview he would be scoring the film.<ref name="JoBlo">{{cite news|url=https://www.joblo.com/movie-news/michael-giacchino-scoring-john-carter-of-mars|title=Michael Giacchino Scoring John Carter of Mars|last=Tassi|first=Paul|date=March 11, 2010|newspaper=JoBlo|access-date=June 23, 2011}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://kusc.podbean.com/2010/02/25/2010-oscar-best-score-nominee-michael-giacchino-up/ |title=2010 Oscar, Best Score Nominee – Michael Giacchino (Up) &#124; KUSC Podcasts |publisher=Kusc.podbean.com |access-date=October 7, 2010 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100311172122/http://kusc.podbean.com/2010/02/25/2010-oscar-best-score-nominee-michael-giacchino-up |archive-date=March 11, 2010 }}</ref> A year and a half later, in his ''New Yorker'' article, Friend documents accompanying Stanton on a visit to Giacchino where they discuss the movie's score and how it relates to the narrative. Stanton had put in the [[scratch music]], the temporary music used to show what mood he wanted the actual score to reflect, himself rather than delegating that task to an editor as is commonly done. He told the composer that he wanted the music to reflect the two distinct plans driving the plot: Carter's and the Therns. Stanton also said he wanted the music for Carter to change in a way that reflected his slow acceptance of himself as John Carter of Mars.<ref name="Friend20110417" />

Stanton had used music from ''[[Perfume: The Story of a Murderer (film)|Perfume]]'' for the Therns; he wanted something similarly choral. With the opening voiceover and battle footage, he had put music from ''[[Syriana]]'' that sounded "dire and Middle Eastern and forlorn, like a culture clinging to its nobility". He suggested something similar to Giacchino as the "Mars theme", but advised against eventually merging it with Carter's theme. "[J]ust because you're master of the high seas doesn't mean you can't have a separate theme for the ocean". Giacchino agreed but suggested a different merger, doing the Mars theme chorally near the end of the film, to accentuate the Therns' apparently inevitable takeover of the planet, an idea Stanton eagerly accepted.<ref name="Friend20110417" /> [[Walt Disney Records]] released the soundtrack on March 6, 2012, three days before the film's release.

==Release==
===Theatrical run===
''John Carter'' was released theatrically in the United States by [[Walt Disney Studios Motion Pictures]].<ref name=VarReview/> The original film release date was June 8, 2012. In January 2011, Disney moved the release date up three months to March 9 of that year.<ref name=Deadline>{{cite news|last=Fleming |first=Mike |title=Disney Moves John Carter of Mars to Same Date as Fox's Prometheus |url=https://www.deadline.com/interstitial/?ref=http://www.deadline.com/2011/01/disney-shifts-release-dates-on-john-carter-of-mars-and-frankenweenie/ |archive-url=https://archive.today/20121209094121/http://www.deadline.com/interstitial/?ref=http://www.deadline.com/2011/01/disney-shifts-release-dates-on-john-carter-of-mars-and-frankenweenie/ |url-status=dead |archive-date=December 9, 2012 |access-date=June 23, 2011 |newspaper=Deadline |date=January 19, 2011 }}</ref><ref name=MovieWeb>{{cite news|last=Gallagher|first=Brian|title=Frankenweenine and John Carter of Mars Change Release Dates|url=http://www.movieweb.com/news/frankenweenine-and-john-carter-of-mars-change-release-dates|access-date=June 23, 2011|newspaper=MovieWeb|date=January 19, 2011|archive-date=January 23, 2011|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110123215126/http://www.movieweb.com/news/frankenweenine-and-john-carter-of-mars-change-release-dates|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=http://heatvision.hollywoodreporter.com/2010/08/frankenweenie-john-carter-of-mars-release-dates.html |title=Disney sets 'Frankenweenie,' 'John Carter of Mars' release dates |publisher=Heatvision.hollywoodreporter.com |date=August 9, 2010 |access-date=October 7, 2010 |archive-date=June 30, 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120630034853/http://www.hollywoodreporter.com/blogs/heat-vision |url-status=dead }}</ref> A [[teaser trailer]] for the film premiered on July 14 and was shown in 3D and 2D with showings of ''[[Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows – Part 2]]''; the official trailer premiered on November 30. On February 5, 2012, an extended commercial promoting the movie aired during the [[Super Bowl XLVI|Super Bowl]],<ref name="Collider Super Bowl ad piece" /> and the day before the game, Stanton, a [[Massachusetts]] native, held a special screening of the film for both the team members and families of the [[New England Patriots]] and [[New York Giants]], the competing teams.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.slashfilm.com/john-carter-screen-giants-patriots-super-bowl-xlvi/ |title='John Carter' To Screen For The Giants and Patriots Before Super Bowl XLVI; Plus New Featurette &#124; /Film |publisher=Slashfilm.com |date=February 3, 2012 |access-date=April 22, 2012}}</ref>

===Home media===
[[Walt Disney Studios Home Entertainment]] released ''John Carter'' on [[Blu-ray]], DVD, and digital download on June 5, 2012. The home media release was made available in three different physical packages: a four-disc combo pack (1 disc [[Blu-ray 3D]], 1-disc Blu-ray, 1 DVD, and 1-disc [[digital copy]]), a two-disc combo pack (1 disc Blu-ray, 1 disc DVD), and one-disc DVD. ''John Carter'' was also made available in 3D High Definition, High Definition, and Standard Definition Digital.{{clarify|date=July 2013}} Additionally, the home media edition was available in an On-Demand format. The Blu-ray bonus features include [[Disney Second Screen]] functionality, "360 Degrees of John Carter", deleted scenes, and "Barsoom Bloopers". The DVD bonus features included "100 Years in the Making", and audio commentary with filmmakers. The High Definition Digital and Standard Definition Digital versions both include Disney Second Screen, "Barsoom Bloopers", and deleted scenes. The Digital 3D High Definition Digital copy does not include bonus features.<ref>{{cite web|last=Wharton|first=David|title=John Carter Conquers The Red Planet on Blu-Ray This June|date=April 30, 2012 |url=https://www.cinemablend.com/new/John-Carter-Conquers-Red-Planet-Blu-Ray-June-30691.html|publisher=Cinema Blend|access-date=May 3, 2012}}</ref> In mid-June, the movie topped sales on both the Nielsen VideoScan First Alert sales chart, which tracks overall disc sales, and Nielsen's dedicated Blu-ray Disc sales chart, with the DVD release selling almost a million copies making $17 million and Blu-ray and 3-D releases selling almost as many copies making $19.2 million, for a combined total of $36.3 million in its first week alone.<ref>{{cite the numbers|id=John-Carter-of-Mars |title=John Carter |access-date=March 3, 2021}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.the-numbers.com/interactive/newsStory.php?newsID=7355 |title=Blu-ray Sales: John Carter Acts Up |publisher=The Numbers |date=June 20, 2012 |access-date=January 31, 2016}}</ref>

==Reception==
===Box office===

Although the film grossed nearly $300 million worldwide, it lost a considerable amount of money due to its cost. At the time of its release, Disney claimed the film's production budget was $250 million, although tax returns released in 2014 revealed its exact budget was $263.7 million after taking tax credits into account.<ref name=Sylt>{{cite web |first=Christian |last=Sylt |title=Revealed: The $307 Million Cost of Disney's John Carter |date=October 22, 2014 |work=[[Forbes]] |url=https://www.forbes.com/sites/csylt/2014/10/22/revealed-the-307-million-cost-of-disneys-john-carter/2/ |access-date=December 7, 2014 |quote=The tax payment to John Carter gave the picture a net budget of $263.7 million which is far more than estimates predicted.}}</ref> Before the film opened, analysts predicted the film would be a huge financial failure due to its exorbitant cost combined with production and marketing costs of $350 million,<ref name=Chmielewski>{{cite news |first=Dawn C. |last=Chmielewski |title=Disney expects $200-million loss on 'John Carter' |date=March 20, 2012 |work=Los Angeles Times |url=https://www.latimes.com/entertainment/la-xpm-2012-mar-20-la-fi-ct-disney-write-down-20120320-story.html |access-date=December 7, 2014}}</ref> with Paul Dergarabedian, president of [[Hollywood.com]], noting "''John Carter'''s bloated budget would have required it to generate worldwide tickets sales of more than $600 million to break even ... a height reached by only 63 films in the history of moviemaking".<ref>{{cite web|url=https://nationalpost.com/entertainment/john-carter-may-set-guinness-record-for-biggest-box-office-flop-of-all-time|title=John Carter: Disney may set record for biggest box-office bomb &#124; National Post|publisher=Arts.nationalpost.com|access-date=January 31, 2016|archive-url=https://archive.today/20130129153001/http://arts.nationalpost.com/2012/03/21/john-carter-may-set-guinness-record-for-biggest-box-office-flop-of-all-time/|archive-date=January 29, 2013|url-status=dead}}</ref> Within two weeks of its release, Disney took a $200 million [[writedown]] on the film, ranking it among the [[List of biggest box-office bombs|biggest box-office bombs of all time]].<ref name=Chmielewski />{{efn|By some measures it is the biggest bomb. Disney's stated $200 million, adjusted to $236 million in modern dollars, is the upper bound of its estimated loss, and the greatest loss for any bomb both nominally and inflation-adjusted. Other estimates, by website [[The Numbers (website)|The Numbers]] put the number lower, at almost $113 million<ref name="The Numbers">{{cite web |title=Biggest Money Losers, Based on Absolute Loss on Worldwide Earnings |work=The Numbers |publisher=Nash Information Services |url=https://www.the-numbers.com/movie/budgets/ |access-date=April 21, 2022 |archive-date=October 26, 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171026191640/http://www.the-numbers.com/movie/budgets/ |url-status=dead }}</ref> ($133 million, after adjusting for inflation), well below the lower bound for estimated losses by ''[[The Lone Ranger (2013 film)|The Lone Ranger]]'' and ''[[Mortal Engines (film)|Mortal Engines]]'', the next two films with losses in that range.<p>The Numbers ranks ''John Carter'' at the low end of its reported range, below ''[[Mars Needs Moms]]'' (to which it attributes $143 million in losses) in its rankings of absolute losses against production costs; if [[Impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on cinema|films released during the COVID-19 pandemic]] (i.e., most films from the 2020s) are excluded, ''Mars Needs Moms'' is the biggest box-office bomb in film history.<ref name="The Numbers" /></p>}} Two months after the release, the Walt Disney Company released a statement on its earnings attributing the $161 million decline in the operating income of its Studio Entertainment division to a loss of $84 million in the quarter ending March 2012 "primarily" due to the performance of ''John Carter'' and the associated cost write-down.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://thewaltdisneycompany.com/sites/default/files/reports/q2-fy12-earnings.pdf |title=Archived copy |access-date=May 12, 2012 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120522224918/http://thewaltdisneycompany.com/sites/default/files/reports/q2-fy12-earnings.pdf |archive-date=May 22, 2012}}</ref>

====Domestic====

On March 9, 2012, ''John Carter'' opened domestically in over 3,500 theaters, taking in almost $10 million, the highest grosses of any film released that day.<ref name="BOM March 9">{{cite web|title=Domestic Box Office For Mar 9, 2012|url=https://www.boxofficemojo.com/date/2012-03-09/?ref_=bo_rl_table_1|website=[[Box Office Mojo]]|access-date=April 21, 2022}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=https://boxofficemojo.com/news/?id=3390&p=.htm|title=Friday Report: 'John Carter' Lands with a Thud|first=Ray|last=Subers |website=Box Office Mojo|date=March 10, 2012|access-date=March 16, 2012}}</ref> It was the only time period for which that would be true.
