==Soundtrack==
{{main|Lost in Translation (soundtrack)}}

The film's soundtrack was released by [[Emperor Norton Records]] on September 9, 2003.<ref name="metacriticost">{{cite web |title=Lost in Translation OST |url=https://www.metacritic.com/music/lost-in-translation-ost |website=[[Metacritic]] |access-date=May 20, 2020}}</ref> It contains 15 tracks, largely from the [[Shoegazing|shoegaze]] and dream pop genres of [[Indie rock|indie]] and [[alternative rock]]. The soundtrack was supervised by Brian Reitzell and contains songs from artists and groups including [[Death in Vegas]], [[Phoenix (French band)|Phoenix]], [[Squarepusher]], [[Sébastien Tellier]], and [[Happy End (band)|Happy End]]. [[The Jesus and Mary Chain]]'s song "[[Just Like Honey]]" and "[[Sometimes (My Bloody Valentine song)|Sometimes]]" by [[My Bloody Valentine (band)|My Bloody Valentine]] featured, and four original tracks were written for ''Lost in Translation'' by the latter band's frontman, [[Kevin Shields]].<ref name="dansby">{{cite magazine |last1=Dansby |first1=Andrew |title=Kevin Shields Found on 'Lost' |url=https://www.rollingstone.com/music/music-news/kevin-shields-found-on-lost-243814/ |access-date=May 20, 2020 |magazine=[[Rolling Stone]] |date=September 24, 2003}}</ref> Other tracks produced for the film include two co-written by Reitzell and [[Roger Joseph Manning Jr.]], and one by [[Air (French band)|Air]].<ref name="dansby" /> Songs featured in the film that are not in the soundtrack include karaoke performances of [[Elvis Costello]]'s cover of "[[(What's So Funny 'Bout) Peace, Love, and Understanding]]" and [[the Pretenders]]' "[[Brass in Pocket]]". A further performance by Murray of [[Roxy Music]]'s "[[More Than This (Roxy Music song)|More Than This]]" is included as a bonus track.{{refn|"[[(What's So Funny 'Bout) Peace, Love, and Understanding]]" was chosen for Bob to highlight his position in an older generation, "[[Brass in Pocket]]" was chosen for Charlotte to show her playful side, and "[[More Than This (Roxy Music song)|More Than This]]" was chosen extemporaneously by Coppola and Murray during shooting, after the two discovered they had a mutual affinity for [[Roxy Music]].<ref name="chumo" />|group="note"}}

During the screenwriting stage, Coppola spoke to Reitzell about the "moody" and "melancholic" qualities she wanted the music to convey in the film, as well as what Reitzell understood to be the "strange, floating, jet-lagged weirdness" that would define the central characters.<ref name="hundley" /> Coppola said she wanted the soundtrack "to be less like a score" and more like the dream-pop mixes Reitzell made to assist her writing of the film.<ref name="mitchell" /> While Shields had released little music since the release of ''[[Loveless (album)|Loveless]]'' in 1991,<ref name="white">{{cite magazine |last1=White |first1=Michael |title=My Bloody Valentine's Kevin Shields: An Enigma Emerges |url=http://exclaim.ca/film/article/lost_in_translation-sofia_coppolas_journey_into_culture |access-date=May 20, 2020 |magazine=[[Exclaim!]] |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190916102334/http://exclaim.ca/film/article/lost_in_translation-sofia_coppolas_journey_into_culture |archive-date=September 16, 2019 |url-status=live }}</ref> at Reitzell's suggestion, he and Coppola enlisted him to help write original music for the film;<ref name="keast">{{cite magazine |last1=Keast |first1=James |title=Lost In Translation: Sofia Coppola's Journey Into Culture Clash |date=October 1, 2003 |url=http://exclaim.ca/film/article/lost_in_translation-sofia_coppolas_journey_into_culture |magazine=[[Exclaim!]] |access-date=May 20, 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190916102334/http://exclaim.ca/film/article/lost_in_translation-sofia_coppolas_journey_into_culture |archive-date=September 16, 2019 |url-status=live }}</ref> Reitzell believed Shields "could capture that droning, swaying, beautiful kind of feeling that we wanted."<ref name="hundley" /> He then joined Shields in [[London]] for some two months<ref name="npr">{{cite news |title=From My Bloody Valentine to 'Lost in Translation' |url=https://www.npr.org/2003/09/15/1431220/from-my-bloody-valentine-to-lost-in-translation |access-date=May 20, 2020 |work=[[NPR]] |type=Audio |date=September 15, 2003 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200204175551/https://www.npr.org/2003/09/15/1431220/from-my-bloody-valentine-to-lost-in-translation |archive-date=February 4, 2020 |url-status=live }}</ref> of overnight recording sessions, and they used the screenplay and [[dailies]] from production as inspiration while they worked on songs for the film.<ref name="hundley" /> Shields commented on the challenge he felt in songwriting for a film, saying "I was barely aware of the language of music that's not essentially just for your ears.&nbsp;... In the end, just the physical movement of the film, that was a delicacy. And I suppose that's why I ended up doing stuff that was so delicate."<ref name="dansby" />

King argues that music often plays the most significant role in setting mood and tone in the film, writing that it is substantial "in evoking the dreamy, narcotised, semi-detached impressions of jet-lag" as well as broader feelings of alienation and disconnection, "making what is probably the largest single contribution to the widespread understanding of the film as a 'mood piece'."{{sfn|King|2010|p=115}} He points to the use of "Girls" by Death in Vegas, featured in the early sequence in which Bob is driven from the airport to the hotel, arguing that it "plays a role equal to if not dominating that of the visuals{{nbsp}}..., creating a drifting, ethereal and somewhat dreamy quality that precisely captures the impressions of temporal and spatial disjunction".{{sfn|King|2010|pp=115–116}} He also points to the use of "cool and distant" tracks like "Tommib", used in the extended sequence featuring Charlotte observing Tokyo while seated in her hotel room window, as playing a significant role in establishing feelings of isolation and disorientation in the character.{{sfn|King|2010|pp=116–119}} In King's view, some sequences feature combinations of music and visuals so as to function as "audio-visual [[set piece]]s", which offer distinct points of appeal in the film for its target audience.{{sfn|King|2010|p=117}}

==Release==

===Marketing===
Coppola did not sell distribution rights for the United States and Canada until she and Flack finished editing the film.<ref name="harris" /> In February 2003, the director showed the film to top executives at the domestic arm of Focus Features,<ref name="harris" /> the company to which it had already sold most of the foreign distribution. The prior contract proved to be significant for Focus, as it received privileged access to the film while competing buyers complained that they were restricted to the viewing of a three-minute trailer in the Focus offices at the [[American Film Market]].<ref>{{cite news |last1=Harris |first1=Dana |last2=Dunkley |first2=Cathy |date=February 25, 2003 |title=Focus frames 'Lost' deal at finish of AFM |url=https://variety.com/2003/film/news/focus-frames-lost-deal-at-finish-of-afm-1117881191/?jwsource=cl |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201028030236/https://variety.com/2003/film/news/focus-frames-lost-deal-at-finish-of-afm-1117881191/?jwsource=cl |archive-date=October 28, 2020 |access-date=May 9, 2020 |work=[[Variety (magazine)|Variety]]}}</ref> Coppola initially offered the domestic distribution rights for $5 million, but she decided to sell them to Focus for $4 million, citing her appreciation for the international deals the company had secured for the film.<ref name="harris" />

Once Focus was involved, it began promoting the film by employing a conventional "[[Independent film|indie]]-style" marketing campaign.{{sfn|King|2010|p=16}} The strategy involved generating positive word of mouth for the film well before its September 2003 release.<ref name="grove2" /> The distributor arranged advance press screenings throughout the summer of 2003 and combined this with a magazine publicity campaign.<ref name="grove2">{{cite news |last1=Grove |first1=Martin A. |title=Focus Heads Focus on 'Translation' Success |work=[[The Hollywood Reporter]] |date=October 10, 2003}}</ref>{{refn|For one example of a magazine article cited by Focus as being part of this campaign, see {{harvnb|Hirschberg|2003}}.<ref name="grove2" />|group="note"}} Posters and trailers emphasized the recognizable star presence of Murray, highlighting his performance in the film's comic sequences, which favored wider audience appeal.{{sfn|King|2010|pp=24–25}} Immediately prior to its release, Focus placed ''Lost in Translation'' in [[film festival]]s and hosted "intimate media screenings" that included question-and-answer panels with Coppola and Murray.<ref name="harris" /> Many of these marketing tacks were designed to promote the film at minimal cost, a departure from more costly strategies often employed in the Hollywood mainstream, such as major television advertising.{{sfn|King|2010|p=16}}

===Theatrical run===
''Lost in Translation'' had its premiere on August 29, 2003, at the [[Telluride Film Festival]] in the United States.<ref name="afi" /> Over the next week, it appeared at the [[60th Venice International Film Festival]] and the [[2003 Toronto International Film Festival]].<ref name="afi" /> It opened to the public in [[limited release]] on September 12, 2003, at 23 theaters in major cities in the United States.<ref name="brooks">{{cite news |last1=Brooks |first1=Brian |title=The Land of the Rising Box Office Shines Bright for 'Lost in Translation' |url=https://www.indiewire.com/2003/09/the-land-of-the-rising-box-office-shines-bright-for-lost-in-translation-79462/ |access-date=May 10, 2020 |work=[[IndieWire]] |date=September 16, 2003 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180528014459/http://www.indiewire.com/2003/09/the-land-of-the-rising-box-office-shines-bright-for-lost-in-translation-79462/ |archive-date=May 28, 2018 |url-status=live }}</ref> The film had already generated speculation about [[Academy Awards|Oscar]] contention from advance screenings and was noted for opening several weeks earlier than expected for an indie vying for awards—a risk being that opening too early might cause the film to be forgotten by the time nominations were made for major prizes like the Academy Awards.<ref name="grove2" />{{sfn|King|2010|pp=16–17}} Focus Features co-presidents [[James Schamus]] and [[David Linde]] commented that the company chose an early release date on the basis of factors including the film's quality and early marketing campaign, as well as a lack of competition from other films.<ref name="grove2" /> The strategy was intended to give ''Lost in Translation'' more time to command the marketplace.{{sfn|King|2010|p=17}}

[[File:Lost in Translation Theater Count.png|upright=1.45|thumb|alt=The number starts at 23 on September 12, 2003, rises to 882 on October 10, and declines to a low of 123 on January 2, 2004. It then rises to 632 on January 30 and then declines to 51 on March 25.|Graph showing the estimated number of theaters in which ''Lost in Translation'' played in the United States, Canada, and Puerto Rico in 2003–2004.<ref name="bom" /> Focus Features expanded its theater presence in January after it received nominations for the 76th Academy Awards.]]
The film grossed $925,000 in its opening weekend and was expanded the next week from 23 theaters to 183<ref name="grove2" /> in the top 25 markets of the country.<ref name="brooks" /> There, it grossed more than $2.62 million over the weekend<ref name="brooks2">{{cite news |last1=Brooks |first1=Brian |title='Scarface' Lashes the B.O.; Docs Continue Strong |url=https://www.indiewire.com/2003/09/scarface-lashes-the-b-o-docs-continue-strong-79447/ |access-date=May 10, 2020 |work=[[IndieWire]] |date=September 23, 2003}}</ref> and nearly paid off the total budget of the film. It entered [[wide release]] on October 3,{{refn|"Wide release" is defined here as crossing the 600-theater threshold.|group="note"}} its fourth weekend, peaking at a rank of seven in the box office chart;<ref name="bom">{{cite web |title=Lost in Translation |website=[[Box Office Mojo]] |url=https://www.boxofficemojo.com/release/rl2388755969/weekend/ |access-date=July 4, 2020}}</ref> a week later, it expanded to an estimated 882 theaters, the film's highest theater count over its run.<ref name="bom" /> ''Lost in Translation'' grossed an estimated to-date total of $18.5 million through October 13<ref name="bom" /> and was noted by ''[[The Hollywood Reporter]]'' to have been performing well even "in smaller and medium-sized markets where audiences don't always respond to this type of upscale material".<ref name="grove2" /> Following this performance, ''Lost in Translation'' saw a gradual decline in theater presence progressing into the new year,<ref name="bom" /> though it was expanded again after the film received nominations for the [[76th Academy Awards]].{{sfn|King|2010|p=22}} The film was widened from a late December low of 117 theaters to an estimated 632 at the end of January, ultimately ending its run in the United States and Canada on March 25 and earning $44.6 million.<ref name="bom" /> Its international release earned $74.1 million, for a worldwide total of $119 million.<ref name="bom" />

===Home media===
The DVD of ''Lost in Translation'' was released on February 3, 2004 by [[Universal Studios Home Video]],<ref name="metacritic2">{{cite web |title=Lost in Translation Details and Credits |url=https://www.metacritic.com/movie/lost-in-translation/details |website=[[Metacritic]] |access-date=May 10, 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180813001028/http://www.metacritic.com/movie/lost-in-translation/details |archive-date=August 13, 2018 |url-status=live }}</ref> and includes deleted scenes, a behind-the-scenes featurette, a conversation about the film featuring Murray and Coppola, and a music video for "[[City Girl (song)|City Girl]]",<ref>{{cite AV media |title=Lost in Translation |type=DVD |date=February 3, 2004 |publisher=[[Focus Features]]}}</ref> one of the original songs composed for the film by [[Kevin Shields]]. Wanting to capitalize on the publicity surrounding ''Lost in Translation''{{'}}s presence at the Academy Awards, Focus Features made the unusual move of releasing the film on home media while it was still screening in theaters, immediately after its Oscar nominations were announced.{{sfn|King|2010|p=22}} The strategy was seen as risky, as the industry was generally concerned that theatrical revenues could be harmed by early home video release.{{sfn|King|2010|p=22}} ''Lost in Translation'' ultimately earned nearly $5 million from its first five days of video rentals and sold one million retail copies during its first week of release.<ref name="saccone">{{cite magazine |last1=Saccone |first1=Melinda |title=Coppola's Oscar-Lauded Film Translates Well to Video |magazine=[[Home Media Magazine|Video Store Magazine]] |date=February 15, 2004 |volume=26 |issue=7 |page=18}}</ref> Early returns showed it was the second-best selling DVD during this period<ref name="saccone" /> while the film screened in 600 theaters and box office revenues dropped 19% from the previous week, which ''[[Variety (magazine)|Variety]]'' described as "relatively modest".<ref name="hettrick">{{cite news |last1=Hettrick |first1=Scott |title='Lost' translates to DVD, bigscreen |url=https://variety.com/2004/digital/features/lost-translates-to-dvd-bigscreen-1117900355/ |access-date=May 10, 2020 |work=[[Variety (magazine)|Variety]] |date=February 17, 2004}}</ref> Focus credited the performance to positive word of mouth and cited the marketing for the film on both media as helpful for whichever platform consumers chose.<ref name="hettrick" />

''Lost in Translation'' was later released on the now-obsolete [[HD DVD]] format on May 29, 2007,<ref name="hdd1">{{cite web |date=May 31, 2007 |title=Lost in Translation HD DVD Review |url=https://hddvd.highdefdigest.com/739/lostintranslation.html |url-status=deviated |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171213173755/https://hddvd.highdefdigest.com/739/lostintranslation.html |archive-date=December 13, 2017 |access-date=May 10, 2020 |website=High-Def Digest}}</ref> and on [[Blu-ray]] on December 7, 2010.<ref name="hdd2">{{cite web |last1=Miller |first1=Gordon S. |title=Lost in Translation Blu-ray Review |url=https://bluray.highdefdigest.com/3283/lostintranslation.html |date=January 4, 2011 |website=High-Def Digest |access-date=May 10, 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170218163407/http://bluray.highdefdigest.com/3283/lostintranslation.html |archive-date=February 18, 2017 |url-status=live }}</ref> In June 2023, [[Kino Lorber]] announced it would release the film on [[Ultra HD Blu-ray]], but the release was cancelled in early 2025, with a post on Kino Lorber's X account saying, "it was becoming [a] very complicated release with lots of people to please."<ref>{{Cite web |last=Report |first=H. D. |date=June 19, 2023 |title=Lost in Translation is getting restored in 4k for release on Ultra HD Blu-ray |url=https://hd-report.com/2023/06/19/lost-in-translation-is-getting-restored-in-4k-for-release-on-ultra-hd-blu-ray/ |access-date=September 8, 2023 |website=HD Report |language=en-us}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Dawn of the Discs - The upcoming @kinolorber 4K UHD of Lost in Translation (2003) has been cancelled for unspecified reasons. #4KUltraHD #4K #Bluray #PhysicalMedia {{!}} Facebook |url=https://www.facebook.com/dawnofthediscs/photos/the-upcoming-kinolorber-4k-uhd-of-lost-in-translation-2003-has-been-cancelled-fo/1064362985651612/ |access-date=2025-03-17 |website=www.facebook.com |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |title=KL Studio Classics / Kino Cult (@KLStudioClassic) on X |url=https://x.com/KLStudioClassic/status/1845124852279042387 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250113140416/https://x.com/KLStudioClassic/status/1845124852279042387 |archive-date=2025-01-13 |access-date=2025-11-19 |work=X (formerly Twitter) |language=en}}</ref>

==Criticism and boycott calls==<!--Please don't change this section to "controversy" per WP:CSECTION.-->

===Accusations of racism===
Critics have argued that ''Lost in Translation'' is [[Racism|racist]] and perpetuates [[Orientalism]], and that its tropes and visual framing rely on [[Ethnic joke|ethnic humor]], [[Stereotypes of East Asians in the United States|stereotypes of East Asians]], Orientalist imagery, and the [[dehumanization]] of Japanese characters.<ref name="wright">{{cite news |last1=Wright |first1=George |title=Hit film gets lost in racism row |url=https://www.theguardian.com/world/2004/feb/27/oscars2004.usa |access-date=May 25, 2020 |work=[[The Guardian]] |date=February 27, 2004 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190816210556/https://www.theguardian.com/world/2004/feb/27/oscars2004.usa |archive-date=August 16, 2019 |url-status=live }}</ref>{{sfn|King|2010|p=132}}<ref name="day">{{cite news |last1=Day |first1=Kiku |title=Totally lost in translation |url=https://www.theguardian.com/world/2004/jan/24/japan.film |access-date=May 25, 2020 |work=[[The Guardian]] |date=January 23, 2004 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200702104422/https://www.theguardian.com/world/2004/jan/24/japan.film |archive-date=July 2, 2020 |url-status=live }}</ref><ref name="paik">{{cite magazine |last1=Paik |first1=E. Koohan |title=Is 'Lost in Translation' Racist? |magazine=[[ColorLines|ColorLines RaceWire]] |date=November 2003 |access-date=May 25, 2020 |url=http://www.arc.org/racewire/031112e_paik.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20050418214717/http://www.arc.org/racewire/031112e_paik.html |archive-date=April 18, 2005}}</ref><ref name=":0" />

On January 31, 2004, the Asian American and Pacific Islander (AAPI) organization Asia Media Watch sponsored and launched a nationwide campaign to petition motion picture industry groups, including the [[Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences]], [[Directors Guild of America]], [[Screen Actors Guild]], and [[Writers Guild of America]], to vote against the film ''Lost In Translation'' in all awards categories at the [[76th Academy Awards]].<ref name="lost-in-racism">{{Cite web |title=lost-in-racism.org {{!}} Campaign - No Votes for Lost In Translation |url=https://lost-in-racism.org/|access-date=2026-05-09 |website=lost-in-racism.org}}</ref><ref name="wright" />{{sfn|King|2010|p=133}} The group, along with its campaign volunteers and supporters, distributed flyers and lobbied voters at film screenings in Los Angeles, New York, and San Francisco, while also conducting email campaigns and contacting the press.<ref name="lost-in-racism" /> The initiative ultimately had little impact on the Academy Awards due to the dominant sweep of ''[[The Lord of the Rings: The Return of the King]]'', which won eleven awards, including [[Academy Award for Best Picture|Best Picture]] and [[Academy Award for Best Director|Best Director]].<ref>{{cite news |last=Morales |first=Tatiana |title=Peter Jackson, Lord Of The Oscars |work=[[CBS News]] |date=February 13, 2009 |url=https://www.cbsnews.com/news/peter-jackson-lord-of-the-oscars/ |access-date=July 24, 2013}}</ref> However, spokesperson Tom Roman suggested that because some voters who were lobbied agreed to return their promotional screening DVDs for refunds, the campaign may have influenced voting at the [[10th Screen Actors Guild Awards]], where ''Lost in Translation'' star Bill Murray, who was previously considered the favorite for [[Outstanding Performance by a Male Actor in a Leading Role]], was defeated by [[Johnny Depp]] for his role in ''[[Pirates of the Caribbean: The Curse of the Black Pearl]]''.<ref name="wright" />

The organization insisted that the film "dehumanizes the Japanese people by portraying them as a collection of shallow stereotypes who are treated with disregard and disdain," claiming that such portrayals and lack of [[cultural sensitivity]] led to discrimination against [[Asian Americans]] in the United States, where a significant minority of the population already holds [[Anti-Asian sentiment in the United States|anti-Asian sentiment]].<ref name="lost-in-racism" /> The group further criticized the film for perpetuating [[perpetual foreigner]] stereotypes, claiming that they also reinforce discrimination and stating: "This film is indicative of a level of mainstream tolerance and acceptance of Asian American discrimination that would otherwise be unacceptable if directed towards [[African Americans|African]] and [[Hispanic and Latino Americans|Hispanic Americans]]."<ref name="lost-in-racism" /> In a released statement, the group asserted: <blockquote>The humor and lampooning of the Japanese in the film has a distinctly racial element … The main characters prey on the Japanese and their inability to understand English. Particularly offensive are the hackneyed stereotypical jokes such as the overdone juxtaposition of L's and R's, mocking them because they bow and are short, and references to their disgusting food. The main characters visibly express disdain, and make insulting remarks and jokes in the direct presence of Japanese characters. There are no redeeming Japanese roles in the film, nor is there any significant dialogue between the main characters and the Japanese characters. They merely serve as buffoons for the main characters to ridicule.<ref name="lost-in-racism" /></blockquote>
Another Asian American and Pacific Islander (AAPI) organization at the time, the Asian American Movement Ezine,<ref>{{Cite web |last=School |first=Stanford Law |title=APILSA Resources |url=https://law.stanford.edu/apilsa/apilsa-resources/ |access-date=2026-05-09 |website=Stanford Law School |language=en}}</ref> criticized the film, comparing its tropes to the history of [[Asian-American representation in Hollywood|Asian American representation in Hollywood]] and [[racism in early American film]]: "To show the culture clash between American and Japanese culture, the film relies on stale stereotypes of the Japanese for laughs: They’re short! They’re wacky! [[Perception of English /r/ and /l/ by Japanese speakers|They can’t pronounce their r’s]]!  The film is replete with racial gags that draw from the same old Hollywood stereotypes, from [[Mickey Rooney]]’s [[I. Y. Yunioshi|Mr. Yunioshi]] in [[Breakfast at Tiffany's (film)|''Breakfast at Tiffany’s'']], to the Japanese car makers in 1986’s [[Gung Ho (film)|''Gung Ho'']], or even [[Sixteen Candles|''Sixteen Candle''s]] infamous [[Long Duk Dong]]."<ref>{{Cite web |title="Lost in Translation" is the Same Old Story |url=http://www.aamovement.net/art_culture/filmreviews/losttrans1.html |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20031110084717/http://www.aamovement.net/art_culture/filmreviews/losttrans1.html |archive-date=10 Nov 2003 |access-date=9 May 2026 |website=Asian American Movement Ezine}}</ref><ref name="lost-in-racism-2">{{Cite web |title=asianmediawatch.net {{!}} Review of Lost In Translation |url=https://lost-in-racism.org/lost.html#reviews |access-date=2026-05-27 |website=lost-in-racism.org}}</ref>

Filmmaker [[Koohan Paik-Mander|E. Koohan Paik]] argued: "The Japanese are presented not as people, but as clowns ... the hilarity is rooted entirely in the '[[Other (philosophy)|otherness]]' of the Japanese people. We laugh at them, not with them. This is why the film is accused of being racist." Paik wrote that it is "the shirking of responsibility to depict them as full human beings, either negative or positive, which constitutes discrimination, or racism."<ref name="paik" /><ref name="lost-in-racism-2" /> Paik also criticized the film's racial undertones within its [[cinematography]]:<blockquote>Even [[Cinéma vérité|verité-style footage]] of authentic locals focuses on the Japanese as a sorry lot, preoccupied with cheesifying all things Western ... These scenes are occasionally 'balanced' by appropriately reverent, but equally inscrutable, shrine-and-temple sequences. Moreover, the film is simultaneously scornful and smug in the knowledge that imitation, no matter how tacky, is the sincerest form of flattery. This sentiment is actually articulated in the dialogue, by Charlotte's husband, galled by a rock-band photo shoot: "Let them be who they are! They're trying to make them [[Keith Richards]] when they're just skinny and nerdy." The subtext here is, when Westerners ape the [[The Rolling Stones|Rolling Stones]], it's normal; but when Asian kids fall prey to the same media hype, they're pathetic wannabees. They should be meditating in a [[dojo]] somewhere, not playing [[rock and roll]].<ref name="paik" /></blockquote>Critics argued that the film portrays Japanese people through exaggerated stereotypes, particularly in scenes involving [[language barrier]]s.<ref name=":1" /><ref name=":0" /> Several scenes attracted criticism for using Japanese accents and English pronunciation as sources of humor; opponents of the film argued that such scenes encourage audiences to laugh at [[Japanese language|Japanese speech patterns]] and mannerisms rather than at the protagonists’ discomfort.<ref name="rich" /><ref name="paik" /><ref>{{Cite web |title=Pop culture lost in Asian stereotypes - The Arizona State Press |url=https://www.statepress.com/article/2004/03/pop-culture-lost-in-asian-stereotypes |access-date=2026-05-09 |website=www.statepress.com |language=en-US}}</ref> In ''[[National Post|The National Post]],'' [[Robert Fulford (journalist)|Robert Fulford]] criticized the film: “''Lost in Translation'' expresses a distasteful racism through romantic comedy. It says, as racists often do, that foreigners, in this case Japanese, are inherently comic and stupid... ''Lost in Translation'' will appeal to all those who find enduring humour in the inability of Japanese to pronounce "r" and "l."  It's a film that prides itself on its own [[wiktionary:provincialism|provincialism]].”<ref>{{Cite web |title=lost-in-racism.org {{!}} Letters From Readers |url=https://lost-in-racism.org/review1.html |access-date=2026-05-09 |website=lost-in-racism.org}}</ref><ref name=":0">{{Cite web |title=The joke's on them: Why can't the protagonists of Lost in Translation see what's around them? -- by Robert Fulford |url=https://www.robertfulford.com/2003-09-23-lost.html |access-date=2026-05-09 |website=www.robertfulford.com}}</ref> ''[[Dallas Observer]]''<nowiki/>'s Gregory Weinkauf wrote: "[After] it's abundantly clear the movie's going nowhere slowly, [the protagonists] encounter Charlie Brown, or "Chalrie Blown" (the director's friend, Fumihiro Hayashi), who's so thinly developed that he makes Bob and Charlotte look like classic [[Dickensian]] creations by comparison."<ref>{{Cite web |last=Weinkauf |first=Gregory |date=2003-09-17 |title=Ad-libbing on Tokyo Time |url=https://www.dallasobserver.com/arts-culture/ad-libbing-on-tokyo-time-6387283/ |access-date=2026-05-09 |website=Dallas Observer |language=en-US}}</ref> Film critic and [[Wake Forest University]] professor [[Peter Brunette]] criticized the film's reliance on [[Ethnic joke|ethnic humor]], writing: "Since all the jokes are at the expense of the Japanese—'these people are, really, just SO weird!!'—the humor grates after a while, especially the ancient jokes about the Japanese tendency to reverse 'r' and 'l' when speaking English. (Needless to say, not one of the Americans ever attempts a single word of Japanese.)" Brunette concluded that "Japan remains little more than one gigantic throwaway line, and the story, and their relationship, could really have happened anywhere."<ref name=":1">{{Cite web |last=Indiewire |date=2003-09-17 |title=Sofia Coppola's Overly Subtle "Lost in Translation" |url=https://www.indiewire.com/criticism/culture/sofia-coppolas-overly-subtle-lost-in-translation-79460/ |access-date=2026-06-19 |website=IndieWire |language=en-US}}</ref> ''[[Slate (magazine)|Slate]]'' critic [[David Edelstein]] argued that there is "something narcissistic and entitled" about the protagonists. He criticized a specific scene, he wrote "Charlotte asks Bob why the Japanese mix up their l’s and r’s and he says, 'for yucks'—which is very funny in a Bill Murray-esque way. But they’re ''our'' yucks, at ''their'' expense. It’s bad enough to make fun of Japanese for their English in [[English-speaking world|English-speaking countries]]. But in Japan? The sense of otherness and of cultural superiority merges uncomfortably."<ref name="edelstein" />
In ''[[The Guardian]],'' ethnomusicologist Kiku Day wrote: "There is only one type of humor in the film that I could see: [[Anti-Japanese sentiment|anti-Japanese racism]], which is its very spine … There is no scene where the Japanese are afforded a shred of dignity. The viewer is sledgehammered into laughing at these small, yellow people and their funny ways."<ref name="day" /> Day also criticized the film for Orientalism and [[cultural appropriation]], arguing that it relies on mocking caricatures of Japanese people while contrasting a romanticized view of ancient traditions. Day wrote that "Those not conforming to [the image of the mysterious East] never have a voice of their own. They simply don't have a story to tell, or at least not one that interests 'us'", comparing this dynamic to "the way white-dominated Hollywood used to depict African-Americans - as crooks, pimps, or lacking self-control compared with [[white Americans]]".<ref name="day" />
Day wrote:<blockquote>The Japanese are one-dimensional and dehumanized in the movie, serving as an exotic background for Bob and Charlotte's story, like dirty wallpaper in a cheap hotel. How funny is it to put the 6ft-plus Bill Murray in an elevator with a number of overly small Japanese? To manufacture a joke, the film has Murray contorting himself to have a shower because its head isn't high enough for him - although he is supposed to be staying in a five-star hotel. It's made up simply to give western audiences another stereotype to laugh at. And haven't we had enough about the Japanese confusing rs and ls when they speak English? … it is reminiscent of the racist jokes about Asians and black people that comedians told in British clubs in the 1970s.</blockquote>Anthony Quinn of ''[[The Independent]]'' noted that the film falters slightly when relying on tropes involving "funny foreigners" for humor, citing scenes with a frantic hotel call girl and a communication breakdown at a hospital. Quinn criticized the presence of "a trace of lumpen-tourist condescension—I am speaking perfect English. Why can't these funny little people understand me?"<ref>{{Cite web |date=2004-01-09 |title=Lost in Translation (15) |url=https://www.the-independent.com/arts-entertainment/films/reviews/lost-in-translation-15-72637.html |access-date=2026-07-20 |website=The Independent |language=en}}</ref> Film director [[Robert Allan Ackerman]] accused the film of stereotyping and racism, stating that he "thought that it had nothing to do with Japan; they could have been on the moon, and the only reason to have Japanese people was to make fun of them."<ref>{{Cite web |last=Hadley-garcia |first=George |date=2009-01-23 |title=Broth in translation |url=https://www.japantimes.co.jp/culture/2009/01/23/films/broth-in-translation-2/ |access-date=2026-07-14 |website=The Japan Times |language=en}}</ref> Film critic [[Mike D'Angelo]] argued that viewers are never encouraged to identify with anyone other than the two white American protagonists, he wrote that he felt "constantly being nudged to find the Japanese hilariously wacky." He cited this persistent "nudging" as a primary reason for his surprise at the film's widespread acclaim.<ref>{{Cite web |last=D'Angelo |first=Mike |title=Lost in Translation 2003 |url=https://letterboxd.com/gemko/film/lost-in-translation/ |access-date=2026-07-20 |website=letterboxd.com |language=en}}</ref>
{{Clear}}
''[[The New York Times]]'' reported that public debate regarding the film's depiction of [[ethnic stereotype]]s and its potential reception among Japanese audiences began prior to its May 2004 release in Japan. Off-the-record comments from Japanese film distribution executives reflected uncertainty over how local audiences would respond.<ref name="rich" /> Critics contrasted the film with ''[[The Last Samurai]]'', in which [[Tom Cruise]]'s character adapts to Japanese culture despite accusations of a [[White savior narrative in film|white savior narrative]] but in ''Lost in Translation'', by contrast, the two protagonists bond primarily over their befuddlement with Japanese behavior.<ref name="rich">{{cite news |last1=Rich |first1=Motoko |title=Land Of the Rising Cliché |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2004/01/04/movies/land-of-the-rising-cliche.html |access-date=May 25, 2020 |work=[[The New York Times]] |date=January 4, 2004 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191018122521/https://www.nytimes.com/2004/01/04/movies/land-of-the-rising-cliche.html?pagewanted=all |archive-date=October 18, 2019 |url-status=live }}</ref> In ''[[The Japan Times]]''' analytical coverage of the film's reception in Japan, it was reported that some of the Japanese crew members “thought this whole thing was very insulting.”<ref name="The Japan Times-2023" /> Co-producer Stephen Nomura Schible, who is bilingual in English and Japanese, also expressed similar discomfort with elements of the script, stating: “It clearly wasn’t a role for the local crew, for the most part, to express about those types of sensitivities — for better or for worse.”<ref name="The Japan Times-2023">{{cite news |last=Hadfield |first=James |title='Lost in Translation' at 20: A Tokyo perspective |url=https://www.japantimes.co.jp/culture/2023/09/09/film/lost-translation-20th-anniversary/ |work=[[The Japan Times]] |date=September 9, 2023 |access-date=August 24, 2025}}</ref> ''[[The Christian Science Monitor]]'' reported that many Japanese critics argued that the film's emphasis on language barriers, cultural misunderstandings, and physical differences reinforced Western stereotypes of Japan.<ref name=":2">{{Cite news |title='Lost in Translation' doesn't translate well in Japan |url=https://www.csmonitor.com/2004/0419/p07s01-woap.html |access-date=2026-08-06 |work=Christian Science Monitor |issn=0882-7729}}</ref> The newspaper also reported that a waiter at the 52nd-floor New York Bar and Grill, who appeared as himself in the film, questioned its use of racial stereotypes, asking, "Do foreigners really have that stereotype about Japanese? ... It will give people in other countries the wrong impression about us." The [[Australians|Australian]] chef at the Hyatt opined that the film reflected the impressions of first-time visitors, stating, "But now that I've lived here for two years, I think it isn't fair to Japanese."<ref name=":2" /> Yoshio Tsuchiya of ''[[The Yomiuri Shimbun]]'' wrote that Coppola's representation of Japan was "heavily stereotypical and discriminatory." He argued that "the film makes fun of Japanese who cannot pronounce 'l' and 'r' correctly ... all of the Japanese characters are submissive, wearing a 'phony' smile." Tsuchiya concluded that "this film is nothing more than Coppola's personal visual interpretation of [Japan] and is hardly a work of cultural critique."<ref>{{Cite news |last=Tsuchiya |first=Yoshio |date=April 19, 2004 |title=映画評 |trans-title=Film review |work=[[The Yomiuri Shimbun]] |language=ja}}</ref><ref name="musetto" /> In ''[[The Asahi Shimbun]]'', another major Japan’s newspaper, author and film critic Kotaro Sawaki said he “felt unusual revulsion against this movie,” adding: “All the Japanese are consistently portrayed as foolish. But the movie fails to point out that what appears to be foolish mirrors the viewer’s own foolishness.”<ref name="musetto">Cited in {{cite news |last1=Musetto |first1=V.A. |title='Lost in Transition' – Japan Critics Rip Flick |url=https://nypost.com/2004/05/21/lost-in-transition-japan-critics-rip-flick/ |access-date=May 25, 2020 |work=[[New York Post]] |date=May 21, 2004 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171030233601/http://nypost.com/2004/05/21/lost-in-transition-japan-critics-rip-flick/ |archive-date=October 30, 2017 |url-status=live }}</ref> Sawaki also drew a parallel to geopolitical conflicts, asking, “Isn't the belief that 'the other person is at fault if I can't understand them' a contributing factor to the events in the Middle East?”, in reference to the [[2003 invasion of Iraq]].<ref>{{Cite book |last=Sawaki |first=Kotaro |title=銀の森へ(Gin no mori e) |publisher=[[Asahi shimbun|Asahi bunko]] |year=2018 |language=ja |trans-title=To the Silver Forest}}</ref> Michiko Shiraishi, a New York correspondent for ''[[Jiji Press]]'', wrote that "Japanese might feel they were betrayed by ‘their true friends,’ Americans.”<ref name="musetto" />{{Clear}}Geoff King, a professor of arts and humanities at [[Brunel University of London]], criticized the film's portrayal of Japanese people and culture, arguing that the narrative relies on racist tropes.{{sfn|King|2010|p=131}}{{sfn|King|2010|p=132}} King argued that the film's humor is derived from the physical appearance, cultural practices, and limited English proficiency of the Japanese characters, writing:{{sfn|King|2010|p=131}}{{sfn|King|2010|p=132}} <blockquote>A good deal of the comedy offered by ''Lost in Translation'' seems to rely on rather cheap and obvious stereotypes, in a manner that is somewhat surprising and out of tune with its broader positioning in the film- cultural landscape. A number of verbal jokes are based around the tendency of Japanese characters to render what should be ‘r’ sounds as ‘l’ sounds ... A similar number of visual jokes relate to the diminutive stature of many Japanese people, some of which do not seem to make much sense other than as arbitrary mocking. Bob bends uncomfortably to get beneath a shower head that is fixed too low and apparently cannot be adjusted sufficiently upwards, for example, although the pole to which it is attached seems to have plenty of further height capacity ... The lack of any other motivation for such examples makes them appear to be egregious cases of crude stereotyping, in search of cheap laughs.</blockquote>King wrote that the film emphasizes the [[Stereotypes of Japanese people|stereotypes of Japanese people as "crazy" or "extreme"]] in scenes such as the one with the prostitute who visits Bob in his hotel room and the chat-show host with whom Bob appears on television.{{sfn|King|2010|p=132}} King noted that Japanese characters exist only as a backdrop to support the main characters rather than as fully realized individuals: "There are some more ‘normal’- seeming Japanese characters, principally some of those with whom Bob and Charlotte socialise on their first night of escape from the hotel, although their nature seems in this context to be shaped by their background function in relationship to the particular experience undergone at the time by the protagonists rather than being given any space to exist in its own right."{{sfn|King|2010|pp=130–132}} He concluded that: "most Japanese are presented as objects for the amusement of the viewer."{{sfn|King|2010|p=134}}

Homay King, professor of History of Art at [[Bryn Mawr College]] accused the film of Orientalism stating that, "''Lost in Translation'' makes but minimal efforts to rewrite the myths of Asia that Hollywood film has been recycling for nearly a century: the [[Orient]] as primitive, feminized, and eroticized; Asian citizens as alternately silly or perilous, enigmatic and cloaked in artifice."{{sfn|King|2005|p=46}} She also noted that the film fails to establish the perspective from which Japanese representations are made, writing that "the film [does not] sufficiently clarify that its real subject is not Tokyo itself, but Western perceptions of Tokyo{{nbsp}}... When Japan appears superficial, inappropriately erotic, or unintelligible, we are never completely sure whether this vision belongs to Coppola, to her characters, or simply to a Hollywood cinematic imaginary."{{sfn|King|2005|pp=45–46}} Kendra Marston, a [[film studies]] lecturer at [[Massey University]], argues that the narrative primarily centers on [[Whiteness studies|whiteness]], "the soul searching of the white American characters," contrasting this focus with what she characterizes as a "heavily stereotyped depiction" of local Japanese characters. According to Marston, "the 'unknowability' of the Tokyo environment aids in perpetuating a cinematic mood characterized by sustained periods of white melancholia."<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Marston |first=Kendra |title=Postfeminist Whiteness: Problematising Melancholic Burden in Contemporary Hollywood |url=https://www.jstor.org/content/oa_chapter_monograph/10.3366/j.ctt1pwt3hk.11?searchText=Sofia+coppola&searchUri=%2Faction%2FdoBasicSearch%3FQuery%3DSofia%2Bcoppola%26so%3Drel&ab_segments=0%2Fbasic_search_gsv2%2Fcontrol&refreqid=fastly-default%3A90baacae9c33bf0e126d871c4d43f57b&seq=16 |journal=[[Edinburgh University Press]] |jstor=10.3366/j.ctt1pwt3hk.11 |via=JSTOR}}</ref> Marston further identifies the specific emotional undercurrent within the film as a "painful yet pleasurable [[neurasthenia]], experienced only by the white and privileged, that the protagonists are unable to alleviate," writing: "The allure of the exotic Other occupies a source of transient fantasy that remains in the realm of wishful thinking, never promising a lasting transcendence over the melancholic state and yet also importantly working to preserve the text’s primary interest in the mysterious nature and nostalgic idealization of [[White identity|white feminine identity]]."<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Marston |first=Kendra |title=Postfeminist Whiteness: Problematising Melancholic Burden in Contemporary Hollywood |url=https://www.jstor.org/content/oa_chapter_monograph/10.3366/j.ctt1pwt3hk.11?searchText=Sofia+coppola&searchUri=%2Faction%2FdoBasicSearch%3FQuery%3DSofia%2Bcoppola%26so%3Drel&ab_segments=0%2Fbasic_search_gsv2%2Fcontrol&refreqid=fastly-default%3A90baacae9c33bf0e126d871c4d43f57b&seq=19 |journal=[[Edinburgh University Press]] |jstor=10.3366/j.ctt1pwt3hk.11 |via=JSTOR}}</ref>

In an article published in a 2004 issue of ''[[Maclean's]]'', [[Steve Burgess (author)|Steve Burgess]] criticized the film as an [[Ethnocentrism|ethnocentric]] "compendium of unpleasant stereotypes{{nbsp}}... indicative of the way visitors and foreign workers often view Japan."<ref>{{cite journal|last=Burgess|first=Steve|date=April 26, 2004|title=Found in Translation|journal=[[Maclean's]]|volume=117|issue=17|pages=38–39|publisher=Rogers Communications|issn=0024-9262}}</ref> In an article for ''[[The Tyee]]'', Burgess also argued that the film relies on the audience's identification with Bob and Charlotte, writing, "The movie would exhibit little appeal for the audience if they disliked the central characters. Clearly, Coppola wants us to sympathize with [them]." Burgess criticized the film for using Japan and its people as a cinematic shorthand for "strangeness," rather than depicting the country with genuine nuance.<ref name="Tyee">{{Cite web |title=Bashing Japan: People Love It! |url=https://thetyee.ca/Entertainment/2004/01/13/Bashing_Japan_People_Love_It/ |access-date=2026-07-02 |website=The Tyee}}</ref> Pointing to specific characterizations, he wrote:<blockquote>Virtually every Japanese person in the film is wacky, creepy, bizarre, or plastic. The worst example is the hooker scene, which even the film’s defenders cannot defend. It’s just over-the-top silly, with the hooker ending up kicking and wailing on the floor of Murray’s hotel room. Those freaky [[Jap]]s. Who can figure ’em?<ref name="Tyee" /></blockquote>

In response to accusations of racism, producer [[Ross Katz]] defended the film, stating he believed "Sofia's love of Japan and love of the people that she's met there is incredibly evident in the film."<ref name="rich" /> Katz added that none of the scenes in the film were "any slight to Japanese people."<ref name="rich" /> 

Director Sofia Coppola stated: "I can see why people might think that, but I know I'm not racist. I think if everything's based on truth you can make fun, have a little laugh, but also be respectful of a culture. I just love Tokyo and I'm not mean-spirited [...] I think that everything you do, people could be offended by—unless you're just trying to be nice about everyone." Coppola further defended the film's humor by noting that specific gags were drawn from her own observations, adding, "Even on our daily call sheets, they would mix up the 'rs' and the 'ls'—all that was from experience, it's not made up. I guess someone has misunderstood my intentions. It bugs me, because I know I'm not racist."<ref name="morrow" /><ref name="wright" />

==Reception==

===Critical response===
''Lost in Translation'' received acclaim, particularly for Murray's performance and for Coppola's direction and screenplay.{{sfn|King|2010|pp=28–29}} On [[Rotten Tomatoes]], the film has an approval rating of 95% based on 234 reviews, with an [[weighted arithmetic mean|average]] rating of 8.8/10. The site's critical consensus reads, "Effectively balancing humor and subtle pathos, Sofia Coppola crafts a moving, melancholy story that serves as a showcase for both Bill Murray and Scarlett Johansson."<ref name="rottentomatoes">{{cite web |title=Lost in Translation (2003) |website=[[Rotten Tomatoes]] |access-date=July 10, 2020 |url=http://www.rottentomatoes.com/m/lost_in_translation/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200605075150/https://www.rottentomatoes.com/m/lost_in_translation |archive-date=June 5, 2020 |url-status=live }}</ref> On [[Metacritic]], which assigns a rating to reviews, the film has an average score of 91 out of 100 based on 44 reviews, indicating "universal acclaim".<ref name="metacritic">{{cite web |title=Lost in Translation (2003) |website=[[Metacritic]] |access-date=May 12, 2020 |url=http://www.metacritic.com/movie/lost-in-translation |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200617160815/https://www.metacritic.com/movie/lost-in-translation |archive-date=June 17, 2020 |url-status=live }}</ref>

Critics praised Murray's performance as Bob, commending his handling of a more serious role that was combined with the comic persona for which he was already broadly known. Edelstein argued that it was "the Bill Murray performance we've been waiting for", adding that "his two halves have never come together as they do here, in a way that connects that hilarious detachment with the deep and abiding sense of isolation that must have spawned it".<ref name="edelstein" /> [[Lisa Schwarzbaum]] of ''[[Entertainment Weekly]]'' regarded Murray's performance as Oscar-worthy and lauded it as his "most vulnerable and unmannered" to date; she praised his treatment of a more delicate role as well as his improvisations in the film's comic sequences.<ref name="schwarzbaum">{{cite magazine |last1=Schwarzbaum |first1=Lisa |title=Lost in Translation |url=https://ew.com/article/2003/09/11/lost-translation-2/ |access-date=May 12, 2020 |magazine=[[Entertainment Weekly]] |date=September 11, 2003 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191206044432/https://ew.com/article/2003/09/11/lost-translation-2/ |archive-date=December 6, 2019 |url-status=live }}</ref> [[Roger Ebert]] gave ''Lost in Translation'' four out of four stars and named it the second best film of the year, describing it as "sweet and sad at the same time as it is sardonic and funny".<ref name="ebert">{{cite news | last = Ebert | first = Roger | authorlink= Roger Ebert | title = ''Lost in Translation'' | work = [[Chicago Sun-Times]] | pages = | language = | publisher = | date = September 12, 2003 | url = http://rogerebert.suntimes.com/apps/pbcs.dll/article?AID=/20030912/REVIEWS/309120302/1023 | accessdate = March 16, 2009 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20141030175843/http://www.rogerebert.com/reviews/lost-in-translation-2003 | archive-date = October 30, 2014}}</ref> ''The New York Times'' critic [[Elvis Mitchell]] had similar praise, calling ''Lost in Translation'' "Mr. Murray's movie" and remarking that the actor "supplies the kind of performance that seems so fully realized and effortless that it can easily be mistaken for not acting at all".<ref name="mitchelle">{{cite news |last1=Mitchell |first1=Elvis |title=An American in Japan, Making a Connection |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2003/09/12/movies/film-review-an-american-in-japan-making-a-connection.html |access-date=May 12, 2020 |work=[[The New York Times]] |date=September 12, 2003 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130523223020/http://www.nytimes.com/2003/09/12/movies/film-review-an-american-in-japan-making-a-connection.html |archive-date=May 23, 2013 |url-status=live }}</ref>{{refn|In the bonus features of the film's 2004 DVD, Murray called ''Lost in Translation'' his favorite film that he has appeared in.|group="note"}}

Coppola received acclaim for her screenplay and direction. [[Kenneth Turan]] of the ''[[Los Angeles Times]]'' commented that ''Lost in Translation'' was "tart and sweet, unmistakably funny and exceptionally well observed—[which] marks{{nbsp}}... Coppola as a mature talent with a distinctive sensibility and the means to express it".<ref name="turan">{{cite news |last1=Turan |first1=Kenneth |title=Bill at his best |url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-2003-sep-12-et-turan12-story.html |access-date=May 12, 2020 |work=[[Los Angeles Times]] |date=September 12, 2003 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200403162030/https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-2003-sep-12-et-turan12-story.html |archive-date=April 3, 2020 |url-status=live }}</ref> Much of the praise was directed specifically at her attention to qualities of subtlety and atmosphere; David Rooney of ''Variety'' praised the film as "a mood piece", adding that its "deft balance of humor and poignancy makes it both a pleasurable and melancholy experience".<ref name="rooney">{{cite news |last1=Rooney |first1=David |title=Lost in Translation |url=https://variety.com/2003/film/awards/lost-in-translation-6-1200539681/ |access-date=May 12, 2020 |work=[[Variety (magazine)|Variety]] |date=August 31, 2003 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180714150754/https://variety.com/2003/film/awards/lost-in-translation-6-1200539681/ |archive-date=July 14, 2018 |url-status=live }}</ref> Likewise, ''[[Salon (website)|Salon]]'' critic [[Stephanie Zacharek]] lauded Coppola as a "stealth dramatist" whose understated narrative style made for an artful depiction of emotion; she praised ''Lost in Translation'' as an intimate story that marks Coppola as an exceptional filmmaker.<ref name="zacharek">{{cite web |last1=Zacharek |first1=Stephanie |title=Lost in Translation |website=[[Salon (website)|Salon]] |date=September 13, 2003 |url=https://www.salon.com/2003/09/12/translation/ |access-date=June 20, 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200703170508/https://www.salon.com/2003/09/12/translation/ |archive-date=July 3, 2020 |url-status=live }}</ref>

In his review for ''[[The New York Observer]]'', [[Andrew Sarris]] called the film "that rarity of rarities, a grown-up romance based on the deliberate repression of sexual gratification ... when independent films are exploding with erotic images edging ever closer to outright pornography, Ms. Coppola and her colleagues have replaced sexual facility with emotional longing, without being too coy or self-congratulatory in the process."<ref name="sarris">{{cite news | last = Sarris | first = Andrew | title = Lonely Souls in a Strange Land: ''Lost in Translation'' Maps the Way | work = [[New York Observer]] | pages = | language = | publisher = | date = September 28, 2003 | url = http://www.observer.com/node/48113 | accessdate = March 16, 2009 }}</ref> ''[[USA Today]]'' gave the film three and a half stars out of four and wrote that it "offers quiet humor in lieu of the bludgeoning direct assaults most comedies these days inflict".<ref name="clark">{{cite news | last = Clark | first = Mike | title = Comedy doesn't get lost in ''Translation'' | work = [[USA Today]] | pages = | language = | publisher = | date = September 12, 2003 | url = https://www.usatoday.com/life/movies/reviews/2003-09-11-translation_x.htm | accessdate = March 16, 2009 }}</ref> ''[[Time (magazine)|Time]]''{{'}}s [[Richard Corliss]] praised Murray's performance: "You won't find a subtler, funnier or more poignant performance this year than this quietly astonishing turn."<ref name="corliss">{{cite magazine | last = Corliss | first = Richard | title = A Victory for Lonely Hearts | magazine = [[Time (magazine)|Time]] | pages = | language = | publisher = | date = September 15, 2003 | url = http://www.time.com/time/magazine/article/0,9171,1005675,00.html | accessdate = March 16, 2009 | archive-date = March 3, 2009 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20090303093606/http://www.time.com/time/magazine/article/0,9171,1005675,00.html | url-status = dead }}</ref> His performance has been likened to the sardonic persona of [[W. C. Fields|W.C. Fields]].<ref name="Gehring2004">{{cite journal |last=Gehring |first=Wes D. |date=January 2004 |title=Along Comes Another Coppola |journal=[[USA Today (magazine)|USA Today]] |volume=132 |page=59|publisher=The Society for the Advancement of Education |issn=0161-7389}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|last=Alleva|first=Richard|date=December 5, 2003|title=About a Boy: Kill Bill-Volume 1 and Lost in Translation|journal=[[Commonweal (magazine)|Commonweal]]|volume=130|issue=21|page=14|publisher=Commonweal Foundation|issn=0010-3330}}</ref>
In his review for ''[[The Observer]]'', [[Philip French]] wrote: "While ''Lost in Translation'' is deeply sad and has a strongly [[Michelangelo Antonioni|Antonioniesque]] flavour, it's also a wispy romantic comedy with little plot and some well-observed comic moments."<ref name="french">{{cite news | last = French | first = Philip | authorlink= Philip French | title = The odd Coppola | work = [[The Observer]] | pages = | language = | publisher = | date = January 11, 2004 | url = https://www.theguardian.com/film/2004/jan/11/philipfrench | accessdate = March 16, 2009 | location=London}}</ref>  In ''The Guardian'', [[Joe Queenan (author)|Joe Queenan]] praised Coppola's film as "one of the few Hollywood films I have seen this year that has a brain; but more than that, it has a soul."<ref name="queenan">{{cite news | last = Queenan | first = Joe | authorlink= Joe Queenan (author) | title = A yen for romance | work = [[The Guardian]] | pages = | language = | publisher = | date = January 10, 2004 | url = https://www.theguardian.com/film/2004/jan/10/features.joequeenan | accessdate = March 16, 2009 | location=London}}</ref> ''[[Rolling Stone]]''{{'}}s [[Peter Travers]] gave it four out of four stars and wrote: "Before saying goodbye, they whisper something to each other that the audience can't hear. Coppola keeps her film as hushed and intimate as that whisper. ''Lost in Translation'' is found gold. Funny how a wisp of a movie from a wisp of a girl can wipe you out."<ref name="travers">{{cite magazine | last = Travers | first = Peter | title = ''Lost in Translation'' | magazine = [[Rolling Stone]] | pages = | language = | publisher = | date = September 8, 2003 | url = https://www.rollingstone.com/movies/reviews/lost-in-translation-20030908 | accessdate = March 10, 2011 }}</ref> [[J. Hoberman]], in his review for the ''[[Village Voice]]'', wrote: "''Lost in Translation'' is as bittersweet a brief encounter as any in American movies since [[Richard Linklater]]'s equally romantic ''[[Before Sunrise]]''. But ''Lost in Translation'' is the more poignant reverie. Coppola evokes the emotional intensity of a one-night stand far from home—but what she really gets is the magic of movies".<ref name="hoberman">{{cite news | last = Hoberman | first = J | title = After Sunset | work = [[Village Voice]] | pages = | language = | publisher = | date = September 9, 2003 | url = http://www.villagevoice.com/2003-09-09/film/after-sunset/1 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20091011192424/http://www.villagevoice.com/2003-09-09/film/after-sunset/1 | url-status = dead | archive-date = October 11, 2009 | accessdate = March 16, 2009 }}</ref>

Praise was also offered for Johansson's performance as Charlotte; Rooney commented that she "gives a smartly restrained performance as an observant, questioning woman with a rich interior life",<ref name="rooney" /> and Turan added that Johansson "makes what could have been an overly familiar characterization come completely alive".<ref name="turan" />

===Accolades===
{{main|List of accolades received by Lost in Translation (film)}}

''Lost in Translation'' received awards and nominations in a variety of categories, particularly for Coppola's direction and screenwriting, as well as the performances of Murray and Johansson. At the 76th Academy Awards, it won [[Academy Award for Best Original Screenplay|Best Original Screenplay]] (Coppola) and the film received three further nominations for [[Academy Award for Best Picture|Best Picture]], [[Academy Award for Best Director|Best Director]] (Coppola), and [[Academy Award for Best Actor|Best Actor]] (Murray).<ref>{{cite news|url=http://www.oscars.org/oscars/ceremonies/2004|title=76th Academy Awards (2004)|newspaper=Oscars.org &#124; Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences |publisher=[[Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences]]|access-date=May 10, 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150402004632/http://www.oscars.org/oscars/ceremonies/2004|archive-date=April 2, 2015|url-status=live}}</ref> The film garnered three [[Golden Globe Awards]] from five nominations: [[Golden Globe Award for Best Motion Picture – Musical or Comedy|Best Motion Picture – Musical or Comedy]], [[Golden Globe Award for Best Actor – Motion Picture Musical or Comedy|Best Actor – Motion Picture Musical or Comedy]], and [[Golden Globe Award for Best Screenplay|Best Screenplay]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.goldenglobes.com/winners-nominees/2004|title=The 61st Annual Golden Globe Awards|work=Golden Globes |publisher=[[Hollywood Foreign Press Association]]|access-date=May 10, 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161220150136/http://www.goldenglobes.com/winners-nominees/2004|archive-date=December 20, 2016|url-status=live}}</ref> At the [[57th British Academy Film Awards]], ''Lost in Translation'' won three awards: [[BAFTA Award for Best Actor in a Leading Role|Best Actor in a Leading Role]], [[BAFTA Award for Best Actress in a Leading Role|Best Actress in a Leading Role]] (Johansson), and [[BAFTA Award for Best Editing|Best Editing]] (Flack).<ref>{{cite web|url=http://awards.bafta.org/award/2004/film?|title=Film in 2004|publisher=[[British Academy of Film and Television Arts]] (BAFTA)|access-date=May 10, 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171113113104/http://awards.bafta.org/award/2004/film|archive-date=November 13, 2017|url-status=live}}</ref>
